translations.text: Book 1.1
The beginning of the book. Here, however, begins the holy man's own discourse.
The book of Saint Mar Nestorius, Patriarch of Constantinople, and the rule of orthodoxy.
Preface. It is therefore proper, I think, for anyone who intends to investigate the truth with all diligence,
not to conduct his argument with a preconceived opinion, but to bring forward everything that opposes the truth and examine it.
Just as experts in gold show the difference between good gold and inferior gold by comparing them with one another,
so that those who wish to accept adulterated gold as genuine, and in preference to genuine gold, may see it.
For many choose evil things instead of good things, and falsehood in preference to truth, because the two seem equal to them.
They place greater value on disputing and defeating one another than on establishing the truth.
Since, therefore, different people profess Christ in different ways, and only in name
are they united, while others dispute even about the name, we must set out the opinion of each of the heresies concerning Christ,
so that the true faith may be recognized by comparing the heresies,
and we may not be shaken as we stumble into one position and then another, like people who cannot see.
1. Why the pagans do not call Christ God. The pagans refuse to call Christ God
because of bodily suffering, [?], and death; and they maintain that these miracles took place through deception.
They do not differ in name, since there is no distinction among them in this respect: they are all pagans.
2. Why the Jews do not accept that he is the Messiah.
The Jews do not acknowledge that he is the Messiah because of the cross and death,
since they expect to receive the Messiah in all greatness of glory and power.
3. Why the Manichaeans do not accept that Christ is also human by nature, but that he is God alone.
The Manichaeans, in turn, and those who sprang from them and alongside them, say that he is not human, but God alone,
because of the miracles. They regard his human experiences as appearance and imagination, not as belonging to his nature.
4. Why the Paulianists and Photinians acknowledge that Christ is only human, and not that he is also God.
The Paulianists say that he is not God, but only human, because of his birth and death.
They attribute the miracles to him as they would to one of the saints.
5. Why the Arians do not accept him as perfect and self-sufficient God,
nor, again, do they accept Christ as a human being, but as half God and half human.
The Arians confess him as half God and half human, consisting of a body without a soul and a created divinity.
They make him less than human beings by saying that there is no soul in him.
They also make him less than God by not calling him uncreated and self-sufficient.
Because of his becoming human, his birth from a woman, and his death, they think that God came to be in a human condition.
They mix his divine attributes with human ones, assigning his becoming human not to his own authority but to a coercive command,
saying that the union with the flesh resulted in one nature, and not as
required for the person in the saving work on our behalf, but as a soul and body are bound together into one nature,
and the soul consciously experiences the body's sufferings, whether it wishes to or not.
Yet on its own and in itself it cannot undergo these things, since it has no body through which to suffer.
In the same way, they also speak of God in a body as one nature, so that he necessarily suffered the suffering of the nature that came into being,
whether he wished to or not, as though he did not belong to the Father's nature, which is free from suffering and need.
They say this solely to avoid showing him to be the one who holds authority and gives commands.
It is as though even the command he received were a punishment—a punishment inherent in his nature, from which there is no escape—
since against his will he experienced the body's sufferings through natural sensation: he hungered, thirsted, grew tired, became afraid, and sweated.
He died and rose, not by his own nature, but by the Father's authority and power.
In short, they say that he endured by nature the things belonging to the nature subject to suffering that he made for him.
6. Which religious groups agree with the Manichaeans. … From among these, heresies sprang up:

some from the Manichaeans, and some from the Paulinians.
7. And which ones agree with the Arians.
8. And in what respects they differ from them, and in what respects they are, in turn, allied with them.

They differ from them.
9. Why I have not recorded the leaders of these religious groups, but only their doctrines.
We wished to refrain from naming their leaders, so that we would not, by first becoming sidetracked by the names,
prolong our discussion, or find ourselves failing to bring any matter under examination to a conclusion.
10. What the statements are of those who say that God the Word became flesh by nature, without taking a body.
For they accuse the Manichaeans, who say that the body of our Lord Christ does not truly have a real nature,
but is an appearance and a fantasy. As for the miracles, for the most part, either because it was impossible,
or, again, because it was unfitting for them to happen through a body, they attribute them to God alone.
Sophronius. He says that the ability to do everything belongs to that nature which can do everything and is unlimited.
All other things, therefore, are bounded by his will, but he himself is bounded by nothing.
And whatever cannot be brought about by another, he himself can do as God.
For he does not derive his being from a nature or some cause greater than himself, so that through this he should acquire the capacity
to be God and the capacity not to be. For this reason they are afraid to confess in this way that he truly became flesh,
lest, by saying this, they take away the Son’s being God. They say:
“How could this happen, when we confess that even the body is God?
For what appears to be flesh is also the nature of God, and it is he himself and not another.”
11. That just as water, he says, freezes in its own nature,
becoming something it was not, without receiving this from outside, so,
they say, God the Word also became a body without taking a body from outside.
“Just as,” he says, “when flowing, liquid water freezes and solidifies, we do not say that it has become something else,
but that it is the same water that has solidified, so too God truly became flesh,
while being God in his nature. He was in all things and acted as God.
And insofar as he was flesh, he truly both acted and suffered as flesh.
He became flesh in the womb, and in what he had become he was truly born and grew up as flesh.
And since he chose to become this, he truly hungered, thirsted, grew weary, suffered, and was crucified, if he truly became flesh.
For just as water, which cannot be broken, can truly be broken when it freezes,
and truly undergoes what affects the nature it has become, so too God, who truly became,
truly underwent everything belonging to the nature he had become, without being driven out of his own nature.”
12. That just as, he says, he appeared to Abraham and Jacob as a human being without taking a body from outside, so too he became human.
Just as he also truly appeared to our fathers Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and the rest of the saints, in a visible nature,
While he walked in that which walks, and spoke in that which speaks, and ate and drank in that which eats.
For nothing done by God was deceptive; rather, everything was real and natural.
For he is the Creator, and the Creator does nothing merely in outward form and imagination, but in nature and reality.
But these things are rightly said of things that do not belong to created nature:
that is, appearance and imagination, because they cannot be sustained in their own nature.
13. How they understand “truly and not fictitiously,” and in how many senses “truly” is used.
Nestorius: So they say that God himself truly became flesh. Sophronius said: “We confess that he truly
became flesh, and not in his nature. For what he became, he became in reality.
And it is a nature, but not by nature, for he was not flesh eternally.
Rather, just as liquid water, when it freezes, has the nature of ice—it was not this by its nature, but became so—
so God also truly became flesh, and is the nature of flesh, but not by his own nature.
For he was not this eternally, but became so afterward.
For this is truly becoming human: that in his own nature he should become flesh and a human being, and not in imagination,
nor in outward form and in [?] without real existence—which is, in truth, not becoming human.
Therefore, anyone who wants to suppose that he became so only in appearance flees from the truth.
14. In what respects those who say these things agree with the Manichaeans, and in what respects they suppose they differ from them.
Has it now become clear to you in what respects they think exactly the same thing, and in what respects they suppose they differ, although they hold exactly the same position?
We ought to leave aside what follows, so that we do not nullify the truth through things admitted without substance.
Nestorius said: I say that we should not neglect this statement altogether,
even if you wish to pass over it as something admitted, although it was stated so rashly that
the hearers even considered it disgraceful—and I think you did too.
Now I shall lay this inquiry open to anyone who wishes, so that what is merely supposed may be brought to light.
For I see nothing in them that [?] anything else, nor anything connected with it.
For they are very far apart from one another—as far as appearance is from reality, and a body from the appearance of a body.
Yet I see many who are very insistent on these matters, as though they were something true and an ancient belief.
For this reason I want you to examine them not superficially, but with every care.
So that statements about the faith may not be unexamined and confused, but clear and known to everyone.
Like things defined by certain boundaries and by natural forms [?].
And not like things whose shadowy outlines, as they are drawn, incline now this way and now that, until they are marked out in the same likeness.
In what way, then, do you say that they say the very same thing, resembling the Manichaeans in the very things for which they rebuke them?
Sophronius: Those who say these things are not rejected by them as people who despise our body.
For both deny that a body was assumed.
Rather, it is because they do not make that other claim, that the nature of the flesh was imaginary rather than real.
Let us therefore also examine their answer concerning these matters: what argument they can rightly make, so that they do not direct their blasphemies where they should not.
15. Refutation of those who say that God the Word became the substance of flesh without assuming a body. Nestorius speaks.
Now state in general terms what they themselves say, going beyond the statements they maintain on their own behalf.
So that they may not suppose that they were condemned because they had no advocate or helper.
For you seem to me to be very well acquainted with what they say.
And you are able to strengthen their arguments with many words,
So that you can even persuade the hearers to believe that things are as they say.
Then compel me also to speak in response to these things. Take each one of the statements I have made,
And also those you have made, and put them to me, so that I may give an answer to each of them, if I can.
And I can, if God wills and gives me what it is right to say, to instruct me according to my capacity.
For I myself am worthy of nothing, except insofar as I am among those who knock and ask at the door of truth, since he is the Truth.
Sophronius: I say that the things I have stated demonstrate divine power:
That he can truly become flesh while being God.
For being truly God gives him the ability to do everything. For he does everything he wills.
He willed to become flesh, and he became flesh—not the appearance of flesh,
But the nature of flesh, that is, truly flesh.
And in this he truly became human: he became human in his own nature, and not in another.
And the Trinity is a Trinity, having received no addition of another substance.
He therefore said in response to these things: For they appear to use ordinary words and concepts,
which it is exceedingly presumptuous to dispute.
16. On the statement that one who has become a body in substance falls short of being God, of being able to do everything, and of being like God.
Nestorius. You have spoken truly, and it is not right to dispute statements that are true.
Moreover, God is capable of everything and does everything he wills. For this reason his substance did not become flesh.
For one who becomes flesh in his nature falls short of being able to do everything,
because he is flesh and not God. For the ability to do everything belongs to God,
and not to flesh, which cannot do everything it wills. Yet while remaining God, he does not will everything.
Nor, again, does he will not to be God, so as to make himself no longer God.
For he is God because he always exists and can do everything he wills, and not because
he can make himself no longer God. For one into whose substance the nature of flesh has entered—
this one has made himself no longer God and no longer able to do everything he wills.
Sophronius. He did not will to cease to be what he is, but to become what he was not.
For this reason he truly became a human being, which he had not been.
That is, he truly became flesh and a human being, but not by nature.
For what he is, he is by nature. But what he became, he is by nature [?]

Yet he truly is what he became.
17. The statement that God the Word truly became a body

is understood in one of two ways: either in substance or in thought.
Nestorius.
Do you take “truly” to mean in substance, or in thought and appearance?
Sophronius. For both are understood as being truly so.
8. On the statement: If God the Word became flesh by nature and remained God,

then God the Word is two substances by nature.
Nestorius.
If what is conceived as existing in substance does exist, then you say that he also truly is God in substance
and is flesh, after he himself became flesh.
And that there are two substances: the one in which he exists by nature, and the one in which he came to exist.
The former is that of God, and the latter that of flesh. Sophronius.
Not one substance and another, but the very same substance of God, which also became the substance of flesh.
And for this reason, one substance. It is like water, whether liquid or frozen:
there are not two substances of water, but one, which exists both in its liquid state and in its frozen state.
And freezing is considered the opposite of fluidity. So too God is himself the same, both a body and without a body,
although in being a body he differs from being without a body.
19. On the statement that things which have no distinction in nature, yet are distinct, are said to be distinct in form.
Nestorius. Then say that they have no distinction in nature.
And things which have no distinction in nature, yet are distinct, are distinct in person.
But in person, nature is a form without an individual reality, in another form.
Or, like the Manichaeans, you speak of flesh and the things belonging to flesh as an appearance and an imagining,
when you concede that the incarnation took place through deception.
Which, then, do you maintain is true? That, when we grant [?]
that flesh is by nature from the substance of God, both substances should become one and should equally be what they cannot be?
This, however, means that he is not God but flesh. Or that he became flesh in imagination?
Sophronius. As for things that ought to be rejected when proposed hypothetically,
by accepting them as natural in your argument, you turn them into impossibilities.
And you really strip us of the Christian faith,
like the pagans and the Manichaeans, who stumble over the cross of Christ. Nestorius.
And who are those who, like the pagans and the Manichaeans, stumble over the cross of Christ?
Is it not those who accept his humanity as a change of substance? For it is the pagans who, in speaking of changes in God's forms,
say that he acts upon the substance in a vessel or [?] through the nature into which he was changed.
And they restore the nature again to what it was in the beginning.
The Manichaeans also took this from them and said that the change of likeness was into a form without an individual reality.
And when you say these things, you are following these people.
And you say these things like those who stumble over the cross.
[?]. On this: Those who describe the incarnation as a change of form acknowledge Christ as neither God nor a human being.
You do not acknowledge him as God in substance, because you have changed him into the substance of flesh.
Nor do you acknowledge him as a human being by nature, because you make him into the substance of God.
And he is not truly God and God by nature, nor truly a human being and a human being by nature.
21. On this: What comes into being in substance from preexisting matter is what it has become,
and not what it was before it came to be, just as a pillar of salt came from a woman.
And there is nothing else besides this: just as a human being made of wood and stone is not truly called a human being,
since its nature is that of wood and stone, so neither is the one who became a human being from the substance of God

called a human being by nature while the divine nature remains.
Sophronius.
Well then, remarkable man, God can raise up children for Abraham from stones,
and a pillar of salt from a human body, and a human being from the earth.
And [?] did not hinder him, nor does anything, in turn, hinder God from doing whatever he wills.

Does his becoming flesh hinder him?
Nestorius. First, then, examine what you said:
that God willed it this way. Show us this. For as to God's being able to do whatever he wills,
everyone is in complete agreement. But once again you are using examples that argue against you.
For someone who becomes a human being from stone or earth has a human nature,
because he has truly become a human being, and does not have the nature of stone or earth.
And what became a pillar of salt from a human body became only the nature of that substance.
For things that are changed from their original substance possess only the nature of that into which they have been changed.
Therefore, if you say that the nature of flesh came into being from the preexisting matter of God's nature,
it possesses the substance that it became, which it had not been before. And it makes no difference, as I said,
whether the substance of human beings comes into being from stone, from earth, or from human seed.
For what comes from an original substance is changed into the nature of what it has become.
And if it does not change, neither does it become flesh by nature. Sophronius.
Divine Scripture refutes this statement for you and does not allow you to insist and speak categorically.
For Moses’ staff, when it truly became a serpent, was a serpent and also [?].
And the waters of the Nile that became blood had the nature of blood and also of water. It is a substance, even though it changed. And for
this reason, the Israelites used the waters that had become blood as having the nature of water,
and Moses used the serpent as a staff, because it truly was both.
For God establishes natures however he wishes. 22. On the statement that when the waters of the Nile were changed [?] into the substance of blood,
they had only that substance into which they had changed. Nestorius.
Again you use illustrations like these, because, I think, you are flustered.
For then both substances would have existed,
if those waters drawn by the Hebrews were both blood and water,
or if those drawn by the Egyptians were both at the very same time.
But if those were only water and these only blood, and afterward they changed—
for as they were drawn, what was drawn changed—
were they, in turn, anything other than what they became?
How, then, is it not evident from these very things that whatever comes to be by nature must in every case
be precisely what it became by nature, and not something else?
Sophronius. Yet look, we see that divine Scripture has spoken of both,
saying that both exist by nature from the very same substance,
when the one who became a human being from dust and earth, and is a human being by nature, says, “I am dust and ashes.”
Unless you are reproaching Scripture as though it said impossible things,
because it says of someone who was a human being, a human being by nature, “I am dust and ashes.”
23. On the statement that a single substance, which is seen in two substances,
exists in one substance by nature, but in the other only in outward form. Nestorius.
If divine Scripture says these things when speaking about human nature, and every person is of human nature and nothing else.
Therefore God the Word, too, who truly became a human being by nature, is dust and ashes by nature.
And he is not from the substance of God, but from dust and ashes, if that from which he came indicates this.
But if everyone is this by nature, while he is not this substance,
but the substance of God, he was not a human being except in outward appearance, as the Manichaeans say.
And the things said about him are also a matter of outward appearance, so that what he is should not be revealed to everyone.
For if one substance is known in two substances, in the one
it is substance, but in the other it is outward appearance, or deception and imagination.
Sophronius. And you grant God nothing beyond this:
that he should truly be God by nature and also be a human being by nature.
The very same nature in both—unless it is God's nature in a human being. And what incarnation,
except that he who became a human being by nature spoke to us in our nature, while naturally enduring everything that belongs to us?
For it was for this purpose that he also became human. But once again, through intermediaries and a garment of outward appearance!
And you claim that God committed such an outrageous act, imitating tragic actors and singers who conceal themselves behind a mask.
24. On this: Someone who can be seen in his own nature does not need to become something else in which to be seen.
Nestorius. But, my remarkable friend, pause to compare the things you have said:
that he appeared to us in his own nature without an intermediary. Why, then, did you say
that he became the nature of a human being while remaining God? For someone who is seen in his own nature does not need to become another substance in which to be seen.
If he was seen in his own nature, you are also saying something impossible: that he himself became his own mediator.
For a mediator is not of one, but God is one. And for this reason he is not God, but God's mediator.
25. On this: If, in whatever form God appeared to the saints,
he appeared through a change of substance, then he became incarnate in many substances and not in one.
Again, be willing to examine this: do you speak of one incarnation of God,
or many? What do you say about this? For you say
that he became the nature of a human being and appeared to Abraham and Jacob,
and that, for each one of the saints, whatever the form in which he appeared, he was changed in nature into the nature in which he appeared.
And at the end of days he changed into human nature in order to become human: you are speaking of many incarnations.
For if you agree that his becoming human [?] is an incarnation,

there are many changes in which he appeared in outward form.
Sophronius.
We speak of one incarnation, because then he truly became human in his nature,
and not when he appeared to particular people, as to Abraham and Jacob, but to everyone.
26. On this point: if the expression
“he became human” is used because he appeared to everyone and not to individuals, as to the saints, then, since he did not appear to all human beings, it teaches [?] “he became human.”
Nestorius. By this argument, he did not even become human, since he did not appear to everyone,
but to those in Palestine. Why, then, was his incarnation partial
and not for everyone? Or because he became a human being by [?], while he became human at all times and appeared to everyone,

do you call this an incarnation?
27. That incarnation is spoken of in his case because he appeared in human nature.
But if there was truly one incarnation, and it was for everyone and not for particular people,
both for those who saw him and those who did not see him, for those who come into existence and those who existed long ago,
and the incarnation was for the whole nature together, we rightly confess that God the Word did not become human nature.
For he is not human nature, who is not human nature but the nature of God.
Rather, in human substance he is truly a human being, from the true nature of a true human being,
in whom, as in the whole nature, he became human for everyone. He made him his own person and was revealed in the things belonging to human beings,
living in human nature, while being God in human nature.
It is like a king in the guise of a soldier, who, as a soldier and not as a king,
goes about on military service among those who need correction.
And he is said to go about in all, because he assumed the outward form of one soldier—the form that clothes all soldiers.
Likewise, in one human being he became human for all human beings who belonged to that same nature, since he was in their nature.

And in him he spoke to everyone, as speaking in his own nature.
Sophronius.
Yes, when he came to be in human nature, he is said to have become human; and through him and in him, for everyone, and not especially for his sake.
For he himself truly became a human being, and in this he would share with the human being who belongs to their same nature.
And the becoming human was real, because he was human in his own nature and had no need of another nature.
Nestorius: For this is not becoming human,
just as a king who makes royal use of a servant’s appearance does not thereby become a servant in the manner of a servant.
Or perhaps, as someone might say, he becomes a servant in name alone.
Likewise, God did not become human either, if it was not by nature, but [?]. Sophronius:
What do you mean by “in a royal manner” and “in the manner of a servant”? Nestorius:
Just as purple robes are royal clothing and not the clothing of servants,
and the clothing of servants is a [?], which belongs to servants and not to kings. When,
therefore, a king wishes to put on the clothing of servants, that is, a [?],
and sets aside the royal purple, he continues to act as what he was, in the servant’s appearance that he has adopted,
without descending from his royal power. Even in this appearance, he retains his greatness and authority over everyone.
But when he wishes to lower himself and become one of the servants, he takes a garment from among those belonging to servants,
as befits a servant, not royalty, and covers himself with it. He speaks with them as an equal
and persuades them without compelling them. He performs royal deeds in the appearance of a servant.
Likewise, when God wished to become human, if he had not come in human nature,
but had become flesh in his own substance, he would not have become human at all,
because he became human for them in his own substance and not in the nature of human beings.
28. On the fact that someone who becomes human through a change of substance belongs to another nature, not to the nature of human beings.
For someone who becomes human through a change of substance belongs to another nature, not to the nature of human beings,
because he has a different definition of nature, not that of human beings, since he is God by nature
and became something else apart from the divine nature—the substance of a human being—so that both would exist by nature.
It is not that he changed from the divine nature into the human nature, nor that he is something else apart from these:
he exists by nature in both. Rather, the human being is human alone, and God is God alone.
Sophronius: And if he did not undertake becoming human in this way, but it took place in another nature,
and not from the substance of God, how does the Trinity not receive an addition in nature?
that it received the substance of another? Or how is this God of the nature of human beings,
and not of the substance of God? 29. On this: that, in becoming human in the substance of a human being,
and not becoming human in substance, he receives no addition either in nature or in person.
Nestorius. Just as a king, when he puts on the clothing of service and is in it,
does not become a double king, nor is he king apart from it, since he is in it.
Nor, again, is he worshiped apart from that in which he was recognized, through which they also knew him and were saved.
So too God made use, in his own person, of the lowliness of poverty and shame, down to death on the cross for our salvation;
and in this he was also exalted to honor, glory, and worship. In that in which he was dishonored, in this he was also glorified.
For the sign of salvation and victory is one of honor, not dishonor.
He did not receive an addition of substance, since the substances remain unchanged. For an addition occurs
in substance when difference of substance acquires sameness of substance.
Nor did he receive an addition to his person, since he took it as his own person and not as another’s.
Not by [?], but by union with his own person, also that of the one in whom he became human.
And in this way his person too is in him, and not in another.
For he put on the form of a servant, and in it he emptied himself. He clothed it with his person and raised his name above all names.
Thus it is worshiped in the person of the Godhead, and not in that of another.
For this reason, there is one person and one name of the Son. 30. Against those who say:
that God did not change into human nature, but changed the human substance into the substance of God.
For those who speak of union through change, an addition of substance and also of person necessarily follows in every possible way.
For the substance that became flesh from God the Word was added to the Trinity.
And this person is plainly a half, and is conceived of as divided:
since the nature of flesh came into being from the substance of God the Word through division, an addition occurs. [?] Where, then, these things have their beginning,
and in what way they are distinct, and again how they are the same, we have already said. Let us turn,
then, also to the other party that sprang from these, which is separate from them and yet mingled with them.
Sophronius. They therefore confess that the body of our Lord is of his own flesh:
And in this they also mock those who say that the flesh existed only in appearance and imagination.
Also those who say that it is from the substance of God the Word, while saying [?]. 31.
What expressions are used by those who say that the nature of the body was changed into the substance of God the Word.
For, they say, he did not come to change his own unchangeable substance and make it a substance,
but to raise this poor and changeable substance of ours to his own unchangeable substance,
and make it divine and worthy of worship—not of itself and for itself, but through union.
And to bring it into union with his own substance, so that there would be one substance and one person of one substance,
because the lesser substance was mingled with and made equal to that of the great and unchangeable divinity.
Just as things thrown into fire become equal to the substance of fire and become the nature of fire,
which made them what they became, so too the divine nature received the human nature and intertwined it with its own nature,
and changed it and henceforth made it one without distinction, both in substance and in person. And neither with respect to
nature nor with respect to person was there truly any addition to the Trinity.
And in this way his becoming human both took place and is understood.
32. In what respects they differ from the Manichaeans, and in what respects they profess the same beliefs as they do.
These people are indeed separate from the Manichaeans in that they truly confess that the flesh is from our own nature.
And it is not an outward form of flesh, but the nature of the Son [?]. And from the others who are with them,
in that those others confess that it is real flesh, but not from human nature; rather, it is divine and from the nature of the divinity.
In these respects they differ and fight with all their strength. And those who are thought to minister in the church
confess that the flesh is from our own nature and substance. And the distinction in this is known to everyone.
For, in common with all of them, they argue against the Manichaeans that it is a substance, and truly a substance.
But against those others, they argue that it is not from the nature of God, but from our ancestors.
But their disagreement with the church lies in their changing the flesh into the substance of God.
Therefore, in not allowing the flesh to remain in its own substance, they agree with the Manichaeans, since they destroy the substance of the flesh.
But in saying that he was divine entirely in the matter of flesh, they distance themselves from the Manichaeans.
Yet these people too, in immediately changing it into the substance of God the Word,
And they are unwilling to acknowledge that he is God with a human body, although they agree with the very same view and the very same suffering.
They eliminate the substance of the flesh as though it did not exist, while insisting that they must either deify the substance of the flesh,
or, so to speak, turn the substance of God into flesh, in the substance of the flesh of the divinity.
33. Those who change human nature into the divine nature do not say that God became human, but that a human being became God.
Therefore, something that is not the human substance of flesh, yet is called flesh, is called this only by sharing the same name.
It is like a man made of gold or silver, or of some other substance, whatever the material may be.
But something that does not possess human nature is not a human being by nature.
And this is not God becoming human, but a human being becoming God.
34. Concerning the fact that those who change human nature into the divine substance
make an addition to the Trinity, both in nature and in person.
If, then, the nature of the flesh that became God remains in that substance in which it became God,
how has the Trinity not received an addition in substance and in person? For there is nothing
of human nature in the Trinity: neither the Father, nor the Son, nor the Holy Spirit.
Rather, it exists alone. But through something that was not eternally with it, but came to belong to it, it has received an addition.
And how is an addition that comes into being not an addition? This too is another fable and a Manichaean tale.
But if that which came to be did not remain as it had been,
but human nature was destroyed by the nature of the divinity as though by fire,
and in this way the Trinity received no addition, this is not even an incarnation, but the destruction of the incarnation.
For whatever brings about the destruction of human nature rather than its preservation is not called an incarnation.
Rather, it is like something that exists [?] into what does not exist.
35. In what respects those who change the nature of the body into the substance of God agree
with those who change the substance of God into the nature of the body.
And in this they agree with those who change the divine substance into human nature.
For it is the very same assertion: that God should become a substance in nature, or that he should change the substance of a human being into the nature of God.
36. Concerning the fact that it is not possible, either through mixture or through a change of substance:
God’s nature should not change into a body, nor should the body change into the substance of God the Word.
For whoever changes the divine nature into human nature brings about the destruction of the divine nature.
And whoever changes human nature into the divine nature brings about the destruction of human nature.
And whoever calls created nature uncreated makes nature uncreated—something that cannot happen.
For the Creator can [?] bring substance together out of nothing and change it from one created substance into another.
But for an uncreated substance to come from something created, and something that has not come into being from something that has come into being, as you say,
is impossible. Otherwise, you completely destroy its existence as a substance.
But there is no possibility that a substance that has come into being should become one that has not come into being, or that a created substance should become uncreated.
Nor, again, can what did not exist become an eternal nature and exist together with the Eternal One.
Nor, again, through a change of nature, or through confusion or mixture,
can a nature that has come into being become one that has not come into being, or can what does not exist eternally become eternal.
Nor can what does not exist eternally be from the substance of the Eternal One.
For either a change of substance takes place through the mixture or confusion of both substances,
into one nature blended from these two, or one of these substances changes into the other.
This is impossible: that the uncreated should become uncreated [?], the eternal temporal, and the temporal eternal;
and that the created should be uncreated by nature; that what is uncreated, has not come into being, and is eternal should become
created and temporal, as though it had come from a created and temporal nature;
or that from a created and temporal nature there should come an uncreated and eternal nature,
and that it should become an uncreated and eternal substance. For these things are impossible and inconceivable.
For how could anyone conceive that, although the Creator is in every respect different from the creature,
and what is made is something different, he himself changes himself? For as long as he is the Creator, he does not change.
For he creates as one who is unchanging by nature. But if he is no longer what he is, he does not create.
For either he is what he is by nature, eternally God, and has not become another nature, remaining in the substance of God;
or, no longer being the nature of God, he is made and does not create. This very notion is absurd and impossible.
37. On the fact that even those who say that the nature [?] changed in part, and not in its entirety, say something impossible.
For even if someone grants that he changed his nature in part, and in part did not change,
that which acts is in every case more sovereign than that which is acted upon and than that which undergoes change.
For nothing is by nature more sovereign than its own part.
Rather, whatever it is as a whole, that is also what it is
in its part. If, then, we accept even absurdities as though they were fitting,
and speak of a part in reference to a simple and indivisible nature, even so one does not [?] what is absurd and not eternal.
For how does that [?] which is not a substance become a substance?
For as long as he is God, he is unchangeable. But when he is not God, he does nothing.
How, then, can this be said, when it cannot even be conceived: neither that God should change into another substance,
nor, again, that another substance should change into the substance of God and become what the Creator is,
namely, unmade and without origin, although it was made and came into being. For these are opposites.
How do these things that have been said seem to you? Has enough been said on both sides,
with arguments supporting their statements as well as ours? Or is something still missing that is proper to their own positions,
which you ought to supply, since you are acting as their spokesman?
For if anything has carelessly been left out of their arguments, let us give them vigorous assistance,
so that, when they seem to many to be unshakable and unchangeable,

although they are not, their rout will then be all the greater.
Sophronius.
I think, then, that the arguments of both sides have been thoroughly worked through, and nothing remains for us. For this
reason I was also glad of the moment of silence, and I want you, too, to pause.
For I have nothing sound and appropriate to say against you,
except perhaps one statement that they confidently use in support of what pleases them.
Nestorius. What is it? Speak confidently, without fear,
boldly and fully employing each one of their arguments in their own manner.
For no one can fight courageously with a divided mind.
Sophronius. This is how it must be with the union, as with bread when it becomes the body.
The body is one and the same, not two; and what is conceived as the nature of the body is one.
And it is no longer conceived according to its original nature, but according to the one whose own it became, as his own.
For henceforth it is not what is seen, but what is conceived.
For this reason the apostle also pronounced a terrible punishment upon those who suppose that our Lord’s body is common,
saying this: “If anyone who rejected the law of Moses dies without mercy on the testimony of two or three,
how much harsher a punishment do you think someone deserves who has trampled on the Son of God,
and regarded as common the blood of his covenant by which he was sanctified—he was sanctified—and insulted the Spirit of grace?” He said this
against those who regarded the blood and body of God as the blood and body of a human being.
And they were mistaken in supposing it to be common, like that of anyone else:
that body and blood by which we were sanctified. And they insulted the Spirit of grace,
because they do not confess that he is the Son of God, sharing the nature of God the Father, but that he is a human body:
that body of the Son of God, who raised his body and blood to his own substance
and did not allow them to be stigmatized with the reproach of human substance, but to be worshiped in his own substance.
38. On the fact that the apostle also speaks against those who regard Christ’s blood and body as common and unclean:
not as though it had actually been changed into the nature of God the Word,
but because they disparage the blood by calling it blood, and the body by calling it body,

and say that they cannot nourish us, as the Manichaeans say.
Nestorius.
Is this proof so insignificant to you that you pass over it in silence? For they draw great strength from it,
and you ought not to have presented it so carelessly.
For this escaped my notice, like those who see the speck but not the beam.
Now that this has come to light, let us examine it from every side, according to what
it is, and according to what divine Scripture wishes us to understand, so that we do not fall under just and divine rebukes.
39. On the different senses in which the word called “koinon” in Greek is used.
First let us also speak about this expression, which in Greek is called “koinon.”
In speech it applies to what is defiled, to what is common, and to participation.
In the sense of “defiled,” as in what he said in Acts: “I have never eaten anything unclean or defiled.”
And in the sense of “common,” as in: “Everything the apostles had was held in common.”
And in the sense of “participation,” as in: “The cup of thanksgiving that we bless—
is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? And the bread that we break—
is it not a participation in the body of Christ?” And again: “The one who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one.
For this reason he is not ashamed to call them his brothers, saying, ‘I will proclaim your name to my brothers, and in the midst of the assembly I will praise you.’
And again: ‘I will put my trust in him.’ And again: ‘Here I am, with the children God has given me.’
Since, therefore, the children shared in flesh and blood, he himself likewise shared in these same things.”
Since, therefore, this term is applied to someone unclean and defiled, and also to what is common,
and also to participation, then this expression, which has three uses,
does not make clear in which sense the apostle said and used it:

“Because of this they trample on the Son of God.” Which of these three is the precise meaning?
Sophronius.
It is directed against those who think that he died not for our sake, but his own death, like everyone else,
and that he was like any other human being, both while alive and when dead, and possessed nothing more.

They do not know that he is the Son of God, and that his blood is the blood of God, not of a human being.
Nestorius.
Are you saying, then, that the body and blood are the substance of the Son of God? Or that the body and blood are from human substances
and have become the nature of the divinity? For the flesh is not flesh, according to what you say,
because through mixture and union it has been changed into the substance of God the Word.
And the blessed apostle, while sharply mocking those who acknowledged his body and blood,

but considered it unclean, said this.
Sophronius.
It was not against those who do not acknowledge a real body at all,
nor against those who change or destroy the substance of the flesh as though by fire,
or make the substance of the flesh impure through mixture, that he said these things.
Rather, it was against those who acknowledge flesh and blood but consider it common.
Nestorius. As it seems to me, the interpretation you hold does not apply particularly well to these people.
But to those who change the substance of God into the nature of flesh and blood,
not believing that the substance of our Lord’s flesh and blood is common to us,
but that it comes from God the Word, and not from human beings [?]. Sophronius.
Then these people deserve not an answer but a rebuke, because they have used contradictory expressions.
But now speak about those who teach that flesh came into being from the substance of God.
[?]. How this statement should be understood: “The one who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one.”
Nestorius. You have overlooked the fact that the apostle did not say two contradictory things.
For this is what he sought to establish: that the one who sanctifies and those who are sanctified should be from one,
and brothers from one substance, not from different substances, and his children as those who spring from him,
when he says this: “For the one who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one.”
Therefore, the blood by which we were sanctified, which was poured out for us, is also from one.
And in this respect we are also his brothers, as coming from one father.
Furthermore, we are also his children, as those who possess one substance, through which we are also children.
For it does not belong to God the Word that he and we should be from one,
or that we should be called children bearing his likeness, so that on this account we should be his brothers,
since we do not have the basis for such likeness, as brothers from one father do.
Nor, again, can we be his children, since we do not share in the very same substance.
Thus, in accusing those who refuse to accept that human blood can sanctify,
and who believe that it is unclean because it is the blood of a human being,
and for this reason consider unclean the blood of the covenant by which we were sanctified
and were saved from death through the real death of a human being, blessed Paul said these things.
And in this respect he tells us that we are from one, and in this respect he calls us his brothers: because of the nature in which he was born from our ancestors,
he also died for us. For insofar as he was born, he belongs to our race, and we are all from one.
But insofar as he died for us and renewed the coming order without mortality or decay,
we are his children, because he is the father of the world to come.
And for this reason, are we not all together one body? For we all partake of that one bread.
In that he gives us a share in the very same blood and also in the flesh, which belong to the very same nature.
And we share with him in the resurrection from the dead and in immortality.
This is how we belong to him, just as the bread is his body. “Just as,” he says, “that bread is one,”
“so we are all one body, for we all partake of that one bread.”
41. On this: If the substance of the body in Christ was changed into divinity,
then we too are changed into the substance of God the Word, for we are all one physical being and one body.
Consequently, we too have been changed into his flesh, and we are his body.
And we are no longer human flesh and blood, but his own body.
For the bread is one; therefore we are all one body, because we are the body of Christ.
“But you,” he says, “are the body of Christ, and individually members of it.”
Is the bread the body of Christ through a change of substance? Or are we his body through a change? Or is the body of the Son of God one
in nature with God the Word? But if they are one in nature, there is no longer bread, nor is there a body anymore.
But the apostle says that those who considered our body [?], that of the Son of God, defiled are trampling on the Son of God,
because they reject and deny him. It is not those who acknowledge that the body is of our nature who consider it defiled.
Rather, it was given for the salvation of us all, since it is pure, without blemish, and free from sins:
he who accepted death for all our sins and became an offering to God.
For if we are not all from one source, we have not been called his brothers or his children
rightly; nor, again, are we bread [?] or his body.
But if all these things truly belong to Christ, we are his body and share his nature,
because we are the very thing that the substance of his body also is.
These people too have become known through the statements of their doctrine: they shift from one position to another because they do not possess the truth.
42. Against those who say that the union took place in the substance of God the Word,
and that the divine nature filled the place of the human nature.
From these, another faction arose, resembling them in some respects and differing from them in others.
They also agree with the Arians, yet in turn they part company with them.
In another way, they assume the appearance of the orthodox, although here too they again depart from them.
In this they fall into the same failing as the former group. They acknowledge that our Lord’s body is of the nature of our fathers.
In this they resemble those against whom we spoke a little earlier.
But they differ from them in denying that the flesh was transformed into the substance of the Godhead,
and they accept a union without mixture or confusion.
But they associate themselves with the Arians by saying that the union resulted in one nature,
not through a change of substance, but through a coming together and a natural composition.
Just as soul and body come together into one nature, and through their natural bond the soul naturally experiences the sufferings of the body,
and the body those of the soul—things that each of them, in its own nature, cannot experience—
through their natural coming together, each experiences them through mixture, so that both suffering and activity take place within a single capacity for sensation.
They did not establish the union merely [?] and in use, but through a natural bond in a nature capable of suffering.
They say that the union took place for this purpose: that they should naturally share in one another’s activities and sufferings.
Yet again they differ from the Arians in that they speak of a body and an animal soul, and say that God the Word is of the same nature as the Father.
Not at a command, but by his own will, he accepted union with a nature in a natural way,
so that he might undergo all the sufferings of human nature for our sake, not in another nature, but in his own.
Apollinarians. They say that he did not merely fashion our salvation in an outward form,
or through a change of appearance, or through a change of substance, so as not to experience our sufferings in his own nature.
For that would belong to someone who did not wish to become human; for he became human by nature.
But whether because he did not wish to, or because it was impossible for him to enter where there was a mind,
he was united in a natural union with a sentient, living soul and a body,
so as to complete and fill out human nature, and to experience natural suffering [?],
and to be handed over to death naturally, from impassibility and immortality, in the nature of soul and body; from
what was not a nature, he became and is human nature. He did not come to be in a human being, but was truly a human being.
[?] with human nature, and he was bound to soul and body, for completion and not for assistance.
For the one who [?] flees from the one in whom he dwelt, and receives neither the nature nor the name of that in which he dwelt.
For this reason, although he dwelt in all the saints, in none of them is he said to have become incarnate and become a human being,
except when he truly became a human being, to bring human nature to its natural completeness [?],
when a governing mind was established naturally in the body and soul,
and he established that he should not be thought to have dwelt as in a human being, but to have been united to the completeness of human nature.
These, then, are their views. But those who wish to follow the orthodox more closely
ascribe to him a body and also an intelligent soul, and agree to the unity of one nature in the completeness of the nature.
Just as body, soul, and mind constitute the completeness of human nature,
so too the union of God the Word with a body and an intelligent soul took place to complete the nature. He truly became a human being, they say,
with his nature possessing everything that belongs to a human being, not merely part of that completeness,
that is, flesh alone, or an animal soul. For this is not what it means to become a human being, when
he has nothing human except an animal body and a soul without reason.
Rather, there is a rational soul, a rational body, and a rational life, not one without reason.
For all the things brought together to complete a nature share in one another and in one nature.

For it shares both in suffering and in activity.
43. Against those who confess a body endowed with a soul,
and an intelligent soul, but hold that the union of the divinity in a composite resulted in one nature.
Nestorius. These statements of theirs are rightly addressed to those people: an animal soul,
and likewise a body belonging to a soul without reason, is not a human body. For this reason, neither is he a human being,
who has nothing human: neither soul, nor body, nor divinity.
For human nature is not constituted from an animal soul, divinity, and a body. How, then, did he become a human being
through a combination of things that do not constitute human nature? Unless perhaps you say that another nature came into being through mixture, outside our nature.
Nothing of this sort existed among all the things and all the natures that existed previously,
and now, after the whole creation had been completed, another nature came into being, different from those that had existed, though it had not existed before.
44. On this point: if the union of divinity and humanity resulted in one nature,
that one nature itself is neither God's nor a human being's, but is another nature, foreign to all natures.
But in general, let these same things also be said to them:
For that which, from a body and a rational and intelligent soul, became the nature of a human being through a natural composition—
this is what we understand and call a human being, and not that which, from divinity and a rational soul and a human body,
became a human being through a composition of natures. For this is impossible.
For human nature is defined, and whoever comes to exist in the nature [?] of a human being must have these things:
those possessed by someone who is a human being in substance and nature, neither more nor less. For the properties of a nature are defined.
Either, then, he is a human being, and the union of God the Word with a body and soul did not result in one nature,
but served the purpose of the saving arrangement on our behalf; or they became another nature,
distinct from that of human beings and that of God, consisting of an ensouled body and God the Word.
That nature is neither human nor divine; rather, that nature which he has is a new one, distinct from all natures.
45. On this: If the union of God
the Word with the body resulted in one nature, he cannot be conceived of apart from the flesh, since it is in this that he must exist in his nature.
For henceforth he is not even God from a nature incapable of suffering, but from one capable of suffering.
He is conceived of on the basis of what came into being through a natural union, and this which was newly created became new.
If, then, God the Word is of the same nature as the Father and the Holy Spirit, he was united in a natural union,
and in this he has what he is; outside it he does not exist, being united and becoming united in it and from it.
Just as a body and soul are united into the one nature of a human being and are not conceived of outside their nature,
but the body is in the soul and the soul in the body, together with their experiences and actions,
the body, the nature [?], and not through a voluntary association, as they perceptibly receive from and give to one another,

through a natural blending and through a mixing that mixes the nature.
46. On this: In a union, two natures are not conceived of as one nature.
Now, in this natural union of which you speak,
which nature is it? That of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit—a nature incapable of suffering and immortal,
eternal and needing nothing? Or that mortal nature, capable of suffering and subject to need, which came into being yesterday and today,
and is neither that of human beings nor that of God nor that of another nature,
but a blend of two natures resulting in the completion of one nature? If, then, they say:
that the essence of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit is united in a natural unity.
This union with the flesh is not a natural unity, but a voluntary one: they are united for the designation of the person, not of the nature.
For those things that are united into one nature are not united voluntarily for a blending,
so that what each one of them does not have of itself and for itself
it may acquire from a natural, rather than voluntary, unity, having been united into one nature.
By whom, then, are these things united in nature? Clearly, by the creator of the nature that came into being.
But if someone says that something is united by itself, I do not think this is sound.
For the uniting of natures in their essences into one nature also involves a change of essence.
And the nature that is united must necessarily be bound by sameness of nature, not by will.
47. On the fact that natures united voluntarily are not said to be united naturally, but personally.
For things that are united voluntarily do not acquire a unity that makes them one nature,
but a voluntary unity of the person of the dispensation.
If, then, they say that the union of the natures resulted in one nature, even if we grant them that it happened voluntarily,
once it has happened, that unity is no longer voluntary, since the natures have acquired it.
And, as one who is united, he suffers whether he wills it or not, and receives the sufferings of the nature to which he was united.
For he is defined by this, and not by freedom from suffering, immortality, and freedom from limitation.
For the boundary and limit of every nature is that within which it must exist.
And if he was united to the nature, he must exist within it, and must also be such as it is by nature.
From this it follows that the Father and the Holy Spirit also, since they are of the very same nature as he,
will be of a nature subject to suffering and created. For whatever the Son received in his nature, the Father can also receive.
For it is impossible for one who is incapable of receiving something to be able to receive it in his nature.
If the Son received this because he was capable of receiving union with this nature,
but the other is incapable of receiving it, how are they of one nature—
those who are opposites [?] in their capacity and incapacity to receive? And through this difference of nature, the argument about unity necessarily leads you to the view of the Arians:
that the nature of the Son was united by the creator of nature.
Just as he who created and made the soul and the body also united them.
For this is an act of creation, and it also requires that you unite the soul
and the body into one nature, since establishing the creation of each of them also belongs to him.
48. On the fact that the act of creating the two is a natural union.
For the union into one nature of the natures that have been united is a second act of creation.
For what each of them does not possess in and of itself—the unity of its existence—it naturally receives from the existence of the two.
For it is not the case that hunger, thirst, and bodily sensation belong to the body in and of itself,
and to the soul in and of itself, and did not come to them from the existence of the two.
Likewise, if God the Word also entered into a union of nature with soul and flesh,
so that what he did not possess in his nature, in and of himself,
he acquired through the union of nature—thirst, hunger, weariness, struggle, fear, and death—
then at once there is the created existence of the two and also the original creatorship of his own essence,
and necessarily for the Creator as well, if he endured these things not merely in appearance but naturally.
And you give the designation “of the same nature” in vain to the one from whom you then necessarily take it away.
And you are compelled to become either Arians or Manichaeans.
For either you accept that he did not suffer naturally in any of these things, or that it was in imagination and appearance.
Or, when you concede that in his nature, naturally, with a capacity for sensation
that is subject to suffering, he underwent sufferings, you exclude him from impassibility, immortality, and being of the same nature as the Father.
And thus he acquired a difference of nature: one that admits suffering and one that does not. Or, if there is no difference of essence whatsoever in his nature,
and that of the Father and the Holy Spirit is without need and incapable of suffering and death,
you deprive him of being God, because he does not belong in every respect to the essence that is without need.
49. On the fact that those who are united in nature endure natural sufferings naturally and not voluntarily.
For through a diminution of a nature that is without need and incapable of suffering, a nature subject to suffering and need came into being.
Just as someone who voluntarily removes his hand, foot, or eye no longer has it as his own after it has been removed,
because he has truly cut it off, so too someone who voluntarily removes immortality and impassibility from himself:
For the perfection of the nature subject to suffering and need, he has neither susceptibility to suffering nor need;
that which he had before, since he was made equal with a nature subject to suffering;
until he acquired freedom from suffering again through [?] from nature, together with a natural union;
when he emerged from the resurrection from the dead, in that nature [?] which became immortal and incapable of suffering;
and not from his own nature, which, before he became a mortal human being in a natural union, while
he naturally accepted everything belonging to the nature that he became, even obedience to the point of death—death on a cross;
and also attaining an exaltation above which there is no exaltation, and receiving by grace a name above all names;
to whom every knee bows, in heaven, on earth, and beneath the earth;
to the glory of God the Father, to whom he subjected himself and rendered complete obedience.
He did not empty himself, nor, again, is he the Father's [?], or did he receive equality anew from the Father.
For he himself exalted him from himself, and emptied himself into a mortal nature [?], and became this nature.
And what he had by his nature, he received by grace.
And from an unmade nature he became a made and created nature, with increase and decreases in natural power.
And a substance incapable of suffering and death became mortal and subject to suffering.
And he died through weakness and lived through the power of God, because he became a weak nature;
and he endured its painful sufferings, experiencing pain and suffering because of the shared nature of soul and body;
being torn away and disturbed in his nature, he was driven outside his nature under compulsion.
And for this reason he does not even undergo corruption at the separation of the soul from the body.
Just as the body endures the suffering of death and is forcibly torn away from a single harmony and from a union
that is natural, through separation, so also for God the Word, who was united in a complete natural union,
it is necessary that he naturally endure all the natural sufferings of death.
For this reason both life and death are shared by those who are united in nature. Therefore, whoever grants this
also grants the rest, whether he wishes to or not, even if he says a thousand times that he is incapable of suffering in his nature.
But he suffered in the nature that he became, whether that of flesh or of a human being, or whatever he may call it.
But let him not say this: that his nature is incapable of suffering.
But perhaps it is as with those who can die but do not die, and who are not immortal by nature.
Let us speak in this way also about God the Word. For God the Word is conceived of in these respects by nature, and he has nothing additional.
And if you say that he is a nature incapable of death, he is in every possible way incapable of natural death.
The union was not for the sake of the nature, but for the need of the human being, in accordance with the divine plan,
as was the incarnation of God the Word, who by nature is incapable of suffering and immortal.
What, then, do they say? I must do both things: set out these objections
and also resolve them, as far as possible, since you have asked me to do both. Sophronius.
For they say this: “How,” they ask, “is the man called heavenly and spirit, unless he is spiritual and heavenly?”
God the Word is so by nature, as God—he who was united to human nature.
And it is said: “Just as the first man was earthly, from the earth, so also the Lord is from heaven.”
“And the first man became a living soul, and the second man a life-giving spirit.”
The man is not called earthly apart from the substance of the body made of dust, nor again is he called endowed with soul apart from the soul.
Rather, this is said on the basis of their coming together into human nature,
apart from the substance of the heavenly and spiritual one, which was [?] to human nature.
[?]. On the statement that if “the second man, the Lord from heaven” was applied to God the Word,
then heavenly human beings also belong to the nature of God the Word.
For as that heavenly one is, so also are the heavenly ones. Nestorius.
Listen, then, to these words also as you read the rest of the text: “As that heavenly one is,” it says,
“so also are the heavenly ones. And just as we have put on the image of that earthly one, so also are the earthly ones.”
For they all possess the very same nature. “And as that heavenly one is, so also are the heavenly ones.”
Because they have the very same nature as that heavenly one, then all of us who expect to become like this
would become human beings from the substance of God the Word, while our soul and body are [?] to complete such a nature.
And each of us becomes what God the Word is by nature.
For, it says, “As that heavenly one is, so also are the heavenly ones.”
And it follows that as many peaceful human beings as there are, so there are also Gods the Word.
In that each one of them consists of God the Word, a soul, and a human body.
Not without the limitation of its nature, while each one exists without limitation.
Rather, it is bounded by the nature of each one of them, and it cannot be conceived as existing outside it.
If this is how you understand the statement, “The Lord from heaven,” and the statement about the second man as a life-giving spirit,
what do you think about the rest: “Just as we have put on the likeness of the earthly one, so we shall also put on that of the one from heaven”?
How, then, did we put on the likeness of the one from dust? What were we, and what did we put on? Were we heavenly and spiritual human beings,
consisting of a soul, a body, and God the Word? Or a spirit without a body and without a soul,
which put on the likeness of the earthly one—a body and a soul—and exhorts us to become the likeness of spiritual beings,
that is, spirits without souls and without bodies? Yet this certainly does not belong to us, but to the Creator.
If this is truly so, how does he exhort us to put on the likeness of the spiritual man, that is, Christ,
as though Christ existed without a soul and without a body? And how, then, is he a human being,
when he has nothing that belongs to a human being? Or how is Christ called a human being,
a spiritual one, who was constituted from the substance of God the Word
as the nature of a human being consisting of soul and body? But unless we become bodiless and soulless,
so that we become like this one, just as he is, having nothing, just as he had nothing.
But this cannot be so. These and similar absurdities necessarily follow from what they say:
in this way, these and similar absurdities necessarily follow from what they say:
those who confess that the nature of God was joined to complete the nature of a human being.
For the conjunction of natural unity belongs to a nature capable of suffering and created, [?] of a nature capable of suffering and created.
And because of this, they fall either into the opinion of the Arians,
who say that God the Word became by nature a human nature capable of suffering and death, experiencing sufferings consciously,
or into the opinion of those who say that he became a soul and a body only in appearance, or into both.
For they will flee sometimes to the one group and sometimes to the other, thinking that by fleeing they escape these absurdities.
51. Against those who maintain that Christ is merely a human being.
So much has been said against these people. Let us now also examine these heresies that he divided:
And confess Christ to be only a man: in what they differ, and in what respects they resemble those mentioned above.
So that we may also distinguish and explain their heresies, lest, because of what is wrongly said, we also reject
what is rightly said, or, again, accept without discrimination what is wrongly said.
For their confession that Christ is a man, both by nature and in truth, is true and is attested by the truth.
And in this no one blames them. But because they reject his divinity,
which is his truly and by nature, they are reprehensible, since they deny the incarnation of God the Word.
52. Concerning those who acknowledge God the Word in name alone.
For the Sabellians among them deny even that God the Word exists in substance.
And they speak of God the Word only as a name, saying that he is the command: “He spoke, and it came to be.”
Likewise, they also speak of the Father and the Holy Spirit as names alone.
In short, they agree with the Jews more than with the Christians.
53. Concerning those who say that God the Word indeed exists by nature, but that he was united not by nature but in outward form,
and that there are two sons. Paulianists. Others, however, blame them on these points,
since they themselves acknowledge God the Word as a nature or hypostasis, and likewise the Father and the Holy Spirit.
But concerning his incarnation they do not agree with the orthodox; instead, they approach those
who say that Christ is only a man and that he lived under the law like one of the saints.
And in obedience to the command, he kept all the commandments. Through outstanding observance, he became sinless as a man.
In this he surpassed all human beings. Or, after becoming sinless, he was shown to be free from death,
and justly received immortality, which is appointed as an honor for those who keep the law without sin.
Or because, while conducting himself in all these things, after keeping all the commandments blamelessly, he undertook to die for us.
And because of his great obedience, he received by grace the honor and title of Son.
It was not God the Word, but the one who lived this way and kept all the commandments, as they put it.
[?]. “For what need was there,” they say, “for God the Word also to share in his deeds and act with him,
as though he could not keep the commandments on his own? And what is this being preserved without sin? Or what kind of victory is this? Is it not the utmost defeat,
that, being unable to conquer, he needed assistance and would conquer through assistance, since he himself was unable?”
For the victory does not belong to this man, but to the one who helped him and is not defeated.
For what struggle is there against God? And what guilt is there? For the one who asks of everyone becomes a savior
. For who considers what there is between him and the ruler who comes and finds nothing in him,
when it turns out that nature itself helped him? And before whom is he judged,
when he himself is the judge who judges and is also [?]? Who received him as an offering on behalf of all human beings,
when he himself is both the one who receives and the one who is offered? Who is the one who reconciles, and who is the one who is reconciled,
when he himself is both? Unless perhaps they pour into a single sovereignty
two things that are unlike one another, and say that the Father became angry,
and the Son reconciled him when he was enraged, as they learned from the tales of the Manichaeans, who spread these things.
Or did he perhaps display his anger against those who went astray only in appearance,
and bring it to an end through favoritism? For he presented himself as both wrathful and a reconciler, so to speak.
Thus, in another way, they also follow those who hold the views of Arius, who say that he was reconciled in no other way
than through the death of Christ, who was God from the beginning, and was God.
But what need was there for this invention? For the one who was in him was not doing this through the death of another.
Nor, again, is it just that someone who does not belong to a nature
should accept death on behalf of another nature for the remission of guilt.
Nor, again, is a genuine remission demonstrated, but only an appearance.
And they say that these things should be divided between two sons, so that some apply to this one and others to that one,
so that in every respect the statements would be neither contradictory nor merely figurative.
Yet there is one divinity, one lordship, and one authority of the Father and the Son, who do not admit an appearance of this kind.
They say these things and others like them, strengthening their arguments
so that they may call the Son and Christ twofold, in person as well as in individual being,
in the same way that the saints received God's indwelling; and they speak of his image in the same way. Nestorius.
Let us therefore also speak to each of these people who go astray and lead others astray, denying that God the Word became human.
And first, let us use their own statements against them.
But take for me those statements of theirs that are persuasive and useful for persuading many people.
And fight valiantly against them, so that they are left not even a single excuse that would let them catch their breath.
For what reason, when the divinity and lordship, authority and knowledge, mind and power of God the Father are one,
and those of the Son, through whose hand everything came into being from God, and without whom not a single thing that came into being came into being,
does he restrict becoming flesh to God the Word alone,
and not say that he made flesh? For he says, “The Word became flesh”—the one who was with
God. He did not say this of God the Father, with whom he was.
For both becoming and making belong to him, without causing a division.
It is not that he is the one and not the other—unless perhaps they acknowledge that there are two Words, like two Sons,

and that one is divinity and the other is susceptibility to suffering, through becoming flesh?
Sophronius.
Who would be so foolish as to confess this? For this is obvious. For this reason the Evangelist also said of him,
“He dwelt among us.” This, however, concerns the Word; the following concerns the man: “We saw his glory, glory as of an only son,”
and not that of the Only-Begotten, “full of grace and truth.” Nor, again, by nature.
For that glory is full not through grace but by nature, and it needs no addition.
Nestorius. Then when the Father says of him, “This is my Son,” and again, “He gave his only-begotten Son,”
and, “The Only-Begotten, who is in his Father's bosom, has told us,”
did he speak about this one who is in his Father's bosom, or did he speak of three only-begotten sons? One is the one
who was God the Word from the beginning; another is the one who had glory as of an only son, but
was not the Only-Begotten; and a third, apart from these, is the one whom he gave for the sake of the world.
Sophronius. What then? Did he give God the Word, his own natural Son, over to death,
although he is immortal and incapable of suffering? And do these statements not contradict one another:
that he is his natural Son, incapable of suffering and immortal, and that he gave him over to death?

Or is it perhaps merely a matter of appearance?
Nestorius. Confess aloud with us that there are not two divine Words,
or two sons [?], or two only-begotten sons, but one, and so forth. Each of these matters
is examined by the two, in the same way and properly: how he voluntarily became human,
although he is by nature immortal and incapable of suffering.
And in what sense is it said that the Son died by nature, and not as he is by nature [?] immortal? Sophronius.
But we say these very things to show clearly, even if you are unwilling, that you speak of two Sons by nature [?]:
one incapable of suffering and immortal, and another capable of suffering and mortal.
54. On the statement that God the Word himself became human, and that there are not two Sons, but one in union.
Nestorius. This is entirely untrue, unless we must first say this about the matter:
We learn what we confess to one another from divine Scripture itself. Let us see, then, what
the evangelist says about God the Word. Does he speak about one God the Word, or about two Words? “In the beginning was the Word,
and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
He was in the beginning with God. Everything came into being through him, and without him not a single thing that came into being came into being.”
