About whom could the evangelist say these things, except the one who is of the same nature and is without a body? And the statement, “In him was life,
and life is the light of human beings. The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not comprehend it”—
did he say this about someone else, or about him himself, as he is? And consequently he called him both life and
light, terms that indicate an immortal essence in relation to those who were in death and darkness,
while he himself does not die, for he is life and an inextinguishable light, and gives life [?] to those who are in death.
For about which light does John testify, so that everyone might believe in him? “For he is the true light, which enlightens everyone who comes into the world.
He was in the world, and the world came into being through him, and the world did not know him. He came to his own, and his own did not receive him.
But to those who received him he gave authority to become children of God, to those who believe in his name, those
who were born not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of a man, but of God.”
Did the evangelist say this about another Word, or about God the Word,
through whom everything came into being, who is life and the true light, who came to his own and his own did not receive him,
who gave those who received him authority to become children of God, who were born not of blood,
nor of the will of a man, but of God? And again, in what sense did he grant those who received [?] him
that they should become children of God? To those who were born from God's nature? Were they, then, changed in nature into the nature of God,
of God, and did they become what God the Word is?
As he was born of the Father? Or did he remain in the same nature in which they are, and did they become children of God,
and were they born of God through kinship and acknowledgment? For just as they received him as God who had become one of their own,
and acknowledged that he is their God, the one who made everything and came to his own,
so he too made them his own and acknowledged them as children of God,
like children who enter into sonship, and not by nature.
55. On the fact that God the Word is one by nature and is so named, and that there are not many who are so named by sharing the same name.
Those who become children through kinship and acknowledgment, of the one from whom
they are born—not from flesh or from blood, but from the will and love of the one who is without a body—
and he becomes a body for them, like a father, through kinship, love, and acknowledgment: so also God the Word,
who came to his own, gave authority to those who received him and acknowledged that they believed in his name.
For they did not have the right to become children of God—those who were born not of blood, nor of the will of flesh [?],
nor of the will of a man; for this already belonged to them in their nature—
but they were born of God through kinship. So, then, the one who came to his own and was received
gave those who believed in his name authority to become children of God.
And he would become flesh for them by taking on flesh, and they would make him their own, and he would acknowledge it as his body through kinship.
For this reason he said, “Because he became [?],” answering the statement, “In the beginning was the Word,
and the Word was with God,” and the rest. He also added this: “The Word became flesh and dwelt among us.”
Just as those who received him became, through adoption, God's own by nature, by an act of will, so also he,
by taking on flesh and dwelling in it, became flesh for them through kinship, and not through a change of essence.
Therefore he also brings forward what is distinctive of God when he says, “And we saw his glory, glory as of the Only Begotten from
the Father.” He is not indicating a resemblance, but an affirmation, when he says,
“Full of grace.” He calls what comes from the very nature of the Only Begotten “grace,”
for this is fullness. For someone who merely shares in it is not full.
For he falls short of the one to whose nature all of it belongs, and who is full of grace and truth.
Not as someone who was changed, but as one who is what he was: the beloved Son,
Just as they received him, and just as they believed in him, so they also saw him who was revealed in the flesh.
Him, and not another God, nor another Word, nor another life,
nor another light, nor yet another Only-begotten, but that very same one who [?] in the flesh.
And from his fullness we have all received, as people who did not have it among us. We received from his fullness, and not his fullness itself.
For fullness is that which lacks nothing, as God does.
And for this reason, God, whom no one has ever seen,
was made known to us by the Only-begotten, who is in his Father's bosom, and not by another.
Rather, it was he who was in his Father's bosom, and came and became flesh and dwelt among us.
And he is in his Father's bosom and with us, because he is what the Father is; and he made him known to us.
It is clear that he did not display the boundlessness and incomprehensibility of the essence,
as he is in his Father's bosom. As one who knew our nature,
he made known to us, in our very nature, the one whom no human being has ever seen.
How, then, is it possible to understand this one as one Son, and Christ as another Son,
and as someone who is merely human and remains in his image through equality and the honor of sonship—
the image of the one of whom you do not say that he himself was sent and himself lived among us? The one who, as in a divine indwelling,
dwelt while being in the form of God.
How clearly the evangelist leads us upward from God the Word and toward God the Word!
And apart from God the Word, he knows no other Word or other only-begotten Son of God, but only this one together with his flesh.
Sophronius. But understand, he says, from what is being said, whom the evangelist means.
"No one has ever seen God; the only-begotten Son, who was in his Father's bosom, has made him known."
He said this about the one who was assumed and sat down at the Father's right hand.
The one who is Son in the image and honor of the Son, the one who appeared to us.
The one who comes after me, who is mightier than I; the one upon whom the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove and remained.
God's chosen one, the Lamb of God, the one from Nazareth, the Son of Man.
"You will see," he says, "heaven opened, and God's angels ascending and descending toward
The Son of Man was not the one who is God the Word in substance, of the same nature as the Father.
For no one has ever seen God, but this one was seen. Yet he did not speak about that one,
but about the Son of Man, who by his grace held the rank of the image of the Son of God.
And in this respect he is Son and Only Begotten by God's good pleasure, because all the fullness of the Godhead dwells in him bodily.
He himself is not the fullness; rather, all the fullness dwells in him bodily, just as it dwelt in each of the saints.
For the one who is Son does not exist from himself and for himself; nor, again, does the Father exist from himself and for himself. For the Son is in the Father, and the Father in the Son.
And for this reason, if becoming human in substance belongs to the Son of God,
it must also belong to the Father and the Holy Spirit, if you call him Son by nature, not by equality and honor.
For he was sent in the person of the Son of God, and he put on his person.
And everything belonging to that one is attributed to this one, as with God in an angel and in a mediator.
For the man Jesus Christ is the mediator between God and human beings.
How, then, did there come to be one Son and a becoming human of God?
Unless perhaps, in the case of everyone through whom God carried out his governance of human beings,
one speaks of God's becoming human. And in the case of those things done through Moses and through the prophets,
and those things spoken or done through angels, it is said that God spoke, God acted, and God appeared.
For because God is by nature invisible and incomprehensible, he requires some mediator through whom to administer these things.
The things done [?] or spoken by these are attributed to him,
as a matter of administration and governance, and not through [?] of nature.
How is someone who is human by nature God by nature, and not by grace and activity,
just as God empowers every nature to act as he wills? Unless perhaps, of everything in which God is present,
someone will say that God and a human being act, and that it is two [?].
It now turns to these matters, for the whole investigation concerns them.
56. On the assertion that in none of the prophets or saints is God said to have become human,
nor did he employ any of them as his own person. Nestorius.
Therefore, since, as they say, they follow the divine Scriptures, arguing against them causes us no difficulty.
For it has never been seen that anyone spoke in God's person as his own person:
neither any of the prophets nor any of the angels. But our Lord Christ said, “I and God are one.”
“Whoever sees me has seen God. And whatever God [?], I too do the same as he does.”
“And just as God has life in himself and gives life to those he wishes, I too give life to whomever I wish.”
“And if you do not believe me, at least believe my works, for I and God are one.”
Nor did anyone among the prophets or the angels dare to say these things.
Rather, concerning what they said or did, they declared, “The Lord said,” and not that they themselves were God [?].
And everything they said or did was what God spoke through them.
They too would say, “God said,” as prophets and as angels.
And in those appearances in which he took the form of a human being or of fire, it is said that God appeared, or that someone saw God.
And elsewhere there is the statement that God gave the law, and again, “The law was given through angels.”
These statements are not false, nor do they contradict one another.
He does not call the angels God, nor does an angel call himself God. Rather, it is because he appeared through angels.
Both statements were spoken truthfully: God appeared through the angel in the fire of the bush, and through him God appeared to him.
57. On the fact that, according to the divine Scriptures, we have learned to confess Christ as God by nature and human by nature.
Therefore, because he called himself both, the apostles and evangelists also say that he is both:
God, through whom everything came into being; and he himself came into the world, and he himself made the world, and he himself was not received by his servants. And to those
who received him and believed in his name, he gave authority to become children of God. And he himself became flesh and dwelt among us, and not someone else.
And once he became flesh and dwelt among us, he brought the flesh into a relationship of belonging to him, as belonging to his own person, who exists in both.
In the former respect, he is of God's essence; in the latter, he is flesh through union and belonging.
Likewise, the flesh, which is flesh by nature, is the Son through union and through belonging to his person,
even though, while he exists in both, he is also called one Son and one flesh.
And for this reason the only-begotten Son of God and the Son of Man is one and the same from both.
He is spoken of in both ways, having made the things belonging to their persons belong to his own person.
And hence, from this and from that, as from his own person, he is [?]:
And he speaks with them sometimes from his divinity, sometimes from his humanity, and sometimes from both.
Likewise, his humanity also spoke sometimes from the essence of humanity and sometimes from the person of the divinity.
For this reason, he both is and spoke as the Son of God and the Son of Man.
58. How God the Word is also understood to have become flesh, and there is one flesh,
and there are not two fleshes; and the flesh is also Son, and there are not two sons.
Was it not the case that, until he became flesh, the Word alone, as Son,
existed? Once he took flesh into his own person, he became flesh.
And the flesh is God because of the person of the Word, so that God the Word is called flesh and a human being, while the flesh is called the Son of God.
For until he took flesh into his own person and was revealed in it, he was called Son on account of his divinity.
For it says, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
Everything came into being through him, and without him not even one thing that came into being came into being.”
But once he became flesh, by taking flesh, he is named from both and in both.
Yet he is one in both, not by nature, but in the one by nature,
and in the other by person, through intimate association and also through revelation. For it says, “The Son, equal to his Father, was revealed in flesh.”
“I and my Father are one,” he says, speaking demonstratively from his own person.
The one who was seen spoke on behalf of the one who was apprehended in thought, as though from his own person.
For he is one and possesses the very same person. From the one, the other is apprehended.
And the one who is apprehended also speaks through the one who is seen, as though from the visible one's own person.
“Even if you do not believe me, believe the works themselves, that I and my Father are
one.” And all statements like these are said primarily of the essence,
and consequently of the person, by intimate association, both in speaking and in understanding, and likewise in acting.
For they are not distant, either in action or in word or in essence, nor divided in love.
These statements are distinguished as referring to one person and another.
For through the love and will of God these statements are understood as referring to his own person, because he took flesh,
and in this he was revealed, and in this he taught, and in this and through this he acts as one who is near, not as one who is far away.
He makes use of the flesh in his own person, since he willed that he himself should be flesh and that the flesh should be himself.
So that those who see the flesh also see God, just as his body is in the bread,
and those who see the bread also see his body, because he took it into his person.
He who is God's equal took the person of the flesh, the form of a servant, and gave the form of a servant his own form.
The name that surpasses every name, namely, Son, at which every knee should bow, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth.
For this reason, there must be two natures: divinity and humanity.
The one who emptied himself into the form of a servant, and the form of a servant that was exalted to the name above every name.
For the one who does not remain in his own essence—teaches [?]—
is emptied and diminished, and is no longer exalted above every name. For this reason he spoke of the form and of the name that it received:
the name that indicates the person as belonging to one; and this same name signifies both the person
and the distinction of nature. They have one subsistence and one person. This one is known from that one, and that one from this one.
Thus this one is, through a close relationship, what that one is by nature, and that one is with this one in the body.
Like a king and lord who takes the person of a servant as his own person and gives his own person to the servant.
He makes known that he is that one, and that one is he. In the servant's person, when he is insulted, he accepts it.
But in the person of the lord and king, the servant [?] is worshiped. For this reason, even if I spoke of this one, I did not say it because of that one.
Even if I spoke of that one, it was this one. For he is the very same in both, since they possess one and the same person.
These statements concern natures that are distinct in essence but united in love and in one and the same person.
59. On this: that we ought to accept the close relationship and the indwelling according to God's will,
and should not shrink from the name as though it were ordinary, because it is used on account of their sharing the name.
For even if, as a mediator, it is only God's person
that the humanity that comes from us bears through a close relationship, yet it also does so through the indwelling of his essence.
And it is not merely through the indwelling of divinity; rather, this indwelling is of such a kind
that it also results in one person, the very same person of the one who reveals and the one who is revealed.
For according to God's will, we must acknowledge and judge both that he is present and that he dwelt there.
God is indeed present in all created things. For in him we exist.
And this is qualified as follows: although he is indeed present in everything, he is said to dwell in particular people.
Of some, however, it is said that he is not even their God.
And he is not said to dwell in everyone in the same way, but according to his love.
In some of us he is said to dwell only in the structure, as in houses, as among believers [?].
In others, however, even when he acts, it is not in the same way, but to a greater or lesser degree.
In others, however, it is as in all the apostles; in others, as in the prophets.
And in others, as in the teachers; and in others, according to the different distributions of gifts.
He dwells in this person, in that person, and in another, and he also acts in all.
They are not all equal and alike, but differ according to the love of the one who dwells in them.
Some of these hold the first rank, and some the ranks that follow.
And step by step, in descending order, they are joined and connected to one another, just as in the body
are its members. Christ is the head of them all, and they are bound together in him.
And the head of Christ is God. For just as he is our head and also our person,
so God is his head, and also his person and his incarnation.
For this reason, we have received from him the right to become children of God; he, however, is the only Son.
So that his flesh might be what he himself is: the Son of God and of the Father.
So that the image of the Father might be the Son of the Father, whose image it is.
For the person of the Son is one and the same, and it is he and no other who is in both substances, without being divided.
60. On this: that it is not as with images, or as with angels, or as with envoys,
who represent the person of someone far away, that we should also think of the archetype;
rather, in his own nature and person he was united to the body and became human,
with his person being used with reference to the body, and the body with reference to the person of God the Word.
Not God; and in the things enacted in an image [?], for there they are said to exist only in appearance,
on the basis of appearance and likeness, while this is far removed from the substance.
Nor, again, is it as with angels and envoys who represent the person of those who sent them.
And in this they are the persons of those others through service and ordinary authority.
But he spoke in his own nature and in his own person when he said, “I and my Father are one.”
And he is what that other is in person, and what that other is in person, he is.
Not by making another form his own form, but in his own form;
and not in another likeness resembling the form of a servant, but in that one's natural form.
So that this one might be what that one is, and that one what this one is, while this one and that one remain.
61. On his receiving, in human nature, a name more excellent than every name.
For this is the supreme advancement of human nature:
that while remaining in human nature, he receives a name more excellent than every name.
It was not through progress in conduct, nor through knowledge and faith, but through this that he became ready to receive:
to be his image and his person, just as his person is also the person of this one. And he is both God and man.
And the form of God, through condescension and self-emptying, is in appearance the form of flesh, like a human being.
And through exaltation the man is what God is, in the name above every name.
For this reason, in self-emptying he humbled himself to the point of death, even death
on a cross, with the person of the one who died and was crucified being expressed in his own person.
And he expressed in his own person these things belonging to the one who died, was crucified, and was exalted.
And for this reason, what is said of Christ is said as of one person.
And each of these things and those things differs in nature as much as the divine nature differs from human nature.
Thus Christ is both: the form of God and the form of a servant—the form that is exalted and the form that exalts.
For even though he is called Christ on account of the flesh that was anointed, he is the one person of both natures.
For the name more excellent than every name is also one. Both, even if it is spoken of on the basis of the divine nature:
for the names of the natural persons are shared in condescension and exaltation.
62. On why the saving arrangement for us had to come from both.
And it was fitting for the saving arrangement for us that both should be taken into that person.
For because God created the first human being in his own image and likeness,
And the persons and God the Creator had not been revealed to us: the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
So that we might also know the Creator, fully acquire instruction in divine knowledge, and fully understand the image of God
and receive it completely, he renewed the whole creation in Christ and made known and showed us who the Creator is:
the one who from the beginning was the Word with God, and was God, the Maker of everything.
“Everything,” it says, “came into being through him, and without him not even one thing that came into being came to be.”
63. On why God the Word built himself the temple of the body.
Just as it was necessarily fitting that our renewal should also come from the makers of nature:
from the one who also, at the beginning, formed us and made us from the earth.
He took a body and made it in his likeness, and established it in his person, in every respect as his own, in the honor and glory of God.
He acted in the nature of the Godhead, but in the person of the Son, for the honor of the Father and the Son is one.
“Just as they honor the Father,” it says, “let them also honor the Son.” Thus he taught us that the one who created everything is God,
and that the Son is with the Father and the Spirit—for the human being lived in him—showing the unity of nature:
that the Father is the Son’s, and the Father is in the Son, and the living Holy Spirit is in them.
And he created the body in a new manner, from a man and a woman.
And because this is an act of creation, he speaks about what is created and about the one who created it.
“The Holy Spirit,” it says, “will come, and the power of the Most High will overshadow,”
pointing to the Creator. “Therefore the one who is born”—that is, the holy one who is created—“will be called the Son of God.”
In speaking of creation, he said “holy” and “Son,” pointing to the image and likeness
that the first human being received at creation but did not preserve.
For, as the image of God, he ought to have offered himself to God without stain and without blemish.
For his willing whatever God wills serves for him as the person of God.
For this is the person of God: that whoever bears his person should will whatever God wills.
For this reason the second human being was created by the Holy Spirit and the power of the Most High, and received from him the gift of being holy and the Son of God.
64. On his receiving sonship from the very moment of his formation, and not through gradual advancement.
So that he would not be like the rest, through obedience in faith and deeds.
But from his coming into being in the Creator’s creation [?], the created one assumed his person, so that he would not first be a man,
but simultaneously man and God, through the incarnation of God in him—that which God is in the first man.
He was the Maker of all, a lawgiver apart from being a king.
Glory. Honor. Power. This one also became a man,
of two, in the things perfected and the things that perfect, so that God would be his person, and he, in turn, would be in God.
65. On how a person ought to be understood in the union, although he has no person of his own.
Just as, when God appeared to Adam in a form and spoke, he was not someone else,
so God will be for all human beings, in the form of the nature that was created,
namely, flesh, appearing and speaking in his own image, and the image in the archetype.
Thus God is seen in the image, although he is invisible.
The image, however, is understood in relation to the one who is invisible. For it is not an image of itself,
but of that one. Now the image and the person—the humanity of the divinity and the divinity of the humanity—are the person of the one who is understood.
“He who,” it says, “was in the likeness of God and equal to him,
took the likeness of a servant and was found in appearance as a man,” in what is visible.
And what is visible is in the one who is understood, in the person and in the name above every name, in honor, glory, and worship.
For he gave him a name more excellent than every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth,
and beneath the earth, and every tongue should confess that Jesus is Lord, it declares.
66. On how the flesh is worshipped in the person of the Son, and how, although it is in no way worthy of this worship, it is worshipped in the person of God the Word.
For a human being is recognized by a human person, that is, by the appearance and likeness of the body.
God, however, is recognized by the name more excellent than every name, by the worship offered by all creation, and by the acknowledgment of him as God.
For in it he took the likeness of a servant and gave the likeness of a servant his own measure, so that it would be equal with God.
Since he himself accepted it as his own person, no one should exclude it, because of its nature, from the worship of the divinity,
in heaven, on earth, and beneath the earth, and from every tongue, even though that worship is by nature above human nature.
For who excludes from worship that which belongs to the Lord of all, and excludes it from his own person and his name? And who, again, refuses to bow
to that to which the Maker of all had at first refused to bow? Yet he bowed to all this.
He whose power to create belongs to him by nature, not in honor or glory,
but in contempt, disgrace, and complete humility, remained so until death on the cross.
“He humbled himself,” it says, “to the point of death—and death on the cross.”
There is nothing more humiliating than death. It was not in the manner in which, with Adam,
it happened: he gave him his image in complete glory and honor. For he subjected [?] everything beneath his feet.
Likewise, to the second man also he gave his image of glory, with honor and power.
But everything was the opposite: [?] he gave the image of God.
(He did indeed take the form of a servant in the person [?] only of the person [?] how long he would preserve it, because of [?]
[?] and it was no longer his [?] he fashioned it in his own person and perfected it.
The form of God in the form [?] he fashioned it for himself in his own form. For the inward assumption made it [?].
67. Why, when he took the form of a servant, he did not take an honored or a despised one.
And for this reason he took the form of a servant, a poor form, a form that had lost the form of God.
It was not for honor, nor for glory, nor for worship, nor yet for authority,
although he was indeed the Son, but for obedience. It acted in the person of the Son according to the mind of God,
having his mind, not its own,
and not whatever it wanted, but whatever God the Word wanted.
For this is the form of God: that it should not have a mind and will of its own,
but those of the one to whom the person and the form belong.
And for this reason the form of God took the form of a servant, so that it would conceal nothing of the humiliation of the servant’s [?] form.
Instead, it took everything, so that it would be the form in every respect, and thus make it conform to its own form without any deficiency.
68. Why he took the form of a servant for voluntary obedience, and not for instrumental obedience, which he declared to be without a will.
For he took it for this purpose: to remove the guilt of the first man
and to give human nature that original image which it had lost because of its guilt.
Fittingly, that which had been condemned, taken captive, and subjected to slavery—
he took it in all those bonds of disgrace and contempt, while from his own person he did not [?] anything divine, or anything of honor or authority.
Just as a son, while still a child, did not acquire the right to be heir or lord of everything through exercising authority, but through obedience.
So too, the form of a servant that he took into his own person, he accepted as the form of a servant:
not for exercising authority, but for obedience. And all this obedience—
that from which obedience without sins is truly born—and he was truly shown
to be without sins. Therefore, when someone is delivered from all the causes from which disobedience arises,
then he is clearly and unquestionably seen to be without sins.
For this reason, he also took from the very nature that had sinned, so that, if he took from a nature incapable of sins,
it would not be thought that his not sinning came from his nature rather than from his obedience.
Instead, although all these things belonging to our nature were present—anger, desire, and thoughts—
and these too grew with the progress and growth of each stage of life, he remained steadfast in thoughts of obedience.
69. Why he did not undertake obedience through different commandments, as Adam did,
but accepted all the commandments, not just individual ones. And through those [?] original commandments,
his return to obedience took place, and not through others, so that it would not be thought that he had been able to overcome because they were easy.
Nor, again, did he practice obedience in circumstances that offered, as it were, the encouragement of honor, fear, and praise,
but in circumstances of poverty, need, contempt, and weakness,
which could bring his thoughts and obedience to light.
These contain no encouragement at all toward obedience, but rather toward slackness and negligence.
And he received no help in anything. He longed only for this: to obey God, and he loved whatever God wanted.
70. Why, in his way of life, he was without care from his divinity in human matters.
And for this reason, although he was in need of everything and was violently battered by adversities,
he did not turn aside in anything from God's purpose, even though Satan used all these things to distance him from God's purpose.
Satan sought this all the more because he saw that he had no one caring for him.
For neither is it apparent that he performed signs from the beginning,
nor, again, that he had authority to teach, but only to submit and to keep all the commandments.
He lived among everyone, where all the commandments surrounded him on every side:
And they showed his courage in disobedience; he conducted himself powerfully among them all.
There was nothing extra or different in the food provided for his nourishment; rather, he used these ordinary things like everyone else.
This was so that no one would suppose that he was restrained from sin because of his strict observance in these matters,
and that without these things he could not restrain himself.
For this reason, while eating and drinking, he kept all the commandments.
And in matters involving hardship and sweat, he remained firm
in his resolve, his will being fixed on the will of God, and there was nothing that could snatch him away and separate him from him.
For he did not live for himself, but for the one to whom the person belonged.
And he kept the person free from stains and blemishes, and through it he gave his nature victory.
71. Why did he receive John's baptism after he had been shown to be without sins?
And because he was fully obedient in everything, he received John's baptism as a first act, just like everyone else.
And although he had no need of it, since he was without sins,
because of his great obedience he received it as someone who needed it. For obedience takes first place:
he was not to act as befitted his honor and glory, but to be obedient to the one who commanded.
And more than this, he was not only to allow him to baptize,
but also to be baptized by him as someone guilty and convicted and in need of forgiveness.
For obedience in everything is like this: he should not seek or demand anything in his own person,
but rather what belongs to the one to whom the person belongs, and he should acquire that one's will.
Since the person belongs to him as Lord, he should regard his person as his own person,
and the person is one. For this reason, the Father revealed him from above, saying:
“You are my beloved Son; I am pleased with you.”
And the Holy Spirit descended in the form of a dove and remained upon him; it does not say that the Son descended.
For he is the Son, the one who took possession of his person, and he made the things belonging to this one his own person, without separating himself from him.
For this reason, he is one also in the birth in the flesh. “The Holy Spirit,” it says, “will come, and the power of the Most High will overshadow you.
For this reason, the holy one who is born from you will also be called the Son of God.”
And he did not say at all that the Son would come, because the one who took him into his person is not someone else.
Rather, he is the very same one who gave him for the dispensation on our behalf, for the reasons we stated earlier.
72. Why he associated with everyone, and afterward was led into the wilderness.
And because he was thought to observe the commandments more than anyone else, because of his dealings with everyone:
But when he lacked many things, it would be easy to oppose him where there was nothing from which he could receive help:
He went out alone into the wilderness to be tempted by the devil.
He was deprived of everything in the world, and of what seemed to be agitation and distress:
Through withdrawal from everything, to this
full height he rose, as far as bodily strength can be raised.
And instead of the impulses of the soul’s desires, he held to what belonged to God, as though he were without a body:
He paid no attention to his body as something belonging to him, but as something outside him.
For this belongs only to the image of God and to someone who preserves the image of God: to desire what God desires.
And because there was nothing else, in everything the devil said,
he put him to shame as someone who was outside the will of God.
He raised his soul toward God, bringing the things he desired into agreement with the will of God.
Thus he would be an image only of the archetype, and not of himself.
For an image in itself is without a likeness; it has a particular likeness, that of the archetype.
And the two are indeed one and the same, and a single appearance.
For through his deeds, in bodily matters, he preserved the likeness of God from all the passions of the body.
And his choice was that the will of God should prevail, and not that of the flesh.
And he made it a likeness of him in [?], so that he would desire whatever he himself desired:
So that there would be one and the same will in both, and one undivided person.
This one is that one, and that one is this one, while this one and that one remain, as he stood firm in everything:
In bodily and spiritual trials, in cities and in the wilderness, with no difference in his observance and obedience.
73. On how, while proclaiming the kingdom of heaven to us, he received honor—a victory without sins.
From then on, as one who had conquered and triumphed in everything, he was given authority as an honor for his victory:
to proclaim and announce the good news of the kingdom of heaven, saying, “Take courage! I have overcome the world.”
“Now is the judgment of this world; now the ruler of this world has been condemned.”
“And when I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw everyone to myself.”
And although he was the Son, he learned obedience from the fear and sufferings he endured.
And he was made perfect and became the source of eternal life for all who obey him.
And he was sent to teach everyone and to perform signs, wonders, and healings, along with all the other things.
It was not so that he might be eager and strive for obedience, but for the faith of those who were learning.
He used all these things for the obedience of his pupils. For until the time of his victory he was struggling
to establish in God the image that had been given to him. But because he had upheld his own image through every trial, perfectly and without deficiency,
and lacked nothing, from then on he acted on our behalf, striving to rescue us captives from the tyrant’s coercion,
to draw us to himself, and to make us all children of his kingdom, partners, heirs, and children of God.
For the tyrant’s defeat would be beyond consolation when he openly cast him down from his position of rule.
And after casting him down, he would also seize his power.
And when he had seized it, his own victory would not suffice for him, but from then on ours too, for which he had struggled.
And those who had been obedient to him, he now brings to himself willingly and not by force.
And he persuades those who come to be saved by him of their own will, and not to become his disciples against their will. [?]

And why do I say “the enemy” [?]? Rather, then, what belongs to the enemy.
74. Concerning the fact that, after the victory,
and after the words “This is my Son” had been spoken about him, he begins other severe battles on our behalf.
For this reason, after his victory in everything, and after it had been said from heaven, “This is my beloved Son,”
he again began other battles [?] leadership, teaching, and the authoritative working of wonders.
Again, he conducted himself with exalted obedience in these circumstances of ours.
But this was amid human circumstances and weaknesses, since he possessed no authority or superiority at all.
He was persecuted and beaten, and he felt the fear that terrifies everyone.
Unlike even a bird or the animals, he had no place to lay his head, as he moved from place to place.
And through all these things he was battered and oppressed for the sake of our obedience.
Although no one compelled him, he was fulfilling his task and teaching with all diligence.
And he endured every trial for the sake of teaching.
And from every place where he was persecuted, he was driven toward those among whom the good news had not yet been proclaimed.
Thus the very thing for which he himself was striving was being accomplished through the efforts of his enemies.
They had not looked ahead to the outcome of the matter, but thought they were hindering him through opposition
and actions full of contempt and abuse, and terror extending even to death.
And after his victory, and after his election by God: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am pleased,”
after he had received authority to proclaim the gospel, after it had been revealed that he was performing divine deeds by his own authority,
after he had said, “I and my Father are one,” he experienced all this weakness and humiliation in these human circumstances,
which it was thought he could not endure
under their burden. Rather, they would bring him distress and ingratitude.
Indeed, there were also many things that hindered him from proclaiming the good news.
And because of this, they also became his accusers on God's behalf,
as though he were the cause of disobedience, while they placed him in a position of humiliation and weakness.
75. Concerning how, in his original honor, he practiced the original obedience:
since Christ also truly became human, and did not reject it as contemptible.
For in everyone's case, humiliation that comes after honor was considered contemptible.
But with Christ in the flesh it was the opposite: in his original honor he acquired obedience extending to death—even death on a cross.
And he showed Satan and every ruler and every authority that greater obedience is all the more a cause of honor,
and not disobedience to God, with which Satan was afflicted when he was deemed worthy of his nature and honor.
And he could not bear obedience to human beings,
since he judged honor and dishonor by the difference between his own nature and that of human beings.
And he thought that this obedience was not owed to God.
Because of this love of glory, he also cast Adam into the same affliction, persuading him not to
to obey God. He did not choose to receive grace and to be obedient without getting anything in return.
Instead, although he had been deemed worthy of God's image, when he was forbidden to eat from a single tree,
he grieved over something not worth grieving over, transgressed God's commandment, and considered God envious.
For all these reasons, God deemed the second Adam worthy of all this honor, because he practiced complete obedience:
an honor beyond which there is nothing, just as there is no obedience that surpasses his.
He did not consider himself to be anything, but sought to be according to God's will,
just as God wanted him to be.
76. Why he made the incarnation his own in person, just as he also became human.
For this reason God himself also became human in a human being, in his own person, and made that human being's person his own person.
There is no comparison for this condescension: that the other's person should become his own, and that he should give him his own person.
For this reason he also made use of his person, since he had assumed it as his own.
Yet he assumed it not by making it honored, but lowly, so that the one who served might show everyone that all
greatness that exists becomes greater through humility, not through exalting itself.
For he took the form of a servant and was found in appearance as a human being.
The form of a servant served him in everything, just as he himself wished.
He wished this in keeping with his nature: not only that he should obey his person on his own behalf,
so that there should be no doubt about his being the Son of God, but also that he should conduct himself on our behalf and die for our salvation.
He did this on our behalf, however, not because we were righteous or good.
For there is encouragement in this—that someone should die for people of that kind—but he died for the unjust.
For scarcely does anyone die for the wicked; for good people, however, someone might perhaps dare to die.
Therefore, because he humbled himself in everything, beyond comprehension, with a condescension beyond compare, once again one mind,
one will, and one purpose were revealed, inseparable and undivided, as in one.
Also in power, in authority, in governance, and in [?],
he shared in all these things with God without division, as from one in one, through the discernment and choice of both.
so that he should acquire nothing human of his own in these human things,
But God's will should be his own will, as he was proved steadfast through deeds and the sufferings of his nature.
Likewise, in divine matters too, nothing belonging to him should come from human lowliness.
Rather, in everything he should remain in the things of God, being, even in freedom from suffering, what he had been in suffering—a human being by nature.
For just as, in emptying himself, he made use of the form of a servant,
so he should share in the exaltation of the form of God, while himself existing in both:
in the form of a servant and in the form of God, with one and the same person belonging to both lowliness and exaltation.
77. On how the incarnation served to instruct the whole of rational creation.
For this reason, through the incarnation of God the Word, it was necessary to teach the whole of rational creation to share in his goodness.
For its sake, although he needed nothing, he did everything, and he disdained nothing in accomplishing this, even the most lowly things.
Finally, he would also give humanity a share in his image, so that, likewise, no one would treat those beneath him arrogantly,
but, through sharing in greatness and according to his ability, would do everything with his eyes on God.
78. On how Satan, out of envy toward humanity, did everything to lead it astray.
Therefore, because Satan had used the things given him by God for the opposite purpose and had fallen away from God's intention,
he did not use the image of God as a likeness and representation worthy of God,
but in envy toward humanity and in leading it away from God.
He deceived the human being and caused him to fall away from his image by failing to observe God's will.
He made him an enemy and a combatant against God, so that through this he might denounce God as unjust,
since he had shown such goodwill toward humanity, and might reproach him for avenging on the human being the dishonor done to him
and exacting from him the punishment he deserved through the things he did to him.
For because Satan had acted in anger rather than with thought, he had forgotten that God does the opposite of what he himself desires.
79. On how God showed the supremacy of his goodness and exposed the supremacy of Satan's wickedness.
For in bringing death, God was not acting to destroy humanity, but to instruct and help it, so that it would not sin
or again be persuaded by the counsels of the wicked, which bring destruction.
For this did not provide grounds for slandering God, but for magnifying his grace.
He had deemed the human being worthy of such honor when he had been nothing.
And that he might rebuke the robber for the deceit he had devised to bring about humanity’s downfall.
And show that he has no intention at all of destroying humanity, but rather of preserving it by grace.
And that he might care for humanity so that it might return to what it had been.
For Satan thought that, after all this love of God toward humanity,
if he again made humanity transgress God’s commandment, God would certainly become angry and destroy it,
and there would be no possibility of restoration and healing for it. But those who had sinned and had been granted salvation,
and then persisted in those very same sins, while they had not yet escaped the first punishment—
wrath would be stirred up against them without reconsideration, since there would no longer be any grounds for deliverance.
Thus Satan himself had already worked out on his own these plans he had devised for humanity’s destruction.
He had persuaded himself and condemned humanity to punishment, leaving it not even a single ground for forgiveness.
And because he was blinded by his anger and envy, he did not himself understand God’s goodness,
because of which God had not destroyed even Satan, the deceiver, despite his being what he was, but had endured his wickedness.
For this reason God also shows patience toward human beings who sin and act wickedly against him,
since it is someone else who leads them astray. He is patient with the deficiency of human understanding and with
the devil’s limitless wickedness toward them.
He has this overwhelming desire: to lead everyone astray and make everyone oppose God,
and to wipe out our entire race through his actions, without its having anyone to intercede on its behalf.
And because Satan took the initiative in displaying all this wickedness, although he had not a single reason for doing evil,
amid all this wickedness, God’s goodness was also revealed.
And he displayed his inexpressible goodness by bestowing his benefits on all humanity alike.
For, in the greatness of his condescension, he had come in lowliness, dishonor, and weakness to the one who had sinned so greatly,
and he was not ashamed of the dishonor endured for the sake of benefit. And through his own person he became that one’s own person,
and that of God, while fulfilling everything belonging to God—that is, instruction, an instructive condescension.
For the obedience of the firstfruits of humanity became a lesson in humility:
it sought not what belonged to itself, but what belonged to God.
And he was united in a single purpose, so that Satan would not have even the slightest opening to introduce disobedience.
And because only death remained as the means of defeat and victory, after everything else he endured this too.
So that, by proving victorious over it, he might abolish it completely. And he accomplished two things
through it: he condemned Satan and stripped him of every pretext for disobedience.
80. On the fact that, when Christ had won, his victory was not enough for him.
Rather, he also chose to suffer injustice for us, so that through the injustice he suffered on our behalf he might obtain redress.
And while many gave way through fear of death, he endured to the point of death.
And he made a just payment on our behalf by exchanging our death for the death that came upon him unjustly.
For this reason, after keeping all the commandments so as to be undeserving of death and to receive the reward of victory on our behalf,
he also undertook this course of action to teach those who were going astray, and died on our behalf as on behalf of those who go astray.
And he brought death forward, because it had to be abolished.
For he did not neglect even to submit himself to death, since he had hope of undoing it.
For this was also why he had first suffered other trials, and not so that he might die unjustly without [?].
For in this very hope he also possessed obedience and immeasurable love:
not to obtain victory for himself, but to seek redress for us.
And not to win on his own behalf alone, but on behalf of everyone. For just as the guilt
of Adam brought everyone under condemnation, so this man's victory also acquitted everyone.
81. On the fact that through these very events God showed everyone
that he had not shown favoritism toward that human nature, since it suffered in all these things.
And from both of them all the rational powers learned that there is no favoritism with God,
but rather the love of a just judge. Through this, humanity won and Satan was condemned.
And God magnified his victory and gave him honor surpassing all names.
And all the rational powers together marveled at his victory,
and they kneel and worship the name that was given to him, because it was justly given.
And every tongue acknowledges the just way things were arranged for the sake of everyone.
through which he made tranquility and peace reign on earth—he who, in all matters, brought them near by persuasion and not by force.
82. Why he took it upon himself to become human, and why he, God himself, carried out the saving plan,
and not through someone else: lest, when that person was in such lowliness and weakness,
his command should be considered contemptible, and envy should once again be stirred up against humanity. Instead, he himself undertook it, he
who can endure everything. And he [?] witnesses to the lowliness of his humanity:
the angels who strengthened him, so that no one would say that it suffered without truly experiencing suffering,
because he himself strengthened it so that it would not suffer, and that for this reason it had no excuse for disobedience.
For everything that could be thought or said about him in doubt, and whatever he knew they would say about him,
even if they themselves were unable to say it, either because they were afraid or because they were obedient,
he acted on all these things, so as not to leave even one cause for doubt. For they did not understand this mystery.
It was hidden even from the rulers and authorities and from all the heavenly powers, and it was revealed to them, as it were, through knowledge.
After this resolution, they all acknowledge that plan which unraveled every plan and overcame them.
And he showed that his becoming human was a saving plan for all,
for all those who agreed with him, with one mind and one conviction, to stand against the enemy of them all,
whom he drove out and whose authority he abolished. There is no longer any room for his deception and envy.
83. Why, when Satan, the enemy of all, had been condemned and rebuked, he did not destroy him but allowed him to act again.
He continues to deceive, however, for his own clear condemnation and that of those who are persuaded by him,
since his deception no longer has such power, and for the victory of those who are not persuaded by him.
For, it says, no one is crowned unless he competes according to the rules.
For this reason Christ continued in his way of life after the victory and after the abolition of death:
that way of life which was abolished in Christ, so that those who are in Christ might also live after Christ’s example,
not only through the grace of the resurrection, but also through the deeds of each one’s way of life.
For the former belongs to all, while the latter belongs to each one individually. And so that it should not be thought
that Christ’s nature had a unique and exceptional constitution, having been constituted to be without sins, and that he conquered for this reason,
he brings it about that the enemy is defeated by many tens of thousands through the way of life in Christ, in our very own nature—by those who keep the strict commandments.
How, falling only a little short of the law, they live in the body the life of bodiless beings.
And amid afflictions and distress, and in [?] weakness, they endure the impulses and movements of nature, together with assaults from outside.
And in this way they prevailed in everything, so that the increase of Satan’s guilt might become their growth in observing the commandments.
He had thought that a very rigorous way of life would make it easy to bring human beings down.
84. For what reason Satan reached such a height of arrogance that he would openly stand against God,
and make himself equal to God. And for this reason, as he rushed here and there, his guilt became great.
From this point onward he increases his wickedness and reveals it, bringing it to its culmination in the Antichrist,
so that he may stand openly against God and make himself God’s equal, imitating his becoming human.
He does not deceive by means of something or from something else, but in his own person and through supreme deception.
And because Christ had undone the deception embodied in their gods and their sorceries, he too, while deceiving, undoes these things of his own.
These are the gods, objects of worship, sorceries, and other things of which he himself is the director.
To make himself great, he places them all under his own person, so that he alone may be thought to be God.
For he uses a human being as an instrument, seizing him and dragging him into immeasurable wickedness.
He also makes the human being share in his lack of divine knowledge, as enemies are accustomed to do.
He does these things out of necessity and anger, because they are being completely undone and abolished, together with all his dominion.
And when he reaches his end and has nothing further to pass on to, so that he might remain
to pour out all his wickedness, and so that it may become clear to everyone that he fought against his Creator in return for creating him,
and in return for giving him such power, and in return for allowing him to use his power and bearing with him while he fought by all these means,
he gathers together all the things that uproot and abolish his tyranny.
For he no longer has any scheme to use against God’s chosen ones, since everything has been fulfilled in every respect:
both his deception and their careful observance of the commandments. And he was defeated in everything, in secret and in [?],
with his persuasions and all his coercion, which he had employed against the weakness and lowliness of clay.
And just as he had acted toward Christ, so he also acted toward the saints,
using every means to cast them into severe afflictions. They, however, were not defeated by these things.
But he, in that he did not [?], when he was defeated by Christ, ceased from his own activity.
And again, when he has been condemned by the saints, does Christ not abolish his dominion through the death that unjustly came upon him?
And it is completely abolished through the death of the saints, which he brought upon them presumptuously, not as something they owed.
And he brings him under a just judgment on account of those whom he unjustly oppressed, fighting to bring about our destruction,
and because of all his schemes and deception, and every kind of ingratitude he showed,
and his arrogance and tyranny against God and against his saints. For the entire period
of God's patience was given for repentance, and so that he might come to his senses
and recognize his folly and his audacity in attempting the impossible.
85. What thoughts Satan conceived against God.
And although he could have afflicted him with suffering and driven him to seek vengeance,
he did not do this, but allowed him to exercise his anger as he wished.
For patience toward those blinded by wickedness causes their wickedness to grow.
Although they see it and understand it clearly, they act in the opposite way, like people who do not see it.
For there is no remedy for the growing wickedness of those who turn things in the opposite direction.
For either they hold this opinion about God's patience:
that because he cannot subject them to suffering, since they possess an immortal nature,
he is therefore patient with them; and for this reason they do things that oppose God.
Or else, while admitting that he can do everything, they themselves act contrary to his will:
although he wishes through his patience to turn them away from their wickedness, precisely because this is what he wishes,
they oppose his will by doing things that are contrary
to what he wishes. For they do not want salvation from him, because of their hostility and their boundless audacity.
Instead, they provoke him still more to destroy them, since they do not even want to be subject to God or to live.
And we shall see him condemned by human beings in a just judgment, when he has not a single means of escape or any accusation to bring.
For God allowed him to do everything he wished, so that there would not be even one ground for his deliverance.
For he neither destroys him in an instant, as he himself desires, nor, on the other hand, lets him go uncondemned.
For by leaving himself not even a single ground for forgiveness, he has prepared himself to be beyond correction in every way.
Whoever, then, is gripped by envy and the love of power
does not cease from his envy until the object of his envy becomes as he wishes; and he is an example of all who are ungrateful.
For God judges him justly, along with all those who, like him, have fallen into this sickness,
and examines them, and condemns them in everyone's sight, and they are unanimously hated.
And in him they see all ingratitude, all insolence and arrogance, and all schemes,
and all deceit, and all the wickedness that has flourished, grown, and reached its fullness, so that it can no longer receive any further increase.
86. On how, at the time of condemnation, Satan is hated by everyone,
even by those who belong to him, as the one who became the cause of their punishment.
For this reason, all this time of patient forbearance has been given to him, and continues to be given to him until the day of judgment, so that he may do whatever he wishes,
so that he may be left with no excuse that he could have done something; rather, he has been given a time of patient forbearance and authority.
And after these things he is fully judged and rebuked by the righteous, together with all those who joined him in tyranny.
He is also hated and accused by these very people, as the one who became the cause of their condemnation.
Thus everyone may love God with pure love, in word and deed, as good and just,
as wise and mighty, as Creator and as God.
And having an example of the just judgment that shows no partiality toward the good or the evil,
all the hosts of rational beings may properly learn the rational discernment of good and evil,
and why God has allowed everyone to choose for themselves according to their own will,
and allows those who choose good things to endure evils,
while toward those who have chosen the opposite of these things and fight against his will,
he is patient, allowing them to do whatever they choose. And in this way
the course of this world continues; in this way it is governed by God until the end. 87. Conclusion.
And after these things, since everything has turned out well, we shall live in everlasting delight,
having no cause to be deprived of it, and no longer needing instruction.
88. On how it was necessary for there to be a union of two natures, and how it was not fitting for it to be otherwise.
For these reasons, then, and others like them, God's becoming human rightly took place.
True God by nature, and a true human being by nature.
For neither of these would have been the case if one of these natures had been left out.
Unless God had become human, and unless this had been in a human being who was of human nature,
it would have been a deception, and these words of Satan would have been true:
that Christ had utterly rejected his handiwork from his image as something contemptible.
For this reason, there would have been no teaching of humility, obedience, and condescension either.
For he is the equal and likeness of God; if he did not take the likeness of a servant,
so as to be found in appearance as a human being, there would instead have been an even greater vindication of Satan's words: that because
he had seen that the human being was inferior by nature to the image and likeness of God's glory, he had despised him.
And all the angels, even though they would have submitted to him as to God and would not have been able to dare to speak against him,
would have been compelled by the situation itself not to blame Satan for anything,
as someone driven to this by an unjustified passion over the immeasurable honor of human nature.
Even if he were blamed on this point: that he ought to have obeyed the command, since it was God's.
And because this passion was in their souls, they would have served him because of the one who commanded them, and not out of goodwill.
89. On the fact that, even if he had been in human form and not in human nature,
the claim of becoming human would not have held true. And even if someone grants that it was in human form,
but not in human nature, that he became human, he is asserting the very same rejection of human nature.
90. On the fact that, even if he changed his own nature into human nature, the claim of becoming human would not have held true.
And even if he changed his own substance into human substance, it appears that he utterly rejected human nature,
in that he came to be in his own substance and not in human substance.
For this substance of his is not from the earth, but from the nature of God the Word, and for
this reason, God the Word appears to have acted cleverly in his human conduct:
so that he who is God the Word in his own substance might remain without sins as though he were a human being.
Thus he also conducted himself as a human being, although he was not a human being by nature,
but was God the Word, even when he fought and defeated the adversary.
And even when he suffered, it was he who was by nature incapable of suffering who suffered.
And likewise with these other things, even if someone says that he assumed a human being,
and changed the human nature into his own substance, he has not undone the victory of those who despise it, who maintain that he is a human being.
And for this reason he changed the nature of the flesh, because it was contemptible to him, so that God would not be dishonored by being in human nature.
In the same way, the conduct, sufferings, and death are not those of a human being, nor, again, are they on behalf of human beings.
And consequently, not even through the death of God—unless God was liable to death.
If he wished to forgive him, he could have released him even without his own death, rather than through the appearance of [?].
But because he was God and not mortal,
he who was not liable to death assumed into his person the mortal and changeable one,
who could fight against the debt through commandments and observances [?], so that victory might belong to his image and likeness, so that he himself
would be the one who had received death as a debt.
And to the one who gave immortality as release from debt, when he was preserved without blemishes in his image.
And just as he condemned him when he was defeated, so also, when he was victorious, he raised him to the name above all names.
And he no longer possessed it through commandments and observances, but through victory, as master, without its being taken from him.
Just as a son, when he grows and reaches maturity, has the authority to be a son,
though previously he was under authority, even though he was a son then too.
91. On this: Even if someone grants a unity through natural composition, or through confusion,
or through an intermingling of nature, the account of the incarnation is not thereby established.
For this very reason, even if someone grants that God the Word received humanity into his nature, whether through mixture,
or through confusion, or through a sharing of substance, and abolishes human nature, he presents human nature as contemptible,
and as unable to remain without sins, because it was not his nature that conquered, but that which came into being from both.
And he shows that Satan was defeated because he was powerless.
And when he condemned the human being who sinned in the beginning, he condemned someone who could not be without sins,
because he was not of the sinless nature of God the Word,
but of the nature of sinful humanity. And Satan was shown to have been arguing a legal case against a human being.
But he was indeed defeated by God, whose nature cannot be defeated by anything.
And both were temporary, in that he commanded Satan and the human being to do impossible things.
But if the things commanded could be done, and the command was not kept, then Satan was justly condemned.
For although he could have obeyed, he did not obey. Instead, he rose against God through the human being’s outward form.
He slandered God before the human being, saying that he was envious, and slandered the human being before God as ungrateful.
He is everyone’s enemy, and he received a just sentence and was publicly rebuked.
For he was condemned by Christ in his humanity, and by his holy ones, because he had openly risen against God and still stands against him.
And he showed that, if he had not been able to lead the first human being astray,
he would from that time have fought against God openly, rather than in the outward form of this one or that one.
And even if he could do nothing, in his mind he claimed sovereign power over whatever he wished to do,
like someone who could do anything, grant permission, and wage war.
And he could have destroyed him immediately, since he deserved destruction. But others would not have learned
that evil is terrifying and destroys those who belong to it, unless they had learned by every means that they had received subjection as a gift,
and through subjection [?] this gift, so that they would not act insolently against God,
and through this they too, along with others, might escape from God.
How, then, would he have made his incarnation subject to reproach through mixture or confusion,
or through a natural union, so that he would be considered neither God nor, again, a human being, but something made from both?
And it is not pure and without distinction. For this reason, then, he is with humanity,
like a judge in a trial and in a genuine contest, possessing it in his own person, while it obeys him in everything.
And he himself is not the one who fights and is brought to trial, except insofar as he brought his own image into close relationship with himself,
and not into the nature of the unconquerable and impassible essence of divinity.
For Satan had no case against God, alleging that God had made him disobey him.
Rather, his aim was to persuade God that the human being who belonged to him did not obey him.
But when God received obedience in everything, offered with a good disposition, he exalted his honor in his own image, to show that he is a just judge.
92. On this: not even if someone were to posit one nature resulting from a natural composition, or flesh without a soul, or ensouled flesh deriving from a soul.
of animals, or with a rational soul in a natural union, the account of the incarnation is established.
In the same way, neither do those who say that flesh was united to God the Word in a natural composition,
as the Arians do, and that he suffered natural sufferings,
nor, again, those who say that the union was with animal flesh, nor those who say that it was with a rational soul and flesh,
so that through natural sensation he experienced the sufferings of a body and of a soul without reason or rationality,
truly establish the account of the incarnation.
And do they not say this: that Satan was defeated through deception by the one who had been defeated,
and that he did not himself defeat him by his own power, but needed a champion—that is, God, who created him—
who fought either openly or secretly?
For although Satan was not engaged in a contest against God, he was defeated by God.
He himself won, since he was showing everyone the injustice of God's love for humanity,
and that the exaltation of humanity served to dishonor all, and to subject every principality and every authority and make them bow down,
and that, if he wanted to do this for humanity, he could have done it even without this deception and trickery.
Whatever he says, he also does. For he was not even concealing himself when he employed this form.
For someone who wants to conceal himself, since he knows that if he is exposed he will certainly be accused, himself
becomes his own accuser. And they are compelled to say the opposite of what they want to say: to accuse God,
and to give the Evil One room to breathe, falsely and with all their might; and they give reasons that run counter to the incarnation of [?].
93. On this: that things composed into one nature must either be the head or be under a head;
and especially that the soul must be the head in the composite nature, if God the Word entered into a natural composition.
For things that are composed and brought to completion as a nature
are established either as the head and governing elements, or as things under a head and governor.
If, then, because the rational soul was not capable of governing, he needed the participation of God the Word,
so that he might be the governor either of the body, or of the rational soul, or of the living being, and through him he gained his victory—
if it is right to call this a victory—that another nature, distinct from, unlike, and unequal to his fellow human beings,
is seen to act under an outward form, forcibly subjecting everyone to himself and bringing them by force under his authority as God:
that the one who had incurred guilt in it by his own choice could not [?] from sin;
nor could he keep the commandments by his own nature, but only through God the Word, who is always victorious. For it is not
something wonderful and worthy of praise that God the Word came to be in a body and kept all the observances [?] of soul and body.
For if he had not remained in his own nature above the nature of the body, or of the soul, or of the mind,
an outcry would have been required, since even a rational soul would have been capable of keeping the commandments.
But if the soul is not capable of this, and for this reason needed God the Word to become human,
so that on behalf of everyone he might endure the sufferings of body, soul, and mind,
in a natural unity that unites him to the nature, he suffers as a body, as a soul, and as a mind, in a mixture.
Yet, since he is not overcome like one of these, it is evident that he is beyond their nature.
For this reason he was not held captive by the things by which one of these was held captive—along with that other absurdity they utter:
they subject God to the necessity of nature and, like the Manichaeans, give matter such power
that it draws whoever receives it under its own authority and compulsion;
and he necessarily experiences bodily sufferings, just as God the Word himself suffered when he descended into a body,
and endured bodily sufferings in his own nature, being tormented by hunger and thirst,
by the body's natural bonds [?], since in his nature he needed these things. He experienced desire and became angry
and was afraid and suffered. He naturally experienced all the sufferings of body and soul, because he was compounded with the nature.
For whoever is compounded with a nature necessarily follows, by nature, all the properties of that nature,
whether human, divine, or some other nature with which he has been naturally united and compounded.
However anyone may wish to put it, it makes no difference to me.
But things that are compounded with a nature necessarily undergo the properties of that nature,
which belong to them naturally, not voluntarily. But for God the Word, it is voluntary, not compulsory.
For he says, “I have authority over my life to lay it down, and I have authority to take it up again.”
Therefore, in no respect apart from this can the words of the divine Scriptures apply to Christ,
except as we have examined and found: they all pertain not to a unity of nature, but to a natural and hypostatic person.
Book 1.2
On the Faith. Sophronius said: Since, then, many accept the creed of the three hundred and eighteen that was established at Nicaea,
including some who believe differently, and who understand the divine Scriptures and other writings differently,
and interpret the words “he became flesh and became human” according to different ideas,
may Your Modesty be willing to examine their ideas and opinions.
And whichever seems right to you and you judge to be sound, write it down and let me know.
Do not give those who seek a pretext to accuse you any such pretext. Nestorius.
1. Some of them say that the incarnation of our Lord Christ took place only in appearance and outward form,
so that he might appear to human beings, teach them, and give the grace of the gospel to everyone.
And just as he used to appear to individual saints, so in the last days he appeared to everyone.
2. Others, however, say that the divine substance itself became flesh,
so that in his own substance there would be the substance of flesh in place of human nature, and he might live, suffer, and set our nature free.
For someone who became human not in his own substance but only in outward form did not truly set us free,
but instead deceived us, appearing in outward form and seeming to suffer for us when he did not suffer.
3. Still others confess that God became incarnate in flesh, taking the place of a soul to complete its nature.
He became incarnate by nature in flesh so that he could act and suffer, and he naturally endured all the body's natural sufferings.
Although in his nature he is incapable of suffering, through his natural incarnation he is capable of suffering.
It is like the soul, which in its own nature does not undergo the body's sufferings, feel pain, or hunger,
but in its natural way of life naturally undergoes the body's sufferings,
being naturally united with it, so that he might live and suffer for us by nature.
And it was not in appearance and outward form, or in another nature, but in his own nature that he freed us from death and corruption.
4. Others, however, confess that he became incarnate in a body and soul to complete the nature, and that God the Word took the place of the mind,
so that he might serve as the mind for the nature consisting of body and soul, and live and suffer for us in human nature.
For he came to abolish the mind that had transgressed the commandment and disobeyed God,
and to take the place of the mind in the soul and body—not in an outward form without actual existence, nor in another nature, nor, again, in a body without a soul.
5. Others, however, say of the flesh in which God the Word became incarnate: he became incarnate in flesh endowed with a soul, though by its nature it had no sensation.
And he did not understand by means of the soul, but understood and perceived through the activity of God the Word.
In God the Word, the soul perceived and also understood.
And the body was an instrument by nature.
And they do not divide Christ into an instrument and a craftsman, since the instrument and the craftsman act together.
6. Others, however, confess two natures in Christ before the union, and that each of the natures is conceived of in its own nature.
God the Word in the Father and the Holy Spirit, and in human beings in the flesh.
After the union, however, two natures are not conceived of, because they have been united in substance, and one results from the two.
They change them from one nature into another, so that he might be human as Lord, while the very same one is also God [?].
So that God might live as a human being, die for us as God, and rise by his own power.
7. Others, however, describe our Lord’s becoming human as flesh animated by a rational and intelligent soul,
complete in its nature, its power, and its natural activities, and not merely in outward appearance,
nor through a change of substances, nor, again, for the natural completion of the nature of the body and the soul or the mind,
or [?] into one nature from the two, or that they were changed from one into the other, or
for the completion of the natural activities, so that the flesh would not act according to its own nature,
but into one person of both natures, while both preserve the properties of their natures.
And the substance of the divinity remains and does not suffer, while it is in the substance of the flesh.
And the flesh, in turn, remains in the substance of flesh, while it is in the nature and person of the divinity; for the body is one.
And both are one Son. For God the Word in the flesh is not said to be someone other than the one who is in our flesh.
Nor, again, does the flesh exist except in the Son, in God the Word.
So that he might live fully in human nature, being a human being,
and rise as God, being God by nature.
He who was without sin, and what he preserved [?], would be handed over to death for our salvation [?].
He preserved the likeness of his own image, so that henceforth he might be that.
It was not for the likeness that he received the name that is higher than every name, so that human nature might be exalted.
For a substance that is no longer that of a human being but of God the Word is not given honor and exaltation.
Our nature was honored in another nature, not in our own nature.
For the exaltation of our nature to that name which surpasses all names
was, in general, an exaltation of the nature as it is—of one who remains in his own substance and can become what
he is in the substance of God the Word. For this is exaltation in the fullest sense, with nothing else like it.
For the transformation of one substance into another is the destruction of the substance that ought to be exalted, and also of exaltation itself.
