Nor is it a descent on the part of God the Word if he is transformed into the substance of flesh.
For it is not the nature that descends; rather, this is what descended.
It is like a king: if he becomes one of his subjects, he is said to have descended while truly remaining king.
And because of the subjects’ clothing that he put on, he is said to have descended in condescension [?], while he [?] his own things through those of that person in outward appearance.
Just as those people are under a law governing their conduct,
so he too willingly comes under the law, while remaining the king and lord of their conduct.
For neither is it exaltation when he is exalted to his own nature.
Rather, it is to give him what he did not have, not to take away from him what he had.
For if exaltation and humiliation belong to the one who existed and was there before,
and humiliation belongs to the nature that he was and already is,
to whom does exaltation belong? First name the substance that was exalted, and then the name in which it was exalted,
which is above all names.
For if you remove the substances capable of humiliation and exaltation, there is no substance that was humbled.
Therefore, apply “he humbled himself” to the voluntary union, to becoming human, and to the manner of humility that he displayed:
that he took the form of a servant. And again, what happened belonged to what was voluntary, not to what was natural.
He was found in outward appearance as a human being, not in substance. For in the form of God, the form of a servant.
The form of God was like a human being in outward appearance, for he was God in his own substance.
Thus humiliation too is to be understood with reference to the one who took the form of a servant,
and exaltation with reference to the form of a servant, in that it received the name that surpasses all names.
And you should not understand this as a transformation of substance, or into a substance, or as a natural composition resulting in one nature.
But the voluntary one, the one involving humiliation and exaltation.
For the natural one is subject to suffering and change.
For the nature is created and made, not uncreated or unmade,
nor is it unchangeable or incapable of alteration.
For this reason, in the incarnation this man attributed nothing to human conduct,
but rather to God the Word, so that he might use human nature for his own conduct,
as with Arius, Eunomius, and Apollinaris.
That is, they call Christ God in name [?], but in practice they deprive him of being God,
by attributing his human characteristics to his essence by nature.
They also invalidate Christ’s genealogy and the promises to the fathers that Christ would arise from their offspring according to the flesh.
For this reason the evangelists mention everything that truly demonstrates human nature,
so that his divinity might not prevent belief that he is also human,
and so that, along with this, belief that he is the one confirmed by the promises [?] might not also be lost.
For this reason he mentioned the blessed Mary as a woman who was betrothed to a man,
whose name, family, occupation, and place he also recorded,
so that there would be nothing to cause doubt or prevent belief that she was a woman.
For this reason he also mentioned his lowliness and, along with everything else, the announcement of his conception, his birth, and the manger,
to identify the one who was born together with the woman who bore him, so that it might be established that he is truly human;
his lying in the manger, his being wrapped in swaddling clothes,
among the things that are natural to infants; the offerings presented on his behalf;
his development, his growth in stature and wisdom before God and before people;
his way of life in the world, his observances, his obedience, the petitions he offered;
his complete fulfillment of the law; his baptism; and the voice that declared to him that he was
the Son—he who was the Son in union from the womb; the testimony to his observance of proper conduct; the Father’s voice;
the manifestation of the Holy Spirit; and the Spirit’s guidance on our behalf, exercised with all diligence.
Not in the semblance or outward form of a human being, but in human nature.
From a human body and a rational soul, which thinks and reasons according to human nature.
So that he might be everything that belongs to human nature, without this being abolished by union with God the Word.
For the union of the natures did not result in a single nature, or in confusion, or in alteration, or in a change of substance:
Either of divinity into humanity, or of humanity into divinity, or in a blending of the natures, or in the composition of a single nature,
With them being blended and suffering together with one another through the natural activities of the natures that constitute them.
For they abolish all these things through a natural and hypostatic union.
They take all these things that belong to him in his nature and attribute them to God the Word as belonging to him by nature:
Human fear, being handed over, being questioned, answering, being struck on the cheeks,
The sentence of crucifixion, his going away, the placing of the cross on his shoulder, his carrying his cross,
Its being taken from him to be placed on others, the crown of thorns, the scarlet garments,
The false testimony [?], the crucifixion, the driving in of the nails, the gall that was offered to him, the other afflictions,
The committing [?] of his spirit to the Father, the bowing of his head, the taking down of his body from the cross, his embalming,
His burial, the resurrection after three days, his appearing in his body, his speaking and his teaching,
So that they would not suppose that his body was an apparition, but that it truly was a body, possessing flesh as well.
For he did not possess a body and soul merely in appearance and deception, but everything was real in [?]; he concealed nothing.
All these human things that they are now ashamed to say about him—the evangelists were not ashamed to say them.
These are the things that they shamelessly make properties of the divine nature,
Through union in a natural hypostasis, with God suffering the sufferings of the body, being naturally united in nature:
Being thirsty, being hungry, being in need, being anxious, thinking, desiring.
So that he might also overcome these human experiences that he undergoes by nature,
And wage war against human nature, abolishing our glory and abolishing our salvation.
And they abolish the distinctive properties of God the Word and make them human,
So that he acts and suffers naturally in his nature, with the sensation belonging to that nature,
Naturally receiving sufferings in his own substance, as the body does from the soul and the soul from the body.
It is a matter of terror and trembling to contemplate this, or even to speak of it to human beings:
those who hold an opinion of whatever kind about the Son, whether he is made or created,
and that he changed from being incapable of suffering to being capable of suffering, from immortal to mortal, and from unchangeable to changeable.
Even if someone makes him of the substance of angels and incapable of suffering, and says
that he acted not by his own nature, activity, and power, but through what he became, he escapes suffering together with this one.
But escape is not possible for one who is united by nature. For if he did not suffer the sufferings of the body by nature,
he suffered as a soul, in place of a soul, because he was there in place of a soul,
which did not think as a mind does; and he was there for it as a thinking being, in place of a mind.
He existed in outward appearance and deceived through the appearance of a human being,
as though he possessed the properties of soul, body, and mind, while these were inactive in their own nature.
But these things are said by those who are supposedly orthodox:
that he is of the Father's own nature, incapable of suffering, without need, unchangeable, and unalterable.
And then, just as the Jews mocked him by calling him the Messiah while crucifying him—
so these people too assign him, in words, a nature that is unchangeable, incapable of suffering, and without need,
yet subject him to every suffering and every bodily need, and make all the properties of soul and mind belong to God the Word
through a hypostatic union, acting like those who change him from his own nature.

Whichever way one wishes to approach it, in any case one arrives at the praise of the orthodox, not at the blasphemy of the heretics.
Therefore, all the things he wished to say against the hypostatic union he wrote openly in his chapters.

But on the basis of unity in nature, I speak of one person, one equality,

In short, in all those things in which the person of this one and of that one exists by nature,

It is in nature, but it is not a nature. For the Son of God the Father is by nature of the same nature as the Father.
Whatever the Father is in his nature, the Son is also.
For what the Son is as a person in nature, the Father is not also.
For he who is Son by nature is not Father, nor is the Father Son.
For he is of the Father's nature and is Son by nature. For they are one and another in person,

Candidianus also went with them, giving them advance warning and solemnly testifying to them
about the things that were newly being done. Testimony of the bishops who did not join Cyril.
The faith of true religion is indeed known, first from the proclamation of the holy and revered Scriptures,
and from the assembly at Nicaea of our holy fathers, who bore on their limbs scars of suffering corresponding to their number.
But because there was inquiry and controversy over various matters, the faithful, Christ-fearing emperor
summoned the orthodox clergy from everywhere to Ephesus by his letters:
While, as is his custom, he was also diligently pursuing this concern for the truth, we all assembled by the grace of God.
But John, the God-loving bishop of Antioch, was absent from our holy assembly.
His arrival, too, is imminent, as his letters recently written to us,
and those of the imperial agents and prefectural officials whom we sent to him,
have informed us; other God-loving bishops from the West are also expected.
Your Reverence has informed us, however, that your continued stay here is becoming wearisome to you,
and that you are eager for the matter desired by the emperor to be examined,
even before the arrival of the God-loving bishops whom we have mentioned.
For this reason we have sent this letter to Your Reverence, asking you to wait for the arrival of the distinguished bishops who are our fellow ministers,
and not to receive, as though it were permissible, people whose deposition has been carried out,
nor those who are, or come to be, under suspension by their bishops.
For it is known what the holy canons prescribe concerning these matters; and those who transgress them
are subjected to no small penalty, one that cannot be set aside by a holy council by any means.
Your Reverence should also know this: everything insolently done by insolent people
will be held against your insolence by Christ, the Lord of all, and by the holy canons.
Nestorius: Read also the warning issued by the illustrious Candidianus, count of the household troops,
so that from this too you may learn of the violence they committed openly and shamelessly.
And that he is no longer merely misleading [?], but after the testimony of the bishops who adopted that pretext for delay [?],
since the bishop of Antioch was close at hand, about to arrive with his Eastern bishops,
as the imperial agents sent to their prefectures had learned from John's own letters—they were saying these things.
When those people heard this, they raised an uproar as though by a single agreement, shouting, reviling, and insulting,
so as to drive out the bishops sent to them and knock them down,
so that even the blows they were inflicting on them could be heard by Count Candidianus.
After they had driven those men out so decorously, they turned against him to hunt him down,
while holding by the hands those who were unable to stand because of hunger and illness.
They did not listen to what he was saying to them, nor to the emperor’s letters sent to them all.
He instructed them that the council was not to be held with only part of its membership,
but that the council’s decisions were to be made collectively by a vote.
But, like a wise man among madmen, he was thought to be raving mad when he said these things, because they did not want to hear them.
He had ordered this imperial command to be read before them,
although it should not have been read before all the bishops had assembled [?].
While doing this, he paid no attention to anything in the letter, which read as follows:
“We have ordered the illustrious Count Candidian to come to your holy council,
without taking any part in the matters you are to investigate.
For we have determined [?] that it is not right for someone who is not counted among the assembly of bishops
to become involved in examining ecclesiastical regulations or investigating the faith.”
For he did not say that he was not to participate in the assembly, but in the investigation of the faith.
He had therefore been instructed not to permit a council to be held with only part of its membership before all its bishops had assembled.
Therefore, because he had been compelled to read this—which should not have been read before the arrival of the bishops [?]—the man who came from
this side was driven out by them amid loud shouting, whistles, and threats:
he would be handed over to death if he participated in the deliberations within the council.
From then on, acting on their own authority, they called themselves a general council.
That is to say, those present were so numerous!
Those who had not joined them in the investigation protested to them, saying:
“We ought to wait for those whose arrival is imminent”—that is, for the head of the council himself.
To keep the count, who had been charged with maintaining order among them, from joining them, they said:
“He is not to take part in examining the faith or investigating ecclesiastical matters.”
But they did everything on their own authority and would not obey the imperial command, which had clearly informed them
that he had been sent for this purpose: to prevent the disturbances and divisions that were occurring.
Hear also the emperor’s letters sent through Candidian. From the imperial decree.
For we had already written what was appropriate concerning the gathering of your reverence for God in the city of Ephesus.
But since it was also necessary to take care that the deliberations of your assembly should be orderly,
concerning the inquiry for which you are assembling,
we did not neglect this either, but instructed you in every respect to remain free from disturbance.
We are convinced that your reverence for God needs no outside assistance to strive for peace.
Nevertheless, it was our responsibility not to neglect care for the investigation of the truth.
That is why we are sending Count Candidian to your council,
without his taking any part in the matters into which you are conducting your inquiry.
For we have judged that it is not proper for someone who is not counted among the assembly of bishops
to become involved in the investigation of ecclesiastical matters and the examination of the faith.
He is to expel from the city the laypeople and monks who have gathered there for this purpose and are present with you.
For it is not proper for such people to be present at your assembly, lest they stir up disorder
and thereby obstruct what you are duly examining and properly carrying out.
He is to take care that no one causes division through contention,
so that your inquiry and the establishment of sound judgment among you are not delayed for this reason.
Everyone is to listen patiently to what is said, whether he is ready to respond or is receiving a response.
In this way, through questions, answers, and explanations, the inquiry concerning the true faith is to be adjudicated without any contention,
and through the joint examination of your holiness it is to reach a good conclusion without contention.
Nestorius: They did not permit these things to be read, nor were they willing to listen to the one who told them to take care
that no one should cause any division through contention,
so that the inquiry concerning the true faith and sound judgment among you should not be delayed for this reason.
Everyone is to listen patiently to what is said, whether he is ready to respond or someone is to respond to him.
In this way, through questions, answers, and explanations, the inquiry concerning the true faith is to be adjudicated without any contention.
And through the joint examination [?] of your holiness, it is to reach a good conclusion without contention.
Because they knew these things, they would not allow them to be read.
For they were concealing that utterance which, as though through divine prophecy,
clearly disclosed the things they were doing.
Or perhaps the emperor inferred from the purpose of what he had done what he was going to do,
and set these things down beforehand in his writings. For even small signs are sufficient
to give a slight indication of the soul’s dispositions, even if such things had not yet come from him.
Even when the things by which it could be known had not yet come to light.
But God revealed everything that was his, so that these things might serve them as judges of the things
that were going to happen, so that they would not be thought to have done this out of ignorance,
and, without knowing the method of inquiry and investigation,
to have recklessly uttered the falsehoods among the things that were said.
Does genuine inquiry begin with division and a cause for contention, for those who genuinely seek,
or with fairness and patience in what is said to those who listen? And with merely setting out all the matters under inquiry,
or with considering them in relation to one another and examining them through questions and answers,
until the inquiry being examined is free from contention? In haste or without haste,
so that, when we receive a question, we give the explanation and answer appropriate to it?
Which of these things was not truly said? But this command did not please you,
because you wanted to win, not to find the truth.
But what am I to do now? Shall I accuse Candidianus of failing to observe the imperial letters,
and of causing such disorder among the bishops against their fellow bishops,
and even against himself, who had been charged with protecting them and maintaining order among them?
But he was trying to persuade with words those who would not submit to listening to words,
who needed him to direct them even against their will, in accordance with the imperial command,
which everyone acknowledged to be just. And otherwise it was not fitting for there to be anything beyond
his establishing his statements, speaking and receiving replies through question and answer.
But they considered whatever served deception to be suited to the occasion. I have nothing more to say.
For he had warned them in his instructions not to do anything before they had all assembled, in accordance with the imperial command.
But they were unwilling to obey even the emperor’s command. Hear, then, his warning as well.
Warning issued by the illustrious Count Candidian, forbidding them to assemble before all the bishops had gathered.
To the holy Cyril, bishop and metropolitan of Alexandria, and to the bishops assembled with him:
Flavius Candidian, the great and illustrious count of the most devoted household guards.
Ever since I arrived in the city of Ephesus, I have asked nothing else of the holy council
except that matters concerning the orthodox faith should be settled in peace and harmony, as the faithful and victorious emperor also commanded.
Your Piety knows—and the testimony of the truth is sufficient for me—that I have been concerned with nothing else more than this.
But when I learned that you intended to assemble in the holy church against the wishes of the other bishops,
while John, bishop of Antioch, had not yet arrived, nor
the bishops with him, from the day before the one on which you were preparing to do this, I did not cease
urging and warning each one of you not to consider holding a council in separate groups.
And again, on the following day, when you had assembled in that holy church,
I did not neglect to come to you with diligence and warn you of what the faithful emperor desired,
although this was unnecessary, since you already knew it from the letters written to you by his authority.
Nevertheless, even though this was so, I explained to you the will of our God-fearing emperor, saying:
His will is that your faith should be defined in harmony, without doubt or disturbance from anyone,
and that he does not wish the council to be held in separate groups,
since this turns our orthodox faith into contention and division.
And again, when Your Modesty asked us that the imperial letter of the faithful and God-loving emperor,
which had been sent to the holy council, should be read, I initially found it difficult to do this.
I do not hesitate to say that this was because there had not yet arrived and assembled
those who had been ordered to attend the holy council. But when Your Piety said
that you were unaware of what the emperor desired and had ordered to be done, it seemed
to me necessary, even without all the bishops being present,
I will present to you his revered and praiseworthy letter.
Furthermore, after the will of his lordship was made known to you, I did not neglect to appeal to you on this same matter,
asking your excellencies and solemnly charging you not to introduce anything new
before all the holy bishops assemble for the council.
Instead, you should wait just four days for the holy John, bishop of Antioch, the metropolis, and those with him,
and also for those who are with the holy and God-fearing Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople.
Thus, when you are together and the entire holy council has assembled in one place,
if there is any matter requiring investigation, or any other matter of dispute,
or one that lies beyond our competence, let it be examined when you are assembled together.
Then, with the agreement of you all, let it become known who is found to hold beliefs improperly and contrary to the canons,
whether you all confess rightly, and whether you revere the faith of our holy fathers.
These things, then, I not only advised but also urged.
But because you observed none of what was said, and I was even driven away by you,
I considered it necessary to notify you through this testimony and solemnly charge you through this decree
not to introduce anything new, but to wait for the arrival of all our holy fathers, the bishops.
Then, when you share a common purpose, let the affairs of the holy catholic Church be judged.
If anyone, acting on the impulse of his own authority,
wishes to change anything that has been decided by the pure and unfailing sovereign authority,
let him know that he has only himself to blame and cannot hold anyone else responsible.
It is no trouble for me to repeat these same things, since your holiness is convinced and knows
that this is what our God-fearing emperor desires:
that, in the presence of all the holy bishops summoned by his authority,
every dispute should be resolved and the true faith revealed.
For this reason, I have also placed above this formal protest the imperial letter sent to your holy council,
as well as the letters written to me by his lordship.
So that, by learning his will through all these things, you may cease doing what you are so eager to do.
Know also that a copy of this document has likewise been sent to our lord, the God-fearing emperor.
Nestorius. When these things had been presented and read before them:
Was their frenzied onslaught human [?]? Or were they ashamed of anything?
Or did they fear the accusations and testimonies? Or did they show any regard for the authorities over them and for the emperor himself,
and for those who were to judge them according to the divine laws and the decrees of the fathers? Rather, they despised them all.
For they had people who kept them informed from the imperial court.
And all these things directed against me seemed to them like some kind of amusement.
And, as I suppose, Candidianus knew these things and was afraid of them.
He restrained them only with words, but in practice he did not dare to act or to trouble those who were doing these things.
On what did you rely in doing these things, which not even barbarians have ever dared to do? Let us suppose that you were not my enemy, nor even a cutthroat.
Yet you were a judge, as you had made yourself, like the rest of the others; indeed, I say, even more so.
The time for judgment also drew near, when they ought to have been tried.
But those who were to judge with you had not come, and you
were compelled to summon them. You wanted to make everyone who was present agree with you.
But I, who wanted a trial, testified to everyone that, as a judicial proceeding, there was no
validity whatsoever to your trial, since you were not judging as you had been summoned to do.
But if it was difficult for you, you had the authority to go and do this:
to state that, because of your own circumstances, you could not judge. It was not that I did not come, but that I could not go.
You ought to have informed the one who held authority about this, and the appointment of the judge would have been decided by him.
For no one believed that you were appointing yourself to act as judge.
And this is how these things happened. Or did God not compel you to write them,
as you breathed out [?] and accused the spirit of Candidianus, John, and Irenaeus,
a man who lived in God, serving him with his possessions, his soul, and his body?
And because what he had done did not please him, they set about accusing him:
As you learn from them of their barbaric, brutish, and wicked insolence.
For when those who had defied the regulation that Candidian had laid down for them, together with those who had acted alongside them, went up to the emperor,
he openly gave them all a reply, one
that you ought to hear, so that from it you may all learn together
how God condemned them all in my favor, out of their own mouths, in the very court.
From the imperial letter sent through Palladius, the imperial agent.
Our Majesty has learned from what the illustrious Candidian, count of the most devoted imperial bodyguard, wrote to us
that what took place in the metropolis of Ephesus occurred amid disorder and contrary to proper procedure,
when not all the God-fearing bishops whom I had summoned to assemble had yet assembled,
and when the arrival of the holy John, bishop of Antioch, together with the other metropolitan bishops, was very near.
Furthermore, even those who were present had not joined together with them or reached agreement with one another. Furthermore,
the investigation of the faith had not been conducted as it ought to have been, or in accordance with the letters repeatedly sent by us.
Rather, the hostility of some toward others is well known, and because of this they were eager to act according to their own opinion,
although they were unable even to conceal their conduct
or to give anyone the impression that they had acted thoughtfully in what they did. For this reason it seemed right
to our Majesty that no one should have any opportunity for insolence, and that everything they had done contrary to proper procedure should be annulled.
Matters concerning the faith are to be examined first, as we have decided and as the council as a whole had also agreed and approved.
These provisions are to be observed from now on, since our Majesty does not accept what was rashly done by prematurely taking the initiative.
These are the emperor’s words. Now hear also the report that these men sent to the emperor,
in which they accused Candidian of having misrepresented them out of friendship for me
and of not having informed the emperor of the truth, while they defended what they had done against me.
For from these things you will recognize their obtuseness and their childishness all the more:
they were speaking as though to a child and treating with contempt the pronouncement [?] that came from him.
For they were being reproached: “Why did you hold a council with only part of its membership before the whole council had assembled?
By this you show that you did everything not out of the fear of God, but out of human hostility.”
And you did not wait with a clear conscience for the whole council to assemble.
They gave him no answer at all concerning these matters, but acknowledged the charge brought against them.
From Cyril’s report sent to the emperor, in response to the report sent by Candidianus.
By these things we show that we stirred up no hostility at all against Nestorius, but set forth the teaching of reverence for God.
When we compared this with the teaching of Nestorius, it became clear which one deserved condemnation.
And from the letters written by Nestorius and from the sermons delivered by him,
we openly pronounced judgment, with the holy Gospel placed in our midst, showing that Christ, the Lord of all, was present.
Nestorius. Like people accused of breaking their oaths,
they sought to persuade others by swearing, “We have not broken our oaths,” rather than basing their defense on the actual deeds.
For they were accused: “Why did you transgress the common rule and not wait for the whole council,
just as you had all been summoned together?” They gave no answer at all to this.
And why did the bishops who were nearby not consult together about this with their fellow bishops
who were with them, as to whether it was right for you all to wait? They gave no answer to this either.
“Why did you not do this with everyone’s agreement,
but instead separate and split the one council away from the bishops who were nearby and those who were still to come,
so that the judgment concerning the faith might be settled through an examination conducted with them?” They gave no answer to this either.
Instead, with undiscerning haste and with the agreement of those who pleased them,
because they did not wish to be fellow judges with them, they treated them as strangers to the faith.
For you did not abandon your insolence, which you had practiced from the beginning;
and because of it you drew even the bishop of Rome into rebellion and nullified an ecumenical council.
In response to all these things, they remained mute and without a sound.
“Why did you not obey the instruction that, before all the bishops had assembled,
you were not to hold a council with only part of them? Why, when the count who had been sent was restraining you
and urging you to wait for the bishops who were nearby and not far away,
did you not wait for them?” They gave no answer to a single one of these things.
If Christ had been sitting there, and you were convinced that he was sitting with you, would you have done these things?
And would you have made Christ a partner in your wickedness, since you treated him this way,
trampling on him as though he were someone unable to rebuke you—him who exposed you so openly?
For how did you suppose that your wicked, hidden intention would come to light?
You had already testified to the bishops about your wickedness, and also to the count who had been put in charge of you,
concerning the matters that he truthfully submitted in an official report to inform the emperor. And for all those who wish to learn about your conduct,
whether through imperial letters or through their reports,
all these things will be confirmed as unquestionably true: that you did not share the views of those who were nearby,
and that you separated yourselves from the bishops who were far away and from those who were nearby,
since you were unwilling to remain even fourteen days at most.
And I was sitting there, saying or doing nothing.
And Christ was sitting in your midst, the one who compelled all of you to say and do these things against me.
“We did not stir up any hostility at all against Nestorius,” they say. Yet while I was absent,
my enemy judged my words and compared them with whatever he wanted, and in whatever way he wanted.
And I was to accept their claim that they harbored no hostility at all against me. Who dares to say
these things when he sees all these wicked deeds and insolent acts through which they wronged me? Should they not
rather be regarded as mockery? For you say these things to the one who was rebuking you for
acting with hostility toward me. Instead, you are like people who beat someone and shame him [?],
and say, “We are only joking,” to the person who reproaches them for their mockery, saying, “It is not out of hostility,
but out of friendship that we are doing this,” while they send him away naked and wounded.
He did the same to me too, while they were being accused and making accusations. But the judge of all does not engage in this mockery.
For even though I have had no human court in all these matters, I have the court of Christ.
“But,” they say, “we ask your authority that no one should be considered worthy of acceptance
from among those who value love for a human being above the fear of God.
For we have perceived that such an intention belongs to the chaste John, bishop of Antioch,”
who wishes to show greater affection, or to have something beneficial to the faith considered.
And for this reason, he neither feared the threat from your authority nor was moved by zeal for the faith handed down to us from above.
Instead, he kept the holy council waiting twenty-one days after
the time limit granted us by your authority. And we were compelled by the orthodox members of the holy council,
we who love the faith alone, to seek the things that belong to the fear of God.
Nestorius: Did they not plainly, without any concealment, make their intention known to him:
that it was not because they were worn out and afflicted by illness, death, and danger to their lives that he did not come to trial,
but because they feared a trial before everyone, and held the trial ahead of everyone else,
before the bishop of Antioch arrived? For what benefit would a delay of twenty days have brought me?
Or what advantage would it have brought you? For what was to be done after thirty days
could equally have been done before all those days or after them all.
For if he had shown greater friendship toward me, he would have made haste to arrive early and reach me,
and he would have persuaded the many who had turned against me. He would not have allowed you to do what you did,
because you would have been restrained by him. But if, so that there should be no examination,
you were employing every means to thwart the trial—let that be so.
Then you ought all the more to have waited for him, so that there would be an examination, and not have given me a pretext for escape.
But not one of these things is true. Nevertheless, let it be so, and let me concede
to you that you waited for a trial to take place. Why did you not act according to the emperor’s command? For you would have shown
that you had not acted for this reason. But you did not wait. Thus, in every respect, your oppressive conduct is exposed from the beginning:
that he was doing this because he was afraid of coming to examination and trial,
and that he was distressed about this and was scheming to prepare all these things.
If, then, you were confident in what you had written,
and had those who testified in your support, namely, the Fathers and the Holy Scriptures,
you would have accused me of doing what I did for this reason, out of hostility and not in truth.
And you would have reproached me: “You have disturbed the world over nothing by raising the question of heretics and the orthodox.”
You ought to have written to the emperor about these things, and about all the others.
If you claim that this was why you did what you did,
as though I were fleeing from a trial because I had no confidence in what I had written.
Rather, it was those who acted out of hostility and not in truth who fled from a trial.
They fabricated a story, saying that there had been a trial and an examination, although neither of these had taken place.
Let him come and stand trial. Let him give an account of the things of which he is accused,
and receive an account of the things of which he accuses others. Let both sides be tried without delay.
Yes, before the Trinity, for whose sake I made every effort.
For why do others stumble over the things in which I have confidence? These things have humbled your power.
You knew that they were true and could persuade, but you did not speak and did not have confidence.
Nor, while fabricating your story, did you say in that fearsome and terrifying voice of yours,
“Let there be a trial, and let an account be given and answered through questions and replies.”
For your voice was restrained by your conscience. But what did you say? “We implore and petition your authority:
so that the council's concern, which springs from zeal for God, may be known, let a summons be sent to the most magnificent Candidianus,
and to five members of the holy council, so that they may establish what took place before your God-fearing Majesty.
For those who hold views contrary to the orthodox faith are cunning
in concealing their erroneous thinking. Thus even some of the holy bishops,
while Nestorius concealed his error, were persuaded to join him and put their signatures to it.
But when they investigated carefully and discovered that his blasphemy was manifest, they withdrew from him and joined the holy council.”
Nestorius. Did he really flee from the council? Look, you plainly need the emperor to send for five of
the bishops to establish what took place! But you said, “With Candidianus,”
and not with their fellow bishops, who would have reproved you as equals.
And five against one—and that one is a layman! Let them bring out the holy Gospel and swear by it,
because they are five, and they are bishops, so that they may be accepted as truthful against a single layman.
For you have been very concerned about the examination of this matter.
For what more or less did Candidianus have to say when he came,
except what you yourselves had already testified and he had reported to the emperor? Or what more did those five have
than what you wrote [?] about him: that he had shown him friendship,
and that for this reason he had brought false accusations against you? But what need is there to speak of your reckoning? Was this why you wrote against Candidianus and the five bishops,
and did not ask either Nestorius or Cyril to come? These were the cause of the disturbance,
and they ought to have answered one another. But you lacked confidence, because there was no substance of truth in your statement.
For you feared nothing else in my words more than the truth.
For suppose that Candidianus had come and said that you had not waited for the whole council, although you knew
that they were nearby, and that he had warned you beforehand and had read documents from the emperor before you,
and that he had appealed to you, but you had not been persuaded.
Would he have said anything else? What, then, would you have accused him of? Would you have accused him of this:
that he had spoken falsely against you because he showed friendship toward me? That was not the case; you did not act that way.
But if you did act that way, let them come, and let there be a trial, even if Candidianus had lied.
But in your memoranda you gave this reason for not waiting for the whole council to meet for debate:
“We were under pressure,” as though you alone had been there.
But in the report you sent to the emperor, you said, “We became aware of this intention of the chaste John, bishop of Antioch:
that he wished to show excessive friendship,” and for this reason you were compelled not to wait.
As though, if you had known that he would agree with you, you would have waited for him, and the place would have caused you no distress!
And in the memoranda you drew up against me, you said that I persisted in these very things:
the things I had written and said from the beginning. And I am also writing openly to you.
But in that report you wrote to the emperor, you wrote the opposite, like someone trying to conceal the wickedness he possesses.
For, it is said, those who hold views other than
the orthodox faith are skilled at concealing their thinking.
Thus even some of the holy bishops, while Nestorius concealed his error,
might be led astray and join him, and lend a hand in the things he was doing.
How, then, do they conceal these things of mine? And again you said openly, “Nestorius was questioned.”
“When,” you say, “we clearly found that he held different views, we deposed him.”
“For even in the metropolis of Ephesus itself he did not hide his thinking, so that we would need other accusers.”
“Instead, he cried out every day, proclaiming before many people his teaching, which was foreign to the faith.”
“We included each of these things in the records we drew up of what happened, step by step,”
“so that they might be made known to your reverence.” Nestorius: In this very statement they contradict themselves.
The one who received these records, namely the emperor, knew what they had done contrary to his command.
But even what they say is contradictory—a crude and shameful account.
For they did not give him an answer concerning the very thing for which he reproached them:
“Why,” he said, “before the bishops of the whole council had assembled,”
“did you dare, contrary to your instructions, to hold a council consisting of only part of them?” Nothing else
do they say except, “Because it pleased us,” although they do not say this openly, because of how offensive such a statement is to those who encounter it.
“Why did you not wait for the arrival of John, bishop of Antioch, when you knew that his arrival was near?”
They had nothing else to say except, “We did not want to conduct investigations with him,”
especially since they knew that he would not agree with them. But suppose that John ought to have been put on trial
because he had taken a bribe and had not arrived on time. He was not to be tried by you, but by the emperor, who had authority over him.
And first this charge ought to have been brought against the bishops from Rome, who did not come when they were summoned.
How, then, do you hold on to those men? For in the same category in which you placed them,
place John as well, with regard to doing what is possible and what is impossible.
Yet you call John to account, although he has a reason for his delay, and everyone accepts it from him,
except you yourself, who are far removed from all love for humanity and from all the feelings of human nature.
You do not blame yourself, not even when you are reproached by the emperor.
Nor do you deny that, although it was very necessary for you to wait four days for them,
so that the council might be free of contention, you would not listen. Instead, you preferred to create turmoil. Just as the kind
of fish called cuttlefish go from clear water into muddy water so that they will not be caught, so you too have acted.
Those who have any sense at all consider these things laughable, and they are certainly not mistaken when they call you to account on these grounds.
Just as grown men, when playing with little children who wrestle with them,
appear to be really wrestling, and pretend, that is, to be defeated by them.
For these words belong not to someone breathing his last, but rather to someone who is merely playing.
The emperor is not merely playing with you; nor, when he reproves you justly, do you satisfy him concerning the things for which he reproves you.
His power was weak, because he was made of gold. But they say: “Those who assembled,” they say,
“and unanimously issued, in accordance with the canons, a sentence of deposition against the heretic Nestorius—

How the position of the heretics was confirmed as though through a judicial hearing and examination by a council.

Let us therefore examine in sequence how they conducted the proceedings against me.
From the records of the proceedings conducted against me at Ephesus.

As he was being choked by the truth itself, he could not conceal his thinking in these statements,

And just as a dog, when forcibly restrained, hides its bad habits,

Statement of Acacius, bishop of Melitene.
As soon as I arrived in the city of Ephesus, I held a discussion with the man mentioned above.
When I realized that his thinking was not sound, I made every effort to correct him and turn him away from his opinion.
I saw that it was only with his lips that he promised to turn away from such a way of thinking.
But when I had stayed ten or twelve days, and some matter again came up for discussion between us,
I began to speak in defense of the true faith, and I saw that he was opposed to it.
I realized that he had fallen into both evils at once.
For, first of all, his improper question forced those who answered
either to deny altogether that the divinity of the Only Begotten had become human, or to admit the impious claim

that the divinity of the Father and of the Holy Spirit had also become embodied along with the Word.
Nestorius.
They themselves asked, and they themselves answered that they were involved in abominations and impiety. They acknowledge and agree with the statement
with which I rebuked them. And by what they admitted, they were condemned as impious.
Does anyone really suppose that it is an injustice for them to record these things in the minutes
and make them all testify against themselves? For let us grant that my question was perverse:
you ought not to have accepted it, but to have exposed the perversity of the question,
so that, by correcting the question, you would not fall into a path of impiety and perversity.
Instead, you accepted a perverse question in the fear of God! Then, through this, you arrived at the impiety
of admitting that either God the Word, the Son of God, did not become human, or that the Father and the Spirit also became human.
Therefore, you ought to have rejected what you agreed to when you were questioned, even if you did not correct it as that other man did.
Let us grant that you did not fall into this disgrace, whether willingly or unwillingly.
Why do you not state that shameful question by which you wanted to condemn me? But—
neither do you state it, nor do the judges pursue it any further.
And if it was so shameful, how was it left without rebuke,
so that it received no rebuke from your entire synod? And if you all left it without rebuke,

Examine it, even if you are judges only in appearance, and write down the question formally for those

But because of your incompetence you stood in darkness, so that you could not even see what was obvious.
Yet God helped you all the more in your questioning, so that you would write these things down,

But from what things, then, were they shown to be so? From those things that they set down in deceitful documents at the trial without condemnation.

The Faith Established by Our Fathers at Nicaea.
We believe in God the Father Almighty, maker of all things visible and invisible,
and in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God, begotten from the Father,

But he passed over such things from the outset and did not wish to begin with them.
Or I, who upheld what the fathers rightly declared [?], and said that we should begin here.
For I also saw the reason why they first set down the names common to divinity and humanity,

first setting down the names of both natures, which indicate these common things,
so that sonship and lordship would not be divided,

But he was explaining the opposite, while I was telling him that this was the starting point,

But he disputed with me, teaching everyone in his wisdom, lest, without knowing it, they should fall short of that wickedness.
Why, then, when you set down the creed, did you yourself not also begin there,

We were investigating how these properties of the flesh and the rational soul, and the properties of God the Word,
ought to be understood and spoken of in terms of nature: whether both belong to God the Word by nature,

But I was saying and affirming that the unity is that of the one person of Christ.

because you want God the Word to be the person of the union in both natures,
leave these things aside as superfluous, and arrange to make your beginning with them.
And from this you pass to that in everything that Christ is by nature and is called.
And since the Christ of the fathers stands opposed to you, you were asked to say who he is.
And, unwillingly, you agree with me that Christ exists in both natures,
and that God the Word does not exist in both natures.
But listen to what he wrote to me, so that you may know that he has nothing sound to say.
Instead, he takes every precaution to prevent a judgment and examination that would reveal that his hostility toward me was not on account of the faith.
“The [?] that came into true union are different,” he says, “but from both there is one Christ and Son.”
Not as though the difference between the natures had been removed because of the union; rather, they taught us all the more that there is one Lord and Christ and Son.
Not as though the essence of God the Word was completed through the difference between the natures:
he remains eternally as he is, admitting neither addition nor diminution.
Rather, through the course of the union of divinity and humanity, one Christ came into being—not God the Word,
for he existed eternally. Christ, therefore, is the person of the union,
but the person of God the Word is not that of the union, but of his own nature. These are not the same thing in expression or understanding.
And for this reason, O remarkable man, the fathers too, following the divine Scriptures,
said, “One Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son,” referring to the person of the union.
Then they teach who those united are, and with whom they are united.
“The one begotten of the Father,” they say, “the Only Begotten, is our Lord Jesus Christ,
the only-begotten Son of God, that is, from the essence of God the Father;
God from God, and Light from Light, true God from true God;
begotten, not made, of the same nature as the Father, through whom everything in heaven and on earth came into being.”
Of whom are you speaking, O fathers? Of something else, or of the one you previously wrote about:
“One Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God”? Who is this, and from whom is he? From the Father.
True God from true God, begotten, not made, of the same nature as the Father, through whom everything came into being.
“Who came down for us human beings and for our salvation”—who is this? Tell me, O fathers, and this man and everyone: which is it? Another,
or the Only Begotten? “We teach you about this one, not another: the one who came down for us human beings and for our salvation.”
And he became flesh from the Holy Spirit and from the Virgin Mary—he who also became human.
For down to “he came down, became flesh, and became human,” they taught us about the things belonging to Christ’s divinity.
But by “he became flesh,” they taught us about his union with the flesh.
The rest concerns his flesh, in which he became incarnate: one Lord Jesus Christ, the only Son of God.
For the statement “from the Holy Spirit and from the Virgin Mary”—
does it not teach us about the birth of the flesh? One Lord Jesus Christ, the only Son of God.
What is his nature? The same as his mother’s, from whom flesh capable of suffering was born.
And he suffered, rose after three days, ascended into heaven, and is coming to judge the living and the dead.
Who is this? One Lord Jesus Christ, the only Son of God.
In both respects they speak of him: of the same nature as the Father and of the same nature as the mother—one Lord Jesus Christ.
They do not say this of God the Word by nature in both respects, but of the one Lord Jesus Christ, the only Son of God.
For the union concerns the person, not the nature.
Nor does it concern the substance; rather, it is a union of substances: the substance of God the Word and the substance of the flesh.
And they are united, but not in substance, for God the Word and the flesh did not become one substance.
Nor are both substances flesh—God the Word and the flesh. And in all these things you agree
with me when you say that the natures of divinity and humanity are different,
and that both natures remain in their own substance, and their differences are not abolished in the union of the natures.
For both natures together constitute one Christ, not one God.
Why, then, do you accuse me? Say it before everyone who reads our words.
For these are the things I say, and I also praised you for what you said and acknowledged,
because in your statement you distinguished divinity from humanity and joined them in one person.
And as for what I said, that God the Word had no need of a second birth from a woman,
and that divinity does not undergo suffering, I said it in accordance with the faith, and said that these statements belong to those who are sound in their faith,
and that they oppose the false belief of all the heresies concerning the Lord’s nature.
Where, then, did I say of Christ that he is a mere human being, [?] two Christs?
And is not the one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God,
one person resulting from the union of two natures? I also told you, as one brother to another,
that we do not separate the union from the person resulting from the union.
Nor, again, do we begin with God the Word as though beginning with the person of the union.
Instead, we begin where the fathers began, who were wiser than you
and were especially well versed in the divine Scriptures. And see how they
uproot, as though from the foundation, and dismantle all those things that bring about alteration [?].
For if you attribute all the properties of the flesh to God the Word,
take care that, by stealing away the properties of the natures, as you said, you do not utter those things
that the three hundred and eighteen fathers rejected with one voice, one mouth, and one mind:
that there was a time when God the Word did not exist.
That is, when his flesh did not exist, God the Word did not exist then either.
And this: that before his flesh was born, he did not exist,
since you said that he made all the properties his own.
And that God the Word was begotten from things that did not exist,
because his flesh came from things that did not exist—
unless perhaps you dare to say that the flesh itself also existed of itself.
And you will say that God the Word is from another hypostasis and another substance,
not from that of God the Father, but from that from which the flesh came into being.
And God the Word is subject to change and corruption because of his flesh, which is subject to these things.
For the fathers anathematize those who say these things about God the Word.
For God the Word is not, in substance, composed of both; nor, again, is God the Word in the flesh;
nor is God the Word composed of two, nor is God
the Word two natures. For he is conceived of only as what he is: God the Word, of the same essence as the Father.
For he became incarnate and was revealed in the flesh. But if he became incarnate in flesh, it is clear that it was in that flesh which came into being.
And he who was regarded as a created being did not turn his own substance into flesh, so as to make the properties of the nature of the substance of flesh
his own properties. Rather, everything he did in his own person was for the purpose of revelation.
For he made use of the likeness and person of a servant, not of a servant’s substance or nature,
so that he would be in both by nature, as in the case of Christ.
Why, then, was he rushing to make other paths for himself, and a beginning apart from what the fathers had established,
so that he would end up anathematizing everything they had said, and necessarily saying
everything for which he had been anathematized by them? Instead, he first quotes these statements of the fathers,
as someone wishing to persuade through them [?], and to say, “I have said what they said.”
But he accuses me as someone who does not say these things.
But when he finds that I do say these things and uphold their statements,
he begins laying down rules and changing terms that they did not use,
and introduces them into the faith, insisting that we ought to hold to these instead of theirs.
“For this,” he says, “is said of God the Word,” when he says, “From
before the ages he exists, and he was born of the Father, and he was born in the flesh of a woman . . .” But where did the fathers say
that God the Word was born in the flesh of a woman? Require him to recite the fathers’ statement,
which they laid down for everyone and which we too ought to follow.
You have spoken well in words and in faith. If, then, you keep your promises in your actions, it is genuine.
For anyone who does not speak as the fathers spoke is guilty. Show, then, that the fathers said this statement,
and condemn me with an anathema as someone who has departed from the Scriptures and from the fathers’ statement,
even if I wear out my breath ten thousand times saying, “In my mind I did not understand it differently.”
Otherwise, do not spare the person who departs from what the fathers said by transgressing against the terminology they established.
For whatever terms have been established must be preserved by every means, even if we sometimes allow them to be explained.
For a person uses them differently as they stand, not to abolish them, nor to change them,
nor to alter them, but while preserving with me, in these very terms, the correct meaning [?]—I mean the meaning of the fathers.
What, then, can you demonstrate concerning this: that I have wrongly used the expression found in the fathers’ statement?
And is it right for me to plead for an explanation? Show me that God
the Word was born in the flesh from a woman, and then explain how you understand that he was born.
For if you yourself first formulate it, and then explain what you have formulated,
you are not accepted by those who accept the statements of the Fathers, which lack nothing.
For this reason they accept neither addition nor subtraction nor alteration.
For someone who explains confirms what is written and does not nullify it.
But if I made improper use of the words of the Fathers,
urging on the basis of their words that the holy Virgin should not be called the Mother of God,
and did not call Christ God, and you were compelled to oppose me, first show me
that I said these things, before people who examine us properly, and not before those who are inclined to follow you.
For before these people you have won, and you have acted as though you were before beings without reason or soul.
You did not present my letter as though you were before human beings—
the letter in which I disputed with you, urging you not to confuse the statements of the Fathers,
but to confess one Lord Jesus Christ, of the same nature as the Father, not another.
Rather, he is one and the same, and he is one person of the two natures,
divinity and humanity, Lord and Christ. You too confessed this.
It is not, then, because I do not confess Christ to be God—for he is indeed God, and he is no other besides God the Word,
who is of the same nature as the Father—but because I confess that he is also a human being. If this were the case,
and I did not confess this, I would have gone on to teach that Christ is God and of the same nature as the Father,
and likewise also a human being of the same nature as us, without passing hastily from the person of the union
and from the essence of the divinity, as from the common person of divinity and humanity.
I would have begun as from one essence of God the Word, which both were.
And everything concerning him, and everything concerning his flesh, I would have attributed to him by nature, since he is both in essence.
Why, then, do you falsely attribute to the Fathers things they do not say? And why, again, do you urge
those who do not wish to accept anything beyond the formulation of the Fathers to accept your statements rather than those of the Fathers? But look to yourself.
Read, understand, and see that this is not what they said. We have not passed over these things out of ignorance or malice.
But you cannot show that the statement, “The one who was born of the Father was born in the flesh of a woman,”
was made by those who wrote to you, if they mention birth from a woman at all.
How, then, can you say, you slanderer, “This is how we found that the holy [fathers] understood it,
and they were so confident that they called the holy virgin the Mother of God. In the same way,” you say, “we also say that he
suffered and rose”? First show us that the fathers call her the Mother of God,
or that God the Word was born in the flesh, or that he was born in his entirety, and likewise that he suffered, died, and rose.
Explain to us how they say that God suffered and rose. But if you have made this up and are making false accusations,
how can anyone accept the rest without doubt? For you have made all these things doubtful,
because you did not say what the fathers said, but changed even the name itself.
For even if you supposed that they designate the very same one, and that there is no difference between “the Lord Jesus Christ” and “God the Word,”
and you understand the very same one by this name and by that, you should not have changed it,
but explained and clarified it, and used the names established by the fathers.
But you could not, through those designations, represent God the Word as subject to suffering and death.
That is why you occupy yourself with this designation, through which you can ensnare those who do not know whom each of these designates.
“In the same way,” you say, “we also understand the statement that he died.”
For God the Word is indeed immortal and incorruptible by nature, living and life-giving.
But again, because his body, by the grace of God, as Paul said,
“tasted death for everyone,” he himself is said to have endured death for us. By
whom? By you or by the fathers? Tell us! Do not lead your hearers astray from the fathers
in the things in which you said you agreed with their words and their teaching.
Read, then: where did they say that God the Word suffered? Or if you say that divine Scripture said
that God the Word suffered, read it out and do not conceal it. But you have nothing to read.
Why, then, do you slander the fathers? Why do you take the faith of the fathers as a means of deceiving
and taking advantage of those who believe simply and do not investigate? Are you really playing tricks on those who read?
Like people who lack understanding? Or are you correcting the faith of the fathers,
because they did not write what they ought to have written? For you first set it down
and say that we ought to agree with it in words and in faith. Yet you do not follow it at all,
nor do you even preserve the order of its wording. You began where the fathers began,
and to this you added everything they said? You did not even think fit to use the very same terms,
nor did you follow their teaching. For being created, made, capable of suffering, and mortal,
and all such things that the fathers reject, you attribute to the essence of God the Word.
For whatever belongs to the Father in his own essence, he too is and is said to be.
For you argue that we should speak in a way in which they themselves did not speak. And then, that is, you explain,
not as though you were ruling out calling God the Word capable of suffering and mortal,
but so as to persuade people to say the things that the fathers refused to have said.
“Thus,” you say, “let us confess one Lord Christ, the one who was named at his birth from the blessed Mary.”
But also a human being; but also in death; but also in the resurrection; but also in the ascension;
but also in his coming from heaven: you now exclude him from all these things.
Thus you said, “Let us confess one Christ and Lord,” in the way that you yourself describe.
Then let us confess what has not been confessed: “Not as though we worship a human being along with the Word, lest an appearance of division be introduced
by our saying ‘along with,’ but we worship him as one and the same.
For his body is not foreign to him, along with which he also sits with the Father.”
Either he said this out of the blindness of his understanding, or he was compelled by necessity imposed by God
to fall into the very things for which he rebukes others, and under the very same condemnation.
For he doubled the expression “along with” by saying, “along with the one who sits with the Father.”
For “along with” is not said of one alone, but of someone along with another.
And how does “along with the one who sits with the Father” not introduce an appearance of division? He says “body,” and “his own body,”
and it sits with him, yet he does not create an appearance of division.
He understands God the Word and also his body as one and the same. And the body
He is conceived, and yet the body is not conceived. And his body is conceived as being with him.
And it is not conceived that his body is with him; rather, he alone is conceived.
And he is conceived as sitting with him, with the Father. And yet he is not conceived as sitting with the Father; rather, he alone is conceived.
Who can express his inexpressible wisdom? But he, it says, took him to himself.
Not as though two sons were sitting there, but one, in union with his flesh.
And you also said: “You introduce the idea of separation when you allow one to be conceived with another—but in union.”
Whose union? Christ’s? Then Christ is the person of the union.
But he says that he took him to himself—the one with whom he too sits with the Father . . . You have posited a person in that very one. What, then, are you rejecting?
As though the statement, “With him he too sits with the Father,” had been wrongly made? Or as though, from the expression “with,”
you were compelled to understand that this was so, although it is possible to understand or conceive it correctly?
Not to indicate that two sons are sitting, but that there is one, in union with his flesh.
And you reject the expression “with,” so that two should not be conceived. But if it is impiety in your view,
as you said, return also to that passage you left out, for that is his intention.
For what did you [?]? Did you not plainly reject it, saying that one ought not to write “with,” while you yourself wrote, “With him
he sits with the Father”? For whoever says these things says that two sons are sitting.
But you reject that statement because two sons ought not to be conceived as sitting. Yet this is how it stands, just as it was set down.
And you have [?] the statement that indicates two sons, yet you say that one ought not to conceive two sons.
But two are necessarily conceived, as it seems in your own view.
But the statement is set down and spoken in this way with a different meaning, and two sons are not conceived.
Why do you accuse me of saying that two are united in one Son,
when by this I intended to show that the natures in the union are not confused,
while using the distinctive properties of the natures? It is not as though I wish to make two sons,
nor, again, to dissolve the union. Rather, on the basis of the one person of the union, I use language referring to two substances,
as divine Scripture also indicates. But by one substance you indicate two substances.
But if I had said what you are saying, it would have appeared to you to be impiety.
But if you, to those who supposedly act in the fear of God, although they cannot examine it [?]—
dared to read these things, you read them to yourself and not to them.
You also fled from examination by the entire synod, because you judged that these things had no way out before a discerning spirit. And when I was absent,
the things you said well, you said on my behalf.
And when you spoke badly against yourself, then too you spoke on my behalf [?].
For if this expression “with” refers back to the statement that the Son is one—and with his flesh, still more with the Father—not because he is worshiped with him,
there are two acts of worship of one Son, while the one who sits with him is worshiped with one act of worship [?].
For the union is in the natures, and you too agree with me: “The distinction between the natures is not abolished because of the union.”
For it is good to repeat many times those statements that have been well expressed.
For you are astonished when you hear my own statements [?] in these statements of yours.
For there is no union that does not disclose a distinction, as with the worship associated with sitting together.
But you make the maker of the natures the starting point of your account, and not the person of the union.
Either, then, refrain from saying “two natures united without confusion,” or acknowledge and say these things.
And it does not seem impossible to you to speak of “one and another” within the union in terms of essence,
not in terms of the union of the person. [?] But if, concerning hypostatic union,
whether as something incomprehensible or as something fitting to you, we are questioned, we fall into saying that there are two sons.
For it is necessary to distinguish and speak of the man
separately, as one honored with the name of Son, and again of God the Word separately, as the one who possesses by nature the title and the realities of sonship.
Therefore it is not right to divide the one Lord Jesus Christ into two sons.
I also told you in the letter that I do not understand the things you say.
And in your presumption you thought that you had gone astray [?]; you did not conceal the things you were preparing to say properly afterward.
And although you should have given an answer concerning these things, written, offered an explanation, and openly rebuked the wrongdoers,
you stood against yourself and me, and disregarded the fathers and the Holy Scriptures.
What do you want hypostatic union to be—a union that does not allow us to understand that there is a human essence,
nor to understand a human being by nature, but God the Word by nature? That is:
And God, who by nature is not what he is in his own nature because of the hypostatic union:
in which there are no distinctions or boundaries belonging to other things.
For this reason, the union itself is a union of things defined by the term “essence.”
And if it is abolished, it is no longer a union,
but something resulting from a union, not a union itself. And if the entire boundary between the natures is abolished,
how has the union not abolished the distinctions between the natures? And if they are conceived neither in nature nor in union, how did you say that he made
the distinctive property of the flesh his own, when you said, “In this respect by nature,
but in that respect by union”? And [?] by nature, even that he died; yet these things belong to him because he made them his own.
How, then, did you think to establish a hypostatic union? What is this hypostatic union that has no meaning?
How are we to accept it without understanding it? Or how have you understood it? How is it exalted and incomprehensible,
and yet not fitting? Teach us. But you do not wish to teach me.
Imagine that the judges are telling you and urging you to teach us and those like us, because we do not know.
But if not, teach the whole synod. For neither you nor the synod is satisfied with the term “union.”
For I too speak of union, but you do not accept what I say, because I divide the union.
If I say of the things that were united that one is bodily in essence and the other bodiless in essence, and that they are distinct from one another:
the one as created, the other as uncreated; the one mortal, the other immortal;
the one eternal with the Father, the other created at the end of the ages; the one sharing the Father’s nature, the other sharing our nature.
For the union does not abolish the essences that were united so that they can no longer be recognized.
You say to me, “You divide,” although you yourself went so far as these words, into which you fell in order to accuse me:
You said these things: “The natures that came into true union are different,
but from both there is one Christ and Son—not as though the difference between the natures had been removed because of the union.”
Do you, then, allow us to think this about the hypostatic union too? Or, like someone who divides by saying
that the natures that were united had various differences, do you snatch this for your own confession,
so that you do not introduce the suggestion of division? And why do I speak of introducing the suggestion [?] of division? And why do I speak
of a suggestion? You understand the actual division of the natures in terms of the definition of the natures and as an absence of confusion.
Although you have no conception at all in your mind of the boundary between the natures, by which you could understand that they were united without confusion.
Just as the fire was united with the bush and the bush with the fire, and they existed without confusion.
You, then, present them as without boundaries and without distinction; I, however, present them as bounded and distinct on all sides.
If, then, you speak of a hypostatic union, speak clearly.
For I admit that I did not understand then, nor do I now. I need you to teach me, so that I may agree with you.
Or, if I do not accept your opinion, I will say that I do not accept it. And if the judges accept
it from you, let them persuade me, or condemn me as someone whose wickedness admits of no change.
Speak, then, of a hypostatic union. Do you mean that we should regard [?] the person as a hypostasis,
just as we speak of one essence of the Godhead and three hypostases,
and understand the hypostases as persons? Then you are calling the personal union hypostatic.
But the union was not of persons, but of natures.
“The natures that came into a true union are different,” he says, “but from both there is one Christ.”
Do you understand this as the one person of Christ, or as the hypostasis of essence and nature,
as in “the image of his hypostasis”? And you speak of the union of the natures as a hypostatic union.
But that is what I myself say, and for this I praised you: you spoke and made a distinction between the natures,
by speaking of divinity and humanity, and of their conjunction in one person.
Or else you did not speak of differences without confusion, and it would have remained without any difference by which it could be divided.
But if you do not allow a difference—and this difference is that of the natures—you are allowing a natural division without knowing it.
But there was no difference in the union, while those things that are in it remain without confusion,
just as the bush is in the fire and the fire in the bush. But you do not appear to be saying these things,
and you accuse me as someone who does not accept a hypostatic union. But another hypostatic union,
one arising from other natures, I do not acknowledge.
Nor do I acknowledge anything else appropriate to the union of different natures except their union in one person,
from whom and in whom both natures are known, as he makes their properties those of the person.
For the body was the temple of the divinity of God the Word:
And the temple was united with the Godhead in a primary conjunction:
so that he might make these things belonging to this one his own, through their appropriation by the divine nature.
It is good to confess this, and it agrees with the tradition of the Gospels—not that he made them his own essence.
What other personal union, then, do you wish to teach me,
in a primary, divine, and indescribable union? I do not know,
unless it is that of one person: that this one is that one, and that one is also this one.
And for this reason I insistently proclaim everywhere that it is not to the nature,
but to the person that the things spoken, whether about the divinity or about the humanity, must be attributed.
This is so that, by uniting the two in essence, there may not be an illusion concerning the humanity.
For not everything said of him expresses what he was in essence; rather, all these things indicate the person.
And God the Word, who is said to have become flesh and the Son of Man, is known
from the likeness and the person of the flesh and of the human being, which he used [?] to make himself known to the world.
For not everything that by nature
is said of the flesh is also said of God the Word—as though he came into being when he did not exist,
or came into being from things that did not exist, or whatever is said of the flesh before it came into being, when it came into being,
and after it came into being, with the changes of growth and decay, and, in short, that it is of the same nature as us.
For it is of the same nature as us in everything. The things said in terms of essence
are said in no other respect, but only in this respect of essence, and it is said to be of the same nature.
For in the things said on the basis of the person and the likeness of the nature, what makes it known is spoken of
as the person of the essence; but what it is by nature is not stated,
because the union was not in essence and nature, but in person. Likewise, the flesh
is not said to be everything that God the Word is by nature.
For it is not without beginning, nor is it uncreated, nor is it incorporeal,
nor is it invisible, nor is it of the same nature as the Father and the Holy Spirit,
even though the flesh too is called Son, Lord, and God, in this manner, through the union.
For the union was in the person of the Son of God, not in the substance or in the nature.
Rather, it was from natures, and not into a nature, but into a person.
For he has everything that belongs to the person, apart from the substance of the person.
What other union in individual being, then, do you speak of that I do not accept,
as you say, either because it is incomprehensible or because it is unfitting?
And for this reason I refuse to speak of two Christs: one a human being honored with the title of Son,
and, separately again, the Word of God, who possesses the name and the reality of sonship?
The one who speaks of one Son, one Christ, and one Lord in the union—
how can he speak of them separately? For then this is no longer called a union, but each of the natures is in its own substance.
For God the Word is not said to have become flesh in his own substance, but through union with the flesh.
Nor is the flesh called Son apart from union with the Son of God.
For this reason there is one flesh in both, and one Son in both.
For what he has through the union, he is and is called;
when they are defined and distinguished from one another, he neither is nor is called that.
Thus God the Word is by his nature God without a body, but through union with the flesh he is called flesh.
And the flesh, which by its nature is a body, is also a body in substance;
but through union with God the Word, the Son of God, it is God and Son.
Those who are distinct in nature and exist in a union of natures are not called two fleshes, nor again two sons. Among
human beings, however, the many who are sons are spoken of with their natures distinct and divided,
those to each of whom this is given only by grace and by membership in the household,
just as honor is given by the king to each of the rulers.
