For what he alone is in his own individual being, he is also for many by grace.
For he exists in his individual being, and in his likeness he made a likeness for himself—not by [?], nor by honor,
nor merely by an equality of grace, but in his natural likeness he made him his likeness,
so that it is not another, but he himself whom we attribute to his own person.
That this should be that, and that should be this: one and the same in both substances, a person represented in the flesh,
and representing the flesh in the likeness of his own sonship in both natures, and one flesh in both natures.
This is represented by that, and that by this: one and the same likeness of the person.
I do not know, then, in what sense you speak of a hypostatic union:
whether it is incomprehensible or inappropriate, so that I may accept it or not accept it.
And for this reason is the man defined and spoken of separately by the designation or honor of Son, and, again, the Word from God separately,
who possesses sonship, the name, and the titles by nature? But how do you speak of their being united?
State clearly the fathers’ formulation of the faith, and prescribe what those who are worthy, including me and everyone else, are to say.
For you have not clarified the meaning: how we ought to think and speak.
How do you say that the nature of the man should not be understood separately, any more than the substance of God the Word,
who is Son, not by nature but by union? Yet you also say that there are differences within the natures,
which were brought together into the union of one Son. And the difference between the natures was not abolished in the union of the natures,
as though the difference between the natures were abolished because of the union.
If, then, the distinctions between the natures are not removed, the nature of the flesh is separately that of humanity.
But he who is Son, of the same nature as God the Father and the Holy Spirit, belongs individually and separately to the divinity.
In the union, however, the flesh is Son, and God the Word is flesh.
For this reason, someone who speaks in this way does not affirm two sons, nor does he speak of two fleshes.
Nor does he speak of two fleshes by nature, nor [?] flesh in it and sonship in it.
In the very same way, they use each other’s natural persons as their own,
just as fire was in the bush, and the bush was fire, and the fire was a bush.
Each one of them was bush and fire, and not two bushes or two fires. For
both were in the fire, and both were in the bush—not in division, but in union.
From both natures, natural persons come into being.
Either, then, do not speak of distinct natures while they persist in their natural distinctions and are not abolished,
or say that they have remained different in nature, and that you define them according to the distinction between the natures within an indivisible union.
Not as though the differences between the natures were abolished in the union.
[?] For if, then, you understand them individually, and not in their natures, but in their distinction from one another,
am I obliged to confess the inseparable union of the two natures in one person? And it is to you, as someone who disputes these things,
that I address my words. But do you perhaps call the hypostatic union one nature,
so that after the union the natures do not preserve their properties? And are you correcting what you said previously?
Rather, you are completely nullifying those statements through your scrutiny of me,
since you want to say the opposite of what I say. For it is not in accordance with the truth,
but out of opposition, like an enemy, that you have come to be unwilling to seek the reason for the distinction.
For this amounts to abolishing the natures, and I do not accept it.
But in your opposition to me, you have fought against the definitions with forceful words,
like robbers, so that you may conceal your thinking and not be recognized.
You say this, and that, and all these things. Yet you do not speak of a hypostatic union for the abolition of the natures,
but of a natural union through composition into one nature.
Just as soul and body form the one nature of a human being, you [?] a hypostatic union.
But even this, although the natures persist, nevertheless the natures become a nature subject to suffering, made and created [?].
Rather, the union results in a nature subject to suffering, made and created.
For the natural union of the two is created.
For what they do not possess in their own natures, they receive in their natures through the union of nature.
But those things that are united in a natural union are united with the other's natural capacity for suffering.
And they do not voluntarily receive one another's sufferings, as in the case of soul and body:
in their own natures they are incapable of receiving one another's properties.
But through the union of nature they share with one another, and give and receive one another's sufferings through the necessity of nature,
and through something blended in nature, so that what did not suffer in and of itself may suffer.
For in the union, the soul does not in and of itself hunger or thirst, nor does it feel pain from cutting, swelling, or a wound.
Nor, again, does a body without a soul have any sensation of these things. Through the union
But in the natural union of different natures, they undergo one another’s sufferings as beings subject to suffering, and share in them through the necessity of the union.
If this is what you mean by a hypostatic union in nature, you are speaking like the Arians.
That it is natural and not voluntary; that he suffered with a natural capacity for suffering. He suffered, he says, as a result of a natural union.
For the sufferings of the soul are the sufferings of the body in a natural composition.
For the unmade one, who is uncreated by nature, was not compounded so as to suffer like a created and made being.
For we do not demonstrate a single nature of the union merely from the fact that the soul is in the body and the body in the soul.
For the soul does not form a union with every body in which it is present,
since it cannot even always give life to its own body, except in the composition in which it was fashioned into one nature by the Maker.
And within a natural boundary, defined and impassable, it is held [?] against its will.
And again, they are unbound and bound together in their constitution, in the union of nature.
If, then, God the Word’s union with humanity resulted in one nature,
even if the natures themselves remained without confusion, nevertheless, in the union of nature,
the Maker and the thing made were constituted through a change, whether he willed it or not.
Because they were named in this way, he too is made and created.
And the one who can fashion everything—that is, God—would be the nature of the union,
and not the individual existence of humanity, which is known by nature as a living being. Just as the body, too,
without the soul is not a living being in its own individual existence, but has the capacity to be a living being through the constitution of a natural union,
if this is so, then the man himself also has the capacity to be a living being in God,
and does not have his own individual existence and nature, but receives them from a hypostatic union that establishes one nature.
For this reason he is asked to say: The man is a man, and in his own individual existence and nature he is a living being.
And God the Word, in his own individual existence, is God the Word,
so that in the union he may maintain his nature and be a living being, not as a result of the union.
For he received his existence as a man through the creative formation of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.
He received his status as the only-begotten Son through union with God the Word,
not from his own nature, nor through a natural and hypostatic union.
For what has its being in a natural union has its [?] not from another, but from a natural constitution.
Thus there is one living being, which comes neither from the body nor from the soul,
nor from both, but from a natural constitution. This, however, is subject to corruption and suffering.
But the union of the natures in the person is not subject to suffering or corruption, since it is an intimate, voluntary association.
And it is not that he has this union apart from the will: in condescension and exaltation, in commanding and being commanded.
And he has such a mind, not through abolition nor
through being abolished, nor through the uprooting of one nature or of the properties of both natures.
But in mind and will, the individual properties are distinguished in their natural characteristics, corresponding to the distinction of the natures in a single equality.
For the will and mind in the union of the natures were one and the same, so that both should will, or not will, the very same things.
And they have a will, and one another’s will. For the person of this one is also that one’s,
and that one’s is this one’s. This one speaks from that one, and that one from this one, as though speaking in his own person,
in one person, that of the union of the natures, not in one individual being or nature.
For the divinity is not bounded by the body, as is each of the natures that are united in an individual being.
For those are bounded by the nature that encloses them within themselves, and they do not exist outside themselves.
For example, soul and body are bound within themselves and do not exist outside themselves.
If, then, you say that God the Word and the flesh are united in individual being,
and you call this an incomprehensible and unfitting union, I do not hesitate to say plainly
that those who say such things are wicked, and that this view does not come from the orthodox.
For if we do not add “of a nature capable of suffering” to “the Son who is incapable of suffering came
so as to experience suffering,” they show that his essence is not incapable of suffering,
but is a nature capable of suffering, from which he was constituted in a union of individual being [?], and in which he suffered.
For someone whose nature cannot suffer does not suffer in his individual being in any way, if he is incapable of suffering.
For someone who suffers in some respect is not incapable of suffering in his individual being, but is incapable of suffering in a particular way.
Similarly, all beings capable of suffering, which suffer by nature, do not suffer in every way, but in the way in which their nature can suffer.
Not everything suffers in the same way: neither light, nor air, nor fire, nor the creatures in the water.
Neither the animals on dry land, nor birds, nor bodies, nor souls,
nor angels, nor demons; rather, in substance and individual being they are susceptible to suffering.
They suffer according to their nature’s capacity to suffer, either from themselves and upon themselves, or through another.
But you do not say that it is through mingling, nor again through a change of substance,
nor through corruption, nor again naturally, so that there would be a single union in individual being.
Then you mean that voluntary union, in which a union is conceived without mingling and without suffering on the part of the natures,
into one person, not through a natural union. For the person that comes into being through a natural union
is spoken of as deriving from both the natures that were united, as a human being is neither body nor soul.
For the union of these resulted in a nature and in the person of that nature. But God,
for his own person and sonship, assumed the form of a servant; he did not come into being from another.
For those things that are united to constitute a nature are of this kind.
He assumed the form of a servant, and human substance was not itself the form of a servant;
rather, the one who assumed it established it as a form and a person.
And he came to be in the likeness of human beings, but he was not human nature,
even though what he assumed was human nature. As for the one who assumed it, he came to be in human likeness.
And with this, he was found in appearance as a human being—the one who assumed, not the one who was assumed.
For the one who was assumed was the substance and [?] of a human being.
The one who assumed was found in appearance as a human being, although he was not human nature.
For he did not assume it for himself to constitute a nature, but to constitute a form,
and the likeness and appearance of a human being, in everything that a person expresses.
As he describes the lowliness of that appearance, he descended as far as death—death on a cross—in which he emptied himself,
so that in the nature he might display the humility of the form of a servant and endure dishonor among human beings.
For it was he whom they dishonored, the one whose condescension is without limit.
He also made known the reason why he assumed the form of a servant, when, in the likeness of human beings, he was found in appearance as a human being,
and humbled himself as far as death—death on a cross. But he did not suffer in his own nature.
They are; but he made use of these things in the one who suffers by nature, in his appearance and his person.
So that he might graciously give him, in his person, a name superior to all [?].
So that every knee should bow to him, in heaven, on earth, and beneath the earth, and every tongue should acknowledge him.
So that the Son should be understood as equal to God and in accordance with God's greatness.
He who took the form of a servant and came to be in human likeness, and was found in appearance as a human being.
And he humbled himself to the point of death—death on a cross.
And he was exalted, in that he was given a name superior to every name, in the appearance of the form of a servant that was taken into union.
But that which is the form of a servant was [?] in appearance, but in substance.
And it was taken into the likeness, the appearance, and the humiliation extending to death on a cross.
For this reason it was exalted to receive a name superior to every name.
But to understand the form of a servant as a substance, he set forth Christ as the one to be understood.
For Christ is both by nature.
For this reason, the properties of both natures also belong together in one person, not that of the substance of God the Word.
Nor is it a person in substance, for he is not God the Word in substance.
Nor is the person of the union that of the natures that were united, so that he might fit together, in the one person of God the Word,
both substances; for he is not both in substance.
Not as though God Christ were someone else apart from God the Word,
but because he indicates the union of both substances, that of God the Word and that of the human being.
Now Christ is constituted from God and a human being, just as you yourself also say.
“The differences of the natures,” you say, “are not lost because of the union; rather, they have all the more fully constituted for us one Lord and Christ and Son,
in one inexpressible and incomprehensible movement toward the union of divinity and humanity.”
Even though you appear to regret the things you said well.
For the substance of God the Word was not constituted from divinity and humanity.
For he does not derive his being God the Word from the union, as Christ derives his being from divinity and humanity.
For becoming human indicates humanity.
The full meaning of his becoming human is not understood from the divinity alone, but also from the becoming human by which it became human.
For this reason the apostle first sets out the person of the union, and then those things from which the union exists.
He first says, “the form of God,” which is equality with God, and then, “It assumed the form of a servant.”
Not the essence, nor the nature, but the appearance and the person.
So that he might share in the form of a servant, and the form of a servant might also share in the form of God, so that, of
necessity, there would be one person from the two natures. For the person is the form.
Thus he is this in essence and that in union, in the statement about humiliation and exaltation.
How, then, do you command us to understand these differences between the natures within the union? For the union did not remove the differences between the natures,
so that we should no longer understand these differences. For the one who assumed the form of a servant
belongs distinctively to the form of God alone. But what was assumed belongs exclusively to the form of a servant.
But the statement that this is that, and that is this, concerns the union of the person, not of the essence.
Thus, just as this is what it is in essence, it should be that in union, and not something else.
That which in essence is the form of God also shares the nature of this essence, in that it is its natural form.
But in the union, the form of God assumed the form of a servant.
And the form of God, which belongs to God by nature, came to be in the appearance of the form of a servant.
But the form of a servant, which is by nature the form of a servant, is in union the form of God, not God's by nature.
Thus we should understand separately the distinctive properties that belong naturally to the nature of each of them,
and the natural distinctions in each of the natures.
And we should understand those things that belong to the union as belonging exclusively to the union, not to the essence.
How, then, do you command us not to consider any of these things separately, on the basis of
the distinction between the natures, which you said are not lost because of the union? But you have no answer to give,
nor can you refute me through the accusations you bring against me. Instead, you accuse yourself
through the things of which you wish to accuse me, and you contradict yourself.
But you, O righteous judges, what have you examined of these things—whether concerning the matters we worked on in our investigation, or from what we said,
or from what I confessed, or from what I denied holding? Rebuke the one who is mistaken, or teach the one who does not know.
For a person is condemned as a heretic not on the basis of what he denies, but on the basis of what he professes.
So it was with Arius, so with Eunomius, so with Macedonius, and so with each of the heretics:
On the basis of what they professed in opposition and argued, they were examined and condemned by the fathers.
Now you too, their imitators: what in what I confessed and argued is contrary to them,
that you should condemn me as a heretic? What did you find in my letter
that is contrary to the fathers’ statement? Tell me whether I said it or did not say it.
He spoke as follows: “Everything attributed to Christ in the divine Scriptures
ought to be attributed to God the Word: birth from a woman, crucifixion, death,
burial, resurrection, ascension, and the second coming, when he comes again—not
from the things with which the fathers began . . .” But I said in response to these things:
“Did the fathers not say these things? For this reason, it is not right to begin here either.”
I also stated the reasoning: “For they did not intend to portray God the Word as subject to suffering,
mortal, made, and created, and as having come into being from things that did not exist.
These are the things that those who begin there are compelled to say.
Rather, the opposite of what Arius said and taught.
For this reason, they made the unity of the person of Christ the starting point of their teaching,
so that both the things belonging to his divinity and those belonging to his humanity
might be accepted in an orderly and appropriate way, without confusion or abolition of the natures.
Rather, they fight against all heresies and stand firmly in orthodoxy as they give their answer,
saying these words: ‘I believe in one Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son.’
Observe,” I said to him, “how they first set down ‘Lord,’ ‘Jesus Christ,’ ‘Only-begotten,’ and ‘Son’—
names common to the divinity and the humanity—as a foundation.
Then they build upon it the naming of the incarnation, the sufferings, and the resurrection.
By first setting down names for both natures, which signify what they have in common,
neither was sonship and lordship divided, nor were the natures, in the unity of sonship
May [?] of destruction and confusion come to Candidianus. [?] What, then, seems right to you,
O righteous judges? For he wrote the opinion that pleased him, and I, in turn, wrote my opinion in the same way.
And once again we choose you as judges. What have you thought about these things? What is your opinion of them? Who is right,
and who is wrong? And by what reasoning have you examined the matter? Tell us your opinion; write to us as righteous judges.
Was it I, then, who lied and transgressed the faith of the fathers because I told him
that they began here—not with God the Word,
but with ‘one Lord Jesus Christ, the Son of God’? You condemned me as someone who added to these things,
but acquitted him, who did not preserve their faith at all,
but thought that they used these names casually and without distinction.
I, however, said that they did not begin here casually, but with a divine purpose. If I acted wickedly in this, show me.
Otherwise, did you perhaps reject as impious the reason I gave him for their beginning here:
that the things belonging to divinity and humanity should be held in common, as the names indicate? And that, for the sake of complete
and careful teaching, they wished to begin with these names,
since the name ‘Christ’ truly applies to both natures, man and God.
But if this was the reason, you ought to have condemned him too.
For he said that the natures brought together in the movement toward union are different,
but that there is one Christ from both—not one God the Word from both.
For the difference between the natures is not removed because of the union.
Thus both natures belong to Christ, and not to God the Word.
Either condemn both my words and his, then, or, on the basis of his words, consider me innocent too, as someone who agrees with them all.
But if not, where he declares that God the Word exists in both essences, let either he or you give an answer:
from what divinity and humanity was God the Word constituted through their combination? For he said that the one Christ exists from different natures,
divinity and humanity, and was constituted in an indescribable way from the combination of the natures.
From what natures? And from what essences? From what divinity and from what humanity was God the Word constituted,
so that God the Word should exist in both natures? Either you or he—tell us even now:
Even if you did not say it at first, say it: God the Word exists in substance in both,
just as you confess concerning Christ that he exists in substance in both:
from different natures, and different natures. The union, they say, did not abolish
the difference between the natures. Rather, you say that God the Word is different natures.
For if two substances came into being from one substance, that of divinity and that of humanity, what occurred was a division and not a union.
But he says that Christ came into being through union and exists in two natures.
God the Word became flesh through union, and not in substance. How, then, does it indicate that he is one and the same:
the one who is two in union and the one who is a nature? Or is he himself both nature and union,
and in nature and in union, and person and substance? For although there is no person without substance,
substance and person are not the same thing. How, then, did you judge us,
O wise judges? What did you think about these statements of the fathers? Did they agree with the divine Scriptures
in their terms and in the meaning of their terms, and did they use these terms carefully and clearly? And from this source,
and not from any other quarter, were they able to make a careful beginning in their teaching,
except from where the Holy Spirit led them, so that nothing should be lacking,
and nothing should be excessive, and nothing empty, and they should not act at random, but do everything with discernment.
Thus, among the things seen in Christ, all those belonging to God the Word,
who has a nature that cannot suffer, is immortal, and is eternal, and all those belonging to humanity, whose nature is
mortal, capable of suffering, and created, and those belonging to the union and to the becoming human,
are attributed to one person, from the very womb and from the becoming human:
to that person who is common to both, that of our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God.
The fathers began with him, and then, making a distinction in their statement,
they taught concerning the divinity that he is from God the Father, of the same nature as the Father,
Light from Light, through whom everything came into being, both things on earth and things in heaven.
Then they spoke of God the Word’s becoming flesh and of his humanity: for us human beings and for our salvation, he came down and became flesh.
Then they spoke of the things belonging to the flesh, of birth and of formation: that he became flesh.
They said, as they taught, that he became flesh from the Holy Spirit and from the Virgin Mary.
They made known the union in which he became flesh and became human.
For up to the incarnation, they taught us everything concerning God the Word.
But from the point when he became flesh, they speak about the union that came about from the Holy Spirit and from the Virgin Mary, about the birth of the flesh in which he became incarnate.
They speak of suffering, death, resurrection, ascension, and the events they made known concerning the body that was united to him, as a body endowed with a soul and understanding.
This is so that we should not suppose that the union came about through confusion, nor again through a change of substance and nature, or
through a mixture or a natural composition resulting in a single living being, but in one person through the saving arrangement made on our behalf.
Thus he would share with us in humiliation reaching as far as death—and death on a cross.
And we would share with him in the name that is above all names,
at which every knee should bow, in heaven, on earth, and beneath the earth, and every tongue should confess.
The soul belonging to his human nature was not without a will, nor was it without understanding.
Nor was the body without sensation: it had the sensation of its own life through the natural union of body and soul.
All the natural properties are present without deficiency in the activity of nature and its power, both acting and being acted upon.
For the union of God the Word with humanity did not take place in nature,
so that the human mind should be without activity,
and he should think with the mind of God the Word rather than with the human mind,
and should perceive, [?] through union with a living soul, but should live through union with the Godhead.
And that he should live and perceive, not through the activity of the soul's sensation, but through the power of the Godhead.
For a union of this kind is subject to suffering. Just as the soul naturally gives sensation to the body,
so, through that sensation, awareness of the body's sufferings is given to the soul.
Thus awareness of the body's sufferings comes from the soul and is given to the soul.
For it is subject to suffering. For this reason, the union is in person, not in nature.
And we do not speak of a union of persons, but of natures.
There is one person in the union, but in the natures there is one and another.
He is known through the common person, so that he gives his own person to the flesh, to the form of a servant.
And he spoke through him as he taught, acted, and brought things about.
And he gave his own form to the form of a servant, and through it he speaks as from his own person and from the divinity.
For the person is shared, one and the same: the form of the servant is that of the divinity,
and the form of the divinity is that of the humanity. The person is one and the same, but not the substance.
For the substance of the form of God and the substance of the form of a servant remain in their individual beings.
For the union of the natures did not take place without will and without thought,
as Arius and Apollinaris said, but for the person and for the work carried out on our behalf,
and for the union of his image and his likeness in our nature, consisting of soul and body,
with nothing lacking except sins alone. He did not live his life on behalf of the divinity;
rather, the divinity worked through him so that he might fight against defeat, fulfilling all the commandments of the law
and its principal observances, so that in his choice and in his observance of the commandments he might also be seen to be blameless.
Thus, being without sins, he might be handed over to death for our sake, the righteous one in place of the wicked.
For what defeat is there? And what victory is there? What equality of recompense is there for the conduct of God and of a human being? For he is the one who directs,
who is united in individual being so as to share in life and conduct, and is held fast in death.
The conduct, death, and resurrection also belong both to the one who directs and to the one who is directed.
For either God remained in his nature, being by nature without sins,
or the events of Christ’s life were deceptive: that God the Word lived as a human being.
For both were being drawn and pulled away from one another, by nature and by will; and he too was being pulled away.
For a way of life is subject to command; it does not belong to a nature that is unchangeable, unique, and without a master,
which is not drawn along by another’s will and thought. But if the manner of life and conduct are truly human,
and the conduct of God the Word belonged to him by nature, and he lived according to the things belonging to that nature,
and was sustained by them, in that he accepted the nature as his own and became changeable and subject to alteration [?],
then he was no longer living the life of God, but that of this nature in which he lived.
What, then, did you find in my letter that makes me wicked,
so that you condemned me and considered this man God-fearing? First, then, I rebuked him:
Like someone who lies about the Fathers and overturns the entire foundation of the faith.
He made its beginning come from him and refer to him, thereby necessarily making God the Word subject to suffering.
And that “God the Word” and “Christ” do not signify precisely the same thing,
neither in the divine Scriptures nor as he himself said, even though Christ does not exist apart from God the Word.
I also taught him the usage of the divine Scriptures and showed him what follows from each of these names.
For the things he said rightly, I praised him, because he preserved the natures and their distinctive properties without confusion:
that God the Word remains free from suffering even in the union.
As for his making the properties of the flesh his own, I showed him that they are attributed not to his essence but to his person,
since the person is his own, and all these things are understood as referring to his person. Not everything belonging to the person
belongs to the essence. For God the Word does not possess everything that belongs to the essence of the flesh.
Nor, again, is the flesh described in terms of everything belonging to the essence of God the Word,
but in terms of all those things that refer and belong to the person,
so that, even with the distinction between the natures, the union may be preserved without confusion,
and the person of the union of the natures may not be divided.
Whatever I did not understand and disputed with him, I told him and did not conceal.
I set before him the reason and the doubt that had arisen in me, so that I would not allow him to say anything of what he had said before.
For what, then, did you condemn me? Because I rebuked him for not following the expressions of the Fathers,
and because, contrary to their intention, he represented him as subject to suffering, created, and made,
and made God the Word one of the things that had not existed,
taking this as his starting point and attributing all the properties to him on this basis? I explained all these things to him.
Was this why you were offended? Or was it because I rebuked him for lying about the Fathers,
because he said that the Fathers called the holy Virgin “Mother of God,”
when they do not even mention the birth itself? Was it for these things that you disowned me? Let no one demand gratitude from anyone.
But if this expression was used in the exposition of the faith by the Fathers at Nicaea,
whom he uses to fight against me, read it out—or if it was spoken by another council of orthodox believers.
For it belongs to heretics—to all those who fight against the divinity of Christ.
But it was not spoken by those who adhered in their faith to the orthodox.
If, however, it is shown to have been spoken by a council of the orthodox, then I too acknowledge
that I have been condemned as an opponent. But if no one has adopted this expression,
you have boldly stood against everyone, introducing into the faith an expression that has not been accepted.
And this was what I was asking of you: to demonstrate that it had not been laid down by the fathers.
But whether it should be laid down or not is for the council to decide.
For it assembled for this purpose, and not for anything else. It was not so that they should agree with me in every respect,
but so that I should agree with what they examine, judge, and choose to accept.
For I called you judges, and I appointed all of you as judges to render a just judgment.
And I did not give to one man what rightfully belonged to the council:
a man who leads by force and compels the whole council to embrace a faith that is not approved.
What, then, have you accomplished concerning the matters for which you assembled? You did not settle what ought to have been settled, and you split away from the council.
You did not wait for those who were far away, nor did you preserve the rights of those who had been summoned to the council.
You did not assemble as you had been summoned. Instead, they became judges as the accused wished.
Instead of treating him as the accused, they seated him as judge over his opponent. And why do I say judge? At the head
of the council itself they seated him. And why do I speak only of those who were nearby? Over those who were far away as well,
and those who had not yet arrived—over all of them you gave him authority:
those who were there and those who were far away, those who were alive and those who were dead. Who would believe these things,
among those who have not encountered the written account they produced concerning the Council of Ephesus? Could a council like this
have rendered a just judgment? But even if I am thought to say these things because I have suffered,
and not to examine them with impartial judgment, let no one be persuaded by my words.
For I do not seek any help for myself from human beings.
For I am now being poured out as an offering, and the time has come for me to depart and be with Christ, for whose sake this man fought against me.
Rather, I have said these things so that people will not stray from the true faith because of the authority claimed for the council’s judgment.
But I said less than what they would have written.
But learn from those very people who condemned me that there was no trial, nor was I condemned through a trial.
For I used to cite these statements of the fathers and these statements of the Holy Scriptures. And I used to look ahead
at the preparations being made against the faith.
And I used to declare beforehand the support that the faith of the Arians would receive from the hypostatic union,
which also encouraged the Manichaeans through the assertion that he suffered without being subject to suffering.
And likewise Apollinaris, who assented to it with both hands and was swept away into all the heresies.
For he ruled out speaking of the properties of each of the natures in the union,
and he was [?] attributing them all to God the Word, even those belonging to the flesh.
And through these things you thought that the orthodox would easily be overthrown by the heretics,
since they have nothing suitable to use against them.
For you surrendered your mouths to them, bound your hands and feet, and handed yourselves over to them,
so that you might either fall through your own fault or suffer evils without any breathing space.
As people who cannot be contradicted, you have vindicated the heresies against the orthodox.
For even if someone happens to be an Arian, he calls you as witnesses against those who assembled at Nicaea,
as people who presumptuously stood openly against Arius, saying things that were not right.
Namely, that the one who is subject to suffering, mortal, and created,
they say is of the same nature as the one who is not subject to suffering, is immortal, and is the maker of all created things.
And even if he is a Manichaean, you testify for him by asserting that he suffered without being subject to suffering—that in appearance
he suffered. For the one who suffers without being subject to suffering is the one who, although he seemed to suffer, did not suffer.
For the one who did not exist by nature did not die either.
At last you have acknowledged the truth and reproached the three hundred and eighteen because, out of partiality, they did not speak
the truth. If, along with this, you also insist on saying that we do not say [?] that God the Word died in his nature,
because the divine nature is immortal and not subject to suffering,
nor merely in the appearance of flesh, but in the nature [?] of the flesh, which is subject to suffering and mortal.
And as for God the Word becoming flesh, the pagan accepts this statement: he accepts it as a change of form.
And you say that the incarnation took place through a change of substance, although his substance and his form did not change.
He suffers in a nature capable of suffering, not before he came to exist in substance.
Why, then, do they not say these things of ours wherever the statement about the incarnation is heard?
But it misleads us with the birth of material flesh, with which God the Word was mixed.
And stories are concocted that are unconvincing and unworthy of belief? And if you say in response to this:
that the incarnation of the one who became flesh and a human being did not take place through a change of substance or a change of form,
but that the man who was assumed, the one who was born
of a woman, suffered, died, and [?], and is to come to judge the living and the dead,
was changed into the substance of God and is no longer thought of as a human being except in name alone.
And by this you say that God died and rose. Again the pagan [?] with you:
the one who serves that religion which asserts the transformation of human beings into divinity, and henceforth seeks his favor and serves him as God.
How, then, do you say, “You hold a pagan view”? You are mistaken:
for until now you have been fighting against me with these things, and through these things you have been misleading people.
And if you say that the incarnation of God the Word took place neither through a change of substance nor through a change of divinity,
and that the body is to remain unchanged in substance, but the Word into unity [?],
and the clay remains unchanged in substance, but he became a human being in a personal and natural union,
again Arius accepts this confession—the one who mocks the three hundred and eighteen.
And you accept him and take no offense. And with hands and feet, to Arius,
who speaks the truth, you give your assent, because he makes the claim that he became a human being in a natural person [?],
and was naturally united in person, while naturally feeling the sufferings of the body through sensation.
You dare to call this one of the same nature—the very one who is capable of suffering.
And if you are questioned about this, as someone who does not acknowledge a soul and a body,
in which the Word acquired existence in a natural person, and suffered because he became capable of suffering in a nature capable of suffering, with natural sufferings—these are the things
of Arius and Apollinaris that he proclaims. For Arius says:
For how does it help you that God should become a nature subject to suffering through a hypostatic union of the soul,
so that he naturally suffers natural sufferings in his body and also in his soul? Does this make him consubstantial with the nature that is not subject to suffering—
this one who is subject to these sufferings? Apollinaris, however, condemns those who say these things
and profess them as people who adhere [?] to his own faith. And he commands them to distance themselves from those who say these things
and to be members of his own party, anathematizing all those who have broken away from him.
If, in turn, this man too is rejected as someone who acknowledges neither mind nor will,
you therefore do not accept him, as someone who does not acknowledge a natural and complete union of the Word with flesh, soul, and mind.
For, concerning all these things that Arius said, suppose that he was united to soul, body, and mind;
the union, however, is hypostatic and natural. You are making an addition, not a reduction.
And you flee from the limitation to the body's sufferings, only to make him subject to many sufferings—
him who is consubstantial with the one who is not subject to suffering. Great is the susceptibility to suffering of those who teach these things.
For you attribute to him the things that make him subject to suffering, because of a hypostatic union,
which is united [?] in a natural composition, so that against his will he suffers the sufferings of body, soul, and mind,
and is united in substance and nature. Just as the soul in the body, with regard to the sufferings
of soul and body, endures them by necessity. Yet you do not call him subject to suffering.
Then it was not a hypostatic and natural union, but a voluntary one,
with a body and a rational, intelligent soul, which are united hypostatically and naturally to form human nature.
But the union of God the Word with these is neither hypostatic nor natural,
but voluntary, as an affinity of will and not of nature.
For things united in a natural hypostasis have a natural affinity, not a voluntary one.
For he took the form of a servant into his own person, not into his nature, nor through a change of substance—
of substance into the nature of humanity, or of humanity into the nature of divinity—
nor was it united and mixed with human nature through confusion, or through a natural composition and an interchange of nature's activity.
For this affinity is subject to change and alteration.
But the voluntary affinity is not subject to suffering or change.
He does not, in his natural substance, involuntarily undergo the sufferings of soul and body.
Those that are naturally united suffer together in their substance,
making the sufferings their own naturally, not voluntarily.
For although he accepted the sufferings voluntarily, nevertheless, when he accepted them and underwent them,
he underwent them naturally, in that he underwent them with a natural property and with sensation.
If this is what you say, you have all leaped up and eagerly said what that man said, who said these things briefly and without concealment.
Those who imposed an unforgiving punishment on the man who said these things anathematized him,
and expelled him from the church and even from the inhabited world, as someone who defiled even the ground on which he walked.
How, then, can you say these things? But if someone should say about me,
“Because he divides and splits the natures into separate parts and separates them from one another [?],
and not because he says these plain things, but because he separates them from one another as distinct parts,
and says, ‘One Son by nature and one son by grace,’ as though there were two sons,
and separates them when he says, ‘For I distinguish in nature, but unite in worship.
Because of the one who wears it, I worship the garment’”—everyone should say to you, “You people have drunk mandrakes!”
For by what you say, you wrong even the Father.
How can you speak of the one who is not divided even in a single word as “the one who assumed” and “the one who was assumed,” and “the one who made him his own” and “the one who became his own,”
and call him “man” and “God”? For all these expressions belong to those who distinguish natures in their discourse,
not to those who say that the substance is one.
“Unity,” they say, “does not destroy the differences between the natures.” But if the differences
between the natures remain in the unity, they are divided by the differences between the natures insofar as they differ.
But how could you say about me that I divide it by spatial distance because I say,
“Because of the one who wears it, I worship the garment”? For the garment is not apart from its wearer,
nor is the one who wears it [?] apart from the garment; rather, he is conceived in that very same form.
For this reason, it is impossible to worship the one who wears it apart from the garment that is with him,
in which he sits with the Father, wearing it. For he does not sit with him without wearing it.
And because he is seated with him, he also receives worship with him.
While seated with him, he is certainly worshiped—not for his own sake, but for the sake of the one who clothed himself in him.
From those, then, who speak of becoming human out of unity, or through a change of form, which is the pagans’ view,
or through phantasms, or in appearance, saying that without blemish [?] he suffered without being subject to suffering,
or who ascribe natural sufferings to God the Word, or say that he exists in unity in hypostasis,
or [?] in flesh, or in a soul without reason, or in a rational soul,
and, in short, that the unity concerned the hypostasis of the nature and was not a voluntary unity of person—we utterly flee from them.
So that we do not make it subject to corruption and change,
and necessarily declare the unity of God the Word subject to suffering, but rather affirm a voluntary unity of person
and not of nature. Or let them be questioned on the basis of my words, since they accept that becoming human happened to the nature:
will they make the unity subject to suffering and change, like Arius, or not subject to suffering, like our fathers?
Which side you wish to belong to is your choice:
either the side of the heretics or the side of the orthodox fathers;
or the side of those who say that he is not subject to suffering or corruption;
or those who say that the unity concerned the hypostasis, or those who say that it concerned the person.
But I say that the unity of God the Word is not subject to suffering, death, or change.
For these things, let whoever pronounces condemnation [?] condemn me.
I have preserved without blemish the faith of the three hundred and eighteen fathers who assembled at Nicaea,
declaring that he is not subject to change or death,
that God the Word always exists as he is in the eternity of the Father.
He did not come into being from things that did not exist, nor from another hypostasis, and there was never a time when he did not exist.
The Father is eternal; the Son is eternal; the Holy Spirit is eternal.
But the flesh that he took on, which came from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary, does not exist eternally.
Rather, there was a time when it did not exist, and it came from another substance,
and from another nature, and from another hypostasis—that of human beings.
And he was not changeable, mortal, subject to suffering, or corruptible from the substance of God the Father. It was not
from the substance of God the Word that he was changed into the substance of flesh,
but flesh in substance and flesh by nature, which did not change from its own substance.
Nor, again, was he changed in his likeness from the substance of God into the substance of flesh.
He is flesh not merely in the form and appearance of flesh, but in the substance of flesh, from the substance of flesh.
The substance of flesh was not changed into the substance of divinity and made divine. He became flesh and became human neither through confusion nor through mixture.
He was not compounded into one simple substance, unique in its kind, nor into a natural composite constituting a single kind of living being.
Nor, again, was he naturally united through a natural union in hypostasis,
and suffered and came into being in a natural union, while they share in the very same things because of a natural sharing in sufferings.
For in every natural composition, they share together in one nature capable of suffering and change,
being constituted from natures. But for the nature of God the Word, it is not through a natural change,
but voluntarily: the union of the natures took place with respect to his person, not his nature.
Rather, the natures remain in their own distinctive properties, and there is one person without division or separation, since he made them his own in his person.
In the substance of humanity, divinity acquired a likeness. And in the substance of divinity,
humanity acquired a likeness, so that there might be one person of the union.
Thus, the things belonging to humanity belong to God the Word, and the things belonging to divinity belong to the humanity in which divinity became human,
so that they may be joined inseparably in one and the same dispensation on our behalf.
For they were [?] with reference to divinity, as to our renewal and our being formed anew,
and to the likeness of the image of the image that had been lost from us; but with reference to humanity, because it was renewed and received its likeness anew.
For humanity ought to have preserved the way of life it had.
For the one who was honored with the honor of the one who honored him, but did not repay him his honor for the honor he had received,
showed that he had destroyed the honor with which he had been honored. For that one too was honored just as this one was.
And that one did not receive him as himself, but regarded him as an enemy.
But when this one came into these circumstances, he preserved himself in this way, making use of what belonged to that one as though it were his own.
This one truly preserved the image of God and made it his own—the one who is the image and the person.
For this reason, it was also necessary for the divinity to renew and create and give a form
to the form of a servant, as though from its own pattern. But it was also necessary for the humanity,
so that the form of a servant might be taken as the form of God, and God as the form of a servant; and this might be that, and that this,
in person, while this and that remain in their own natures, preserving sinless obedience [?] because of his original obedience.
And for this reason he was handed over to death for the salvation of the whole world.
For it is not as Arius and Apollinaris, who venture to say
that in his goodness God the Word accepted an earthly way of life and obedience to death in his incarnation.
For this reason, the incarnation took place in a semblance of a human being, in a natural union,
so that the divinity might naturally become human in place of a soul,
and live and truly suffer with natural sensation, so as to be handed over to death on behalf of everyone,
and naturally accept the death belonging to the soul’s capacity for suffering [?], in the unity of a natural hypostasis, being torn away by compulsion.
For this reason, they assigned to the incarnation of God the Word
a single human nature in a natural composition, and an incomplete human being,
so that the substance of God the Word might take the place of what the flesh lacks to complete human nature,
while he receives commands and does the things that belong to those who receive commands,
and truly endures the whole human way of life, with difficult, painful, and distressing observances, against his will.
What he wishes to do, he does not do, for fear of transgressing the commandment,
while thirsting and hungering and experiencing human fear, while willing
with a human will. And he is in the body with all the things that belong to the soul,
which acts within the bodily frame through its formation and the form of sensory perception, while understanding,
while learning, while being perfected in the flesh in the nature of a soul, in a natural and hypostatic union.
And they abolish that voluntary union of the natures in the person,
while establishing a natural, rather than voluntary, appropriation, so that God the Word shares in the sufferings of the soul and the body.
And this appropriation comes from compulsion, not from the will, but is natural, arising from the hypostasis:
a natural union of a natural hypostasis, so that it is a nature that suffers.
But we ought not to be Arians, nor again Manichaeans, holding that the incarnation was only an outward appearance.
Or, in their account, attribute everything to the nature of God the Word: his way of life, sufferings, and death.
For it was not the nature of God the Word that sinned or transgressed God's commandment, so that he should lead a life of obedience and keep all the commandments,
and, as one found through his conduct to be without sins, die on our behalf.
“Through a human being came death,” it says, “and through a human being came resurrection.”
For this reason, the incarnation of God the Word also required a complete human being, complete in body and soul,
so that he might live in human nature and maintain the obedience and conduct proper to human nature.
And they eagerly desire and honor the name [?] “Mother of God,” so that they may say that God died.
And again, concerning this expression from our fathers, those who, even to the point of death,
stood against the heretics who say “Mother of God.”
Yet they did not [?] these names there, nor did they use them in the writings of the synod.
Was it because they did not know it? Or because they hated it? Or did they have some consideration in mind,
by which they adhered to divine teaching and paid no attention to the deceit of their opponents,
and gave no opening for diminishing his divinity by making it subject to suffering and death?
For someone who speaks of divine things in name alone is not said to speak of divine things.
Rather, it is someone who speaks of divine things in reality as well as in name, and gives no permission to those who are ready to make him something made and created.
It is not someone who supplies material for blasphemy and does not accept that God the Word actually came forth from the Virgin Mary,
as one who exists and has existed from the beginning.
And concerning the fact that a human being was born from her, as one who had not existed and came into existence, he is questioned:
“Do you, then, speak of God the Word as God and a human being in both natures?
And, as one born a human being, does he exist in the nature of God the Word, or was he changed into another substance, that of a human being?
And is this how you say that he was born?” “For,” he says, “he did not have his existence from a human being, but from God the Word.”
And he makes use of a human being's outward form, but not a human being's substance.
Book 2.1
But Athanasius does not allow you this, when he says: “... These things did not happen merely by borrowing.”
Far be it! [?] as some people supposed, but truly and really.
When our Savior became human, he became salvation for the whole human being.
For if he was in a body only in a borrowed sense, as they say—and what is spoken of in a borrowed sense is an illusion—
then it follows that the salvation and resurrection of human beings were only apparent,
as the wicked Mani said. But our salvation is not an illusion.
The body that came from Mary, then, is a human body, according to the divine Scriptures,
and it truly belonged to our Savior. [?] No one accepts speaking of God the Word as being in a body only in a borrowed sense,
but rather of God as God the Word, who existed beforehand and exists eternally.
He became embodied and is also in a body, without passing from his own substance into the substance of flesh,
and he underwent birth in the flesh, but from our substance. [?] For the nature that came from Mary is human,
as the divine Scriptures say, and it truly belonged to our Savior.
For it is over the substance of God the Word and the substance of the human being that I differ with you, not over a name.
For I do not object, I said, to the expression that the Virgin gave birth to Christ.
Rather, I acknowledge as honored the woman who received God, from whom the Lord of all came forth.
You do not accept these things. And how can anyone leave you alone
and believe you as someone who says that God was born in this way? What came from the blessed Mary, then, is human,
even if you rejoice a thousand times against Athanasius. God the Word was in a body,
in that which began to exist from the blessed Mary; he himself did not begin to exist.
In the beginning was the Word, and God the Word existed eternally.
Confess the natures as they are; confess as you were commanded; confess in accordance with God's will to save you through the body.
And confess that the body was not changed from the substance of God the Word into the substance of flesh, then molded and given shape,
and grown and brought to completion in human nature and born.
Rather, it came from the bodily material of which we are formed, from human offspring. For he was Abraham's offspring.
Why do you turn the things belonging to the body into mirages and do away with the things belonging to its physical existence,
and attribute them to God, so that you cast doubt on both births?
When you make the birth of the body from God the Father beginningless.
For you call God the Word a body and a human being, subject to a beginning and subject to completion,
and say that he was born of the blessed Virgin, [because he became a human being].
How do you speak of the birth of the body? For you attribute birth from God the Father only to God the Word,
and birth from the Virgin. Speak clearly, and acknowledge the human nature
that comes from blessed Mary, as the divine Scriptures say.
And the question is resolved: God's substance is not subject to beginning, growth, and completion,
even if it is spoken of in this way through gradual manifestation.
Why do you abolish the names that indicate humanity?
Do you also wish to persuade people of the same thing about the divinity? But as something that does not constitute a denial,
and the statement that the divinity came forth from her, as indicating that it did not take its beginning from her,
you abolish; and you abolish the humanity that was born of blessed Mary.
For you say, “She did not give birth to a human being,” but act like deceiving demons, who show a human being as not being human.
For you acknowledge a human being, but God the Word; and you acknowledge God the Word, not a human being.
For you mislead people: you change substances by means of names.
For you say “a human being,” but posit the substance of God the Word.
And again you say “God the Word,” but posit the substance of a human being,
and you have exalted it with the name “God the Word.” They have nothing to say.
What comes from [?] Mary is a human nature. Therefore she is the mother of a human being.
He who took his beginning from her, developed, and reached completion is not God by nature,
even if he is called this because of gradual manifestation. [?] Therefore, by nature she is the mother of a human being,
but by manifestation she is the mother of God. If you say that by manifestation
and not by nature he was born of her, then he came forth united with the one who was born of her in the flesh.
Why do you set them out piecemeal and abolish them, like wonder-workers,
who make visible things invisible?
And do they do in appearance the things that are seen and those that are not seen? Christianity exists in truth.
Do not be mistaken ... The one who was born of the blessed Mary is human ... the one who had a beginning, advanced, and became an object of wonder.
He is not God by nature, even if he is called this because of his gradual revelation ...
Do you believe those who said these things, regarding them as truthful? Do you believe what you have written?
For you yourselves wrote these things. Or do you not believe them? Or do they speak of a mere human being,
because they say these things about Christ? Is it not figuratively that they say he is God in the flesh?
With reference to his manifestation, they say of God that he began and advanced.
For how can things that are united be called simple? Rather, you consider simple those things that are not both the same in essence:
the divinity, which is not humanity, and the humanity, which is not divinity.
But it is disgraceful, I think, for someone who has said that the distinction between the natures is not abolished by the union to say these things.
So you are saying what I too say when I offer praise:
that the divinity exists united with the humanity, and the humanity exists by nature and is united
with the divinity. And do you anathematize what belongs to my teaching? Anathematize these statements of your own as well,
if it is right to call them yours—these statements in which you have no confidence as being true,
while you persist in opposition to the Fathers and to the divine Scriptures.
For this discovery of heresy is wonderful and praiseworthy: you say all these things,
which no one acknowledges, and you alone have established your own doctrine against everyone—a doctrine that you supposed was accepted by everyone.
On the contrary, since you have treated everyone with partiality, everyone hates you as a person who shows partiality.
Thus the truth that everyone recognizes may be revealed: you certainly know it, but you do not dare to state it.
These things, then, are enough for those who want to know your thinking to learn on what grounds you criticize me:
as though I were someone who says that the essences are separated by distance in space,
but share equally in association and love,
and not in what they are by nature. It is in speech, then, that we distinguish the natures.
For divinity is one thing and humanity another.
But through their association, there is not one person and another.
You have put it this way so that they may grumble against me. Yet what I say appears to be the opposite of what you accuse me of.
I do indeed unite the substances. But from the union
of the substances I speak of one person, with a single equality in everything that belongs to the person,
who has both one substance and another—not in division and separation, but in the very same person.
But let us also pass over the other matters as quickly as possible,
lest anyone [?] that there is blasphemy in these things, or that through those things these too are condemned.
[?] As we were saying, then: “Do not be afraid to take Mary as your wife.”
“For what is begotten in her is from the Holy Spirit.”
For whether you say “what is begotten in her” or “what came into being in her,” this takes nothing away from the meaning.
“For what is begotten in her is from the Holy Spirit.” For if we say that God the Word was begotten in the womb—
for being present with the one who is begotten is one thing, and being begotten is another.
For it says, “What is begotten in her is from the Holy Spirit.” That is, the Holy Spirit created what was in her.
Look, then, at the fathers, as experts in the divine Scriptures.
If we apply “was begotten” to the one who became incarnate, God the Word turns out to be a son of the Spirit,
or to have two fathers. But if we say “came into being,” God
the Word turns out to be a creature of holiness. Avoiding the expression “birth,” they wrote:
“He came down for us human beings and for our salvation, and became incarnate.” What does “became incarnate” mean?
That he did not change from divinity into flesh? For by saying “became incarnate from the Holy Spirit,” they drew close to the evangelist.
For the evangelist too, when he came to the subject of becoming human, avoided speaking of birth in connection with the Word and used “becoming incarnate.”
How? Listen: “And the Word became flesh.” He did not say, “The Word was begotten through flesh.”
For wherever the apostles and evangelists mention birth,
they state that the Son was born of a woman. [?] Consider what was said, I ask you.
Where they use the name “Son” and say that he was born of a woman, they use the expression “was born.”
But where they mention the Word, none of them has dared to speak of birth through humanity.
Listen to the blessed John the evangelist when he came to the Word—to the subject of his becoming human:
Listen to what he said: “The Word became flesh.” That is, he took flesh, “and made his dwelling among us.”
That is, he put on our nature when he dwelt among us. “And we saw his glory, the glory of the Son.”
He did not say that we saw the birth of the Word. I therefore gave the reason that I thought was sound:
the reason why the fathers, in their formulation of the faith, did not say
that he “was born of the Holy Spirit and of the Virgin Mary,” but that he “became incarnate,”
so that they would not call the Holy Spirit the Father or the creator of the Son,
but rather [“he became incarnate of the Holy Spirit and of the Virgin Mary”], so that they would attribute the expression “he came to be” to the flesh, because he became incarnate.
For this is an account of creation. But what do you say? Say it openly.
Clearly rebuke those who blasphemed by saying, “He was born of the Holy Spirit.”
If he was born, the Holy Spirit is the Father of the Son, or the creator of God the Word.
For I said that the fathers [?] did not say these things, and I do not say them either.
Did I blaspheme by saying these things? Or did I wrong the fathers? If you can show that they said these things—
the fathers—say so openly. Which of these is he? Is he a creature, or the Son of the Holy Spirit,
God the Word? And if the flesh, which is fleshly, is a creature, and is not even a creature of the Holy Spirit,
say so openly. As for “he became incarnate,” he is certainly said to have become incarnate in his own nature.
It is not when someone else became incarnate that he is said to have become incarnate.
Rather, he himself became incarnate in his own essence, in the flesh that came into being and was born of the Holy Spirit.
For the expression “he was born,” according to you, contradicts what you said:
that when he was born, it is the flesh that is said to have been born, since he made the birth of the flesh his own. Yet not
that it was assumed [?] by appropriation, but in his own essence. Thus “he became incarnate” and “he was born” do not mean the same thing.
For this reason they set down “he became incarnate,” and not “he was born,” because they applied “he came to be” to the flesh.
For this reason the evangelist also said that he became flesh, and did not say that he was born,
so that with “he came to be” he does not place a limit on God the Word, but refers to the flesh that came into being: it became his flesh.
And God the Word made his dwelling among us. God the Word did not come into being, for he already existed.
And listen to them, for you are not being questioned by those men from whom you brought against me gleanings of [?].
Speak, then, Ambrose: do not neglect someone who is being wronged.
Do not become the mouthpiece of oppressors, and do not condemn innocent blood before you have heard the case.
I am speaking of the flesh that came from the Virgin Mary, not of God the Word.
For I confess that he is neither made, nor brought into being, nor created. Yet all these people stand against me like swords.
They are not even willing to hear the sound of my voice at all, and on these matters they bring you forward as a witness.
It was not death that I feared when I was wronged in this way, but that I was condemned as a wicked man by you yourself.
I spoke concerning [?], and I do not deny what I said, even if they raise a sword against me.
I said these things: “This one, then, is destined after these things to come from a woman, just as he did.”
Apply this not to the divinity, but to the body that was assumed.
He came from a woman through the body that was assumed. For this is the one who came down; this is the one whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world.
Does not Scripture itself teach you that it is not the divinity that needs sanctification, but the flesh? If, then, they have deceived,
they have deceived themselves, not me. What [then about you too, Gregory the Theologian?] Concerning these things,
what is your opinion? I ask, not because I do not know, but because the truth is being wronged in your name.
How do you understand the one who came from the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary,
who began, progressed, and reached completion? I am speaking not of the person, but of the substance. What, then? Are you giving something else,
besides what you gave them in your writings—that the man who was assumed [?] For the one who begins, grows, and reaches completion
is not God, even if this is said because of his gradual manifestation.
For those things of which our Savior consists are different from one another,
if indeed the invisible and the visible are not one and the same:
God who became human, and a human being who was made divine. [?] Speak also, wise Athanasius.
For you were subjected to many such injustices and endured them at the hands of the Arians, on account of
the tradition concerning the Son, God the Word.
What is your opinion concerning the one who was born of the Holy Spirit and the Virgin Mary—in nature, and not in the person resulting from union?
For we say that it was the one and same Son who was born of holy Mary, and not another,
but that one alone who was born as Son.
Christ is God the Word with his flesh, and he is one flesh with God the Word.
But in substance, God the Word is from God the Father.
And the flesh is flesh that he took from the Virgin in order to become flesh.
We do not speak of one person and another, for the person of the two natures is one.
For who is the one who came into being by nature from the Holy Spirit? And what is his nature? And of which nature is the Virgin the mother? For this is what must be asked.
Listen, all of you. [?] I said that the one from Mary is a human being.
According to the divine Scriptures, and it truly was that of our Savior.
For if the Word was in the body in a figurative sense, as they say,
then what is spoken of figuratively is an illusion.
It follows for him that the salvation and resurrection of human beings took place only in appearance, as the wicked Mani said.
But our salvation is not an illusion, nor is it the salvation of the body alone.
Rather, the salvation of the whole human being, of soul and body, truly took place.
The one from Mary is therefore human, as the divine Scriptures say, and it truly was that of our Savior. [?]
[?] Thus, he says, we also call Christ in the flesh God because of his conjunction with God the Word.
While we recognize the one who is seen as a human being.
Listen to Paul, who speaks of both: “From the Jews,” he says, “is Christ in the flesh, who is God over all.”
He first acknowledges the human being, and then, because of his conjunction with God the Word, he calls the one who is seen God.
So that no one should suppose that Christianity worships a human being.
Look and consider: he accuses me without cause, as though I were speaking of some ordinary human being who is far removed from divinity.
I speak of Christ in the flesh, just as I also speak of that very same one in his divinity.
For I did not say “the fleshly Christ,” but “Christ in the flesh.”
I speak of Christ’s flesh, because of its conjunction with God the Word, as something united,
and not separated from God the Word. It is united not merely in equality, but to God the Word himself.
And I said that the one who was visible in substance was from the Jews, not God the Word.
For I acknowledge that the human being, in substance and nature, is from the Jews, and not God the Word in his nature.
And I call him a human being by nature, apart from the nature of God the Word.
But he is God through the union that took place in the person.
Is this why you are angry with me? But listen to what Athanasius cries out to you:
“What came from Mary, then, is human, according to the divine Scriptures.
Our salvation and the resurrection of human beings are not a mere appearance or a fantasy, as the wicked Mani said.
Nor was our salvation truly accomplished for the body alone, but for the whole human being, both soul and body.
What came from Mary, then, is human, according to the divine Scriptures,
and it truly belonged to our Savior.” … Why, then, do you deny our salvation? Why, then,
have you condemned as wicked someone who does not deny it but confesses it? For either you deny that it is human, like the Manichaeans,
or, if you do not deny it, you cannot condemn someone who does not deny it but confesses it.
Listen to Gregory as he cries out that it is a human being who was assumed:
“For the one who begins, [?], and reaches perfection is not God, even if he is called this because of his gradual manifestation.”
Do you see that he says that the one who was assumed, who begins, progresses, and reaches perfection, is a human being by nature,
but God by manifestation? What darkness, then, has spread before your eyes,
so that you cannot see these things? But if you accuse these statements of mine,
should you not have compared these with those, since they support them?
But if you accept those statements and others like them, you should not have written these down as wicked statements.
I addressed those who deny the humanity that was assumed from us
and make their confession like the Manichaeans: I composed these words of mine, and not without qualification.
Rather, I set out with precise distinctions the properties of the natures and of the one person.
And again, in some respect, two: in one respect, as regards the natures, and in another, in conjunction.
But you have taken their role upon yourself.
So you are in every respect an enemy of those who accept my words, as someone who belongs to that group.
For we take from these statements and set them before you, crying out: “Our salvation is not a fantasy, O man!
The nature that came from Mary is human, as the divine Scriptures say.” … The one who begins, progresses, and reaches perfection:
He was not God, even if, because of his manifestation, he is occasionally called this.
[?] But just as we call the Creator of all God, and Moses god.
For he says, “I have made you god to Pharaoh.” And we call Israel the son of God: “Israel is my firstborn son,” he says.
And just as we used to call Saul anointed: “For I will not lay my hand on him,” he says, “because he is the Lord’s anointed.”
And Cyrus likewise: “Thus says the Lord to his anointed, to Cyrus.” And we call the Babylonians holy: “For I
will command them; they are holy, and I will bring them.”
In this way we also call our Lord Christ God, Son, Holy, and Anointed.
But although the sharing of names is similar, the honor is not the same.
Why have you taken offense at these things, you oppressors and wise men? Because I said that just as we call the Creator of all God,
and Moses god, so we also call our Lord Christ God of all and Maker? And it is not because Moses is called god—
whereas Christ is God and consequently the Creator of all—that we speak of Moses as we do of Christ.
Or because Moses is Pharaoh’s god, do we consequently say that he is the Maker of all? Certainly not!
For sharing names does not bring about a sharing of honor and equality.
For the honor of the Creator of all is one thing, and that of Moses another. The former is honored as Creator;
the latter, as a creature appointed to be a leader. Likewise, both our Lord and Israel are called son.
For sharing names does not bring about a sharing of honor.
In this way, however, he says, he is God by nature, of the same nature as the Father, the Creator and Maker of all; but the other is not.
Likewise with each of the remaining names. Just as we speak of God, the Creator of all,
so we also call our Lord Jesus Christ God, Son, and Anointed.
Yet in relation to each of those called by the same name, the Creator
of all differs in nature and in the honors that are bestowed as gifts. For equality and honor surpassing all belong to his nature.
For I said that the name Christ and the name Son signify two natures:
divinity and humanity—that which has nothing equal to it in the things that have been stated.
Thus we ought to look not at the name, but at what it signifies. Christ is indeed God of all and Creator;
but Moses too is called god. For he is not called God in this way, nor is he understood as God.
[?] For they think they are mocking me on account of the humanity.
For, they say, if the one who came from Mary is a human nature, according to the holy Scriptures, yet is God,
by manifestation and not by nature, you call him God, Son, and Holy One by grace, as one of these.
But I say only this to you: if, like Gregory and Athanasius, you acknowledge a nature,
a human one, in the one who came from Mary, and that he began, advanced, and reached perfection, but is God by revelation,
and is distinct from every human being in the meaning of that name which he used to express the distinction,
as great as that between the Creator and creation, because he is one person, then I too acknowledge this.
But if you do not acknowledge a human nature that began, advanced, and reached completion,
or that he did not begin, advance, and reach completion, as Athanasius and Gregory said,
you are not even to be questioned as orthodox believers. Instead, take your stand with the Manichaeans.
And Gregory, Athanasius, and Ambrose silence you: if the flesh shares our nature,
and if the soul shares our nature, whatever he is, he too is of human substance.
He is therefore a human being, distinguished from us in honor and dignity.
Just as Israel is called a son, and Moses a god,
so too is Christ in the same likeness—not God by nature, nor the Son of God by nature.
And how did that God become human, except in human nature? He became human in the one who came from Mary.
But if he did not become incarnate in a human being, he saved him, not us. But if he saved us, he became incarnate in us,
and came to be in the likeness of human beings, and was found in appearance as a human being, but was not himself a human being.
Say these things and things like them openly, then. Why do you pretend that you do not say these things,
while you argue about them like those who say them, yet do not say them yourselves? And the things you do say,
you say only outwardly, and you are unwilling to call the one who came from Mary a human nature,
as is stated in the Scriptures. Whoever does not call him a human nature, like one of humankind,
from the natural body of our fathers, from whom we too derive, consisting of soul and body, and possessing all the qualities
of a rational soul, apart from sin—this person, like the Manichaeans,
Gregory [?] him. For, he says, the one who begins, advances, and reaches perfection:
He is not God, even if he is occasionally called this because of manifestation.
As regards his humanity, he is not divine by nature, but by manifestation.
