But in the nature of his divinity, he has a great distinction from all those called gods, lordships, or Christ.
But in humanity he resembles them all. And he is one person in two natures [?].
He is God, and he is the Lord, and he is Christ.
For he does not make use of a person characterized by division, but he made use of this one as his own person.
For he has everything belonging to the essence through union, and not by nature. Or do you not accept Christ in his divinity,
that he is God, the maker of everything, and not like Moses [?], even though Moses is called God?
For sharing names does not bring about a sharing of honor.
For the honor of the servant is one thing, and that of the master is another, even if, as regards the body, he is distinct from servants.
But if you say that the body and the nature of the body, and the rational and intelligent soul, remain without change and without alteration,
but do not accept those things that characterize [?] the soul and the body—
some of them through union, and some by nature—but instead attribute them all to one nature,
you falsify the truth, making yes into no, and no into yes.
And as if to deceive, you speak of a human nature, the one from Mary,
in accordance with the divine Scriptures, but you do not make the things belonging to humanity his by nature.
Yet in person you exalt him above all humanity, as someone different in essence:
the one who exists eternally as he is, and neither began, nor advanced, nor was perfected.
But the one who began, advanced, and was perfected is another;
and in union, in manifestation, in one person: God who became human, and a human being who became divine.
He was not altered or changed from his divinity, just as Christ’s humanity is not different in nature from human beings,
but in honor and in person. For he is God of all, and Lord, and Son;
and everything that divinity is in essence, humanity is in honor.
Not in another honor, but in that very same honor of the one who assumed it as his person,
with humanity making use of the person of divinity, and divinity of the person of humanity.
That this was assumed, and that the other assumed it—not as someone who would not acknowledge the one that was assumed, but as someone who would acknowledge it.
Therefore acknowledge the one who assumes as having assumed, and the one who is assumed as having been assumed.
But in what sense is one distinct from the other, and in what sense are they one and not two? In the same manner as in the Trinity.
In his own likeness, as his own [?]. From the fifteenth quire. Have this attitude in yourselves:
the attitude that was also in Jesus Christ, who, although he was in the form of God, emptied himself and took the form of a servant.
He does not say, “Have this attitude in yourselves, which was also in God the Word,
who, although he was in the form of God, took the form of a servant.”
Instead, he used the name “Christ,” which indicates both natures without danger.
He names both the form of a servant, which he assumed, and the form of God in connection with him, while the things said are distributed without reproach between the two natures.
These statements too should be used to examine everyone's thinking, and mine first of all, to see whether it is as this man says:
that I speak of one and another, and separate the divinity into some portion, as though by spatial distance,
and do not acknowledge that he is one and the same. But I said “without danger” because he named the form of a servant and God.
We understand neither the nature that assumed nor the nature that was assumed separately.
Rather, the nature that was assumed is contemplated in the nature that assumed, and the nature that assumed is itself contemplated in the nature that was assumed.
For henceforth the nature that assumed [?] is not contemplated independently and on its own, nor, again, is the nature that was assumed,
unless it is in that person belonging to both the nature that assumed and the nature that was assumed.
So it is not for this that you rebuke me, but because I distinguish the individual properties belonging to each of the natures,
so that each of them subsists in its own individual reality. I do not say that these properties are attributed to God the Word
as though he were both natures in essence, or that the properties of flesh without an individual subsistence are attributed to God,
so that he merely appears in the likeness of flesh, makes use of it, and experiences everything belonging to flesh;
or that he was changed into the nature of flesh, or that they were mingled into one nature;
or that, through confusion or change, the properties of flesh are transferred to the essence of God;
or that, through a natural composition, to complete that natural composition, he experiences the body's sufferings as one susceptible to suffering,
while the body, in its own nature, contributes nothing to the saving work undertaken on our behalf and performs no human actions,
neither through the soul's will, nor through human thought, nor through bodily sensation.
But with the thoughts and will of God, and also with God's faculty of sensation, he experienced everything human.
But he has a body in name alone, without individual existence and without activity.
And for this reason you call him a human being only in expression and name, as though this were something superfluous,
since you do not agree to speak of a human being's essence and activity.
And let there not be two natures, each with its own properties, individual existence, and essence.
But perhaps someone says, “Because you do not acknowledge that it is the very
same one who is God the Word and Christ, you therefore rebuke those who say that Christ is one
and God the Word another, apart from Christ.”
If, then, I called Christ one and God the Word another apart from Christ,
or Christ apart from God the Word, you would be speaking correctly.
But if I have not said this and do not say it, but rather that it signifies something different, I am still saying this very thing now.
Do not distort what I say; in that very statement you can find the distinction in what it signifies.
For I said that the name “Christ” signifies two natures, whereas “God” signifies one nature.
But a name that signifies two is different from one that signifies one, without the thing itself being something different.
Likewise, someone might say about a human being that the name “human being” signifies one thing and “rational soul” another.
This does not mean that the human being is one being and the soul another, apart from the human being.
For someone who says “human being” does not speak of him without a soul, because apart from a soul he is not a human being.
Rather, the term “human being” signifies the unity of two natures, soul and body.
The other term, however, signifies a nature. For a nature is one thing, and the unity of natures is another.
What then? If God the Word is not something different apart from Christ, nor Christ apart from God the Word,
why do you not use the names without distinction, as though the same thing were signified by this name or
by that one? Instead, you make a distinction, saying, “I am not speaking of God the Word, but of Christ,”
as though Christ were one being and God the Word another.
But listen also to [?]: they are not one being and another.
For they would be one being and another if Christ existed apart from God the Word.
But it indicates one and another, if he is not one and the same in essence, visible and invisible.
And those things from which Christ exists remain in their own essences.
And God the Word does not exist in the nature of both.
You acknowledge distinct natures, those of divinity and humanity, but one Christ from both.
You do not say that God the Word is different natures, but one; yet he has a distinction in relation to the other.
Then you call Christ one and another, because you say that he is different natures:
those of divinity and humanity. But the nature of God the Word is one; he is not different natures.
Or, as I said, he is not one and another,
since Christ does not exist apart from God the Word, nor, again, does God the Word exist apart from Christ.
But it indicates one and another, because Christ exists in union from God the Word and from humanity.
But God the Word is one nature, and not from two natures.
And it is not through union that he has his existence as God the Word.
You too bear witness to these words that I am saying, even though you are unwilling.
Indeed, you bear witness when you say, “The natures that came together in union are different, but Christ is one from both.”
For if you do not indicate one and another, why did you not first venture to say what you urge me to say:
“God the Word is one from both”? But you could not say it,
or I could not bear to hear your impiety stated so nakedly, and for this reason you passed over it without expressing it.
So that you could not deny this and would have no escape, you were compelled to acknowledge the truth plainly.
He indicates one and another, this one and that one; yet he is not one thing and another.
For those from whom our Savior exists are one and another, but he is not one and another—far from it!
This is also the case with the Trinity. But you attribute to God the Word the things belonging to the flesh:
that he sees and speaks and experiences the sufferings of the body, while merely making use of the flesh,
as the Arians say, assigning the activities and sufferings to the divinity by nature.
And as Apollinaris says, he takes the place of the mind and by nature performs the functions of the soul and the body.
Likewise, this man too makes use of God the Word in everything, and of a body and a rational soul.
that he should experience the sufferings of the body and perform the actions of the rational soul, as the activity and conduct of God the Word.
And the things belonging to his person, to the nature of God the Word
he attributes, and not to the person of the humanity, which is moved by humanity as a human nature is,
but by God the Word. But who is a complete human being
who does not act and undergo things as human nature does? He is a human being in name only,
and a body in name, and a rational soul in name, if he is not moved in his own nature:
neither as a soul, through thought and will, nor again as a body, through sensation belonging to the soul.
Instead, God the Word was established as the will, thought, and sensation in the body and soul,
so that God the Word might perform and experience these bodily things [?],
and these things belonging to the soul: anger, rage, desires, fear, trembling, and thoughts,
and actions, judgment, and voluntary choice. All these things he himself performs and experiences in place of the soul and in place of the body,
so that, through the victory of God the Word, a victory subject to suffering and belonging to him by nature, the nature that had been defeated might conquer,
when he gave it his own victory, so that it might conquer through him and in him who had assumed its nature.
All these things alter the nature of God the Word when they are attributed to him as things he experiences by nature;
and you call his nature capable of suffering, change, and alteration.
For one who in his nature was incapable of suffering, but whose nature became a nature capable of suffering,
is capable of suffering, corruption, and alteration. For one who by nature is incapable of suffering and is not
subject to change or alteration does not in any way suffer in human nature what he is not capable of suffering in his own nature.
But if you say that one who is not capable of suffering in his nature suffered by nature,
it is a fiction to say that he suffered in another nature. Whoever resorts to fiction is certainly deceiving,
and, like the Manichaeans, makes our salvation something that happened through deception.
Tell us, what do you say? Which is the choice of the orthodox:
that of those who teach that God the Word is not subject to change or alteration,
or that of those who say that he has a human nature from Mary? Those who consider him to have a rational and intelligent soul and to be a complete human being,
and then deny the distinctive properties of humanity and do not acknowledge that they exist as they do in human nature:
And birth, growth, upbringing, and gradual advancement in stature, wisdom, and grace;
and the commandments, their observance and fulfillment, and suffering, the cross, death, and resurrection—
they attribute all these to God the Word as to someone subject to change and alteration.
What are you saying? Teach people:
how should they think and confess? Is God the Word by nature two substances,
or do you think that the man is by his nature two substances,
of divinity and humanity? Or is God the Word one substance, and his substance received no addition,
remaining as it was eternally? And is the man's substance one, belonging to human nature,
and did he both exist and conduct his life according to human nature? Do not confess these things and then deny them again.
God the Word became human so that in himself he might make humanity the likeness of God and renew it in himself in human nature.
Then he renewed his handiwork and showed it to be without sin through the observance of the commandments,
as one who alone was able to renew the one who had originally fallen by transgressing the observance of the commandments.
Or did he give himself in his place to keep them, because he could not be kept free from sin?
Then our fall remains without healing.
It is like a paralyzed man who is healed yet continues not to walk; instead, the physician walks in his place or carries him,
and does not say to him, “Get up and walk, for this is why you were healed: so that you could walk.”
For this reason he took the form of a servant, which was without sin at its creation,
so that through the observance of the commandments he might also receive a name more excellent than every name,
and so that what existed in the renewal of his handiwork might be confirmed through observance and vigilance.
For this was also the purpose of the renewal of the handiwork, because of the incarnation:
that through him he might struggle against sin. But if that was not accomplished
for which he became human, then it did not happen at all. Instead, all these things are mere appearance and invention:
those concerning the first man's disobedience, and also those concerning his condemnation to death.
For someone who did not have a nature capable of keeping the commandments could not keep them.
For this reason, [?] the second man kept them; rather, God conducted his life and kept the commandments in his place.
For he was by nature one who does not sin.
And if this is so, what need was there for the conduct of his humanity to demonstrate
that he who was God the Word could observe the requirements of human life,
which he who was a human being could not observe? Otherwise, was it to demonstrate that he had no authority,
since, although he wanted to save him from death, the Father was unwilling? He himself lived on behalf of everyone and was kept free from sins,
and, as one who had not sinned, gave himself as a ransom on behalf of all human beings.
These are the teachings of the orthodox, who confess one essence of the Father and the Son, and one will and one power.
These are the teachings of those who confess that the things pertaining to Christ are neither fiction nor mere appearance.
He was not acting in pretense [?] when he was hungry, thirsty, and afraid, or when he learned what he did not know,
and in all the things that could establish that he was a human being. For
he was truly God by nature, and a human being [?] and in truth.
For this reason, it was necessary for the divinity to renew the human being, and for the humanity to be renewed,
and to receive the image of the one who created it, and not his essence.
And it was necessary for it to observe carefully the conduct required of the human being who had fallen, because it had also been created for this purpose:
to conduct itself according to the law inherent in human nature and to preserve the image of the Creator
uncorrupted through observance of the commandments, while the divinity made use, in its own person, of the likeness of a servant,
so that, in the very person in whom humanity had been defeated, its victory might be established when it conquered.
For from the newness of its formation it possessed the image of sonship from the one who created it.
But it also needed the reward for observing the commandments,
so that the person might be common both to the one who gave the image and to the one who received it because of his obedience.
Because Adam did not preserve that image, although it had been given to him from his formation, it was taken away from him.
Therefore, do not destroy the purpose of the incarnation, but acknowledge the distinctive properties of the divinity,
and acknowledge the distinctive properties of the humanity, and acknowledge one person of the union.
All these things are true, and all are orthodox. If you wish to listen,
hear these very same things, on these very same points, from the testimonies that you yourselves have brought forward.
I said: “Have this attitude in yourselves, which was also in Jesus
Christ, who, although he was in the form of God, emptied himself and took the form of a servant.”
He did not say: “Have this attitude, which was also in God the Word, who, although he was in the form of God, took the form of a servant.”
Instead, he used the name “Christ” as a designation indicating two natures, without risk.
By it he names both the form of a servant that he took and God. Yet Christ is one and the same.
I said “two natures” of the form of a servant that he took and of God, without separation.
Say these words of Gregory: “There are indeed two natures, God and man, but not two sons.
For those things from which our Savior is constituted are one thing and another.
But he is not one person and another—far from it! Rather, he is one through the blending: God who became man, and man who was made God.”
And again: “The one who begins, advances, and reaches perfection is not God,
even if he is spoken of in this way because of his gradual revelation.”
He did not say that God the Word was two natures, nor that he came to be from two natures.
Nor did he say that the man was two natures, or that he was constituted from two natures.
Rather: “Two natures, God and man.” For he used the designation common to the natures: “Son” and “Savior.”
Without division, he names him God and man. And he distinguishes that twofold being into two natures, those from which our Savior is constituted.
In the union, one is called what the other is. Thus:
“God who became man, and man who was made God”—not that he was changed from his divinity.
“The one who begins, advances, and reaches perfection is not God, even if he is spoken of in this way because of his gradual revelation.”
Whom, then, did he call one? And in what respect two? And whom did he describe in terms of substance, and whom in terms of union?
Ambrose too said the very same things, not anything different, about the union of God and the flesh:
“The Son of God speaks in both, because both were in him. The Son of God speaks,
because both natures were in him. Look at him: the glory belongs to God, but the sufferings belong to man.”
For he too speaks of the union of both natures, not of one nature being two natures,
but of both natures being in the one person of the Son. The glory belongs to the divinity, but the sufferings belong to the humanity.
For he does not call the Son one person and God the Word another Son.
Rather, it signifies something else, such as person and essence.
Just as with the name “God,” so also with the name “Son.” The one designates the natures;
the other, the person [?] of the Son. He himself is God and Son, and is one person of both natures,
and not of one essence. Therefore both are one Son, and both natures are in one Son.
The two natures are not one God the Word, nor are the two natures one divinity.
For there was no confusion, no mixture [?], nor, again, any transformation of the essences into one nature of essence;
nor, again, any natural composition into a composite nature.
What, then, did you hear in my words that was foreign, and condemn,
and set down these things? For he uses the name “Son,” and that of “Savior,” while Athanasius uses that of “Lord.”
But how did those who are called Christians dare to disagree,
if the Lord who was born of Mary is Son in the essence and nature of God the Father,
but was born in the flesh from the offspring of the house of David? For the flesh is from Mary the virgin.
For you too know that what comes from Mary the virgin is human nature.
In nature and essence he is the Son of God, in the essence and nature of God the Father.
But in the flesh, he is human nature from Mary. For he used the common name “Lord,” which is understood as belonging to nature and in nature.
There are also expressions that indicate the properties of the natures, as he makes both known: divinity and humanity.
The one is from God the Father by nature, and the other is from a woman by nature.
When he calls the one from God the Father human, he is not saying that he is from God the Father in his human nature.
Rather, he also makes both natures known through their natural properties.
He does not make the human nature without a person and without a hypostasis, nor the divine nature either.
Nor did the incarnation for our sake take place as something superfluous that accomplishes nothing,
so that we should attribute human things to God, as the Arians say:
that he suffered our sufferings by nature, in his own nature and person, while the flesh contributes nothing.
Rather, just as humanity is understood in its completeness as the nature of a human being, everything that belongs to human beings
he possesses completely, both in acting and in suffering, as is possible for human nature.
In his own likeness, while his own [?]: from the sixteenth quire.
“At the name of Jesus,” he says, “every knee shall bow, in heaven and on earth and beneath the earth, and every tongue shall confess that Jesus Christ is Lord.”
Because of the one who put on the garment, I honor the one who was put on; and because of the one who is invisible, I worship the one who is visible.
God is not separated from the one who is visible. Therefore I do not divide the honor of the one who is not separated.
I distinguish the natures, but I unite the worship.
I ask and implore you to examine everything carefully,
so that no one blames me as though I were presenting and dividing the divinity and the humanity into separate parts,
like things that are separated from one another in isolation.
For how can the wearer be separated from his garment, or the one who is hidden from the one who is revealed?
As we also added in those very words of ours: God is not separated from the one who is visible.
But you say to me, “I distinguish the natures.” How, then, are the natures confused—
those that are not separated? For they are recognized in thought as essences [?], without confusion and without mixture,
so that in the union both natures are preserved in their natural properties and in the characteristics
of their essence, according to nature, so that the divine nature is conceived in the nature [?] of God,
and the human nature is conceived in the nature of humanity, in its essence. This divides into separate parts:
the one who said that humanity is conceived by nature in divinity, and that humanity is not conceived as divinity.
Nor is God the Word conceived in both natures, whether in outward form, or without the subsistence of the flesh,
or in susceptibility to suffering, or in the activity of the senses and in the nature of the flesh. For if he is not conceived in this way,
neither is he conceived in any other way. Nor, again, is it otherwise possible, apart from this,
for us to circumscribe by a distinction the one who is without limit and cannot be circumscribed.
For in that very statement he made in his letter, he holds this same understanding:
“The differences of the natures,” he says, “are not abolished because of the union.”
For through their natural differences he distinguishes the things that are united, while making the distinction without separation; for he distinguished them in the account of their essence.
For the account and conception of divinity is one thing, and that of humanity is another.
For those things that are distinguishable are distinguishable.
But I speak of two natures: the one who put on the other is distinct from the one who is put on.
And there are two persons: that of the one who put on the other, and that of the one who is put on. But you too acknowledge that he is from two natures.
Each of them is known through the differences between the natures, not without a person and not without an individual subsistence.
Two persons of sons are not conceived, nor again two persons
of human beings, but of one human being. For this takes place in exactly the same way also on the part of the other.
For the union of the persons took place with respect to person, not with respect to essence and nature.
It is not as though a single essence were conceived without an individual subsistence, as one that had been united into a single essence.
And there is one person of one essence.
But they maintain the natures in their persons and in their natures, and in the person of the union.
For the other also makes use of the very same natural person of the one because of the union.
And thus there is one person of both natures.
The person of one essence makes use of the very same person of the other essence. For which essence
do you wish to make without a person? That of divinity? Or that of humanity? Then you must not call God the Word flesh,
nor call the flesh Son. But if you call God the Word, in both natures,
God and man, but call the man nothing at all, something else must be considered concerning your position.
Either you speak merely of the name and outward form of a human being, without any nature, from which God the Word receives his designation;
or you hold that humanity contributed nothing by its nature to the person of the saving dispensation on our behalf;
or that it was so that God the Word could be revealed and undergo human sufferings without his will.
For while the humanity suffered without awareness, God the Word was undergoing the sufferings of the body
and the sufferings of the soul and the sufferings of the mind. And he was acting and being acted upon.
And for this reason you make all these things belong to God the Word, and exclude the humanity.
If you draw back from this statement about two natures, which you acknowledged with me,
then, by the very same reasoning, draw back also from saying that God the Word became flesh,
and also from the flesh in which he became flesh or became human. Likewise, also concerning the man and concerning God.
But someone who speaks in this way does not make two Gods the Word, nor two fleshes.
Rather, he makes a complete confession, without deficiency, of the divinity and of the humanity in which it became human.
The humanity must not be conceived as a mere appearance, nor, again, as a change of substance or a change of form
from the nature of God the Word into human nature. And since this is so,
the human nature is not conceived in terms of mixture or confusion, or a change of substance, nor, again, in terms of composition.
All these are objectionable and destructive, and are suited to paganism and to heretics,
and they destroy the distinctive properties of every nature. But, excellent judges,
are you willing to bring forward the testimony from the Fathers that you have written down, so that I may use it? By my using witnesses beyond dispute,
you will learn that I too said these very things. Yet you condemned me as someone who had not said these things,
and you condemned me, as it were, in brutish anger and darkness. For what
else did I say beyond what Gregory said? “For those things of which our Savior consists are one thing and another,
since the invisible is not the same as the visible, nor the timeless the same as what is subject to time.
But he is not one person and another—far from it! For both are one through mixture: God became human, and the human being became divine.”
For notice that he calls the clothing visible, and the one who put it on invisible.
For God and the human being are one thing and another. But he is not one person and another;

to choose whoever was suitable? Did I not appeal to the bishops themselves, when I said,
“It is your responsibility to choose and appoint a bishop”? And I likewise appealed to you.
Did I not leave the matter in your hands all this time, patiently allowing you to make your choice without pressure,
so that haste would not cause me to make a mistake about the person chosen? Or did you make a choice and I refuse to accept your choice?
Do you want me to say something against you? Shall I speak of their campaigning, their running about, their gifts, their promises, and their oaths,
and everything they wanted to accomplish as though by purchase [?]? From among these,
whom did you want it to be? But I pass over these things.
Which choice did you want to prevail? Yours? Or his? Or someone else’s? For different people were choosing different candidates.
They were not acting as in an election, as though putting forward their own people [?], but against those who were wicked.
Everyone honored the person to whom he was somehow attached [?], and spoke maliciously about the person chosen by others,
and made accusations against him with vicious [?]. But you did not agree on a single person.
And you would not agree to the person whom the people had agreed on.
I read out before you the people’s acclamations concerning each of those who had been chosen.
What, then, ought I to have done that I did not do? You
monks did not agree with the clergy, nor did the clergy reach a common judgment, and the bishops were divided.
The people were likewise divided, and one person fought against another.
Even then I did not claim authority for myself, but left the choice to you.
But when you all remained in turmoil, you all came and gave me permission to choose whomever I wanted.
Then, after I had been persuaded only with difficulty, as you were all pleading with me,
I decided that no one from here should be appointed, lest he incur hostility and be hated.
For they all hated one another and were hated by one another, as people who had been campaigning over the matter.
Instead, I wanted an outsider, someone who was not known to the people here,
and who did not himself know them, someone distinguished in his speech and conduct.
For they informed me that there was such a man in Antioch, speaking of Nestorius.
For this reason I sent for him and brought him, although I distressed that entire city. For that was how the whole city was.
And I brought him for the sake of your [?], which I valued more highly than theirs.
But when it happened, you did not consider it to be so.
What, then, ought to have been done to the man? You did not [?] him, so that he might breathe concerning the accusations against him.
And your bishop was not judged on equal terms, but that the bishop of Alexandria should be
and of Rome, as someone who did not believe correctly; and he was supposed to submit to their decision.
But he sought and awaited a trial, as someone who had been wronged.
And he reproached them for having accused him unjustly.
For he was a bishop, and he ought to have been summoned before a court of bishops, not before my court.
Nor was someone such as he was to be a judge.
Nor was it right for the bishop of Constantinople to have his case heard before a single person.
Did I judge as I pleased? I gave authority to the council. Who asks for a trial
and is not granted one? Who is in the right: the one who longs for a trial and asks for it, or the one who runs away from a trial? Could he not have imitated them,
doing to them what he himself had suffered, and assembling the bishops under his authority
and those in the East who obeyed him, so that they might judge and accuse that man as guilty? But who did this?
Instead, he longed for a trial, especially to resolve these divisions.
For there is no law that the bishop of Alexandria, or of any other city, when brought to trial,
should not be tried. But even when the council had assembled and taken its seat, they appealed to him once and twice,
and he refused even to give them an answer. Why? Tell me; do not conceal it.
For I have not forgotten what happened. It was done so openly
that the arrangements they made cannot be concealed. For he was not being summoned by a court,
but through the arrangements of a council assembled in a partisan manner to judge those who did not please us.
Such a gathering is not even a council, when an opponent sits among the judges.
And did we not also command that nothing should happen before the whole council had assembled?
For we call the assembly of us all a council, not an assembly of certain individuals.
For we had foreseen the preparations and the deceit that took place,
we ordered that no council should be held with only part of its members, but that they should wait for all the bishops to assemble.
The examination of the matters under investigation was to be conducted through questions and answers.
They, therefore, dissolved the ecumenical council and set aside the law governing the court.
It was they who treated our wishes as nothing, and the bishop of Antioch did well by them
when he removed them from their episcopal rank, so that they would not remain in their offices and bring dishonor upon them.
What wrong, then, had the man committed who asked them to wait for those who were far away, and not to set aside the directive that had been given,
or cause a division in the council? For these things, should the man have been deposed who had violated none of the provisions laid down for the proceedings,
but was ready to be judged by anyone, although he was not being questioned?
When he had finished saying these things, he added, “I cannot find even a ground for reproach against this man.
I and the royal rule of my family are innocent of this wickedness.” They hurried to seize upon this statement and held him to it,
namely, that he should relent [?] and let stand what had been done against me through their actions.
Dalmatius and those with him cried out, “Let this guilt be upon me, O emperor!
I stand surety for you and yours in these matters. I will give up my spirit over these things before the judgment seat of Christ,
for it was I who did the deed—this deed . . .” And when he had received this assurance that he could be free from anxiety
concerning [?] those who were condemning me, he made his decision and confirmed what had been done against me.
This was how I was judged, and this was how the examination was conducted. When these proceedings, which they had prepared against me, were completed,
a decree [?] of condemnation was issued by the imperial authority. Others circulated other reports against me.
They carried Dalmatius along as he reclined on a bed that had been made up and covered.
Mules carried him through the middle of the city, so that everyone would know
that he bore the triumph of the emperor’s [?] decision, accompanied by a great crowd of people and monks,
who danced, clapped their hands, and shouted whatever could be said against someone who had been unjustly deposed.
When it became known that they had won over the emperor,
all the heretics whom I had previously deposed joined them.
All together, with one voice, they shouted out an anathema against me, taking what had happened as license to speak openly.
Everywhere in the city, but especially in the [?] of the sanctuary.
So that the crowd of people would join them in acting wickedly without concealment.
They openly persisted in this, clapping their hands and saying nothing else
except, “God the Word died.” And there was no distinction between the heretics and the orthodox:
all stood together against God the Word.
And against those who would not be persuaded to attribute suffering to the nature of God the Word,
they fought as against merciless evildoers, saying:
“The immortal was not joined to the mortal to put the mortal to death by his immortality.
Rather, on the contrary, he was joined to the mortal so that the immortal might become mortal.
And thus he rose, having died with him, through the immortality of the one who rose. And how could he be immortal at all?
So that he himself, in his nature, might admit both immortality and mortality, according to the power of the one who commands—
the power that can make the immortal mortal and the mortal immortal.”
These things were said outright by both sides and by other heretics; in houses, in marketplaces, and in all
the churches they were sung and accompanied by clapping.
From these things you could not distinguish what was being said in the churches,
or identify the churches themselves as belonging either to the heretics or to the orthodox.
For there was such agreement and zeal in holding to the faith and confessing a God subject to suffering.
They used arguments like these, on the very grounds on which they themselves were being accused,
and over these very things they were breathing their last.
They all had one mouth, one heart, and one common resolve against God the Word.
Consequently, the services in the churches and courtyards were neglected, and they devoted themselves to strife, persecutions, and deeds like these.
Those who supplied them with possessions, provisions, and luxury out of everything they gave
also made preparations for them and demanded that they occupy themselves with these things without respite.
The emperor therefore decided that I should be deposed, and that Cyril and Memnon should likewise be deposed.
It therefore seemed that he was doing this to compel us all to come to an agreement and mutually to accept one another and be accepted.
And to bring us all to one mind, he was patient about my release.
And he continued without reconciling with them, so that he might involve me too, by every possible means,
in their efforts and their petition on Cyril’s behalf, so that it would appear that imperial wisdom had prevailed
over their thinking. But this was not actually the case.
Rather, either his thinking, which had been sound at the beginning, had changed,
or he had held this opinion from the beginning and had only been pretending in his dealings with me,
as long as he found that patience was sufficient for his trafficking in possessions.
But however it may have happened, this was the situation I reached.
Now when Count John, who was in charge of the treasury [?], was sent to Ephesus,
and it was thought [?] that I would address the council [?], and that henceforth the affair would be beyond further inquiry,
in every respect it became a source of fear and astonishment to them.
Such was their fear and trembling at speaking with me and at having a judgment made concerning our statements
on the matters under investigation. Yet the impetus did not run its full course; instead, it slackened.
For that thing which people love had struck him—that very thing which even then was being spoken of as a rumor.
But in the end, the one who reveals hidden things exposed him and brought it to light, making him known before everyone.
He put him to shame during his lifetime, and after his death he was reproached—the man who had sold the truth, namely John.
And the one who was greater than he, namely Cyril, when that gold gained through injustice was being demanded
of him. But let this be set here: as these things happened, they cried out as though with a voice and made themselves plain,
to teach all people. For after John had come to Ephesus, he ordered everyone to come.
Memnon fled from what was happening. While they were bringing him out of the sanctuary, John summoned him as though for a friendly conversation,
and handed him over to be kept in custody, so that nothing would be lacking in what was required for the authorities’ examination of what everyone ought to do.
But when we had all assembled to hear the emperor’s letters together,
his resolve slackened in this way, and he became a different man, seeking to pass the time
rather than apply himself to matters that so deserved his attention.
For when the imperial letter, which had been written to everyone, was about to be read [?],
Cyril and those with him persuaded him that I should not come before him, but should listen from inside the doorway to what the emperor had written.
He did these things without giving any thought to what was proper, because he had already been bribed.
When they realized that the statements concerning me were being read, they praised the emperor with many acclamations.
But when he came to the statements concerning Cyril, they shouted and swore that these should not be read. With such childish boldness
they behaved—those who had been trembling from the outset and were eager to sink into the ground, if that were possible—
although they had no room even to breathe, either concerning what they had dared to do contrary to the command,
or concerning the examination of the faith. But after I had been placed under guard,
and Cyril likewise, ostensibly so that we should not enter and reach our cities,
which had already been ordered earlier by the emperor,
so that we should not be received by the authorities or by those entrusted with the administration of the cities,
he finally ordered me to live in my own city, wherever I pleased.
This was not a concession on his initiative, but a response to my request. For I had asked many times,
and had sought a favor from those who could speak freely with the emperor and were thought to be my friends:
that they should inform the emperor that I had no concern for the human glory of the episcopal office.
Rather, I long for my own monastery [?]. Do me this favor.
And before this, let there also be an examination of the faith without me,
so that their hostility toward me should not cause them to fall away from the faith.
For I had seen the preparations and the battles previously directed against me,
and when there was no ground for an accusation against me personally that would allow them to expel and dismiss me from Constantinople,
they turned against the faith. Through their hostility toward me, they also became hostile toward the faith.
And it seemed to me useful and helpful that I
should disregard my own interests, so that what was more urgently necessary might take place.
For when enmity is dissolved, how often people come back to their senses!
He had given me as a pledge of favor the very thing that he had sold to Cyril.
This too was revealed after his death, through the admission concerning me that was found among the written documents.
For at the very moment when this confession was made, death had gone out—that death which exacts its due from everyone and spares no one.
I was making use of help of this kind.
But while I became drunk with such honor, Cyril was kept under guard for a time.
Yet he, who was being guarded with every precaution, had hidden himself from those guarding him in Ephesus,
and from the officials who had been ordered not to let him travel to Alexandria.
He had left Ephesus and taken possession of his city, without being stopped by anyone.
For he had already bought this too with his wealth: he was not leaving the city by force,
but was contravening the imperial documents, against the emperor’s will.
He had also escaped the distress and punishment due for his violation of the imperial command.
But all these things were indeed allowed to happen in this way,
because of that anger against him, which was, as it were, a deceptive fabrication.
The affection toward me was of the same kind. For this reason, what appeared to be affection toward me
was always a reproach to me, because it was something purchased, not something that belonged to me.
For the hostility toward him was in practice transferred to me. These things against me, then, were done in this way from the beginning.
They left nothing undone that could convict me of having spoken falsely. Yet they are convicted by what they themselves wrote.
For anyone who wishes is free to examine the matter with complete precision,
and not to pass over with preconceived judgments the things they wrote to Ephesus,
so that, by reasoning consistently from their writings, he may understand who set all these things in motion and why he set them in motion,
and why that man did not act appropriately, as a brother toward his brother, reproving and advising,
asking and examining these matters between himself and the other man. Instead, he had first made them public, sent out letters, and filled everyone
with confusion, conflict, and hostility through the letters he had written. Why?
When I wrote a reply to his letter and accepted those things in it that were rightly stated,
while concerning those things about which I had doubts, as being improperly stated,
I also explained to him the reasoning for which I did not accept them, he gave me no reply,
either by way of instruction, or as someone who had not understood, or to say whether it was indeed so.
to uphold what had been written? Why did he stir up the Egyptian and Roman synods concerning the charges against me?
Did you perhaps ask me to defend my statements, as one living person before another living person [?]? Instead, on your own initiative and for your own advantage, you decided to collect my statements
and pass judgment against me while I was far away from you.
Why did you not come to me with your synod, as someone questioning me or reproving me,
as your predecessors did with those whom they saw needed them to come,
as Alexander did in the case of Arius, and Timothy in the case of Gregory,
or Theophilus in the case of John? For there was no one preventing you,
nor anyone denying the accused the opportunity to speak in his own defense.
No one who is absent and seeks a trial passes judgment on someone else.
No accuser acts as judge over his opponent while absent.
Why, when you were summoning an ecumenical council, did you refuse to come with a provincial synod
and defend yourself concerning the matters over which you accused and condemned me while I was absent? Why, when you came, did you not wait for the council that had been agreed upon,
but instead shrink from it? Why, when I was pleading with you and holding you back,
and adjuring you to wait for the council, did you refuse to await the arrival of the eastern bishops? And for the count who had been put in charge of
maintaining order, you did not wait, but instead treated them all alike with contempt? Why,
after all the bishops had arrived and the emperor had ordered—as though there had been no previous inquiry or examination—
that the matters between me, you, and the bishops of the East should be investigated,
did you do everything to prevent an examination and a trial? His aim was one and his intention was one, from beginning to end:
that there should be no trial or examination concerning the matters over which he accused me.
My intention, however, was that there should be a trial and examination concerning the matters over which he accused me,
even though this did not happen, because this man's flight and haste prevailed.
Why was I pressing forward while you were refusing,
if you were confident in the evidence you had from the Scriptures and the Fathers? But he was afraid of me because of the support from the emperor,
which, as they know, resulted in greater betrayal of me in these events, not in support. But suppose this was so:
who, then, was preventing a trial without the emperor's support? For once it had already been decided that I should leave Constantinople,
The synod of the East wanted a judgment and an examination of the faith to take place, even without me.
The king had also ordered that the depositions of both of them, as they had been deposed by the synod [?],
should stand without examination. Seven bishops were to be chosen from each side and sent from the two
synods to Constantinople, so that they could speak before the king about the matters requiring investigation,
and the rest were to be dismissed. Did they, then, speak with one another? But because they had gone to Chalcedon in Bithynia on the authority of imperial letters,
both groups of bishops who had been sent by the synod were received.
When he asked the Easterners about the reason for the division that had arisen, they said, “They introduce a God who is subject to suffering.”
They would not agree to make peace before these matters had been investigated.
“For even if you compel us by force, O king, are we to be persuaded [?] to accept a God who is subject to suffering?
For one whose nature has no impairment [?] has the nature of one who has such an impairment.
But if the one who does not suffer is of the same nature as the one who suffers, then even the one who has not suffered can suffer.”
The king appeared to tremble, and his ears could not even bear to hear these blasphemies.
He shook out his purple robes, saying, “I have no fellowship at all with people who are like this.”
Nor did he order that they be compelled by force. On the contrary, he ordered them not to let the matter drop,
but to seek the truth in every possible way concerning the matters under examination.
With this he dismissed them with many expressions of praise, ordering them to be ready for this examination.
When this was heard, these people again became agitated, seeking to prevent a judgment and examination of these matters.
But your imperial authority sent the Easterners away, while it ordered you—
by “you” I mean [?] those who shared your views, who were pursuing your cause—
to go to Constantinople and appoint another bishop in my place.
Where, then, had the trial taken place? And before whom? Tell me!
In whose presence? Even if it was a fabricated trial, tell me, you who wrote down what happened:
how did it take place? For there are many. Do not trust anyone on our side,
lest you say that he wrote out of personal affection. Follow your own people who put what happened in writing.
But you cannot erase the things that happened in this way and were written down at that time.
But perhaps someone will say, “What happened is plainly a fabrication.”
Yet it is undeniable that he did these unbelievable things, which call for much forgiveness.
For it is hard to believe that these things were done in this way; nevertheless, this is how they were arranged:
not against me alone, but also against the faith.
For its sake I was moved and took care to write and explain what happened, just as it happened,
so that they would not suppose that a trial and an examination had taken place, dismiss the whole matter, and abandon the faith. For the providence
and judgment of God were revealed to everyone, although there are some who see and yet do not see, who rose against me out of hostility from the beginning.
For even now he wanted to incite and spur everyone to hostility against me, so that I was condemned without a trial.
And before everyone alike he put up a barrier, so that I would no longer have any opportunity to reply.
By this he had hemmed in the party of the Easterners and those from the other regions, who had not joined them in what they did,
and who had given me help. And I knew nothing of what was happening.
Nor had I planned beforehand to bring charges against them and accuse them unjustly in court.
And I appealed to an ecumenical council against that council which represented only one part,
so that it might become plain to everyone why they had done what they did.
For it was not on account of the faith that he was confident and zealous, but so that his case and mine would neither be examined nor judged.
Through letters and various other means he had corrupted those close to the emperor and the empresses,
and was urging that no council be held. This was reported to the emperor, and he was severely reproved in writing,
so that he could not conceal it. For he ought to have welcomed a trial, if these things were not a pretense,
and eagerly sought to show the emperor that his thinking was upright and just. For this was done so
that he would have no excuse, as though he did not know what he was accused of and denied it.
And he obstructed the trial, not once or twice, but until death.
The emperor, however, acted in the opposite way toward the man whom he had rebuked.
But me, who had been praised and commended, and for whom many testified that I had been wronged, he condemned.
The shameful deeds were so numerous that they could not be concealed. But so that their injustice might be revealed,
he fittingly made even that man a witness and judge for me, so that the injustice would be without excuse.
For they all testified, “We can find no wrongdoing,” yet they condemned me without cause.
And while I was among them, while among them [?], they acted among themselves without examination and without trial.
And he changed everything concerning me. Concerning what happened when Cyril came to an agreement
with the Easterners, and before seven representatives from each side were sent.
But let us speak briefly. Perhaps someone will ask, “How, then, did the Eastern synod also condemn you,
so that not even one excuse for [?] in spirit would now be left to you?” For at the urging of the imperial government—
and everyone is fully convinced of this, and no one can conceal it—
it is one and the same matter concerning everyone: those who were at peace, who were in agreement with me and used to welcome
me and fight alongside me, and those who were accused along with me and suffered insults along with me,
although they had not received from me a single reason to change, they themselves changed sides and joined them.
Tell us yourself the reason they turned away from you. For because of your insolence toward me,
and your writings and the chapters you composed, they had anathematized and deposed you at Ephesus.
And you cannot deny it—neither you nor they—in view of what you put in writing.
So, when they did these things, they testified to both things concerning me: my orderly conduct and my fear of God.
But you, by contrast, they accused as an opponent, as an insolent man, and as a heretic.
They summoned you for trial to convict you on both counts, and they judged that you deserved deposition.
And when you were summoned by the emperor as [?] for trial, they had already accused you.
For they were convinced of your insolence and tyranny, and of all the evil things you had done at Ephesus.
For even at Chalcedon, before the trial took place, you closed all the churches to them so that they could not enter and pray.
You blocked the roads to the emperor, and you confronted them with stones and sticks.
And you drove them into confined places,
into places from which strangers could not escape—people unfamiliar with the roads,
who had come expecting the emperor to maintain order. And so they barely escaped
from those who were harassing them, until the emperor sent soldiers to help rescue them.
The crowd of those engaged in the uprising was beyond counting.
Then you were summoned from Ephesus, at that time by the Egyptians and by the monks in Constantinople,
and by those who had been rejected from monastic life, and all those who had been expelled on that account,
and who were eager to stir up disturbances.
Because of their monastic dress, they were thought to be acting out of zeal.
Then. Then they would receive food [?] and provisions from the monasteries, along with clothing,
which were given to them as though in payment for the fervor of their love. With these things they would fatten their [?] instead of practicing endurance.
These came from what you used to send for and bring from the storehouses and the warehouses of wine, oil, flour, and every kind of clothing.
You filled with them the monasteries that had been set apart for this purpose, as well as other places,
so that even the holy places of prayer were overcrowded,
and they filled the shelters [?] and entrances of every place that could accommodate them.
These things were in full view of everyone. And you supplied them with what are called blessings,
which were given as payment for these things—something that you had not done before that time,
nor did you do it afterward. You carried out these things
in such a way that you would not be thought to be sending these supplies to prepare an uprising,
but as though they were things coming to the monasteries and being received from the monasteries,
so that the recipients would not be reproached over the person on whose account they were receiving them.
They openly caused disturbances and turmoil, while being regarded as zealous men.
For you allowed them to do anything at all.
And you did everything to keep people from believing that they were doing these things. Tell me, then,
why did you allow these things to happen? And on what grounds did you drive away those who were suffering these things,
so that they were not even considered worthy of a hearing about why they were being driven away? What opinion did they have of you, and what opinion of me,
when they returned to the East? Each one of them warned his own city not to agree to the measures stirred up against me.
Why was an edict sent by the emperor through Aristolaus,
to compel them to accept what had been done against me? And as people of what sort, and with what attitude toward me,
was he sent to them? Why did he order them to accept you among the bishops? And what was the reason that persuaded them?
that they should [?] you among the bishops? You did not see one another or speak with one another,
nor did you say or hear for what reason you were [?].
And when there had been no trial, no examination, and no synod, how could you accept in a trial what you had not accepted,
and they accept what they had not accepted? Instead, you deliberated on your own and for yourselves;
you reached agreement with others about those matters for which you were rightly removed,
so that you might justly annul both synods, whether through fear,
or through forbearance, or through favoritism, or through all these together.
What defense do you have before those who accuse you
of having made a sham peace through favoritism and deceptions? “It was the emperor’s command,” you say. “It was the emperor who commanded us and prepared us for this.”
Tell me, then, why do you ask me how they accepted my deposition,
when they had not accepted it before? You should not be questioning me; rather, I should be questioning you:
How did you accept the faith that you had not accepted before? How did you conceal your chapters,
because of which you were deposed? How did those who had not accepted your standard accept you? And how did they accept the deposition pronounced against me,
when they had not accepted your wicked chapters? Do these things call for a question or for an answer? For it is not
the case that the affair in which I was openly condemned by everyone leaves me without a defense,
whether they are willing or unwilling. On the contrary, it also makes another defense necessary for me.
For those, therefore, who wish to examine the matter, these very things show how they happened,
and you yourselves agree with me about this. For they undo their own position,
and by their own judgment they have condemned themselves. For they had not accepted the matters examined by a synod,
but rather those which the two of you, acting together, agreed to annul,
whether you are willing or unwilling, apart from all the others.
Thus they would not annul in the name of a synod what they had once investigated, whether properly or improperly,
but would show that they had done what pleased the emperor by accepting what had been done against me, although previously they had not accepted it.
Moreover, they were also eager to avoid any mention of the chapters. They held to these two opposing sides:
you to my deposition, and they to the annulment of your chapters, because of which we endured all this turmoil.
But I endured every suffering and did not give in; and let it be said that, with God's help, I will not give in
until the final departure of my breath. Therefore, by accepting these things which they had
not previously accepted, they condemn themselves and also invalidate what was done against me.
For when the chapters are annulled, my deposition is annulled along with them.
Or was it not because I refused to accept these things that I was removed? For there is no other reason for my deposition.
But you say, “I did not annul the chapters.
Rather, I accepted John, who made the same confession as I did and agreed with me in the faith opposed to you.”
John also said these very things: “I accepted you, Cyril, because you agreed with me in the statements of faith.”
Who, then, was the one who accepted the other? And who was the one accepted? For you both say precisely the same things,
and you try to persuade those who separated themselves and withdrew from the deceptive peace you made.
You, for your part, because they accepted my removal, which they had not previously accepted,
were suggesting that they had also accepted these chapters which I had refused to accept.
But he, because he does not agree to include your chapters in the statement of faith,
those concerning which you insisted that they agree with you, on matters for which they rightly accused them.
For was not our entire inquiry, battle, and struggle concerned with these things,
so that we should not accept them? But it may be said that it was not because they had been annulled that they were omitted from the statement of faith
when peace was made, but because they were beyond dispute and inquiry.
If our entire inquiry and controversy concerned the annulment and abolition of these things,
it was for no other reason that they were not included in writing when peace was made,
except that they had not been accepted by common judgment and agreement.
How, then, do you hold to these things as though they had been accepted,
when they were not accepted in your confessions? For these things were not left open within the agreement
so that you and those with you [?] could use them as orthodox teachings, while those in the East treated them as heretical.
For this is not a single agreement in faith, but disputes and divisions.
But why were these things not annulled in the written [?] confession, but instead left standing? First of all,
For they were yielding to imperial coercion and wanted everyone alike to make peace.
After this, because they wanted to do him a favor, he was not to anathematize the chapters [?] in writing.
For it was enough for them not to accept them or even to put them in writing:
those which he had previously wanted to have accepted by force.
But why had he agreed that they should be left out of the written documents,
if he wanted them—as indeed he did—to be accepted as orthodox?
First, so that he would not be forced into a debate and be defeated, with the Easterners standing against him
and demanding, before anything else, that he be deposed over these matters as someone who had been condemned. This was what he feared.
For when he was pressed and cornered, he would necessarily have to state clearly what he believed:
either he would be seen to believe what was contained in the chapters and his letter, or else he did not,
and he too held the same views as the Easterners. In either case he stood accused.
Either he said the very same things and was seen as an evildoer, or he was clearly exposed as a heretic.
To avoid suffering this, however, he willingly agreed and accepted that there should be peace between them,
without written statements concerning the chapters. Afterward, however, those opposed to me were to grant him
what he wanted, namely my deposition, so that there would no longer be any possibility of my return.
For they all agreed together against me—something he had been striving for from the beginning.
Nevertheless, he did not succeed, because it came from imperial coercion and not from a just judgment.
Cyril’s letter to Acacius, bishop of Melitene:
Concerning those who criticized him over the peace he had made with the Easterners.
“And as for their attitude toward those who criticize the peace that has been made, I breathed a sigh.”
He, for his part, breathed a sigh as someone who had not accepted your chapters,
but had rejected them, those chapters for which you had all been so zealous.
But this man says that he had not agreed to anathematize them, although they had been very eager to have the chapters anathematized.
“And what you were insisting upon,” he says, “but did not believe would happen, I have accomplished:
they willingly accepted the deposition of Nestorius, and through it they also accepted the chapters.”
But he does not deny that he accepted his deposition.
But because you accepted and acknowledged in writing the faith by which the deposition is annulled, saying:
“You give us your assurance in writing, without dispute, that our statements are correct:
that you distinguish the natures and the divine expressions concerning both natures.”
What we were all urging you to acknowledge, but you did not acknowledge—this, he says, has now happened.
For it anticipates and establishes, in every possible way, what it obliges him to accept in faith.
Nor did we prevent the confirmation even of those who had been wronged over these matters; rather, we made the way still easier.
He, for his part, says: “I made them say ‘Mother of God,’ which they had not previously accepted.”
And he boasts and exalts himself over those who had opposed this confession.
But he acknowledged this: “I accepted ‘Mother of God’ [?] in a bare sense.” For the meaning must be stated:
the meaning through which God's personal and natural union is abolished, along with his natural birth from a woman.
For he says: “We acknowledge holy Mary as Mother of God, because God the Word took flesh and became human from her.
And from the very moment of conception, he was united in her to the temple that was assumed.”
It was not that he was born, but that he was united to the temple that was assumed and was born from her.
For we are not being questioned about the term ‘birth,’ but about the personal union of God the Word. For this reason, we caused it to be abolished.
He, for his part, says of God the Word that he is perfect God and perfect man, and that he is both in essence.
And for this reason, he says, he wrote: “Before the ages he was born from the Father in his divinity.
But in the last days, the very same one, for us and for our salvation, was born from the Virgin Mary in his humanity.”
He says that it is the very same one who was born from the Father and from the Virgin Mary in humanity.
Here again, because they did not examine clearly how to establish what was required or is required:
namely, the one Lord Jesus Christ, a complete human being consisting of a rational soul and a body, inasmuch as he is Christ
and Son and Jesus in both essences. And he is God in every respect, just as he is human by nature.
And in every respect he is human by nature, just as he is God the Word.
Both exist in essence; for this reason, each of them is from him and belongs to him.
Because these things were set down without comparison, he attaches to them a meaning suited to his own purpose.
And a spirit goes out to those who share his thinking and leads them astray.
Although no one has actually been wronged, each person pulls his companion toward his own goal.
And he accuses me of not having accurately stated what was said by the Easterners.
They say that God was born of a woman, whereas I do not say this. And he presents my words as hearsay.
For he says, “He said: ‘We have learned from divine Scripture that God passed through the virgin who bore Christ.
But nowhere do we learn that he was born of her.’”
And in another place in his exposition, he says, he stated: “Nowhere, then, does divine Scripture say
that it was God who came from the virgin who bore Christ, but rather Jesus Christ, the Son, and the Lord.”
For because he says these things, he divides our Lord into two sons.
For, he says, one is the one who dwelt separately [?], the Son and Christ and our Lord: God the Word, who was born of God the Father.
And another, again, is separately Son and Christ and Lord [?]: the one who was born of the holy virgin.
How can you conceal the truth? That is the only thing he does not say openly. They,
however, call the holy virgin the Mother of God because they speak of one Son and Christ and Lord,
perfect in his divinity and perfect in his humanity.
But he added what you yourself accepted and acknowledged: that there was a union of two natures.
And for this reason we confess one Christ, one Son, one Lord.
And do not mislead the wise Acacius, and through him the rest.
For it would not escape a man like this how he might be reproached for the faith he holds in opposition to you.
Perhaps you will likewise seize upon these statements of mine, and especially those concerning orthodoxy, which you accepted amid all this turmoil.
For I confessed two united natures, but you were denying
that from divinity and humanity there is one Christ, one Lord, and one Son.
He was born of a woman not in his divinity, but in his humanity.
It is not as God that he is one Son, who is from two united natures,
but he is one as a human being. Where, then, do I speak of two sons:
one who is separately Son and Christ and Lord—God the Word, who was born of the Father;
But another Christ, from himself and for himself alone, from the holy Virgin? You do not even understand these excerpts that you wrote:
“We have learned from divine Scripture,” he says, “that God passed through the holy Virgin who bore Christ.” These things that you wrote
that I say—how, then, can you cry out that I say: “One Christ, separately, is God the Word, who was born of the Father,
but another Christ is the man [?] from holy Mary”? About whom, then, do you say that the statement was made, “God passed through her”? Clearly, it was about God the Word, who was born of the Father.
How, then, [?] do I speak of Christ as someone other than God the Word, who was born of the Father? I said:
“He also passed through blessed Mary, without taking from her the beginning of his birth, as did the body that was born of her.”
For this reason I said that he who is God the Word did indeed pass through, but was not born,
because he did not take his beginning from her. But when both are united, he is, and is called, one Christ:
he who was born of the Father in his divinity, and from the holy Virgin in his humanity. For the union was of two natures.
And it is right for us to say to you, Acacius, that you have confessed one Christ in two natures without confusion.
In one nature, namely that of divinity, he was born of God the Father;
but in the other, namely that of humanity, from the holy Virgin.
How, then, can you call her the Mother of God, when you have confessed that he was not born of her? For if you said
that he was born in his divinity from the holy Virgin, she would be called the Mother of God on account of the nature in which he was born of her.
But if you too confess that he was not born in his divinity, in that
in which you confess that he was not born, how do you acknowledge her as the Mother of God? How can you accuse that man of speaking of two Christs,
when you yourself have confessed that Christ is two natures: one nature of divinity, which is called Christ,
and one nature of humanity, which you also call Christ? Either you confess two Christs through the difference of the natures:
one, the humanity that was born of the holy Virgin,
and the other, God the Word, who was born of God the Father;
or you speak of one, as that man said, by union, and nothing more.

And why did you go to all these lengths, and bring others out with you to do these things against a man who said these things?
Cyril.
“But,” he says, “God the Word, who is from God the Father, is not one Son,
and he who is from the holy Virgin yet another, as Nestorius thinks. Rather, he is one and the same.”
For this is clarified and explained afterward: he goes on to explain what “perfect God and perfect man” means.
He who was begotten of the Father before the ages in his divinity;
but at the end of days, for our sake and for our salvation, from the Virgin Mary in his humanity.
Of the same nature as the Father in divinity—he himself, the very same one; of the same nature as us in humanity—he himself, the very same one.
Therefore they do not divide him—Son, Christ, and Lord
and Jesus. Rather, they say that the very same one exists before the ages and at the end of times.
It is clear that he who is God from God the Father is also a human being from a woman in his humanity . . .
For how can he be conceived of as being of the same nature as us in humanity, when he was begotten of the Father, as you said, in divinity,
unless the very same one is conceived of and called God and a human being? And if it is one and the same essence of God the Word
that was begotten of the Father and of the Virgin Mary, why do you confess two natures of the union,
and not one for the very same one who was born of a father and a mother, as you wish,
and as you also compel us to conceive of him, and to allow you, too, to conceive of him? But those who accepted this confession
do not allow you to drag them wherever you wish.
Instead, they press and constrain you as a deceiver, requiring you to stand by what you confessed along with them.
For you confessed a union of divinity and humanity, since it was a union of two natures.
You confessed two, yet you say that they confessed one.
How astonishing you are! You confessed a union, yet you say that they confessed a division of the union.
How can one and the same essence be divided into two essences unlike one another—that of divinity and that of humanity?
And how can one essence [?] be of the same nature, when it is divided into essences that are unlike and different
from one another? For one essence cannot be conceived of as two essences that are unlike and different from one another.
And those that are alike are of the same nature as one another, in keeping with that likeness.
For in what nature is the Son the Son of the Father,
and in what nature is he of the same nature as us? For the essence of God the Father and our essence are foreign to one another.
Therefore he is also foreign to himself, and he is from two natures that are foreign to one another.
How, then, can he be conceived of as being of the same nature as us in humanity,
when he does not exist in the essence of humanity? And how is he of the same nature as the Father,
that he does not exist in his own essence? Or how is he in essence, when he is from the essence of God the Father
and from our essence, while the essence is one and the same—two essences alien to one another,
each of the essences both existing and being conceived in one essence? But if this is impossible,
and cannot even be accepted as conceivable in a truthful account, he is not in his own nature a nature from the essence of the Father
and from the essence of humanity, so as to be of the same nature as both.
Rather, in the essence of God the Father alone, he is of the same nature as God the Father.
But in our essence, he is of the same nature as we are. And he both is and is called one and the same,
from the nature of God and from our nature, in the person of the union. For in the natures he is naturally
distinct, because of the difference between the natures, which do not share with one another, according to the account of the essences.
And you cannot undo what you have bound. A union of two natures, he says, and not two natures that are one nature.
For a union of the difference between distinct natures is conceived and said to have taken place,
not a union of differences within one and the same essence. For coming into being belongs to a single essence.

Union, however, is a coming together of essences.
Cyril.
But, he says, these things do not appear this way to Nestorius. Rather, his aim looks entirely in the opposite direction.
So he said while preaching in church: “For this reason God the Word is also called Christ,
because he has a permanent conjunction with Christ.”
And again: “Maintain,” he says, “the conjunction of the natures without confusion. And we acknowledge God who is in the man.
We honor the man who, through conjunction with the Godhead, is worshipped together with God Almighty.”
Do you see how far astray his statement is? For it [?] great impiety.
For he said that God the Word was called Christ separately, but that he has a permanent conjunction with Christ.
Does he not, then, in fact speak of two Christs? Does he not acknowledge that the man who is worshipped together with God is honored? Do these things, then, our brother,
seem to agree with what those men say? They do not have even one
meaning in common. The former, indeed, spoke of two in actual fact.
But they acknowledge and worship the one—that is, one Son and Lord and God,
the very same one from the Father in his divinity and from the holy Virgin in his humanity.
They say, to be sure, that a union of two natures took place; yet they clearly confess one Christ, one Son, and one Lord.
Nestorius. It would have been right to say to you, wise Acacius:
Why are you misleading us? For you have confessed a union of two natures that are unlike one another.
And in the very matter for which you accuse Nestorius, you appear to confess the same thing as he does,
even though you do not say that two Christs are spoken of.
For it does not appear [?] that Nestorius, either, confessed two Christs.
But on the basis of the statements you report about him—that he speaks this way without confessing
that two Christs should be spoken of—you too appear to speak of two Christs.
For you have not said that Christ exists in one nature,
but that he exists in two complete natures, which are unlike one another in their essence.
Christ exists in divinity and humanity.
For since he is two, both natures are also called two Christs, under the one and very same name of Christ.
For whenever two natures that are unlike one another are called by the very same name, they are spoken of as two
with a shared name. But you have said that he is one by union. Nestorius also said this: two natures, one Christ.
They are preserved in their own natures and do not need to constitute one another,
so as to be constituted through their union; rather, they brought about the saving work on our behalf.
Divinity does not depend on humanity, nor, again, does humanity depend on divinity,
because in their own nature they are without need.
For divinity does not owe its being God to union with humanity; God is not dependent.
Nor, again, does humanity owe its being human to union with divinity,
but to the creative activity of divinity in the common nature, even though its union also existed from its creation.
For the union with divinity did not take place to complete a single essence, but for the person of the saving work on our behalf.
Nor, again, did humanity have divinity for the completion of its nature, but for the person of the saving work on our behalf.
For they bear one another’s person. And for this reason, the person of one nature
is used by the other nature as its own—not both indiscriminately in one and another.
