It was not by composition to complete a nature, as soul and body complete human nature.
Rather, in the person of one nature, another nature is [?] in that very person as in its own.
And for this reason, from the humanity that was anointed, the divinity too is called Christ because of the union. And he is
Christ from two natures, divinity and humanity: one Son, one Lord.
Through the union of divinity and humanity, he himself is Son and Lord and God.
For those things that are called one in union—that one, insofar as it is united, exists in nature.
And they are not spoken of separately, like things spoken of merely under the same name.
But if you [?] them, that one is not divided along with them.
For the substances exist together in his own nature, and in both of them he is named from his own nature.
Just as soul and body united together are called one living being, and are not called two living beings: soul and body are one living being.
For the body does not live by a life of its own, but through union with the soul.
And for this reason, if they are separated, life is not divided.
Rather, it belongs to the soul alone, from whose nature both are called one living being.
Let this, then, also be taken as an illustration concerning divinity and humanity: there is one person, though in distinction there are two.
It is not possible to conceive of that one without union. Rather, the human being is a human being, and God is God.
Both are one Son, one Lord. For when they are separate, it cannot be said of them that this one is what that one is.
For this reason, you too acknowledge a union of two natures,
and that these are two natures unlike one another: divinity and humanity.
Complete divinity and complete humanity. One Christ, one Son, one Lord.
Or do you perhaps call one nature Christ, and not two natures one Christ,
so that union without confusion of the natures is superfluous? But if the one Christ is of two natures,
you say that it is through union, as Nestorius does, that one is named from the other.
And why do you run outside to hunt down others, while exhausting yourself on their behalf,
when both are within you—these things and their opposites? [?] And again he sets out these very same things.
For, he says, he did not assume a nature in the way that some earlier heretics supposed:
But we maintain that the Word who is from God fashioned this body for himself out of the divinity.
Rather, following the divine Scriptures in everything, we affirm that he took it from the holy Virgin.
While in this [?] those of whom there is one and only Son, Lord, and Jesus Christ:
as we understand them in thought, we speak of two natures united.
But after the union, since the difference between the two natures has now been removed,
we confess that the nature of the Son is one, though he became human and became flesh.
But if it is said that the one who became flesh or became human was God the Word, this would exclude the notion
of change. For he remained what he was. Let us also confess a union without confusion.
Nestorius. For you acknowledge that, in those of whom Christ consists—that is, divinity and humanity—
you have acknowledged a difference in substances and their remaining without confusion.
But they remained without confusion as the natures that they are.
Therefore they remained so in the union as well. How, then, do the natures remain without confusion,
if after the union they do not remain as they are by nature? . . . For, he says, after the union,
the distinction between the two has ceased, and we confess that the nature of the Son is one.
For if they did not remain in the union as the natures that they are,
but their distinctions, by which they are understood as two, are abolished,
then even in the union, while the natures remain without confusion, confusion occurs.
And confusion involving change and alteration is the coming into being of a single nature.
What, then, is your view? Did the union take place without confusion in the natures that were united?
Then the two of whom there is one and only Son, Lord, and Jesus Christ are two even in the union.
And the natural differences by which they are understood as two are not abolished.
For this is not that in substance, nor is that this in substance.
For you must not think this way and yet fail to speak as
you think. How, then, do you accept in your thoughts the two of whom Christ consists,
but after the union, as though abolishing the distinction between the two natures,
Do you say that the Son has one nature? Above, you say that those from which the one Son exists are two.
And below, you say that the Son has one nature, as though the union of the natures took place in nature, and not in person.
As for the natures of those two that were united, they became one.
For this union involves alteration and change, since it brings about a nature and the completion of a nature.
This is not from two complete natures, but from two incomplete ones.
For every complete nature, in order to exist and live, does not need [?] in order to exist.
For in a natural composition it is evident that not one of the natures from which it exists is complete.
Rather, they depend on one another to exist and continue in existence, just as the body depends on the soul to live, for it does not live by itself.
And the soul depends on the body to perceive. Otherwise, it would see even when it had no eyes,
and it would hear even when deprived of the organ of hearing. The same applies to the other senses.
For how can you speak of one nature from two complete natures,
when the humanity is complete and does not need union with the divinity in order to be human?
For it does not derive its human existence from union with the divinity, but from the creative power of God,
who brought into existence everything that did not exist, even though the union took place at the same time as its creation.
Nor did the divinity depend on the humanity in order to know or perceive human things.
How, then, did the union of the Son result in one nature? Then abolish the two natures completely,
and there is room for the claim of one nature: without a soul, as Arius said,
or without a mind, as Apollinaris said. And you assign to the human being one nature outside all the natures.
And after this, God the Word is not self-sufficient, because he is not a complete nature,
since he depends on the human nature. But now you say all these contradictory things at the same time:
both that there are two complete natures from which the Son exists, and that the union resulted in one nature of the Son.
It can therefore no longer be understood from these statements that he is one Son. You spoke of two natures that are united,
and again of one nature of the Son, and you eliminate that of the flesh.
For this reason, after the union you abolish the distinction between the two,
since the nature of the flesh has ceased to exist, either because it was destroyed or because it was changed.
And you believe in one nature of the Son, but one that became human and took on a body.
Which nature and which other nature did you say the one Son is from? And what is
the one nature of the Son? Now those things that are united from two natures into one nature
are conceived of as coming from both the natures that were united, as, for example, composite things come from simple things.
Therefore the one nature of the Son is composite, and for this reason you said, “But embodied.”
How, again, is the distinction between the two abolished, so that he is not conceived of together with flesh? Yet you speak of two,
and say that two should not be conceived of after the union, as though abolishing the distinction between the two.
And you speak of one nature of the Son, yet necessarily concede that two are conceived of,
by saying that he is embodied after the union. For he has taken on flesh through flesh, which is flesh by nature.
Therefore you attribute two natures to the Lord after the union: one, the nature of the Son, and one, the flesh through which he has taken on flesh.
Or distinct natures are conceived of before the union: that of the Son’s divinity and that of his humanity.
And then they were brought together so that one nature was abolished.
But in this way the Son is not conceived of as being from two natures, either before the union or after the union.
Or do you say this: that they remain neither united nor separated,
and the nature of the Son [?] apart from the nature of humanity, as though abolishing the distinction between the two?
And before Acacius, as before a dog that is provoked and growls against you, you throw
the statement that after the union the distinction between the two is abolished, and you say, “We believe that there is one substance
of the Son.” And again, before the Easterners, you add, “But having taken on flesh,” so that they will not be provoked.
You also said this: that the union took place perfectly, without confusion. And you give everyone what he wants.
Acacius. But indeed, how often do our opponents say
that these people plainly name two natures when making a confession of the orthodox faith,
and distinguish the utterances of those who speak of divine things according to the difference between the natures?
And see how these statements are not contrary to those statements of yours:
for you do not agree to divide the utterances between two persons or hypostases.
Cyril. But, wise man, I say that they are written in chapters:
Whoever distributes the sayings between two persons or hypostases,
and assigns some of them to a human being understood separately, apart from the Word of God,
but others, as befitting God, to the Word from God the Father alone—let him be condemned.
But we have in no way removed the distinction between the sayings; we have also rejected dividing them
between the Son alone, the Word from the Father, and, again, a human being separately, a son [?] from a woman.
For the nature of the Word is truly one, for we know that he took flesh and became human.
Nestorius. Was it, then, through reasoning and a connected examination that he had persuaded
Acacius with these words, and was he not, rather, treating him like someone held by reins,
pulling him along to follow wherever he wished? For he said that there was a union of two natures,
from which there is only one Son and Lord and Jesus Christ, and, quite explicitly, that the union took place without confusion.
How, then, is the nature of the Son one, when you said that he is two natures?
That is, in the natures, that [?] the union was confusion.
How, then, is the nature of the Son one, when you said that he is two natures?
That is, what is he in the natures from which he exists? For there is no nature that is two natures,
from which he would be one and not two.
But, he says, it is in union that he is to be one; and yet again, it is not in union that he is one.
And we are to conceive of two without confusion, and of the distinction between the essences; and yet again, we are not to conceive of two, but one.
Who understands confusion without confusion, and dividing the sayings between two persons or hypostases,
and not dividing them between two persons or hypostases? These things require much examination,
a precise examination of [?] and otherness.
“If anyone,” he says, “distributes the sayings between two persons or hypostases.”
And again: “But we have in no way removed the distinction between the sayings.”
The one who said that the sayings must not be distributed between persons or hypostases
also, in turn, in no way removes [?] the two distinctions between the sayings.
For in what sense must the sayings absolutely not be distributed between persons or hypostases? From
You rule out two for us. How, then, is the difference in expressions
not something you have removed in any way? Even if, as you say, we have excluded dividing them, assigning them to the Son:
separately to the Word who is from the Father, and again to the man who is separately recognized as a son born of a woman.
For the nature of the Word is truly one; for we know that he took on a body and became human.
In what way, then, have you not abolished the difference in expressions?
But do you say that the eternal Son is by nature God the Word? Say so, and in union,
and not merely in contemplation, attribute flesh to him as well.
What is the difference in expressions that you have not removed? For there are differences between the realities set before us,
and differences are indicated by expressions.
For when there is no difference, the difference in expressions is also abolished.
He confesses two natures belonging to one Christ and Son, and also two differences. And according to the differences between the natures,
he makes distinctions between the expressions, and also distributes the expressions of those who speak of divine things.
How have you associated them with those who divide, when you accept the one who divides them
with a distinguishing expression [?]? How do you confess two natures in union,
belonging to one Christ and one Son, and again one nature of God the Word? For you said, “One nature
of God the Word we confess, and not two that are united.”
You speak of one Son, for you speak of the Son as two natures without division.
And again you attribute only one nature, and no longer two without division, to God the Word.
And you say that he is an incarnate Son, and again that he was not in the flesh.
Unless perhaps you call God the Word, incarnate in one nature, one Son,
and the Son who is from two united natures another—the one Christ and one Son.
You do not dare to say “one incarnate nature,” yet you confidently declare “one nature of God the Word who is incarnate.”
What, then? Is God the Word, one nature, one Son,
while the Son in two natures, from which he is one Son alone, is another?
For the nature of God is not said to be two natures, but one nature.
How can you say that Christ is one Son in two natures?
Yet these are the very things you say: both two natures of one Son and one nature of God the Word.
You say that the Son is from two natures unlike one another.
And again you [?] him, and give him only one nature.
You set aside one—I mean humanity—so that you do not confound the Son in the union.
By the term “natures,” you compel us to distinguish the properties of each of them, whether you wish it or not.
For why did you say “one nature of God the Word,” and not “two natures united”? Nor, again,
did you dare to say, “From them there is one God the Word alone,” as you said, “From them there is one Son alone.”
Let it be as you said: “We speak of two united natures apprehended in thought.”
Say likewise also about God the Word: “From them there is one God the Word alone—two [?].”
For my part, I speak of two united natures, following the divine Scriptures and the divine teachings,
and say that “God the Word” designates the nature, while “Son” designates the person.
Yet God the Word is one and the same. Just as “God” designates the nature,
“Father,” “Son,” and “Holy Spirit” designate the persons. For this reason the divinity is one,
but the persons are three. For the Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God.
The persons are not without substance. Again, it is the same way also with Christ:
two natures, one of God the Word and one of humanity.
But there is one person of the Son, that very person whom humanity also makes use of.
And there is one human being, that very human being whom divinity also makes use of.
This is not in nature, but in the natural person of the natures. For even in the union the natures remain without confusion.
There are neither natures without persons nor, again, persons without substance.
Nor did the union occur as it does in the nature of a living being, to complete a single living being, which, in order to be
complete, received from both of them. Rather, there are two complete natures, and one is spoken of in terms of the other through their close relationship.
This is not in nature, but in the natural person of the natures, and not in another nature.
What is different is spoken of as different in nature. For God the Word is by nature the Son of God.
In the same way, “the selfsame” is also applied to the humanity through the affinity of union, and not by nature.
For, it says, “Christ is the same yesterday, today, and forever.” He is the same in person, not the selfsame in nature.
Why do you congratulate yourself, while admitting that he is not the selfsame in substance?
Or, as you said, in the natural mode of humanity and divinity.
If it is right to call nature a mode? And again, the nature of divinity and of humanity:
You admit that they are united without confusion. You understand two that are not confused and that are brought together with one another.
You also acknowledge them according to their natures, because they remain without confusion.
Yet in the nature of each one of them they are conceived as one, since you confess this not in person, but in nature.
And you abolish the two that you acknowledged to be without confusion.
For you admit that two were united without confusion.
And again, like someone abolishing the distinction between the two, you say that two are not conceived when there is one.
If you did not have in mind the absence of confusion between two substances, because they were brought together into one substance, how then do
you say that this union must be confessed to be without confusion? And again, that we should not conceive as having been united without confusion
those things that were united without confusion? Or, as in what you said, that a union took place from two natures into one Son.
But after the union, you remove the humanity from the union into one Son,
so that it has been driven out of the union into one Son and is henceforth conceived outside the union.
The substance of the Son, however, is conceived by itself, and those things from which he exists are no longer conceived in one Son,
but only one nature. Yet you say that he is only one nature.
But, it is said, when the manner of the incarnation itself is examined,
two things, joined to one another inexpressibly and without confusion in one union,
are certainly seen by the human mind. But once they have been united, it does not separate them at all.
Rather, it believes that he is one from both, and is God, Son, Lord, and Christ.
In what sense do you say that he is one? In the person of the union of the natures that were united? Thus, then, the human mind shows
those things that are united without confusion. They are without confusion in their own natures and in their own substance,
and they remain and are conceived in this way. This is not conceived as that in substance, nor is that conceived as this.
For when speaking of substances, a distinction exists in the nature of each of them:
it is both conceived and exists. But in the union of the natures, in them,
in their very selves, there is one person, without separation and without division.
In the natural person, one nature uses the person of the other nature as its very own.
Thus, then, the natures that have been united are without confusion, and they are never divided within that same union.
Since they exist as natures, they are conceived according to the distinction between their own natures. Cyril.
But Nestorius’s wicked thinking, he says, is something entirely different from this.
For he makes a show of confessing that the Word, who is God, became flesh and became human,
but he does not understand the force of the statement that he became flesh. He names two natures and separates them from one another,
setting God apart by himself, and likewise the human being by himself,
joined to God only through closeness, equality of honor, and authority.
For he says this: “God is not separate from the one who is visible. For this reason, I do not separate the honor of the one who is not separated.
I distinguish the natures, but unite the worship.” ... But our brothers in Antioch, accepting those things from which Christ is known
as considered simply in thought alone, speak of a difference of natures.
For, as I said, divinity and humanity are not the same thing by nature.
Yet there is one Son, Christ, and Lord. And since he is truly one, they say that
his person is one, and they do not separate in any way the things that have been united.
Nestorius. And yet, if this had really been so,
you too would have relied all the more on this statement, which I cannot confidently understand.
But, as you say, I use it as an outward form.
You ought to have rebuked me before the whole synod.
Even when I earnestly begged you, you should not have concealed it, but should have maintained it before the whole synod.
And when you were summoned again to the synod, you should not have excused yourself.
For how many times did you do this and rebuke my wicked thinking?
Then I would no longer have been able to use any means of escape [?]. For someone who is exposed as thinking the opposite:
For whenever he shows partiality toward you [?], he condemns the wickedness of his own thinking on every count.
But perhaps it is not so, but the opposite.
How do you know that I confess that God the Word became flesh and became human,
yet do not say that he became flesh and became human? For whoever becomes flesh becomes flesh in [?].
But someone who says that they are divided and separated from one another does not confess the incarnation at all—unless perhaps he confesses that what did not
become flesh became flesh. For those things that are kept apart from one another so that they are not united—
how do they become flesh? If, then, I confess two natures and that he became flesh,
how did you suppose that I say the natures are separated and distant from one another,
so that I would not acknowledge the incarnation and the becoming human of God the Word? For you said that he said:
“God is not separated from the one who is seen. For this reason, I do not separate the honor of the one who is not separated.”
How does someone who says, “God is not separated from the one who is seen,” separate them? For the one who is seen from the one who is not seen—
you said that he does not separate them, nor does he separate the honor of God, who is not separated.
But if you say, “I do not separate God himself from the one who is seen; because he is not separated, I do not separate the honor either,”
whom did you say is not separated? And from whom is he not separated, so that for this reason you say, “I do not separate the honor of the one who is not separated either”?
“But,” he says, “he said, ‘I distinguish the natures, but unite the worship.’”
Just as you too have accepted the union of the natures, whether in reality or in outward form, without confusion.
Whether you wish to or not, you distinguish the natures by speaking of substances,
from which Christ is conceived, since you also speak of a difference, and say that
divinity and humanity are not the same in their natural character, as you yourself say.
For someone who says that divinity and humanity are not the same distinguishes them by a difference of nature:
this is not that, nor is that this. Now a difference of nature is a distinction.
Thus, distinction arising from a difference in the substance of the natures is one thing,
and separation arising from distance between the substances that have been brought together and united in a conjunction is another.
So the unity consisting in the conjunction of the natures, of divinity and humanity—
I have described it as being without separation: God is not separated from the one who is seen.
As for the union of the natures without confusion, I said that they are distinguished by their natural difference.
But I said that the worship of those which are thus both undivided and distinguished is one.
For they were brought together into one person, not into one substance or one nature.
For the union of the natures did not come about through confusion, nor, again, through a confusion that would produce one complete nature.
For the union did not come about from incomplete things, but from two complete natures.
For every union that occurs through natural composition to produce a complete nature comes about from incomplete natures.
But a union formed from complete natures results in one person and is established in this.
For it was not a body without a soul, nor a soul without
will and without thought that he used; nor did God the Word take the place of soul and mind for the body and soul.
But the church of the Arians and Apollinarians departed from this, since it does not accept two complete natures that have been united.
Nor do I separate the natures that have been united from one another by removal and isolation.
Nor do I speak of an association through love and closeness,
such as exists among those who are far apart, who are united in love but not in their substances.
Nor, again, did I speak of the union as consisting in equality of honor and authority, but as a union of natures, and of complete natures.
And I place the union without confusion in the coming together of substances.
But into one honor and one authority. For I spoke of a union of natures,
not of honor and authority. Otherwise, show it in what I said.
God is not separated from the one who is visible; for this reason, I do not divide the honor that is undivided.
Where, then, in these statements did I say that I separate the natures from one another,
and speak of God the Word on his own and the man on his own, saying that they were associated through the closeness of love
and equality of honor or authority? For I said, “I do not separate God from the one who is visible.”
It was not closeness, nor equality of honor, nor equality,
but God himself in his nature whom I said I do not separate from the visible nature.
And because God is not separated [?], I do not divide the honor either. For he himself is one thing, and his honor another;
and his substance is one thing, and what the substance is, another.
But even if I said that I distinguish the natures and unite the worship,
I did not say that I distinguish the natures from one another by a separation that sets them apart, as you unjustly accuse me of doing.
For if there were no other way of distinguishing the natures except the one that sets them apart,
you would rightly draw the conclusion against me that this is how I distinguish them. But if there are many other ways,
especially in the discussion of the natures, which is the whole subject of our inquiry,
and I said that the union of the natures took place without confusion or change,
how is it that this lies before your eyes, and you examine it above and below,
yet act as though I said that I distinguish the natures in this sense? And you assert that they do not divide [?] in any way those things that have been united.
You yourself had already spoken first concerning those who distinguish [?]: “Our brothers, however,” you say, “those in Antioch,
accept those things through which Christ is known merely in thought alone,
and speak of a difference of natures. For, as I said, they are not one thing
in their natural character—divinity and humanity—but there is one Son and Christ and Lord.
And we say that he is truly one and that there is one person.”
But you say that they do not in any way divide the natures that have been united, although they spoke of a difference.
We say: In this way he is shown to be complete God, his nature being diminished in no respect by the union.
And in the same way, again, he is a complete human being,
in no respect diminished by the union in the activity and sufferings belonging to his own nature. For whoever refers to the one person of God the Word
both what belongs to God the Word and what belongs to humanity, but does not in return attribute the person of God the Word to humanity,
steals the union of the orthodox and imitates it with that of the heretics.
For you learned from the orthodox, in the testimonies they wrote,
that they attribute what belongs to humanity to divinity, and what belongs to divinity to humanity,
and that what belongs to this is said of that, and what belongs to that of this, as concerning complete and united natures.
And they unite without confusion and make use of one another’s persons. How, then, have you allowed him whatever he wanted,
O wise judges? Either refute these statements of the fathers whom you brought forward as witnesses,
or, if you do not, you are necessarily obliged to accept on their side the one who speaks in accordance with their teaching.
Two in nature, and one person in union, in mixture, in manifestation, in conjunction.
God who became human; a human being who became divine. This one, on account of that one, is said to have become human;
and that one, on account of this one, is said to have become divine. What, then, have I said that is foreign to them,
for which you condemned me? Was it not right to confess two natures? Is it not right to confess one person of two natures?
This is what he said, in his formulation, that he confesses together with the Easterners. For if there is no distinction of natures,
how did you say that they spoke of a difference of natures? And how was it not the very same thing, since divinity and humanity exist in a natural manner,
being divided in nature according to the difference that exists? For in this matter, if he supposes that I speak of a natural distinction, he is not lying.
But the definitions do not belong to interpreters of inventions, for these are not inventions of mine.
Rather, they are the apostolic faith and the teaching of the fathers, and indeed your own confession too,
while you are under pressure and turn it this way and that, to say it and not to say it.
And you confessed that those from which Christ exists are two natures, and that they are foreign to one another in substance.
“We should not,” he says, “think that God the Word took something from his own nature—that is, the divine nature—and fashioned a body for himself.”
Following the divine Scriptures in every respect, we affirm that he took it from the holy Virgin.
Those from which there is one only Son and Lord and Jesus Christ, as we understand them in thought:
we confess two natures that have been united, and the natural distinction does not pass away.
For the indication of the natural distinction lies in their being called two.
And it is in respect of natures that they are called two. For the natural distinction belongs to natures,
by which you confessed two, except that they are united without confusion. For this reason, they are also two.
Again, you say something else to the contrary: that after the union there is one nature.
Because the distinction of the two has already been removed, he cannot agree with the Easterners in both these statements of his.
Yet you say that it is not even an indication of the distinction of the two;
the distinction, however, concerns not the union but the difference of substances.
But you, O wise man, in all your wisdom, also confess two after the union.
And after the union you decide to confess that there are no longer two natures. For you spoke of two natures that are united.
It is clear that they are united after the union, and not before the union.
How, then, do you confess two natures even after the union,
yet reject confessing two natures after the union? Which statement are we to believe? The first,
or the second? Or your own statement, that you confess along with the Easterners who confess two natures?
But Acacius does not: after the union it is not right to confess two natures, but one,
because the distinction between the two has already been abolished.
To everyone, as you wish . . . But, he says, they do not accept a natural distinction;
rather, they only define and distinguish the expressions concerning our Lord, saying that they are appropriate.
And they do not say that some of them apply separately to the Son, the Word from God the Father, while others apply to yet another son,
the one born of a woman. Rather, some apply to the divinity, and others, in turn, to his humanity.
For he himself is both God and a human being . . . And he wrongs me, lying about me as though I spoke of two sons.
Even these passages that he brought against me from him cry out, whether from the letters or from the homilies that they were excerpting for him.
As for what he has now said—that they do not accept a natural distinction, but only define and distinguish the expressions concerning our Lord—
let us see what those from the East said, and how he uses their words.
“As for the expressions in the Gospels concerning our Lord,” they say, “we know that those who speak of divine matters
treat some of them as common, as referring to one person.”
Do you hear how they confessed it? Referring to one person, not to one nature.
Why do you alter their confession, when they treat these expressions as common,
as you said, referring to one common person? You make it common, and nothing else.
With respect to whom do they treat them as common, when there is no sharing except among those who make use of one person? Say, then, “a common person.”
Speak of these expressions that make the one person common. He makes his one person common.
For something becomes common when it is constituted from contrasting elements, so that it is no longer individual, but
common. Just as a snake, then, receives a wound and coils itself around the wound,
covering the wound, but from pain stretches itself out again and exposes it against its will,
so you too dare to hide what you confessed, and afterward you confessed it,
although you are unwilling to accept what was confessed. For listen to your own confession:
For they required you to confess with them these things that you wrote ... concerning the expressions in the Gospels and the writings of the apostles that are spoken about our Lord:
We know that those who speak of divine things treat some of these expressions as common, as referring to one person.
Others, however, they distinguish as referring to two natures: those, they say, that are fitting for God, according to Christ’s divinity.
Others, the lowly expressions, they assign to his humanity. ... You agreed to hold and teach these things.
Why, then, are you concealing this now? For you said that the expressions they distinguish refer to two natures,
and not to one nature; nor are divinity and humanity the very same thing.
Rather, the things belonging to divinity are assigned to divinity, and those belonging to humanity to humanity.
They did not call one nature by two names, distinguished only in expression and not in substance, as you suppose.
For you say that the differences between the expressions were not abolished, but that through the expression they made known the natures and the distinction
between the natures. And you acknowledge that one may say there is a distinction between the natures.
For you said that they distinguish the expressions as referring to two natures.
Those among them, you say, that are fitting for God are assigned to Christ’s divinity,
and not to that very same substance in humanity, but in the nature of divinity.
For they do not speak of divinity as two natures, but as one nature, and of humanity as one nature.
For two natures are not named from one nature, nor one nature from two natures.
For he said that the distinction should be made with reference to two natures, and not to two expressions that indicate one nature,
but that they indicate two natures through the distinction in substance between the two natures.
These expressions are treated as common, as referring to one person.
Others, however, are distinguished as referring to two natures: those fitting for God are assigned to Christ’s divinity.
The person common to both natures is Christ, in whom, in that very same person,
the natures also make use of that very same [?], in that in which and from which both are known in substance:
divinity and humanity, without distinction and with distinction.
The common person is neither divinity nor humanity, for it belongs to both natures,
so that through this and from this both natures may be known. For he is one in substance.
For the substance of humanity also makes use of the very same person of the substance of divinity—not in substance, but in person.
of humanity: the essence of divinity makes use of it as such, and not in essence, as you maintain.
And, they say, we do not apply some of them exclusively to the Son, the Word who is from God the Father,
and others to another Son, namely the one from a woman.
Rather, some apply to his divinity, and others, in turn, to his humanity.
For he is God, and the very same one is also a human being. . . . If you say “exclusively” with the natures separated far apart,
you are not speaking to those who confess that the natures are united and that he was united into one person,
and that there are two natures, and that two [?] make themselves known and are known in him and from him.
But if you say “the very same one” in nature, so that the divinity that was born from God the Father is one nature,
and you likewise speak of birth from a woman, you are saying that God differs from a human being only in expression, but is the very same in essence.
You are speaking contrary to your own confession, and once again you are rushing to wage war against yourself.
For how did you confess, together with the Easterners, the distinction relating to two natures:
some of the expressions, those fitting for divinity, to Christ’s divinity,
and the lowly ones to Christ’s humanity? For the humanity is humanity by nature, and the divinity is divinity by nature.
Not to the divinity of God the Word, nor again to the humanity of God the Word.
For God the Word is not two natures and from two natures,
or two names or many names, with one essence having these names.
Nor is divinity conceived of as a nature, but only as an expression.
Why do you drag Acacius along with you, a man who loves you and is your kindred spirit,
whom you ought not to dismiss so casually? Is he to agree with you that you divide the [?] merely by a bare name and an expression,
not in their essences, but in expressions that have their existence in the mind?
Like expressions that indicate neither a definition nor a nature,
they have no distinction in nature or in essence, because they are not essences at all.
They have a distinction only in the expressions for the natures, because this is also how they have their existence.
In this way you also spoke of two natures in Christ—not in natures and essences,
but you say that they have a distinction only in meaning and in expressions.
“Our brothers in Antioch,” he says, “concerning those things from which Christ is known:
they speak of a difference of natures as people who accept it in bare thought alone.”
For divinity and humanity are not one thing, as I said, in natural kind ... You said “in kind,”
and not “in essence.” But a kind is not the nature of an essence,
but either the form of an essence, or of a nature, or of something without essence,
or a view predicated of natures in bare thought alone. This kind does not have a natural difference
of natures, but a difference of natures without essence.
Rather, he says that they are merely expressions in thought of natures without essences.
And concerning this he says, “Those things from which Christ is known:
they speak of a difference of natures as people who accept it in bare thought alone.
For they are not one thing, as I said, in natural kind:
divinity and humanity ...” But those from Antioch do not accept this, either to say it or to listen to anyone who says it.
Rather, they say, “As for the statements in the Gospels concerning Christ [?] our Lord,
we know that the godly men treat some of them as common, as referring to one person,
but distribute others between two natures ...” They said that they do distribute them:
they said that the statements concern two natures, and not that they accept a difference in bare thought alone.
Not in statements, but in statements concerning two natures, which are distinguished in respect of their essences.
The two natures are distinct, being distinguished by the expressions that signify them.
Not natures without subsistences, nor in thought without the subsistences of the natures,
do they establish them through expressions in thought, but in thought concerning natures that have essences.
Rather, they establish the thoughts and the natures in essences and natures. For this is very different from that.
For he says that they accept expressions for a difference of natures in bare thought alone,
and he does not accept the thought of natures that have essences.
Rather, without subsistences or anything to sustain them, they have their beginning from thought itself, and at its end they cease.
The one who says that the thought and the expressions of the natures signify them in essences, and that their beginning is in thought and in natures and in essences.
Thus, for someone considering the nature of substance, there are three corresponding modes:
the substance itself, the conception of the substance, and the expression that makes the conception known.
But whoever says that they exist simply in thought alone speaks of two modes:
the conception alone and its expression. For this reason, he allows a difference only in the conception of nature,
and not in substance, but in the mode in which nature is contemplated and imagined.
In the form of nature, and not in the substance of nature. For it is a mode of nature, and a form and appearance of substance.
For he brings and gathers everything to this conclusion: that it is without substance.
Who could have confidence in someone who treats divine matters so contemptuously? He does not have a single clear and reliable conception,
and he thinks about everything in the same way. He merely toys with those whose distress has reached their very souls and who are eager to learn the truth.
He imitates Origen, who says everything in such a way as to be accepted by everyone, granting everyone a favor in whatever
he says and persuading everyone by the very things for which he is hated by everyone, while overturning and nullifying through contradictions what he has put forward.
For everyone wants to remain with the things that please him.
For someone who changes these things like an enemy is an enemy to everyone.
They do not rejoice and find rest in what they have put forward. On the contrary, they are deeply distressed by what they have put forward.
For they do not rejoice in the things that satisfy him, since they consider these things to be outside the truth.
Rather, in those things in which they rise up against him as against an enemy of the truth,
he vents his anger—that is, concerning the faith of the Easterners—
and he did not preserve their expression in its own sense, unmixed, as it stands. Cyril.
For the children of Arius's wickedness, while wickedly mixing falsehood with the force of the truth,
say that the Word who is from God came from a human being, but made use of a body without a soul.
They do this craftily, so that, when they explain him through human expressions
and show that he is inferior to the Father's exalted status,
they may tell those whom they mislead through these expressions that he is another nature, separate from him.
The Easterners, therefore, are afraid of this: that perhaps the glory of the nature of God the Word might be diminished
by the things spoken in a human manner because of the dispensation with
flesh: we distinguish the expressions, without dividing the one Son and Lord into two persons, as I said.
Rather, we assign some of them to his divinity and others, in turn, to his humanity. Nevertheless, all of them belong to one.
Nestorius. For if they attribute the divine and human expressions to the one nature of God the Word,
making distinctions only in the expressions, how do they avoid saying
that the human expressions do not belong to the substance of God the Word? But concerning the human expressions you said
that they do not exist separately, although they are foreign to the nature of the Father, which is one.
For he is different in nature not merely in expression, but also in substance.
For the substance of the human being, as you said, is the substance of God. He is, you say, God and a human being.
Then he is foreign to the Father in every possible way and inferior in everything, according to your thinking,
since you think that in that very same single substance he is also a human being.
For you will not proceed by force while acting cleverly, nor will you be truthful.
They had distinguished the expressions so that they might be thought to distinguish them as referring to two natures of substances.
And they are reproached for providing support against God the Word, so that they might conceive of these as natures without substance, in thought alone,
as you understand it, since you speak of both these and those.
But they understand them as referring to two natures that exist substantially,
and distinguish these expressions according to what they truly are.
And they repel the Arians’ attack against God the Word.
For whoever attaches both sets of expressions by nature to one nature and the very same substance
provides support and assistance to the Arians in every possible way, to say that God the Word is foreign to God the Father. Cyril.
Surely this has not escaped Your Holiness: when they poured the faults of Apollinaris’s thinking onto my letters,
they also gave the impression that I say that Christ’s holy body is without a soul,
and that there was a blending, confusion, mingling, and transformation of God the Word into flesh,
or that the flesh was changed into the nature of the divinity,
so that nothing was preserved in its purity, and neither remained what it was.
Along with this, they also gave the impression that I am entangled in the blasphemies of Arius.
Because I was unwilling to recognize the difference between the expressions and to say that some of them are appropriate to God,
while others are human and are more particularly appropriate to the dispensation in the flesh.
But your Perfection itself bears witness on my behalf to others that I am free of such things.
Nevertheless, it was right that those who had stumbled should be reassured.
For this reason I wrote to your God-fearing self that I had never held the views of the followers of Arius or of Apollinaris.
Nor do I say that God the Word was changed into flesh, or that into the nature of the divinity
the flesh passed. For the Word of God is unchanging and unalterable,
and incomprehensible in every respect. Nor have I ever abolished the difference between the expressions.
Rather, I know that our Lord speaks both as God and as a human being, because he is both God and a human being.
Nestorius. How could you say, “All these things are suspected of me,” because you are unwilling to recognize the distinction between the expressions,
when you have not abolished the difference between the expressions? How, on the basis of what you have not abolished,
could it be suspected that you hold the views of Arius or those of Apollinaris:
that God the Word was changed into flesh, or that the flesh was changed into the nature of the divinity? For in defending yourself
against some people's suspicion that you are unwilling to recognize the difference between the expressions,
by the very reason you give in your defense, you accuse yourself of having given them grounds to suspect you.
But in the statements by which you defend yourself, when you say,
“I have not abolished the difference between the expressions,” you accuse your own self and those who suspected you
without finding grounds for suspicion—especially Acacius, who was particularly suspicious,
since he himself had accepted these expressions, which you did not accept at first.
Or how does he know that you have not abolished the difference between the expressions, and that you are thought
to hold the opposite? Or how could you say that God the Word was not changed into flesh, nor the flesh into God the Word,
and that the difference is only one of expressions, and not also of substances,
and that the substance of the divinity remained in its own nature, and the substance of the flesh remained in the nature of flesh,
if their substances were not changed? Or how do you attribute the human and divine expressions to one nature of God the Word,
so that God the Word, in that very same nature, is both God and a human being?
And was he not changed into flesh or into a human being? For it is impossible for both to exist in one and the same substance,
without that substance becoming the other, and likewise the other becoming that one.
Or does it perhaps become something without becoming it? And is it what it became, and is it changed into what it became? That is,
into the substance of a human being, and the substance of a human being also into the substance of God.
If he is God and a human being in one and the same substance and in one nature,
with the distinction between the two abolished, how do the substance of the flesh and the substance of God remain themselves, without his having changed,
unless they are conceived in the natures in which they exist without change? But if they are conceived without change,
how can those that are two not be conceived as two? How is the distinction between the two removed and abolished? Would these things not stir you and bring you to an awareness of their absurdity,
even if you were a stone, even if you were a demon who takes no pleasure
in anything good? For he cries out that the deed is his own, and he does everything like people who are utterly insane.
He said these things—these and others, everything and nothing. And yet he makes everyone
follow absurdities like these, without understanding either what they are talking about or what they confidently assert.
For they do not hold one and the same view about one and the same thing; instead, they deny it.
And they persist in the very things they deny professing, as though these were the true faith.
They hold in faith to things that belong to unbelief.
And they do not believe things that are evident and acknowledged by everyone. For faith is one thing, and nature is another.
For someone who says that things evident and known in their substance are something else by faith
does not abolish what they are by nature, but seeks to persuade us of things about them that they are not by nature.
But what it is by nature is, in power, what the person is.
For example, when he says of the bread, “This is my body,” he does not say that the bread is not bread,
or that his body is not a body. For he spoke of bread and body in a way that indicates what each is in substance.
But we are convinced that bread is bread in nature and substance. As for believing that the bread is his body,
this is by faith and not by nature. He seeks to persuade us to believe that it is what it is not in substance,
so that it may be this by faith, and not in substance.
If it is so in substance, what purpose does faith serve? For he did not say, “Believe that the bread is bread.”
For everyone who sees bread knows that it is bread. Nor again, in the case of a body,
do we bring about belief that it is a body. For everyone sees and knows that it is a body.
But he asks us to believe that it is what it is not, so that through faith it may become this for those who believe.
Therefore, in the case of things that are of different substances, it is impossible to believe of one that it is the other, as it is said to be,
when it is not so in its own substance, and for them to remain two, foreign to each other in substance.
But whoever abolishes the substance in these things also abolishes, along with it, what is understood by faith.
Therefore it is in no way right for someone who speaks this way to express himself openly.
Rather, he deliberately misleads, since he both accepts and abolishes these things, to show everyone that in him there are truths and falsehoods,
both orthodoxy and heresy, as though it had obeyed him in whatever he wished.
Not in a single one of the things I said were they able to show that I am a heretic; rather, in all of them
they showed me to be orthodox. And the things he had not raised at the beginning he raised in the words with which he breathed his last.
Thus even now he breathed his last on behalf of the Easterners, although shamelessly and deceitfully.
But someone says, “Why did the Easterners accept your deposition for impiety, for which they accuse him?
Even if you taught nothing foreign, nevertheless, in the very matters for which you accuse this man,
let them also be seen to bring accusations in those same matters. They reject these things, and they also accept these very things,
and there is nothing more.” For we ought to question this man about these things, and those men likewise.
But if you wish to learn from me as well, I will explain the matters to everyone, one by one.
It is not so that I may be accepted and helped by anyone.
For I have no concern for any human affairs. For I have died to the world, but I live for the one for whom I live.
But I will speak for the sake of those who have stumbled—not because of me or anything of mine, but because of this man, whom Christ compelled to breathe his last on my behalf.

For they said nothing else except that they had been compelled by the emperor’s command to accept all these things.
Cyril.
The bishops in Constantinople, he says, said, “The God-fearing Bishop John ought to anathematize

the teaching of Nestorius and acknowledge his deposition in writing.”
Nestorius.
So until then I was a bishop in the eyes of the bishop of Antioch and the Easterners, the orthodox bishops.
So when the God-fearing emperor very gladly agreed with them in these matters,
My admirable lord Aristolaus, the tribune and notary, was sent to put this right.
Cyril. When the emperor’s command was made known to the Easterners,
as though it accorded with the wishes of the holy bishops who had assembled in the great city of Constantinople,
though I do not know what they had in mind, they gathered around the holy and God-fearing Acacius, bishop of Aleppo,
and had him write to me about an agreement for peace among the churches.
It ought not to be otherwise than as it seemed right to them.
But this was a harsh and burdensome demand:
for they wanted everything written in letters, tomes, and books about the events that had occurred to be annulled,
after the coerced peace. Nestorius. Until the time when they wrote these things, this man too was among the heretics,
while everyone knew and took offense at what this man had written—not merely a few individuals.
What, they say, was it that drove them by force, when there was nothing
standing in the way of doing the opposite of what they wanted?
Understand, all of you who hear us: someone did sympathize with us
under the coercion imposed by the emperor’s command—not to add the sort of coercion they brought upon me.
But one becomes angry: why did they not stand by what they had once decided? For, compared with what was done against me, they showed less concern
for the correction and confession of the faith and the peace of the churches.
Rather, like a tyrant who comes to take captives but cannot capture the city,
he wants, as a pledge of peace, to receive the death of the man who fights against him on their behalf,
so that, once he has taken him, the city may be condemned. In the same way, this man also demanded that my deposition be granted without a trial.
Let this happen: as for me, what has happened to me does not matter to me.
Only let there be peace among the churches; for the good order of the churches, I endure everything.
But everything turned out the opposite way. For after he had received what he longed for,
and had subjected them to his authority for the sake of a merely apparent peace, he knew that he had gained nothing by what had been done against me,
but that the confession of [?], on account of which war had been waged against me, had been confirmed.
And it had become clear that it was hostility and coercion, and that it was a demonstration of these things that had happened.
and that they can also easily be concealed. But so that this would not happen, and so that my enemies would not in turn
become his accusers—those who had previously helped him in what was done against me—
he begins to attach himself to the confession of faith; he lowers himself and speaks on both sides, making contradictory confessions.
But they knew and had carefully ascertained that people had grown weak.
And they had suffered greatly, without having received even a single instance of help.
For this reason they do not readily dissolve the peace they made through the letters written to them by one another,
wishing to be left with those very things and to think in this way.
But because he had been accused [?] by those who held to his views and shared his confession, as someone who had departed from their common position,
and because he alone, through his domineering conduct and his contempt for them, had undone the efforts of them all,
he was afraid that they might withdraw from him or rise against him, and he strove to do more than they were asking.
And just as those captured in war, when they want to show that they share their captors’ views,
spare neither friends nor children nor parents,
so as to make them believe that they hate their own people, so this man too
immediately proceeded to stand against—against the fathers who had died long before:
against Diodore and Theodore, who were fathers to everyone, both while they were alive
and after they died. They were also this man’s fathers—the very same men who were ours.
Yet this man singled them out as enemies of everyone, although he himself had been in fellowship with them
and had regarded them as fathers and as orthodox. And their statements concerning the faith
he himself had also embraced with the greatest zeal, and he had ordered them to be sent to everyone.
But when he wanted to convince others that he had not slackened in his hatred toward me,
he wanted to anathematize those against whom no one had expected, or even imagined, that he would dare do anything of the kind.
And, most disgraceful of all to say, he was even undoing what had been done against Apollinaris,
and upholding the teachings of Apollinaris, saying that this was the faith of the church.
For which side should a person support? The side of Diodore, whom the holy fathers throughout the inhabited world,
and indeed the whole inhabited world, praise, and who opposed Apollinaris, Arius, Macedonius, Eunomius, and all the heresies:
With a single purpose, she regarded them as a common mouthpiece:
Or are you on the side of Apollinaris? Let us grant that I became your enemy because I did not obey you in what you asked of me.
Why do you fight on my account against those who died in the orthodox faith? Or is it on their account that you fight against me?
But I will tell the truth: because of your wickedness in everything, you fight against everyone.
Tell me yourself: were there not, in the days of Diodore,
Basil and Gregory? Were there not also bishops in Alexandria renowned for their conduct and their teaching? Were there not accomplished men in Rome,
who were capable of presiding over the churches? And were there not those throughout the inhabited world who were teachers, to preside
over the churches? They did not live amid purple robes, glory, honor, and luxury,
but amid persecutions, afflictions, conflicts, and fear; they guarded and held fast to the true faith without wavering.
From the man who was a heretic and was in error—that is, Diodore.
He was on everyone's lips, was circulated in writings, and was a terror to heretics.
Through the word of his teaching and through divine grace, he set himself against the imperial decrees
on behalf of God's people, and he did not destroy them, but increased them many times over.
And he secured all this peace for the churches. At that time he was not a heretic, either to the people of that time,
or to you yourself, or to your followers, or even during that disturbance which you stirred up against me.
But after you had grown powerful and taken control as you did,
and had attained this tyranny of peace, then Diodore became a heretic in your eyes,
along with Theodore and the rest of the others. For the way would also have been open to you against Basil, Gregory, Athanasius, and Ambrose,
and against the rest of the others, who all said these very same things.
Who would not groan that he came to this way of thinking? While they were strengthened by imperial decrees, fear, and punishments,
they were coercing the Easterners, and after peace they would lead them back and forth like captives and take them around,
so that they would anathematize their fathers. This is the peace and harmony they attained! This is how they came to think with one mind!
This is how they found relief from suffering harm: by handing me over to my enemy.
Because they were afraid, they said, “It is better for one man to be wronged and for the faith to hold firm.”
If only this had been true, so that this would not have happened to me!
But on the contrary, I was truly glad when the matter they were pursuing was being set right.
But on the contrary, they were distressed at what they had allowed me and at what they had permitted to be said.
And they no longer allowed them to speak, on the grounds that I too was saying exactly the same things.
And on these grounds they had expelled me; after that, they attacked Theodore.
And after him, Diodore. Then also each
one of the rest of the others; and they were devising the same plan,
insisting on their expulsion along with me, on the grounds that these men said these things and nothing else.
And it was right that they should either be expelled with me on exactly the same grounds, or that they should accept me too and also accept these men.
But they did not dare to say that I should be accepted.
For they had already expelled me once, and it was necessary that, even in sorrow, they should expel those men too.
And afterward, on these very same grounds, they would expel these men too.
For these men themselves hold and teach exactly the same things, and maintain that these things are true.
And with this audacity he thought he could stand against all the saints, accepting things and then turning back and undoing what he had accepted.
For this man revealed himself through his confessions from the beginning, gradually adding and subtracting while saying exactly the same things.
And he denied them, using coercion and authority, acting and scheming until he could abolish the assertion that there are two natures,
those from which Christ is. And he places the natures in names, not in substances.
And he prescribed, as though by law, that one nature should be confessed,
then struggling to undo and overturn those who spoke of two natures—not all of them at once, however, but
first certain individuals, so that, once he had gained strength against these,
he might gradually attack the rest as well, as people who said the same things as those men.
For in the passages they used as testimony, those men had said these things, and they themselves were saying them too.
And it was no new discovery: he was expelling these men as heretics.
And I too say what those men say; and thus they confess as heretics.
And they were extending this shameful wickedness against everyone, all of them together.
For it was not to show that I was a heretic that he brought forward these statements of the orthodox and of those teachers from earlier times [?].
But, on the contrary, he was setting these views of mine against theirs, to show that they were heretics.
These things they said are similar to my own views.
Let us also show what happened after these events, and let us begin with him.
Book 2.2
Concerning what happened in the time of Flavian. For after Proclus,
Flavian became bishop of Constantinople, a man who conducted himself with uprightness and chastity.
But he did not have the ability to speak openly and make his views known.
But the man who accused all the bishops had grown bold—the one who
alone remained after the rest of the others had died, namely Eutyches.
And because he was not a bishop, he used imperial authority to establish himself in another way,
as a bishop of bishops. For he directed the affairs of the church,
using Flavian as though he were a deacon in carrying out the orders given in Constantinople.
Because of his great humility, Flavian did not know what was being prepared.
He was expelling from the church as heretics everyone who did not share his views.
But those who supported him he established in office and helped.
Outside the church, he made use of the emperor's authority, an authority on which he relied.
And he did not want two natures to be spoken of in Christ, even as a mere expression.
He ridiculed the fathers who spoke in this way, accusing them of showing favoritism:
through favoritism they were concealing the truth, or they had expressed these views of mine as heretics.
For their teachings ought not to be accepted as a standard for judging the faith.
Thus, while he was confirming and [?] these things through imperial authority and decrees,
the whole East was thrown into turmoil over these matters, and there was no place that had not been shaken.
For he was overturning all these things as though they were things
that existed only in outward form. And already he was openly compelling them
either to say what they did not wish to say, or to suffer harm and receive punishment.
For Flavian had heard that the churches had again been thrown into turmoil over these matters,
that the monasteries had become divided, and that the people were split into factions,
and that already a fire was blazing throughout the inhabited world because of those who were going back and forth,
and that different people were proclaiming different things, full of impiety.
And he sent word to him, as they say, asking and imploring him to have pity on the churches of God,
which had been severely battered by the disturbances that had occurred previously. What had been imposed on them when peace came was enough for them.
And he asked him not to stir up against him these things that had not been stirred up against those who came before me,
“so that you may not be thought to have refrained from acting against them out of fear,
but in my days out of excessive disregard. For I admit that I am a poor man.
But who could be more at your disposal than others? Yet because of my humility,
you too exercise authority in this bishopric. And I have done everything you commanded without question.”
But he, in reply, said, “I am helping you
in your episcopal office, and you ought to rejoice in the change,
so that these measures, which were not attempted against your predecessors because of favoritism, may be attempted in your days without favoritism.
For now, that is, it appears that people have been cleansed of the teachings of Nestorius, yet they cling to his teachings.
And we appear to bear a merely personal hostility toward the man, rather than to oppose him because of his impiety.
For we condemned him, but left his faith free to run rampant.
Instead, we must completely eliminate the things he said and professed.
For he was not banished on the grounds that he professed two Sons separated from one another, each of them a Son in and of himself,
but because he professed two complete natures and one person consisting of two.
These must necessarily be called two Sons, since in each of the natures a Son is designated—one Son.”
Now Eusebius of Alexandria, who was bishop of Dorylaeum, had also come to Eutyches—
the man who was regarded as a confessor because of the statements made against me.
And he praised the boldness he had shown against me in the matters in which he had testified against me.
He said, “It befits your boldness to uproot those who are growing strong in the impiety of Nestorius.”
For this reason too, God himself sent you, not because you needed anything—for everything had already been provided and prepared from [?]—but so that
you might enjoy the fruit of your toil, if this too should be within your power. But if you approach the emperor in this way,
while you are being criticized by those who insist on accepting two, or rather, if you say that they should not be annulled—
those things that took place at the council in your days . . . But this man, thinking that he would not be disturbed,
was no longer concerned about these things. But because he was very devout, he said to him, “Be quiet,
and do not labor in vain, seeking to bring about things that are impossible.
Neither the whole council held at Ephesus nor Cyril himself annulled them; rather, he came to an agreement with the Easterners.
And afterward, peace was again established on these very terms, and he allowed those things that had been properly established to remain in force.
For it is impossible to abolish from the church the teaching that there are two natures in Christ, without confusion:
that of fatherhood [?] and that of humanity. He is of the same nature as his Father in divinity,
and of the same nature as us in humanity.” . . . Eutyches became agitated against him and said, “May God rebuke you!
For even Nestorius had not originally said anything about God, except as a troublemaker and a lover of glory.
For how can someone who has said these things that Nestorius said stand against Nestorius? For these words belong to that man,
whom you handed over with such great effort.” But Eusebius said
to him, “I do not know whom you mean.
For it is not because he spoke of two natures that I dispute with him, nor did the council condemn him on that account.
Rather, it was because he divides and sets them apart, placing God on his own and the human being likewise on his own,
so that they share, and are spoken of as sharing, only the very same honor and equality.
In this way he spoke of two sons, and said that the holy Virgin is not the Mother of God,
because God made that birth of his flesh his own.” And Eutyches said, “You are slandering him,
because you hold his views, so that you may not be thought to hold his views.
For he himself cried out countless times, ‘I do not speak of two sons; I speak of one.
I speak of two natures, not two sons. For the Son of God is twofold in his natures.
For this reason she did not give birth to the Son of God, but gave birth to the humanity, which is Son because of the Son who is united to it.’
And again: ‘God is not separated from the one who is visible.’
How, then, am I dividing the honor of him who cannot be divided? For it was not because he had plainly spoken of two sons,
nor because he had said that the natures were not united. “For I confess,” he says, “one who is twofold;
but I worship the two in one because of the union.” Rather, it was because, even after the union,
he speaks of two natures, and says that the Son is twofold in his natures, and that the union resulted in one person, not in one nature.
Yet you too, even while condemning him, say this very thing and nothing more.
All who show partiality ought to be humbled in the dust.
For after the union I recognize no other substance in our Lord.
Nor do I even entertain the thought that our Lord, who is our Lord and our God, is of the same nature as we are,
though he is of the same nature as the Father in his divinity. And Eusebius said to him, “Whether Nestorius said this,
as you say he did, or not, it is not my task to investigate that now.
But I do say this: whoever said these things spoke correctly.
You, however, do not join the orthodox in confessing and saying that the flesh is of the same nature as ours.
Either you abolish it, or you change it into the nature of the divinity.
For this reason, these matters must be investigated—the things you say belong to Nestorius,
on the basis of which he accuses the council and Cyril of lying about him, although they themselves hold these views.
And you confirm his accusation: that it is true that he holds these views.
Everyone condemns this opinion as impious. I will demonstrate this at the appropriate time. For if there is no nature in our Lord,
and he is not of the same nature as ours, then the substance of the flesh has been abolished.”
He had accused him of these things before Flavian and before the council assembled with him in Constantinople.
He had admitted them and persisted, displaying his impiety by not confessing that Christ’s body was of the same nature as ours,
as though speaking of two natures, but rather as of one nature.
This had stirred the emperor, and he wanted him not to be deposed.
But when he was not obeyed, he then made every preparation for Flavian’s deposition and Eutyches’ reinstatement.
He had already enlisted on his side the bishop of Alexandria and the bishop of Rome,
through letters concerning [?] that had been done against Eutyches. One agreed, and the other did not.
For the bishop of Rome had read these accounts of what had been done against Eutyches,
and had condemned Eutyches as guilty. But when I found that document and read it,
I thanked God that the church of Rome professed the faith correctly and without fault, even though they took a different position concerning me personally.
But he also estranged the rest of the bishops from him and made them run to Eutyches,
while he insulted those who sided with Flavian and deprived them of freedom to speak before him and before the officials.
They were indeed accused, but they were not given a hearing
concerning the accusations against them. Instead, people assailed them with insults, arrested them, and put pressure on them.
He also estranged the clergy from him, oppressing and persecuting them by withholding [?] their means of support.
And the payments that he had ordered should not be demanded from the churches, on pain of [?] being disowned by the church and by God—
these he ordered to be demanded from them with savage fury, accompanied by insults for which no one was held accountable.
The heads of households were openly arrested and accused before crowds.
Every bishop who was not a supporter of Eutyches was arrested.
And all the taxes on their churches’ properties that had been remitted for them by him and by the emperors before him—
he ordered the taxes for all those years to be demanded from them at once.
And from those who were prominent or came from prominent families,
instead of the honor they had enjoyed, he openly demanded a quantity of gold.
Under these same measures, he also ordered payment to be demanded mercilessly from Eusebius, the accuser of Eutyches.
For both these things were imposed, together with all the afflictions of famine, destruction, and captivity,
which were beyond counting; and he had made the Roman Empire fall to its knees and groan.
When Flavian was caught up in all these troubles, he waited for the feast of Easter, when the emperor would enter the church.
He did not regard him as an enemy, but took the holy Gospel so that he might have mercy on them,
with all the bishops and clergy gathered around him, and the baptized in their own attire, while the people cried out with him.
He fell on his face and threw himself down in the church, begging them to receive him so that he might breathe his last, for he thought that the Gospel was being disowned.
But he thrust him away with insults, threatening him as someone who had insulted him by what he had done to him,
while the bishops and clergy pleaded with him, and the baptized lay prostrate on the ground.
along with the people's chants; and they pursued them as though they were evildoers.
From that time on, he had withdrawn even from entering the church.
He had ordered that what he owed should be demanded from him with humiliation, and that he should be given no respite,
so that he was now forced to send word to the emperor that he had no possessions of his own, because he was poor.
Even the church's possessions, if sold, would not suffice for the amount of gold being demanded from him.
But he had the church's sacred vessels, which the emperor himself and his royal ancestors had donated.
“I am compelled to melt them down, because I am being
forced.” But he said, “I do not want to know. I want gold, by whatever means possible.”
Because of this, he brought down the church's vessels, and they were melted down publicly.
This brought weeping and cries from all those who sympathized with the people from whom these demands were being made,
as though they were undergoing persecution. But when the emperor heard what had happened,
he became exceedingly angry, fiercely and savagely, as though he had done these things to provoke him.
He ordered an ecumenical council to be assembled against him and proceedings for the deposition of Flavian to be undertaken.
40. But when Flavian was hard pressed on every side and saw that everything he did and said
was being turned into grounds for reproach and accusation against him, and that he had no help from the imperial government—
for, as they say, it was through his sister's choice and efforts that he had attained his position—
she did not want to exercise authority in any way in these internal affairs,
since she supposed that he was being mistreated on her account.
He decided to free himself from the office of bishop, go to his monastery, and live there.
He submitted a petition requesting release and handed it over.
When the emperor learned that he had done this, he sent after him to bring him back,
as though he had done even this to discredit and insult him.
And if he did not return to his church, he would be in danger. “It was not
for your harm,” he said, “that I ordered a council to be held,
but for a genuine examination that would reassure the heart about the truth of the matters in question.”
But when he returned, he immediately had accusers ready, who said:
“The records of the proceedings held at Ephesus against Eutyches were fraudulent.”
The accusers were those who had sought refuge with Eutyches.
They themselves had put in writing what had been done against him.
They were accusing themselves even more than Flavian, so that they might receive greater praise rather than be condemned.
With the freedom granted them by the emperor, they did everything by force.
The intention was that, under pressure and without any respite from all the accusations against him, he would suddenly lose his mind, be bewildered, and perish.
But because he was able to endure, he was subjected to all kinds of humiliations, and he did everything without hope.
For even the bishops who were in attendance [?],
and who ought to have sat as judges, he had already approached and won over, making them his own.
Such were the bishop of Ancyra and the bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia.
He sent for them and questioned them, as though distressed by what had been done to
Eutyches, asking whether the things done against him had really happened.
He said that the account of what had happened at the synod was incomplete, and that the accusers were standing ready.
“We wish to examine these matters before the imperial officer and before your God-fearing selves.”
With these words he encouraged them not to accept what had taken place, but to leave everything to the emperor’s wisdom.
All these things were being done so that there would be no examination of the faith.
Instead, Flavian was to be deposed through the external measures being prepared, and they were to accept the teachings of Eutyches without examination.
