If, then, Flavian had told him these things—that Christ is from two natures,
and that the natures continue to exist after the union, as natures united without confusion,
and that in his divinity he is of the same nature as the Father, and in his humanity, from his mother, of the same nature as us—
and they had cut these expressions out of his words and altered those that suited the judges [?],
and condemned him as someone who held the opposite opinion, then the man deserved support, because he had truly been wronged.
But if they had deposed him, not as someone who had failed to say these things, but as someone who still persisted in these very views of his,
while confessing that this was his belief and classifying as heretics those who did not believe this way:
Why do they abandon the investigation concerning him? And they assume that those outside possess
barbarity, because they were among the accusers. [?]
For they were the ones who wrote, and they took great pains over the matters under investigation.
For suppose something was omitted from the judicial verdict, or from these things by those men:
was what led to his deposition at their hands also omitted?
Why, then, did you not investigate what was omitted, with reference to the things for which they rightly deposed him,
the things in which he had not truly agreed with them? For the man who says, “They omitted things to my disadvantage;
I was indeed wronged,” denies having said the things for which he was accused and deposed.
But if he admitted that it was not two natures that were united, and also that our Lord’s body is not of the same nature as ours,
and even now shows that he continues to hold these very positions, what is it that was omitted,
as though these things were not enough to show him to be a man with an alien belief? Yet he did deny some of the things he had said,
and through these he was strengthening his case against his accusers who had deposed him.
This, then, had already been examined, and he had also received a judgment. What other judgment or examination was needed,
beyond the one conducted by the bishop of Rome? For after receiving the accounts of what had been done by both sides,
he praised the one but condemned the other with
divine discernment, and he did not pass sentence on them casually.
And because they had been put to shame by the bishop of Rome, they turned to the bishop of Alexandria,
as to someone who was eager to rush into such matters and who was an enemy of the bishop of Constantinople.

On what happened at Ephesus concerning Flavian.
For once again they had reached Ephesus,
which [?] was designated and set apart for the deposition of the bishops of Constantinople.
And again the bishops of Alexandria and Ephesus had made an agreement,
and were helping one another against the bishop of Constantinople.
The bishop of Rome was not there, nor the seat of Saint Peter, nor the apostolic dignity, nor the loving head of the Romans.
Instead, the bishop of Alexandria sat in authority and seated the bishop of Ephesus beside him as well.
And the bishop of Rome was being consulted. But let Julian tell us:
The one who represents the holy bishop of Rome, if he is in agreement with the holy synod,
and wishes to read in this record what took place at Constantinople? He therefore asks
like someone who has authority, and speaks while also passing judgment against them.
Yet they grant him their consent, not so that he should accept whatever they wish, nor again so that he should grant them supremacy,
but so that, if the bishop of Rome agrees with him, they may also receive him on his side.
But if not, and he is found to oppose them, they will thrust him aside as someone who has no authority in any respect.
He wanted to show everyone that they should not look to the bishop of Rome, since he cannot help the bishop of Constantinople.
For after Julian had said, “We agree to this:
that the account of what took place should be read, provided that the letter of our father Leo is read first,”
and after him Hilary, the deacon of the holy bishop of Rome, had said,
“It was after these proceedings, which you now wish to read, had been read before him that he sent what he sent,”
when he had heard these things and had nothing reasonable to say, he ruled against them.
He said, “This is the proper and indeed good order: that what took place should be [?],
and then the writings of the God-fearing bishop of Rome.”
What sort of order is this, or how is it good? That first these things
should be read, and then those, while they are being read and your own decision—the one you want—is being imposed upon them? Afterward, on what grounds do you order them to be read,
when you leave no room for reading them? Is that when you order them to be read,
because you wanted to nullify his opinion? For you knew—
you knew very well what Leo had sent about these matters to the emperor, to the empress, and to Flavian himself.
Yet you took the opposite road, the one that led here, to which you also enslaved yourself,
and abandoned the one that led to God, giving it little thought.
I said “little,” but in fact you considered it nothing at all, and therefore despised it.
You also brushed aside the solemn appeals of the bishop of Antioch, who had adjured you with fearsome oaths
by the holy mysteries not to press for Flavian’s deposition or to do him harm.
One ought, indeed, to consider not what will satisfy the emperor’s heart, but what will be stirred up by these things.
“For,” he said, “I am testing him and persuading the emperor to make an effort, not for condemnation but for acquittal.”
For otherwise we cannot help him, however much we exert ourselves, while the emperor is fighting against him and is angry.
And when he is so angry, it turns into punishment unless the one who calms his anger gives way. Thus, with these words
he had deceived him and brought him under his control. So he drew him on with this statement, which he made as though in confidence:
and he had accepted him and joined him in the rest of the other matters.
He fought against him and deposed both him and the others,
and anyone who was thought in any way to hold Flavian’s views. And concerning these matters, this was what seemed good to the emperor.
For I pass over the things that were brought up concerning me personally and concerning Flavian,
and all the things by which they sought the expulsion of those who did not even wish to anathematize us.
Nevertheless, in the end they deposed him too on those very grounds. Others who were wronged were deposed without a trial.
For they saw neither a trial nor a court, nor any opportunity to defend themselves, nor were they allowed to speak.
Instead, they deposed and expelled from their cities anyone whom the emperor and Eutyches pleased.
And they had ample opportunity to defend themselves before people concerning him—those who were from the man of Antioch—
whereas he was not granted this. For through the things he had done against others,
he was now being strangled without help, suffering those very things himself, and not on behalf of others.
And what brought him to all these things was something that could not even be denied:
namely, his violence and his breaking of his oaths, from which there is no escape. For he had made the man of Antioch
an instrument against the bishop of Rome and against the bishop of Constantinople.
He claimed that this was what he thought, although he was certainly not unaware
whether he thought this way, for they had written to one another many times about these matters.
Nevertheless, he made use of the holy bishop of Antioch as someone of this sort.
He used him until he made him unfit and unworthy for the work of a bishop,
and he rejected him and cast him aside while the oaths were still on his tongue.
Either he was someone who was no longer useful to him, or he feared him as someone who had experienced the breaking of oaths.
For this reason he deposed him on this very ground, through which he could also pursue his claim in another way.
But if he had this intention, he was afraid not only of him, but also of the emperor.
And he did everything out of fear that, after he had done all these things to him according to his wishes,
the emperor might afterward turn against him and hate him as someone untrustworthy who broke his oaths,
and who had done all these things unjustly to please the one in power; and might then act against him too and bring him down.
For this was indeed his character toward anyone who pleased him: he would bring him close to himself, and in whatever
he wanted, he would help him and advance him.
He would do everything and convince everyone that he had an undying love for him.
And when he seemed to love him all the more, once the benefit he wanted from that man had run out,
without any intermediary he would [?] the man, and from then on become his enemy, turn away from him, and harm him.
He would hand him over to his enemies to be humiliated, as though he were a thoroughly wicked man
who had acted unjustly against his wishes, behaved disgracefully, and broken his oaths.
And because he knew this, he wanted that man to hate him too, so that he might suffer injustice in the very matters in which he had acted unjustly.
In this way he could gain the upper hand through these things and slander the man before everyone.
He had already experienced these things at this man's hands, for they had happened not long before.
Concerning what happened to Cyril when gold was demanded from him.
For Cyril, who had given large sums on our account, when the benefit of what he had given him had run out—
since the emperor knew that he still had possessions, and he owed two thousand pounds of gold under written agreements,
as they say, for the confirmation of the things he had stirred up against me. But because they had been confirmed,
and the man who had made an agreement with him that he should give it to him, namely John,
had died in disgrace and contempt, together with the man who had worked with him on what was done against me at Ephesus,
and because the written agreement he had made came to him, requiring him to collect what remained as well and release the man,
what did he do, according to what they say? He wrote him an affectionate letter, begging him to listen to him and come with him as far as Ephesus,
because he had a vow concerning himself and concerning what had been done at Ephesus,
which he was to bring and fulfill at the church of Saint John, concerning the death that was in his hands.
“And if,” he said, “there is anything I have done wrongly because I did not know, I ask to be corrected by you.”
“And I will pay you the honor I owe you,” explaining his flight from Ephesus,
and what he had done against him; these were the things he wanted to set right.
Concerning those who rejoiced at his flight from Ephesus and supposed that, because he hated him,
he was gathering people on behalf of Nestorius and seeking his return, so that everyone might be persuaded and not think these things.
“So that they may not become opponents while entertaining an empty hope, we will bring them all under your authority.”
But he, knowing nothing of these things, diligently
carried out the undertaking. He filled ships with all kinds of ornaments and gifts intended for the emperor and the members of the imperial household,
and for all the officials according to their ranks and their dignity, as much as would suffice for them.
He came to Ephesus, gave his gifts, received honor, and astonished everyone.
In keeping with his distinction, he was on everyone's lips. He was honored with every honor,
so that he sat with the emperor in the first seat—I mean the emperor's seat—while the emperor would sit in the second.
This happened in the imperial palace, in the carriage, and in public,
so that the emperor's seat might be sanctified by his sitting there. For this reason he also brought him into Constantinople,
so that the emperor's brothers, the imperial household, and the city might also be sanctified by his arrival.
But after he had satisfied people's desires with gifts here too, and now had nothing left,
then orders were given to demand the gold that he owed under written agreements: two thousand pounds.
He could not even deny these debts, lest, by denying them and being exposed, he should also be stripped of his honor.
But when he recognized and became aware of the suffering from the great calamity that had come upon him,
he provided guarantors for these debts and traveled by sea amid storms and great turmoil.
He fled, lest he fall into further troubles through the accusers who were bringing charges against him.
[?] But I return again to that point, concerning the just judgment of Dioscorus,
who had inherited from Cyril both leadership and hatred toward the bishop of Constantinople.
For their aim was not to hold fast to the truth, but to gain strength by any means whatsoever.
For before Flavian entered the assembly, as they say,
this very man had taken the seat and place of the bishop of Constantinople.
He had arranged for others to go before him, so that he would sit in the last place, as though out of humility.
But the other man had thought nothing of the kind and had sat down.
But that man, wanting to display his tyranny, had first set this in motion.
And this had made the Roman take the hint, as they say.
He had stood up and pressed him, brought him over, and seated him in his own chair.
Then the counts who had been put in charge of this were preventing the bishops who had assembled and wanted to speak in his defense
from doing so, as though they had no authority to speak,
except about the matters on which they were questioned by the bishops of Alexandria—this man whose authority was firmly established.
And those who had come from elsewhere to testify about everything that had happened previously,
and who could refute Eutyches, because he had been saying these things even before the accusation,
to show that there was no oppression—I mean those confined in the monasteries—
and all those who were thought to have come on Flavian’s behalf,
they forced into hiding and made afraid because they had come,
as though they had recklessly and presumptuously committed themselves on behalf of that man,
who had even been removed from Constantinople by the emperor.
But all the monks who sided with Eutyches enjoyed great freedom and authority,
so that whatever they wanted to happen through the exercise of power would be carried out by their hands.
They even handed over everyone they recognized to the officials and the townspeople.
For everyone was subject to them and served them, whether willingly or unwillingly.
For many were displeased by what was happening, but they were compelled and wept.
Nevertheless, they carried out what they were ordered to do.
They dragged people away, some from ships, some from marketplaces, and some from houses,
and some from churches while they were praying. Others they pursued
to make them flee. Those who were hiding in caves and holes in the ground they searched for and hunted down with every effort.
And it was a matter of great fear and danger for anyone to speak with Flavian’s associates.
from among those who lived in the pavilion and kept watch,
and acted as spies, watching those who went in to see Flavian.
As a result, more and more people went over to the party of Eutyches.
Some did so because they feared suffering harm, and others
while they [?] and secured his support, spoke and told many lies.
Whatever they told him against that man, he endorsed, as though he found pleasure in what they told him.
They had separated Eusebius, bishop of Dorylaeum, who was Eutyches’ accuser, from him, and would not let him draw breath.
They had also separated from him the entire synod that had heard the case and deposed Eutyches at Constantinople,
which ought to have spoken alongside him and upheld what it had done. They isolated him on every side
and made everyone his accusers, since they were troubled by the fear that they might suffer harm.
For whether someone agreed or refused to agree, it was in any case clear
that he would suffer harm unless he accused Flavian of lying and became a supporter of Eutyches.
Thus they had arranged his situation beforehand and stripped him of support on every side.
They left him without hope or freedom to speak, so that he could not utter even a sound.
For they had all prepared themselves not to listen to him, but to condemn him in any event.
They brought him into their assembly while insulting him and allowed him no breathing room concerning the accusations against him.
In the presence of the counts who had been appointed, they intimidated and terrified him, ordering him not to speak.
But listen also to the cry that arose under compulsion and distress, making a mockery of this man’s trial.
For when the records of the proceedings held at Constantinople against Eutyches were being read,
along with the agreement and signatures of the bishops against Eutyches,
beginning with that of Seleucus, bishop of Amasia in Pontus, who had condemned him,
they conducted their examination with no judicial procedure and no order,
such as asking him to confirm his signature, what his opinion was, and whether his statement had been correctly expressed.
Instead, they passed judgment without examination, and as though amid a tumult,
confused and indiscriminate, with neither leader nor discipline, they shouted:
that they are not those of the bishop of Amasia: “Do not divide the indivisible.”
so that by this they might intimidate the man into agreeing with the accusations they were bringing against him.
And they would make an example of this, so that others too would be afraid
and would repudiate the decision they had made, and would coerce Flavian in exactly the same way.
For this was shared by all those who had accepted him and agreed with him.
Therefore the judgment, too, ought to have been shared by those who had condemned him and agreed with him,
and had withdrawn their signatures from the action taken against Eutyches. Yet they were doing these things to show
that Flavian certainly deserved condemnation, as someone who had disparaged their words and their verdict,
and that they had no other way to gain relief except by accusing Flavian.
Dioscorus, who was conducting this examination, while silencing the disorderly assembly,
was himself shouting in his disorderly way: “Be quiet for a little while,” he said, “so that we may hear some more blasphemies.
Why do we blame Nestorius alone? There are many Nestoriuses.”
The one did not rebuke him for holding these views of mine, nor, in turn, did the other allow him to mistreat him on my account.
Rather, what he was saying to me, he was also saying to him. For this man too was among those who spoke correctly.
Yet he was saying that I said one thing and he another.
And he denied that I said these same things, either out of ignorance or out of fear.
So, without giving him any room to breathe, he hurried to condemn him,
lest, if he gained breathing room, the truth should be established about the statements for which he was being accused: that they were not those of Nestorius,
but those of the divine Scriptures and of the holy fathers who preceded the three hundred and eighteen,
and those of the three hundred and eighteen themselves, and of those who came after them.
For he had every means at his disposal to show that they were orthodox.
So, to prevent these statements from being examined, since they could not deny that they were orthodox,
and to avoid accepting them as orthodox and consequently abandoning what they were eager to do—
to condemn Flavian and acquit Eutyches—they passed over these statements and turned to other grounds for accusing him,
as though he were indeed disparaging the verdict. And they gave him this pretext for gaining breathing room:
And not that on account of which and by means of which Cyril and the council at Ephesus were exposed by what they had said.
For the supporters of Cyril and Eutyches were collecting those statements
that agreed with them, and choosing those that pleased them.
The members of Flavian’s party, who opposed them, did the same.
But Cyril was the father of many heresies, and he would say these things, those things, and other things at one and the same time.
This was so that, when they used contradictory statements, they would not
be forced to uphold what had happened in Cyril’s time and what had happened at Ephesus,
and necessarily uphold my words, thereby invalidating what had been done against me,
and have no room left for what was being done against Flavian because of Eutyches’ accusation.
For these reasons, they would not let Seleucus draw breath, or even confirm what he had written.
Instead, they resorted to decisive shouting, so that no one else would dare draw breath,
but would say what they wanted against Flavian:
things that discredited him for taking action in passing judgment on Eutyches, so that they would accept such a signature without a word.
For their intention had become clear to everyone from these things; it becomes especially clear from Atticus’s signature.
For Atticus was a man from the countryside and was simple-minded,
and he could not manage even obvious matters. For he had difficulty speaking,
and he had been brought up indoors like the slaves, having been placed in the great household of the imperial court.
Having thus gained the confidence that comes from power and high standing, he had been chosen to be one of the bishops,
although he was neither practiced in nor understood such methods, fabrications, and schemes.
They were pressuring him to say falsely that it was indeed deficient.
But he pressed them to speak and explain the difficulty to him, since he did not understand what they were saying to him.
For Bishop Atticus had said, “I suddenly came up to Constantinople
and looked at the hearers and at the monk who was saying, ‘My lord, sign.’
I said to him, ‘God! [?] Let me look.’ And I heard him reading something false.
After this he said to me, ‘My lord, sign.’ I said, ‘I cannot sign.’”
I do indeed know, but I cannot say anything.
Nevertheless, I say that if anyone does not believe as the three hundred and eighteen fathers at Nicaea did, and as those at Ephesus [?] did,
let him be accursed in this world and in the world to come. And Dioscorus, as though dealing with a boy under accusation,
was ordering Atticus to deny it and make himself out to be a liar. He himself was saying what he wanted
him to say: “These things that have been read, then, are lies and fabrications.”
Atticus did not know what he wanted him to say, and said, “But I know.”
For they were signaling to him to say, “They are lies and fabrications,” but Atticus did not understand.
Again, he questioned him differently, signaling to him: “You did not say these things?” And only with difficulty, as they prodded him,
did he understand what he wanted him to say. And Atticus said, “No.”
And again, when they wanted to confirm what he wanted him to say,
he felt confident enough to question him about those very same things. Dioscorus, that is, was saying:
“Have you heard what was said—by you, that is?” He himself was saying what he wanted him to say and coaching him,
because he was afraid that he might give him one answer instead of another. And Atticus said, “I have heard.”
And Dioscorus signaled to him, saying, “Then you did not say them?” And Atticus, signaling along with his teacher,
himself repeated the very same words: “You did not say them?” In this way, both before the emperor and before other people,
he employed the very same preparation, so that they would disavow their signatures
and act openly and unjustly against Flavian. These statements from those men he would accept without examination.
But those statements made under compulsion, which were derogatory,
he accepted without question. Flavian, however, wanted to speak against them,
and although he was under such severe distress and coercion, they would not leave him alone.
Instead, they were beating him, as the counts say, so that he would not even speak until the signing against him was completed.
Thus the claims of Eutyches would be confirmed, and what they were striving for would be brought to completion.
For by then they had gathered as though over a dead man.
For when the proceedings recorded in the minutes against Eutyches were being read, and Flavian spoke against them,
they would say, “This man is lying about our signatures.” And they were beating him, as they say.
Then, after the judgment and sentence against him had been confirmed as they wished, Dioscorus ordered him to speak, saying:
“If the God-loving bishop Flavian knows anything that can help him, let him state it in writing.”
What ought he to have said to someone who knew perfectly well that his truthful statements had been suppressed by such coercion?
And now, when they were ordering him to speak as a mere formality, what more could he say than what he had already said:
“You have blocked all my truthful statements by accepting every injustice against me without distinction”?
But to show that this too was a mere formality, and how they had stifled his defense,
they recorded all his truthful statements in the minutes, even though they did not want to.
Dioscorus said to Flavian, “The holy synod knows whether I have used force against you.”
And Flavian plainly described the coercion he had suffered: “I was not left free or permitted even to speak.”
And to make it clear that what was being said was mockery, he said, “Say whatever can help you.”
And he said, “There is nothing invented or false in the proceedings recorded in the minutes.
My lord Eusebius and my lord Thalassius also know this, since they undertook the examination with me.”
They rejected his statement, saying that Thalassius and Eusebius had not conducted the examination.
Then, since their only intention now, after the sentence, was to mock him,
Thalassius repeated what Dioscorus had said: “No one is preventing Your Holiness from speaking.”
And Dioscorus mockingly turned to each of the bishops,
who were aware of this arrangement, saying, “My lord Eusebius, speak.
If these things are not so, investigate, so that he may be found free of condemnation.”
But you yourself stopped him from speaking, and now you encourage him to speak again? After he had spoken to him, he repeated the very same things:
“This proceeding took place and was examined before my lord Thalassius and my lord Eusebius, with my lord Magnus the silentiary also present.
Nothing of the sort was found. Let each of the bishops who were present there,
those who gave an account, say, as before God, whether anything was falsely stated.”
Dioscorus, again mocking him, said, “Surely this man is not out of his mind!”
But he thought that he was genuinely inviting him to speak and allowing him to examine these matters.
And again, sneering, he turned to Stephen and said to him, “My lord Stephen, did you prevent him?” And to them all: “All of you, speak.”
He spoke about the man in this way: he was unaware of, and did not know, the wickedness and deceit of the Egyptians.
He thought these things were done in the fear of God. As for the things being circulated through slander,
they were eager to say more than was true. Once he knew what they were doing,
and that there was no need for any [?] or demonstration, he was reassured.
He declared before everyone, saying, “With God’s help, I have no part in any of the things you have done to me.
For I have neither professed nor thought anything at all differently, nor do I now profess anything differently.” From then on he stopped answering
him, treating him as an obvious heretic.
For this reason they had prepared him to speak. He remained firm in this confession and entertained no improper thought.
He did not imitate the bishops of his time in this world, who agreed to everything that was asked of them.
Nor did he change his way of thinking. Instead, he remained firm, giving himself over to suffering.
He neither considered nor thought of saying, “This man is uneducated, and I am far removed from such precision.
Even previously [?], we were teaching and persuading Eutyches.
I condemned him because I had been persuaded by his accusers, who seemed to know something,
following the judgment of the majority rather than my own.
And now, if it has seemed right to all of you together, and you have examined these teachings of Eutyches and found them orthodox,
I too accept what all of you accept.
I join hands with you in upholding these orthodox teachings.
Count me too among these bishops who need forgiveness.”
For everything would have been settled by this statement, including the anger of that emperor whom slander had gripped [?]
and who had been incited to tyranny, for which he had also convened the council.
But he had not been persuaded even in Constantinople, although everyone
was urging him and begging him to do this.
Nor was he persuaded later in Ephesus, when disaster was already near and death hung over him.
Everyone was saying that this alone would give him an escape from death,
while he saw all those who were deserting him and joining Eutyches, and were being saved because of this.
And I myself was proof of this: removal from the city's episcopate was not enough in my case.
Nor was silence, intended to avoid giving them a pretext for disagreement; instead, it became the reason why I suffered evils.
For it was being heard everywhere that I was among the living. For as long as you live, expect death at the hands of the wicked.
Therefore, so that you do not betray the faith, keep all these things before your eyes, ready to endure them.
For immediately after what was supposed to be a deposition,
he was being seized as though by wolves and lions—by those counts before whom this deposition had taken place.
He was being torn at and thrown down, while different people were saying and doing different things.
He was being bribed and harassed by them all, and his spirit was distressed.
They handed him over to soldiers and ordered them to drag him out of the holy places. They drove him out and confined him
in prison, a man who could not breathe. And before he could come to himself,
catch his breath, breathe in fresh, clean air, and take nourishment to gain a little strength, they handed him over to the governor.
They threatened him into sending the man away in his broken condition, unable to endure the hardship of the journey,
as though the emperor did not care about his life, but wanted to punish him rather than keep him alive.
And so they forcibly brought him down and handed him over to a murderous man, so that they might destroy him
and send him away without mercy—nominally to his homeland, but in reality to destruction.
And so, being torn at and dragged along, he was only able to survive four days,
as they say, while every day his soul was being loosened from his body. They regarded his death as a festival for themselves.
And evils increased against all those who agreed with him and shared his faith.
And again I was among the first, amid severe persecutions and flight,
exiles and wanderings everywhere, since they were given authority to act against those who held these views.
That is, the very same views that I [?] and Flavian held.
The people were given authority to drag people away, seize them, and hand them over. Slaves
were accusing their masters over these very matters, and authority was given to them by an official command.
Every effort was made to make them turn their own souls astray,
even souls who considered or thought that God the Word is not mortal.
And the wicked among them used to speak in such a way as to force people to say:
That it was the very essence of God the Word that died. And he had given them authority against everyone,
since they trusted neither the rulers, nor the bishops, nor the whole world, nor their enemies,
nor the slaves, but regarded them as falling short of their own desire and zeal.
Against those who said that God the Word was immortal and incapable of suffering,
they appointed those who were especially eager to search and investigate to hunt down those who were fleeing.
He surrounded them with everything that inspires fear. The expectation and anticipation of suffering were worse for them than the sufferings themselves.
And this was plainly a Pharaoh-like struggle against God.
An enumeration of some of the disasters that occurred in the inhabited world,
because of the transgression against the true faith in God, who cannot suffer, together with a prophecy.
But since these things were certain to happen through the belief and the controversy directed against God the Word,
that he is neither immortal nor incapable of suffering, from then on it was as though the immortal God did not care about them.
For those for whom God was no longer immortal began to be attacked and enslaved,
in one way and another, and some of them in every way. And there was no one to turn away the wrath.
Things that happened through earthquakes and wars. 1. Through devastation, famines, and lack of rain,
and through hail, burning heat, extraordinary earthquakes, captivity, terror, and flight,
they were overwhelmed with every kind of disaster, yet they did not come to recognize the cause of such disasters.
Instead, they became still more inflamed and embittered against anyone who dared to call God the Word incapable of suffering,
as though they were suffering these disasters because they called God the Word capable of suffering and immortal. And there was no place of escape.
2. A twofold upheaval from the barbarians and the Scythians shook them:
they were destroying everyone and taking them captive, and there was not even a single hope of deliverance.
Yet they still did not understand that all this was not merely a human affair.
3. Along with this, he also shook the earth with earthquakes unlike any that anyone could remember.
For it shook so violently that it seemed it was about to overturn and collapse,
or at any rate be destroyed. But when it again grew quiet and settled as before,
It looked as though someone were holding it in a way contrary to nature.
The one who was moving it was himself moving with it. Only, it did not show to the eyes
the movement of the one moving it or the firmness of the one holding it upright; yet it brought these things to the awareness of all people.
And in the single greatness of all these things, it communicated more to their minds than a voice could.
4. For the barbarians had approached and struck the Romans, bringing them to utter despair.
5. In Constantinople, the imperial city, the towers of the wall, which had been built together with it, had broken away.
They had let go of the wall, although it had suffered no damage from the things that had shaken it.
And they remained as though they had not been shaken, with not
even a single sign of shaking on them. And in some places, from the middle of the structure,
stones had leaped out of the whole structure and from around the structure. Everyone, too, had been shaken.
6. Other things were plainly appearing in a different way on another side of the city:
they were not being shaken by a general tremor, but as a rebuke.
For the one doing these things was not mortal; he had authority over them.
7. In the Forum of Theodosius the Great. For even stones that had been fastened with iron and lead had come loose.
They were carried through the air and remained floating for a long time, and then fell.
And when those who were to receive them came out, they fell immediately.
And countless other things were happening in other places and being reported,
filling people with trembling and fear, so as to bring them, unwillingly, to supplication
and to pleading with God to have mercy on them. Yet it was not as he wished:
for different people made different pleas according to their own thinking, and prayed to him according to the beliefs they held.
One would say in his pleading, “God, who suffered and died for us,”
while others spoke differently, as though they considered this expression shameful.
For they were angry and furious with
those who dared to say, “Not subject to death or suffering.”
And because of this, afflictions were being prepared for them all the more, along with terrors more frightening still.
As their calamities continued to afflict them, so that they would have no time to spare
to mistreat the God-fearing people among them. On “Holy God.”
But when he wished to bring them to an awareness of their blasphemy, and to make them turn away from it,
because they had not come to this themselves, God himself gave them a form of supplication—for no one was found who had been doing this—
so that they would say: “Holy God, Holy Mighty One, Holy Immortal One, have mercy on us.”
Everyone agreed to this with one mind, and they abandoned the things they had desired,
things in which God took no pleasure. They inscribed this publicly in the basilica,
setting it down in this form: “Praise and thanksgiving to the Holy and Immortal One, God, the Savior of all.”
And for a little while they [?], and gave thanks to the immortal God.
They did not deny what they had embraced at that time; rather, this was sung everywhere.
But once the earthquake had subsided and wars became infrequent, they again stirred themselves up and openly opposed God.
They concealed their confession of God,
like people who did not remember that God is holy, mighty, and immortal, and that he was able
to bring wars to an end even without human power.
For his might was in himself, and did not come from resources outside himself.
They had experienced this in practice, yet now they had ceased even their supplication.
A little earlier, before the war with these barbarians, the cross alone had been teaching them
and bringing them to believe in God, especially in him who overthrew the warriors without weapons.
Before this, however, when human power had been mobilized, it had been struck down by thunderbolts and lightning.
For the Scythian people were great and numerous, and from ancient times they had been divided into peoples and kingdoms.
They had acted like bands of raiders and had not done much harm,
except through sudden, hurried plundering. But in the end they established a kingdom for themselves.
Once they had become a kingdom, they grew very strong, so that in their greatness they surpassed all the military resources of the Romans.
And God showed them that he had not grown weak—the one against whom they had long ago conspired, and whom they had subjected to suffering and death.
They had intensified persecutions against those who confessed God as holy, mighty, and immortal.
They had abandoned the one in whom they had placed their hope and through whom they had been saved from death, and who had given them understanding
to reject the death of God, but to know him and acknowledge that he is immortal.
But because this had happened, and they had not turned to praise God, who had saved them,
but instead to blaspheme and compel everyone to confess the death of God, while fleeing from the Immortal One as though from wickedness,
the barbarian once again rose against them, killing and sweeping over the whole land of the Romans and overthrowing everything.
There was no way out and no escape. They were trembling with fear, and there was no hope.
He had hemmed them in and made them powerless in everything they undertook
for their deliverance. And because they had not understood their earlier deliverance,
he had sent the man whom he had taken from tending sheep, the man who had exposed the secrets of the king’s heart.
He had already been stirred by God and had ordered a cross to be made.
And as though he did not believe him, he had made the wooden object with his own hands and sent it against the barbarians.
He had also engraved another cross in the royal palace,
and another in the forum of Constantinople, in the middle of the city, so that everyone could see it.
Thus, when the barbarians too saw it, they fled and were struck down. And the king himself had gained confidence to remain,
although he had previously been preparing to flee. The sinews of the city, which had grown weak, were strengthened.
All these things had happened in this way. For when the barbarian had fled, stricken,
although no one was pursuing him, and the king had been strengthened to stand firm in his resolve to rule,
and the city had been filled with great courage, they could find no other cause for this sudden change,
because there was no one else doing this—striking down the one and encouraging the other—
except only the cross that had been set up, deriving from the one who had been crucified in his nature and in truth.
That is, the body that had been crucified in its nature. And we are given to understand that we should not be ashamed to say
that this died, and not God, who strengthened the weak, suffering, mortal body—the body that suffered and died on the cross.
For this reason, even the wood on which he was crucified became a means of deliverance. For in the case of someone who did not believe
and despised the cross of the mortal body, the one who was able to save
commanded him to make the cross out of wood, to bring about through it such deliverance in the city and among the barbarians.
So that we may not doubt that it was the body of the one who gave life to the whole world that was crucified, and not God:
he who had performed such a mighty deed through the crucifixion of the body and the cross.
But because they had devised a clever argument about this too, as though the cross belonged to the divinity and not to the body,
they persisted in opposing the God-fearing, who said that the cross did not belong to the divinity,
but to the body of the divinity, and that for this reason he saved us through the cross.
Once again, against this Pharaoh-like thinking, God stirred up the fury of the barbarians and the earthquakes.
And because he also wanted to restrain them from attacking the God-fearing and from inflicting suffering on them—
for only then did the God-fearing gain relief and freedom—he was teaching through both:
that the wicked thinking which included an acknowledgment of death in him did not please him.
For although they represented the death caused by the barbarians as death caused by human beings,
they could not make this claim about the death caused by the earthquake.
But since even in this way they had not come to recognize the glory of the incorruptible God,
and were attributing death, suffering, and weakness to him despite such might and immortality,
he then taught them through these very words: “Do not attribute blemish or injury to God,
because he is holy and free from all suffering.
Nor attribute weakness to the one who displayed mighty strength through the weak cross,
and possessed all might. Nor attribute death
to the one who alone is immortal, and who showed through our death that he is immortal,”
through the confession that he is holy, mighty, and immortal.
But because they did not stand by what they had been compelled to confess, and did not believe in the mighty and immortal God,
who can put an end even to wars, they became slaves of the barbarians,
and were reduced to servitude, paying them tribute with written acknowledgment.
They even gave to those who were waging war against him.
There was nothing he did not do, he who made the barbarian appear as master and the Romans as slaves.
Thus supremacy passed to the barbarians, as though the Romans had no God who was over all.
Holy, mighty, and immortal. For this reason, the rest of the nations also fled to him.
But they fled from the Romans, since the Romans could not even save themselves.
And because they had arranged their rule in this way, as though they had no need of divine help,
they did not come to their senses, nor did they remember the confession that they held on their lips:
that he is holy, mighty, and immortal. Instead, they again argued the opposite, concerning the sufferings of the divinity,
thereby showing that he was none of these things.
For along with suffering and death, this too was attributed to him: that he was not even holy
by nature, and not mortal by nature, and not mighty by nature.
Until God in turn raised up some of their own number, whether they wished it or not,
to rebuke their wickedness, to bring relief to those who had suffered cruelly,
and to instruct those who had previously gone astray—Flavian and Eusebius, whom they were killing.
For they were carrying out God's retribution, confessing him to be holy, mighty, and immortal.
And they persisted with laws, decrees, and penalties
against those who confessed God the Word to be holy, mighty, and immortal.
And with plunder, exile, and executions, until Theodosius was removed from their midst,
the man who had risen up against God. Then mouths were opened to confess, praise, and worship
God, who is holy, mighty, and immortal, as they spoke without fear.
For it is not the person who calls Christ a God subject to suffering and death
who confesses Christ as God, but the person who speaks of Christ in his divinity, which he possesses by nature,
and confesses God as by nature free from suffering, immortal, mighty, and holy.
But he is subject to suffering in his humanity, since that person confesses him to be human by nature.
But someone said, “What connection do you have with Flavian and with the things that happened to him and on his account? For you
have been anathematized and publicly denounced by everyone. And so, by the things you keep adding,
you are working to give yourself a bad name and to bring about your condemnation, not to obtain straightforward and just relief.”
To him I have said repeatedly, throughout and at every opportunity: “It is not fitting for me to be loved by people like these.”
But I also earnestly desire that, through my being condemned, they may be saved from blasphemy.
And let those who are saved acknowledge God as holy, mighty, and immortal,
without exchanging the image of the incorruptible God for the image of a corruptible human being,
or stitching paganism into Christianity.
Rather, let them acknowledge God according to what his image is, and the human being according to what he is in his image.
Thus let both the one who can suffer and the immortal one be acknowledged in the images of their respective natures.
In this way Christianity will profess neither a transformation of God nor, again, a transformation of the human being, after the likeness of pagan wickedness.
But let there truly be a yes that is yes and a no that is no: the savior and the one who is saved,
so that Christianity may acknowledge that Christ is truly and by nature God and a human being.
He is by nature immortal and incapable of suffering as God, and by nature mortal and capable of suffering as a human being.
He is not God in both natures, nor, again, a human being in both natures.
My aim and earnest endeavor, then, are that God should be blessed and glorified on earth as in heaven.
Let Nestorius be condemned, but let them say about God what I pray that they will say.
For I am among those who are with God, not among those who are against God,
who insult God under the guise of reverence for God and deny that he is God.
For he fights for the things for which I fight, and those who fight against me fight against him.
And for this reason I am bound to endure and suffer everything for his sake.
If only, through my endurance, everyone might succeed in being reconciled to God!
For nothing is greater or more precious to me than this. Nor would I have hesitated to say the opposite of what I say,
if I had known that they wished to say the opposite of what I say in every possible way,
and that they would belong to God, and that through these things I would be honored before God,
on account of these things that belong to God, because I had thought as God does and not as a human being.
[?] Again, in another way: I did not recount these matters concerning Flavian casually either.
Rather, I brought them forward as evidence of the things done against me in wickedness and injustice,
so that people might not be misled by the name of a council, but might investigate what happened with complete truthfulness.
And let them judge by these things before God, even if they happened otherwise.
For Satan disguises himself as an angel of light and leads
people astray, to turn them away from God. Again, however, [?] I judged in my mind
that to conceal the [?] accomplished through the power and wisdom of God
is a great wrong, utter wickedness and ingratitude—not to show and reveal these things to all people.
For he had done these things for their sake, to undo their schemes and expose them:
those who were strengthening wickedness and shedding light on it, while I was not believed in what I said.
But they were doing this, and they had also done at their gathering in the synod
all the things that I was suffering, and they did not believe me.
But it was not possible at the synod to rebuke and undo these things that had arisen.
The will of wickedness had grown stronger than the will of God,
through which the wicked were exposed as wicked, and those who feared God as not fearing God.
And they struggled to the death and preserved the purity of mind that they owed to God.
For without this intervening time, which came about through God's patience,
during which these people suffered and those people made them suffer, they would not have been revealed: neither the wicked as wicked,
nor those who were deemed worthy of such care, which was turning them back from fighting against God.
Through these very events he was fighting and standing against them, restraining them from kicking against
God's goads. Nor, moreover, would they have turned back from their wrongdoing in this way,
while those who feared God were neither dismayed nor discouraged as God showed patience,
so that they might suffer throughout their lives while remaining faithful to God's purpose.
For this reason one can find the care and assistance recounted by those who received it
and neglected the circumstances in which they found themselves. Yet care was shown to them,
while they were ignorantly devising plans concerning things that ought to have been set right—things that those people had despised and also undone.
For it was right to put an end to the things that had gone badly, not to conceal them.
These things, therefore, which came from God as a means of correction,
Those who conceal them did not belong to God, but to those who undo what belongs to him.
For why do you suppose that those who held the inhabited world as their [?]
became the property of barbarians? Was it not because they failed to make proper use of the authority given to them,
so that the nations might recognize the grace given to them? Thus, because they did not teach as masters,
they would learn as slaves what was required. Why, again, was it not from the orthodox
that they heard the message of the gospel, but from worshipers of created things? And they did not
submit to royal authority, nor again [?] to the religion under which they had lived.
This was so that they might know that, when they received royal authority but did not preserve the supremacy of their religion within the kingdom [?],
for this reason they did not remain rulers in anything else either, since authority passed to their enemies.
For in the very matters in which they neglected the gospel, they were also rejected from authority.
They also joined the worshipers of created things in faith, although they differed in name and in the expression “of the same nature.”
Just as those people confess “created” and “uncreated,” and inconsistently say “of the same nature” as an expression of praise,
while by distinguishing between creature and Creator they posit a difference of nature,
so these people too, through “subject to suffering” and “not subject to suffering,” “created” and “uncreated,” posit a difference of nature,
and inconsistently use the expression “of the same nature” as though it were some expression of praise,
in name alone, while holding to authority and religion on the basis of opposition,
and not on the basis of an open confession of nature.
For until what concerns nature is also purified, so that authority may receive religion, and religion authority,
being established by God, so that just as he is glorified in heaven he may also be glorified on earth, and there may be glory in heaven and peace on earth,
God does not cease to guide and teach us through his direction of these events. Like those
who teach children, he makes use of appropriate blows and rebukes
to teach us and convince us that we are going astray; and a spirit comes forth on behalf of those who are silent and reveals their innocence.
For what have I invented [?] from these events that happened as they did,
and not God himself? For there were betrayers of the tradition of the fathers,
and the mouths of those who were demanding the rightful claims of the fathers were shut.
For this reason, some of them were turning aside to Arianism from what they had professed;
and some to Manichaeism, some to Judaism, and some to other teachings, both new and old.
God raised up men from among them, from their own ranks, just as he used to raise up judges from among the Jews,
to rebuke them for their transgressions against God: namely, Flavian, who was occupying my place,
who in this matter would naturally have been my enemy, as indeed he was, whether through ignorance or for some other reason;
and Eusebius, who used to fight against me. Without any cause for fear, they made their confession,
and fought against Cyril’s party, who were blaspheming and seeking to prevail.
God did not leave them alone until they had exposed the contradiction in Cyril.
For one group brought forward his words against the other, while the other group in turn selected those statements
that contradicted the former statements and set them against them. Both sides disputed on the basis of Cyril himself and his own words.
One group said that the others were Manichaeans, because they attributed everything to God the Word, even the properties of the flesh.
The others, however, accused these of holding my views, since I too say these things.
They attribute the properties of God to the divine nature, and the properties of humanity to the humanity.
They acknowledge that the union took place in the person, not in the nature.
Almost everyone was disputing with his neighbor, rebuking him on my account, on the grounds that I had indeed been wronged.
These views of mine were being proclaimed with the utmost zeal.
One group reproached those who said that I taught two sons, on the grounds that I had never said this.
The others rebuked those who [?] spoke of one nature,
because they said that God was subject to suffering, just as I used to accuse them of saying.
Who was compelling them to proclaim these views of mine, which decrees had forbidden anyone to read,
so that, of their own accord and among themselves, they were fighting to proclaim them with the utmost zeal? And while I was silent,
and my authority to proclaim them had been taken away, and I was not believed,
God had raised up people who were believed when they proclaimed these views of mine,
that they were true, without there being any grounds for suspecting
that they were saying these things out of friendship or love for me. God was doing these things, not for my sake.
For who is Nestorius? Or what does his life mean? Or what does his death mean in the world, except for the truth he gave to the world?
He was free from misleading pretexts, and he rebuked those who led others astray.
And because they were prejudiced against me and did not believe what I was saying,
as though I were concealing the truth and preventing certainty from coming, God provided a herald for this:
Leo, who was free from this prejudice and proclaimed the truth without fear.
And because the council’s having taken place beforehand had misled many, including the representative of the Romans,
so that they did not believe what I was saying, and my statements remained unexamined,
God allowed these contrary events to happen, to change the bishop of Rome,
who had exercised authority over the arrangements for the council at Ephesus against me,
and to make him agree with and confirm what had been said by the bishop of Constantinople.
And the man who had been capable of everything was counted as nothing.
This was Dioscorus, bishop of Alexandria. I say that he was counted as nothing
because he resorted to flight and devised ways to avoid being deposed and sent into exile, so that, through what they were suffering,
they might also believe what the Egyptian had done against me at the first council.
And because of the supposed friendship of the emperor and the officials of the imperial court, I was thought to be putting pressure on the council.
This did not move me to abandon the truth or compel me to agree with the emperor because of what had been done against me.
For because they had not actually examined anything, they thought I was a blasphemer.
But so that God might show that the emperor’s love for me was deceitful,
and was not sincere but motivated by possessions, he revealed his support through Eutyches and Flavian.
As could be seen from what happened, he gave no permission to assemble, and they did not allow those who had assembled to say anything
except what they were ordered to say. Instead, under fear and coercion, they even condemned themselves.
Again, they supposed that I had been summoned for examination and trial, and that I was simply making things up.
But they had summoned me not for a trial, but for deposition and a plot to bring about my destruction and death.
To expose them as murderers,
God allowed Flavian to enter the council and suffer what he suffered at their hands.
For it is clear that these are the very things they had also been doing against [?] from the beginning.
And because it was thought that those who were bishops would not be induced
to do anything outside the judgment they approved, whether out of love for the king, or through fear, or amid disturbances,
God again exposed them as they acted to the contrary, and rebuked them before everyone. They left nothing to which they had not borne witness.
Rather, through all these things he exposed the pretexts of deception and proclaimed them on the rooftops,
so that there would not be even one excuse for those who fashion themselves [?] in ignorance.
But just as Pharaoh was rebuked by God through all these things—
and I call him inexcusable, because neither through the coherence of the words, nor through the deeds themselves,
nor through rebukes from human beings, nor again through those from God, was he willing to be persuaded,
and he died in his blasphemy—so these people also persist without excuse.
[?] So when I saw these things being done by God,
did you want me to remain silent and conceal all this providential activity of God? [?] God's prophets would not have been distinguishable—
those who were anathematized as false prophets by false prophets who claimed to be prophets—
if they had not accepted being anathematized for God's sake by false prophets.
They would not have been worthy of the glory and teaching of the prophets
if their descendants had observed the anathema pronounced by the false prophets. Nor would they have been redeemed and saved—
those who became Christians from among the Jews—if they had upheld the unjust judgment their ancestors passed against Christ,
as though it came from holy and righteous people.
They would not have become Christ's apostles if they had followed the whole assembly of the Jews, and the priests,
and the teachers [?] of the law, and the rulers, as teachers of the law and the prophets [?].
They would not have believed in Christ, nor would they have died for Christ,
if they had regarded death and contempt not as an honor but as a disgrace.
Nor would they now be honored by assemblies, rulers, and lords,
if they had not endured death and humiliation at the hands of rulers and peoples.
They would not have been considered worthy of such care from kings, rulers, and armies,
If they had observed the commands and laws of kings, judges, and rulers,
our fathers would not thereby have been regarded as orthodox teachers,
if they had sought to escape condemnation by a council of heretics and to say what those men were saying,
and had shown partiality. Nor would we be worthy of the instruction provided by their labors,
if we accepted without examination the decision against them as though it came from a council.
To put it briefly: Meletius and Eustathius would not be bishops of Antioch if they had accepted the partisan decisions and judgment of a council
of heretics against them. Nor would Athanasius be bishop of Alexandria,
if he accepted without question the judgment of those who deposed him, as though it came from orthodox men.
John would not be bishop of Constantinople,
if he accepted without examination the judgment and deposition imposed on him as though they came from a council.
Nor, again, would Flavian have been bishop of Constantinople,
if he had submitted to the gnashing of teeth of the ecumenical council that deposed him, as though it were the gnashing of teeth of a council.
There would have been no one, from whatever city he might be, who suffered these things for my sake,
and they would not have shone like the sun, if I had looked to accusers rather than to God.
And I too was deemed worthy to become what each one of these men had become in God.
For the deed is not mine, but Christ’s, who strengthened me. Everyone will give an account to God,
for what he said or did, or for causing others to stumble, or for making every effort to remove stumbling blocks.
But if, although someone does everything he can, the person who stumbles is not persuaded,
let him stumble because of himself, not because of the person who speaks and cries out to him, whom he refuses to obey.
Now, many people repeatedly reproached me
for not writing to Leo, bishop of Rome, to inform him of all the events that had arisen, just as they happened,
and of the alteration of the faith, addressing him as a man upright in his faith.
And I too had been given a portion of the letter concerning the judgment against Flavian and Eutyches,
in which it was revealed that they had not been afraid of the friendship of the imperial power.
That was why I did not write, not because I am an arrogant and senseless man.
But so that I would not hinder the progress of the one who was running well, because of prejudice concerning my person.
I agreed, however, to endure the things of which they accused me, so that, while I was being accused of these things,
they might accept the teaching of the fathers without hindrance. For I have nothing to say about those who rose up against me.
And for this reason I did not write again, lest I be thought to be fleeing the struggle because I feared the hardships
of many years, when I had not even a single respite,
nor any human consolation. For these calamities that have come upon the world are sufficient
to reveal to everyone, more clearly than I could, the wrong done to the true faith.
But because you reproach me as though I had failed to speak clearly about what happened, O my holy superior,
Sophronius, now hear for yourself the things you know, and bear witness to the truth of what is being said.
For immediately, as you know, you first saw that death had snatched away the daughter of the man who was reigning at that time.
And after this, that demon, the chief instigator of adultery, who had cast the empress into disgrace and shame.
Then the cities of Africa, Spain, and Muzicanus [?], and the great and celebrated islands—
I mean Sicily, Rhodes, and many other great islands—
and Rome itself were handed over to the Vandal barbarian to be plundered.
Indeed, the barbarian’s second arrival at Rome came soon, not after a long delay.
During it, even Leo, who had held firmly to the faith,
but who, in the matters concerning me, had consented without investigation or judgment to the injustice of those who acted against me,
handed over the sacred vessels of divine worship into the barbarians’ hands with his own hands.
And with his own eyes he saw the daughters of the emperor who was reigning at that time being led away into captivity.
But I endured the devastation of my life and of everything belonging to me in this world as though it were the hardship of a single day,
and I have not changed throughout all these years. For now I have already reached the point
of being released, and every day I implore God to release me, whose eyes have seen the salvation of God.
Conclusion. Rejoice for me, desert, my beloved, my nurturer, and my dwelling place, and exile, my mother,
which, even after my death, will keep my body until the resurrection, by the will of God. Amen.
The copying of the book called The Bazaar of Heraclides is finished. It was composed by Mar Nestorius, illustrious among the saints and blessed in every way.
Bishop of Constantinople, a daily witness [?], and the glory of orthodoxy;
a true herald of the glorious Trinity. To him be everlasting glory. Amen.
[?]. 1. Commentary and letters of Saint Cyril of Alexandria and Saint John of Antioch,
and of Saint Athanasius and Saint Proclus of Constantinople, concerning the incarnation of our Lord.
Explanation of the Twelve Chapters by Cyril, Archbishop of Alexandria.
Everything is easy for those who understand and straightforward for those who find knowledge, as it is written.
For those who approach the divine words of the Holy Scriptures with the clear and pure eyes of their minds
gather spiritual benefits from them for their souls, like a heavenly treasure.
But those who have a mind inclined toward falsehood, following the [?] speech of human beings,
and loving impure knowledge, become partners
of those about whom the blessed Paul wrote: those whose minds the god of this world [?],
those who do not believe, so that the light of the gospel of the glory
of Christ may not shine upon them. For they are blind and are guides of the blind.
They fall into pits of destruction, just as our Savior himself said: “If a blind person leads a blind person,
both fall into a pit.” For some people undermine the teaching of truth,
and, with their minds full of the devil’s wickedness, they eagerly seek to distort the mystery of godliness.
They bring a grave accusation against the saving work of the Only-Begotten in the flesh, understanding
neither what they are saying nor what they are arguing about, as it is written.
There were indeed many others who devised wickedness like this in former times.
But now Nestorius and those with him fall short of their wickedness in no respect,
standing against Christ like those Pharisees of old and crying out insolently:
“Why do you, though you are a human being, make yourself God?” It was therefore necessary
that we too prepare ourselves to oppose their words and condemn their impure and defiled teachings,
remembering God, who said through the voice of the prophets: “Priests, listen and testify to the house of Jacob,
says the Lord Almighty”; and again: “Pass through my gates, and remove the stones from the road.”
For it is right [?], as we contend for the teaching of truth, to remove
the stumbling blocks from the way, so that the nations, without stumbling in any way,
may travel along a smooth road to the holy and divine folds,
saying of each of them, “This is the gate of the Lord, through which the righteous enter.”
Therefore, since Nestorius put a collection of alien and wicked blasphemies into his writings,
we set this down out of necessity, as people concerned for the lives of those who encounter them.
We did not indiscriminately set down whatever came into our minds in the letter of admonition written to him,
but, as I have just said, we were excluding and rejecting from the teaching of godliness
the inventions of his deficient understanding. But perhaps some people are angry at what we have said,
either because they do not truly understand the force of what is written,
or because they support the filthy heresy of Nestorius and share in his wickedness, since they think as he does.
The truth, therefore, does not elude those who are accustomed to thinking rightly.
But because people often follow the inventions expressed in these men's words
without understanding how and in what manner they arose, it seemed right to me
to explain each of the anathemas briefly and to describe their force as clearly as possible.
For I think this undertaking will provide a source of benefit to those who encounter it.
The First Anathema. Whoever does not confess that Emmanuel is truly God, and that therefore the holy Virgin is the Mother of God—
for she gave birth in the flesh to the Word from God who became flesh—let him be anathema.
Explanation. The blessed fathers who once assembled in the city of Nicaea,
when laying down the definitions of the orthodox faith, [?] maker of all things visible and invisible,
and in one Lord Jesus Christ, his Son, and in the Holy Spirit,
said that the Word was begotten of God the Father, the one through whom all things came to be, Light from Light,
true God from true God, who became incarnate and became human, suffered and died, and rose again.
For although he is God by nature, the only-begotten Word of God took on the offspring of Abraham,
as the blessed Paul said, and in this way shared in flesh and blood, just as we do.
For he came to be in the flesh from the holy Virgin and appeared as a human being like us.
Not that he fell away from being God—far from it!
Rather, being what he had been, he remained in the nature and glory of his divinity.
We therefore say that he became human, not by undergoing a change into what he had not been, or an alteration. For eternally
he is what he is, and he cannot undergo even a shadow of change. Nor do we assert any confusion,
or mingling, or blending of his nature with the flesh.
Rather, we say that the Word was united to flesh possessing a rational soul,
beyond understanding and beyond expression, in a way that he alone knows.
Thus he remained God even in taking on flesh.
And he is the one Son of God the Father, our Lord Jesus Christ, the very same before all times and ages,
inasmuch as he is known as the Word and the radiance of the Father's being, and in the last times as a human being for our sake, according to the saving plan.
But because some reject his birth in the flesh, which took place from the holy Virgin for the life of all—
not that he calls this the beginning of his existence as God, but that he became like us to rescue us from death and corruption—
for this reason, the first anathema that we issued cries out against their ungodly belief.
It professes what is right when it says that Emmanuel is truly God,
and that therefore the holy Virgin is the Mother of God. Second anathema.
If anyone does not confess that the Word from God the Father was united in his own person to flesh,
and that Christ with his flesh is one—that is, that the very same one is God and human—let him be anathema.
Explanation. Blessed Paul, the interpreter of the mysteries,
of God, writes: “Truly great is the mystery of godliness: he who was revealed in the flesh, was vindicated in the Spirit,
was seen by angels, was proclaimed among the nations, was believed in throughout the world, and was taken up in glory.”
What does “he was revealed in [?]” mean? It means that the Word from God the Father became flesh.
This was not through a transformation or change of his nature, as we have already said,
but rather, having made the flesh from the holy Virgin his own, he is called the one and same Son.
Before becoming human, the Word was still without flesh. After becoming human, the very same one had a body.
In this, then, we say that he himself is both God and a human being.
We do not divide our understanding of him, setting the human being separately, existing on his own, and God the Word separately,
so that we do not conceive of two sons. Rather, we confess that one and the same is Christ, Son, and Lord.
But as for those who think these things are not so, or wish to believe otherwise,
they split the one into two sons and separate from each other what has truly been united.
They say that the human being’s conjunction with God came about only in honor and authority [?].
We say that they are strangers to the upright and blameless faith.
Therefore, even if he is called an apostle [?], and even if he is said to have been anointed and is designated the Son of
God, we are not ashamed of the saving dispensation. Rather, we say of the Word who is from God the Father
that when he became a human being like us, he was then also called an apostle and was anointed with us in a human way.
For he who became like us, although he remained what he was, does not hold himself aloof from what belongs to us.
Rather, along with the limitations of humanity, he accepts these human things for the sake of the saving dispensation.
Yet none of this diminishes his glory or his nature. For even so he is God and Lord of all.
The Third Anathema. Whoever separates the persons in the one Christ [?] after the union,
joining them only by a conjunction of honor or authority or power [?],
and not rather by their coming together in a natural [?] union, let him be anathema. Explanation.
When we examine the mystery of the Only-begotten’s saving dispensation in the flesh, we say that, in a wonderful
and inexpressible way, the Word from God the Father was united to the holy body that has a rational soul within it.
And thus we understand there to be one Son, as can also be seen in us:
the nature of the body is different from that of the soul, yet the two are composed into a single unity.
But some people do not think that these things are so.
Instead, they posit a human being separately, existing on his own, and say that he was joined to the Word
who was begotten from God the Father, as though only in honor and authority,
and not in a natural union—that is, a real union—as we believe.
For divine Scripture [?] also said this: “We were by nature children of wrath.”
As also with the rest of these things. But he used “by nature” in place of “truly.”
We must not, then, separate the hypostases after the union and set each of them apart on its own,
that is, the man and God, and introduce a connection between them based on honor alone.
We would necessarily establish two sons, whereas Holy Scripture speaks of one Son and Lord.
Therefore, after the indescribable union, even if you call Emmanuel God,
we understand this to mean the Word from God, who became embodied and became human.
And if you say “Son of Man,” we likewise recognize the very same one, who, as part of his plan, came down to the limits of human existence.
We say that the one who cannot be touched became touchable, and that the one who cannot be seen became visible.
For the body united to him was not foreign to him,
the body that we also say is touchable and visible.
But those who do not believe this, but instead, as I said, separate the hypostases after the union,
and introduce a mere connection between them based only on honor and authority,
are excluded from those accustomed to think rightly by this anathema set out above.
The fourth anathema. Whoever divides between two persons or hypostases the statements found in the Scriptures and those of the evangelists and apostles,
or those spoken by the saints about Christ, or by him about himself,
and assigns some of them to a man understood separately, apart from the Word from God,
but assigns others, as befitting God, to the Word from God the Father alone, let him be accursed.
Explanation. Although the Word who is from God the Father exists in his likeness and equality,
he did not consider it robbery to be equal with God, as it is written.
Instead, he lowered himself to a voluntary self-emptying and willingly entered our condition,
without changing from being what he was.
Rather, even in this condition he remained God, and he did not disdain the limits of human existence.
Therefore, all things divine and human belong to him.
For how did he empty himself if he resents the limits of human existence? And if he hesitates to take on these human things,
who brought him down, as though by necessity and force, to become like us? Therefore, all the statements in the Gospel:
We attribute the human and divine things to one person. For we also believe that Christ Jesus is one Son:
that is, the Word of God who became human and took on flesh. ... Therefore, even if he said
something human, in keeping with the measure of humanity, we consider these human things his own, for the humanity too is his own.
And if he speaks as God, since we believe that the one who became human is God,
we likewise consider the utterances that transcend human nature to belong to the one Christ and Son.
But those who separate him into two persons necessarily introduce two sons.
For just as it is not permissible to divide a human being like us into two persons,
even though he is understood to consist of soul and body, but he is one and the same human being, so too with Emmanuel:
because he is the Son and Lord, the Word of God who took on flesh and became human, his person too is necessarily one.
And we assign these human things to him because of his coming in the flesh,
and these divine things in turn because of his indescribable birth from God the Father.
But those who separate and divide off the human being on his own, as though he were another son,
apart from the Word who is from God, and God on his own, as though he were another son, thereby speaking of two sons,
are rightly subject to the force of the anathema set out above. Fifth Anathema.
Whoever dares to call Christ a human being in whom God dwells, rather than saying that he is truly God, as one Son also
by nature, since the Word became flesh and shared in blood and flesh just as we do, let him be anathema.
Explanation. The blessed John the Evangelist said that the Word became flesh,
not that he was turned into flesh through a transformation or change of his nature, as we have already said.
For, as God, he possesses the quality of being unchangeable.
Rather, he shared in blood and flesh just as we do, and became a human being.
For Holy Scripture customarily calls a human being “flesh.”
For it is written, “All flesh will see the salvation of God.”
But those who praise the wicked teachings of Nestorius and those with him,
that is, those who think as he does, do make a show of accepting the term “incarnation.”
Yet they do not say that the Word of God truly took on flesh, that is, that he became a human being like us.
while he remained what he was. Instead, as in a man, one of the saints,
they contend that the only-begotten Word of God dwelt in the one born of the holy Virgin,
so that there would no longer be one Christ acknowledged as Son and Lord and worshiped,
but rather a man recognized separately, in and for himself,
honored only through a conjunction consisting in a unity of honor, who is to be worshiped and glorified together with him.
For the God of all dwells in us through the Holy Spirit,
just as he also said long ago through one of the holy prophets: “I will dwell in them
and walk among them. I will be their God, and they will be my people.”
The blessed Paul also expresses his distress: “Do you not know that you are temples of God,
and that the Spirit of God dwells in you?” Christ himself also said concerning the holy prophets
