and the righteous people of old: “If he called those to whom the word of God came ‘gods,’
do you say to the one whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, ‘You are blaspheming,’
because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?” But it is not in the same way that God dwells in us
that he also dwells in Christ. For he is God by nature, who appeared like us.
And he is one Son, even when he became flesh. Therefore, those who dare to say that he is a man in whom God dwells,
and not rather God who became human, necessarily fall under the anathema set out above.
Sixth Anathema. Whoever says that the Word from God the Father is the God or Lord of Christ,
and does not rather acknowledge the very same one as both God and man,
since the Word became flesh, as it is written, let him be anathema. Explanation.
Our Lord Jesus Christ, since he is truly the one and only Son of God the Father, even when
the Word became flesh, rules over all together with the one who begot him. Every knee bows to him, of those in heaven [?], those on earth, and those beneath the earth.
And every tongue acknowledges that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.
He himself is therefore Lord of all, because he is recognized as God and is God,
even though he was not apart from the flesh after becoming human. But he is not his own God or Lord.
For thinking or speaking in this way is utterly shameful—that is, truly full of every kind of impiety.
It was therefore rightly on account of this that the anathema set out above was pronounced. Seventh anathema.
Whoever says that God the Word worked in Jesus as in a human being, and attached to him the glory of the Only Begotten,
as though he were someone else apart from him, let him be accursed. Explanation.
When the blessed Gabriel announced to the holy virgin the birth in the flesh of the Only Begotten Son of God,
he said, “You will give birth to a son, and you will call his name Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.”
Christ too was anointed, since he was anointed along with us as a human being, according to the words of the psalmist:
“You have loved righteousness and hated wickedness. Therefore God, your God, has anointed you with the oil
of gladness beyond your companions.” And although he himself is the giver of the Holy Spirit,
and does not give the Spirit by measure to those who are worthy,
for he is full, and from his fullness we have all received, as it is written,
in the divine plan he is said to have been anointed as a human being, when the Holy Spirit rested upon him [?],
so that the Spirit, who departed at the beginning because of Adam’s transgression, might dwell in us too.
Thus the Only Begotten himself, the Word of God, was called Christ when he became flesh.
And he performs wonders because the power proper to God is his own.
Those, therefore, who say that the glory of the Only Begotten was attached to Christ’s capacity,
as though the Only Begotten were someone else apart from Christ, conceive of two sons:
one who acts, and another in whom the action takes place, like a human being who is one of those like us.
And by this they fall under the force of the anathema. Eighth anathema.
Whoever dares to say that the human being who was assumed ought to be worshiped together with God the Word,
and glorified together with him, and called God together with him, as one person with another—
for the word “with,” which is continually added, necessarily conveys this meaning—
and does not instead honor Emmanuel with one act of worship and offer him one glorification,
since the Word became flesh, let him be accursed. Explanation.
We have been baptized into one God, the Father Almighty, and into one Son, our Lord Jesus, and into one Holy Spirit.
The blessed Paul also said, “Do you not know that those of us who were baptized into Christ,
Was it into his death that we were baptized? Therefore we were buried with him through baptism into death.
So that, just as Christ rose from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too might walk in new life.
Therefore we have believed and been baptized, as I said, into one Son, our Lord Jesus Christ.
That is, into the Word from God the Father, who took flesh and became human.
And we have learned to worship the one who is truly God. With us, the heavenly powers also worship him.
For it is written: When he brings the firstborn into the world, he says, “Let all the angels of God worship him.”
The only-begotten became the firstborn when he was revealed as a son like us.
For then he was also called the brother of those who love him. Therefore anyone who says:
That he is worshipped alongside him separately as a man, being someone other than the Word from God,
And does not bring them together in a true unity as one Christ and Son and Lord,
Honoring him with one act of worship, is rightly placed under the force of the anathema.
The Ninth Anathema. Whoever says of the one Lord Jesus Christ that he was glorified by the Spirit,
As though he were using an external power belonging to the Spirit,
And received from him the ability to act against unclean spirits and to perform divine signs among human beings,
And does not instead say that the Spirit through whom he also performed divine signs is properly his own, let him be anathema.
Explanation. When the only-begotten Word of God became human, he remained God even so.
He is what the Father also is, except for being the Father.
And having the Holy Spirit, who is from him and is in him by nature, he performed divine signs.
Therefore, even when he became human, because he remained God even so, it was by his own power
That he performed miracles through the Spirit. But those who say that, as a human being like us,
That is, as one of the saints, he was glorified through the activity of the Spirit,
And that he used not his own power but an external power befitting God,
And received from the Holy Spirit, as a share of grace, his ascent to heaven, are rightly subjected to the force of the anathema.
The Tenth Anathema. That Christ became the high priest and apostle of our confession,
Divine Scripture has said, and that he [?] himself for us as a fragrant aroma to God and the Father.
Whoever says, then, that the high priest and apostle of our confession is not the Word who is from God,
when he became flesh and a human being like us, but rather another human being, born separately from a woman, apart from him;
or if anyone says that he offered a sacrifice for himself, and not rather for us alone—
for he who knew no sin had no need of a sacrifice—let him be anathema.
Explanation. We acknowledge that human limitations belong to the Word who was begotten of God.
Nevertheless, they are not contemptible, because of the work of salvation.
For although he is by nature Lord of all, he lowered himself to our condition, taking the form of a servant,
and was called our high priest and apostle, being given these titles according to this human condition.
He offered himself for us as a pleasing fragrance to God the Father.
For by one offering he perfected forever those who are being sanctified, as it is written.
But I do not know how those who think otherwise maintain
that it was not the Word from God who became a human being and was called the apostle and high priest of our confession,
but another human being apart from him, who was born separately from the holy Virgin.
They say that he was called apostle and high priest, and that he attained this through his development.
And he offered himself as a sacrifice to God the Father, not primarily for us, but for himself.
This is entirely foreign to the right and blameless faith. For he committed no sin.
He who is above all shortcomings and entirely free from every sin had no need of a sacrifice for himself.
But because those who think otherwise reject what is right
and once again introduce two sons, this dispute became necessary, openly exposing their impiety.
The Eleventh Anathema. Whoever does not acknowledge that the Lord’s flesh is life-giving
and belongs to the Word from God the Father, but instead belongs to someone else apart from him, joined to him in [?],
or possessing God merely as an indweller, and does not acknowledge that it is, rather, life-giving,
as I have said, because it became the very flesh of the Word who is able to give life to all—let him be anathema.
Explanation. We celebrate a living, holy, and bloodless sacrifice in the churches.
We do not believe that what is offered belongs to someone like us, being merely an ordinary human body.
In the same way, also the precious blood. Rather, we receive them
as the body and blood of the Word who gives life to all. For ordinary flesh cannot give life.
Our Savior himself bears witness that this is so when he says, “The flesh is of no benefit; it is the Spirit who gives life.”
For because it became the life-giver’s own, it is thereby recognized as life-giving,
just as our Savior himself said: “As the living Father sent me, and I live because of the Father,
so whoever eats me will also live because of me.” But because Nestorius and those who have fallen into the sickness of his thinking
undermine the power of the sacrament through their deficient teaching, this anathema was most justly formulated.
The Twelfth Anathema. Whoever does not confess that the Word from God suffered in the flesh, was crucified in the flesh [?], and tasted death in the flesh [?],
and became the firstborn from the dead, as one who is living and gives life as God, let him be anathema.
Explanation. The Word from God is neither subject to suffering nor mortal.
For the divine nature, which cannot be described, is beyond suffering.
He gives life to everything and is free from corruption and from everything that ordinarily causes distress. Yet, although the Word is these things
by nature, being from God the Father, he made flesh capable of death his own,
so that, in what is ordinarily subject to suffering, by taking upon himself suffering on our behalf and for our sake, he might deliver us all from death and corruption.
God brought his own body to life, and he became the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep and the firstborn from the dead.
For he was not an ordinary human being, regarded separately and in his own right, apart from the Word from God the Father,
who endured the honored [?] for our sake and tasted death. Rather, the Lord of glory himself suffered in the flesh, according to the Scriptures.
But because these new and wicked [?] wish to intrude upon the firm and spotless faith,
saying that an ordinary human being endured the cross on our behalf, this anathema was necessarily formulated,
showing the enormity of the wickedness within them. Here ends the explanation of the twelve chapters by the blessed Cyril.
The letter that Saint Cyril sent to the blessed Valerian, bishop of Iconium.
To my lord, my dearly beloved and fellow minister Valerian: Cyril sends greetings in our Lord.
It is sufficient, as I believe—that is, as indeed
it is true—that the vigilance of Your Holiness should be able to stand firmly against the empty words of certain people.
For in their foolishness they turn everything upside down and throw it all into confusion.
And they pretend to investigate closely the mystery of the incarnation of the Only Begotten, and give the impression that they understand it.
Yet they readily turn it into something improper and understand it in distorted ways.
This is the bitterest thing of all: they lie and pretend that they want to think rightly.
And while they give themselves an appearance of plausibility, as though they were inclined toward this,
they put it on their faces, while pouring the gall of the wicked Nestorius over the souls of simple people.
They resemble those accustomed to treating bodies, who mix honey [?] into bitter medicines to make them appealing to the taste.
But their thoughts do not escape us, for we have the mind of Christ, as Paul says.
For if someone were to say that the one who was born of God the Father,
the Only Begotten, God the Word, the maker of the ages, received the beginning of his existence from the holy Virgin,
it would seem consistent with their position that they rightly say:
“If God the Word is spirit by nature, how could he be born from a body,
when our Lord said, ‘What is born of [?] is flesh’?” But because the teaching about the mystery of Christ
follows another path, one that is plain and straight and has nothing crooked in it, for
what reason do they babble pointlessly, without understanding what they are saying
or what they are agreeing to? For we say that the Only Begotten, God the Word,
is spirit as God, as it is written, and that for the salvation of us all he took flesh and became human.
He did not turn his own nature into a body, nor did he abandon what he was,
nor was he changed or altered. Rather, he took from the holy Virgin a body without blemish, endowed with a rational soul.
And he made it his own through a union that is inconceivable, without confusion, and utterly inexpressible.
And this body is recognized as his own, not someone else’s. In this way the Only Begotten entered the world and became the firstborn among many brothers.
He is not counted among created things, since he is God. Therefore, when he is said to have been born of a woman,
[?], the qualification “in the flesh” follows, so that no one may suppose that he received his beginning from the holy Virgin.
For God the Word exists eternally with his Father, long before the ages.
But when, by the Father’s will, he took the form of a servant, then he is also said to have been born bodily of a woman.
Therefore, since it is known that what comes from flesh is flesh, and what comes from God is God,
Yet both together are one Christ, one Son and Lord, together with his body endowed with a soul.
That is what he is, as I have said. Therefore, let them not divide the one Son into two for us,
setting up the Word and Son separately, and separately the man from a woman, as they say.
Instead, let them know that it was not a man who was joined to God the Word.
Rather, he himself is said to have become a human being, taking from the offspring of Abraham, as it is written.
And he became like his brothers in everything except sin. Now likeness in everything includes, above all,
birth from a woman. In our case, this is understood in a human way, but in the case of the Only Begotten, in a way surpassing this.
For it was God who became embodied, and for this reason the holy Virgin is called the Mother of God.
But if they say that God and a human being came together and formed one Christ,
while the person of each of them was preserved without confusion, they are not understanding or expressing this correctly.
For it is not, as they say, that God and a human being came together and formed one Christ.
Rather, as I said before, while being God the Word,
he shared in flesh and blood like us, so that he might be recognized as God who became a human being.
He took our body and made it his own, so that, just as among us one human being is recognized,
whose constitution consists of soul and body, so he too may be confessed to be one Son and one Lord.
For the nature and constitution of a human being are confessed to be one, even though he consists of different things that are not
like one another. For the nature of the body is different from that of the soul, yet it belongs to the soul.
It completes the person of one human being, and this is not obscured in the thought and understanding of what has been said.
But their combination, or their inseparable coming together into one, makes the human being one living being.
Therefore, the Only Begotten, God the Word, did not take a human being to himself and come forth as a human being.
Rather, although his birth from the Father is beyond description, through the Holy Spirit he made himself a temple in a way surpassing nature, and became a human being.
For this reason, in this very condition, he is recognized as one, even though in thought the nature of his body is understood to be different from him.
But confess everywhere that his body was endowed with a rational soul.
I have learned, however, that some people have reached such madness that they are not afraid to say:
God the Word dwelt in the man Jesus, who was born of the Virgin, and made this man God.
But we say to them: This, our beloved, is not what it means for the Word from God to have become incarnate and become human.
For him to dwell in a human being as in one of the holy prophets is not the fulfillment of the mystery.
Rather, as we have already said, he willed that the Word who was begotten of the Father should become flesh,
as it is written—not through a change of nature, or an alteration, or a transformation into flesh.
Instead, he made a body endowed with a soul his own. He was born and came forth as a human being, not by attaching himself to a human being,
nor by dwelling in one, as they say. But the claim that a human being became God because of the one who dwelt in him,
as they say—this we reject completely.
How does it not display madness? For it conflicts with the purpose of divine Scripture.
For the glorious apostle, speaking of God the Word, who is in the likeness of the Father and equal to him in everything,
said that he did not consider his equality with God something seized by force.
Instead, he emptied himself and took the form of a servant, and became human in the likeness of human beings, and humbled himself.
But they turn everything into its opposite and sell away the force of the [?].
And they say that a human being became God. Who, then, was the one who emptied himself,
our beloved? And how was he humbled? And what form of a servant did he take? Tell me! For their statement apparently presents
a human being, one of us, who was exalted and who rose from our emptiness to the fullness of divinity,
and who passes from the form of a servant to the form of lordship.
How they say that the Only Begotten was emptied, or how he endured our lowliness, I cannot understand,
unless they say that his emptying was precisely this: that he honored the human being with his own glory.
And if, by honoring, he suffers loss, and by glorifying, he is emptied, how would one not say instead
that it would have been better for him not to honor or glorify anyone? For he would have remained in his greatness
if he had not honored and glorified that human being who, as they say, was attached to him.
Are these things not worthy of laughter and full of folly, though they deceitfully present them as wise? But the account of the truth
does not hold that he was ever emptied in any respect; rather, he is full and perfect in his nature.
Nor does it suggest that he was lowly in any respect; rather, he is high and exalted above all, and afterward descended to become what he had not been.
And it knows that the one who took the form of a servant was by nature free from the beginning.
And it does not recognize the one who became human as a human being before he became human.
Divine Scripture, then, speaks of an emptying, the likeness of a servant, and also humanity.
And it says that the one who willingly accepted these things is God the Word. Why do they turn it into its opposite—
this arrangement full of wisdom—and say that a human being became God,
so that Christians would be no different from those who worshiped creation rather than its Creator? Or do they perhaps suppose
that even the holy angels went astray along with us, those whom Holy Scripture commanded
to worship the Firstborn who entered the world? And how does the title Firstborn apply to the Only Begotten,
unless he became human? For if it is true that he is recognized as the Firstborn because of his many brothers,
then he came down to share brotherhood with us when he became a human being like us and became like us in everything except sin.
For devotion to God, it is enough for us to consider and understand that what has become the body of God, who gives all
life, possesses his power and activity and is rich in indescribable glory.
But those who hold these views inflict another injustice on divine Scripture and say that it is not
to the person of the Only Begotten that the humiliation inflicted by the Jews belongs,
nor bodily death either, but to another son, the one who was born of a woman.
And I do not know under what pretense of an appearance of devotion to God they abandon the straight road and leap onto the road to the pit
and to the depths of Sheol, as it is written. For he is truly God, neither subject to suffering nor tangible,
because he is without a body. Rather, he is beyond intelligible and visible creation and is incorporeal in his incomprehensible nature.
But because the Only Begotten, God the Word, took a body from the Virgin Mary, and,
as I have said many times, made it his own and offered himself on our behalf as a pleasing fragrance,
an unblemished sacrifice to God the Father, for this reason we say that he himself endured everything that happened to his body.
For whatever is a body is subject to all these things belonging to the body, except sin.
And because God the Word became human, he remained free from suffering in his divinity, while making the sufferings of his body his own.
And he is said to have suffered in the body, although he does not experience suffering insofar as he is God.
Thus, a pretense of devotion to God leads them astray
from the truth. And they do not understand that his freedom from suffering is preserved insofar as he is God.
But it is written about him that he suffered for us in the flesh, because, although he is God by nature, he became flesh.
In the flesh, because, although he is God by nature, he became flesh—that is, a complete human being.
For who was it who said to the Father, to God who was in heaven:
“You did not desire sacrifices and offerings, and you did not ask for whole burnt offerings for sins, but you prepared a body for me.
Then I said, ‘Here I come to do your will, O God’”? For he who, as God, is without a body
says that a body was prepared for him, so that in it he might undergo suffering for us and heal us all by his wounds, according to the prophet’s saying.
But how did one die for many, and how was he worthy to die for everyone,
if the suffering belonged to someone who was a human being? But if he suffered as a human being, as one to whom the sufferings of his body belonged,
then we rightly say that the bodily death of one was worthy to be weighed against the life of all.
This was not because he was like one of us, but because, although he is God by nature,
he became a human being, according to the confession of our fathers. But if some people remove from the Only-Begotten
suffering in the flesh, as something unsuitable and unworthy of him, let them also deny that he was born in the flesh of a virgin.
For if it is unworthy of him to say that he suffered in the flesh, his birth in the flesh comes before that. And consequently,
by these things the work of the divine plan is nullified, the mysteries of the Christians are nullified, and the hope of our salvation becomes empty.
But they say, “How can one who does not experience suffering suffer?” It is acknowledged [?]:
as I said, God the Word is not subject to suffering by nature.
But he is said to have suffered in his flesh, according to what is written, for he was in a body subject to suffering.
Peter also confirms this when he writes about him: “He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree.”
Thus the Word is not subject to suffering insofar as he is God, but the sufferings of the flesh are regarded as his own in accordance with the divine plan.
Otherwise, how could the firstborn of all creation, through whom rulers, authorities, dominions, and thrones came into being,
in whom everything holds together, be the firstborn from the dead, who also became the firstfruits of all who have fallen asleep, if a body capable of suffering
had not been made his own by God the Word? For just as he was born bodily of a woman,
sharing in our birth as a human being, even though he has his birth from his Father,
so he is said to have suffered in the flesh as a human being like us, although by nature he is not subject to suffering, since he is God.
For in this way Christ is known to be one, and in this way he shares his Father’s throne. Not as
a human being honored by the indwelling of God the Word, but as a true Son, even when he became human.
For the excellence of his nature is preserved, even though, in carrying out his saving plan, he came to be in the likeness of a servant.
So then, as we have said, although he shared in our nature by becoming human,
nevertheless, he was also God, above all creation.
But I have learned that some people, when explaining the reason for his ascent into heaven, say:
“He went to a protected place where he would not be harassed. He was also deemed worthy to share the Father's throne,
so that the enemy of our nature could not approach and harm him.” Tell me, then: did heaven become his protector?
And was his ascent from among us, in which we glory, an escape rather than an ascension? But if, as it seems, he was afraid
that the evil one might fight against him again if he did not ascend, and would harm him even after his resurrection,
who would not flee from this deluge? And who would not distance himself and turn away from this error,
and abandon those who dare to say such things? Nothing is more absurd than these statements,
for their argument borders on madness. For after Christ had completed his saving work on our behalf,
trampled Satan, shaken all his power, and abolished the dominion of death, he opened up for us a new and living way
by ascending into heaven and appearing on our behalf before God the Father, as it is written. And he shares his throne,
even bodily—not as a human being conceived of separately as another son apart from God the Word,
nor as one who merely dwelt in a human being, but as the true Son, one and only.
Even though he became human, he sits as God with God, as Lord with the Lord, and as Son with the Father,
with whom he truly shares the same nature, even though he has a body.
For it would have been possible to refute their foolish statements at length.
But if we were to speak at length against their absurdities, perhaps their tediousness, together with their folly, would burden us.
Yet it is necessary to append to what I have said the things by which they think they can frighten the Lord's congregation,
as it is written, “to shoot in the darkness at the upright in heart”—that is, at those who are accustomed to live with simplicity of mind
and who preserve the richness of the faith in their hearts as something entrusted to them, keeping it sound and undisturbed.
For those who are skilled in error and devise twisted questions draw the untrained away from the truths.
And they ask questions insincerely, just as their fellow heretics are accustomed to ask:
They do not understand what is written: “Woe to anyone who gives his neighbor stirred-up dregs to drink!”
For those who support the wickedness of Arius say that the only-begotten Word of God is of another nature.
They place him second to the one who begot him. They call him created and made,
and count him among created things—the one through whom everything came into being.
Again, when they investigate the mystery of his incarnation, they deceitfully undermine the power of the truth.
Already infected with the thinking of Apollinaris, they say
that God the Word did indeed take a body, but, they say, there was no rational soul in it.
Rather, he is in the body in place of a mind and soul. But they are soon caught acting deceitfully in this.
For, to prevent us from thinking that the words spoken of our Lord in human terms ought to be understood with reference to his incarnate life,
and in a way appropriate to Christ in his humanity, because he became a human being,
they steal the rational soul from the body and lower the Son beneath the nature of his Father.
They make him take the place of a soul for the body, and gather statements from the Scriptures as a pretext for their wrongdoing.
But look, even now, those who rival these men in their lack of discipline
have burst out bitterly with the new words of Nestorius, to wage war against the faith with their questions.
For they say that the blessed Paul said about Christ our Savior: “He emptied himself and took the form of a servant,
and came to be in the likeness of human beings, and was found in appearance as a human being.
He humbled himself and became obedient to the point of death—even death on a cross.
Therefore God also highly exalted him and gave him a name that is greater than every name.”
And again, in another place: “For God was in Christ, reconciling the world to his majesty.”
And again: “In him all the fullness of divinity dwelt bodily.”
They also repeat the words of Peter, who said: “Jesus of Nazareth, whom God anointed with the Holy Spirit and with power,
who went about healing all those who were afflicted by the evil one, because God was with him.”
And again: “God overlooked the times of error, but now commands all people everywhere to repent,
since he has [?] appointed a day of judgment on which he is going to judge the whole earth through the man he has chosen.
And he turned everyone to faith in him by raising him from the dead.”
They apply these, and those expressed in another way in human terms, to these things.
And immediately they spew bitter words from their evil minds.
“To whom,” they say, “did God give the superior name? To God the Word? And how,” they say, “can this be accepted? For he was always God,”
as one who is naturally begotten from him. For this is the name superior to every name.
For what is [?] higher than being God by nature? And whom did he anoint with the Holy Spirit? Or with whom was God?
They add other things to these, babbling and disturbing the minds of simple people.
They make distinctions everywhere, for they are worldly people who do not have the Spirit.
And by dividing the one Christ, who is the Son and Lord of all, into two sons, they fall into the very thing they reject.
For they pretend to confess one Christ and Lord and Son, and they say that he has one person.
Yet by dividing him again into two individual beings alien to one another, they deny the mystery in every respect.
For they say that the one born of a woman, or that form of a servant, received the superior name separately and on his own.
And he, they say, was anointed with the Holy Spirit, and he is the one with whom God the Word was.
But with these words they spew corruption and a foul stench at us.
For they are evil and cannot speak good things, according to the saying of our Savior.
For he was always truly God and Lord,
the one who was begotten from God the Father invisibly and in a way that cannot be expressed.
But because he came to be in the flesh from a woman, gloriously and beyond our nature,
through the coming of the Holy Spirit and the overshadowing of God's power, and underwent birth like ours,
for this is how he is said to have emptied himself, humbled himself, and become obedient even to death on the cross,
on this account he is said to have received the name superior to every name, and every knee bows to him,
in heaven, on earth, and beneath the earth, and every tongue confesses that Lord
is Jesus Christ, to the glory of God his Father.
For the intelligent and rational creation did not fail to recognize that the one who became human was God the Word.
For although he entered into our circumstances and shared in flesh and blood like us, nevertheless,
he did not cease to be God, nor did he abandon being what he had been [?], remaining as he was.
For he remained worshiped, to the glory of God the Father. For it is the Father's glory that his Son should reign and be worshiped with him,
even though, in carrying out the divine plan, he became a human being for the salvation of those under heaven.
Therefore, when angels and we human beings believed, even while he had a body,
that he is truly God by nature, then he is said to have received a name superior to every name.
This does not mean that he actually gained something by way of an addition. For what he had always been,
how could he receive as someone who did not have it? Rather, because God the Father shone in everyone's hearts,
he did not allow them to forget that the Word who became incarnate is God by nature.
For he says, “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me [?] him.” His anointing, however, was on account of his humanity.
For although the only-begotten Son, begotten of him, is holy by nature like his Father,
he is said to have been anointed like us, or sanctified by his Father, because he became a human being. For
the wise Paul wrote about him and about us that the one who sanctifies and those who are sanctified are all from one.
For this reason he was not ashamed to call them his brothers, saying, “I will proclaim your name to my brothers.”
Therefore, although the Only-begotten is holy by nature and sanctifies his creation,
because he became a human being and a brother to us, he is said to have been anointed in his humanity.
This is something proper and fitting for humanity, while his stature was not diminished because of his humanity.
For this is also what he said to the glorious John: “It is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness.”
But if it is also said that God was with him, how did these crafty sophists forget
that the Father is always with the Son by nature, and that he is in him? Or do they not remember that Christ said,
“Have I been with you all this time, and you have not known me, Philip? Whoever has seen me has seen the Father.”
And, “I and my Father are one.” “Do you not believe that I am in my Father and my Father is in me?” He also said,
while speaking with his disciples, “The hour is coming, and indeed is now here, when you will be scattered, each to his own place,
and you will leave me alone. Yet I am not alone, because my Father is with me.”
For it is not as those filled with alien conceit suppose: that God the Word, being one Son, was
with another son, a human being who had been assumed. For this is a division and a separation
of two sons. Rather, God the Father was with the Son.
That is, with God the Word, who became incarnate and became human. For the Father is not separated from the Son.
But if someone supposes that the statement that God is going to judge [?] the earth through the man Jesus means that Scripture said:
that the only-begotten Son is going to judge the earth through that human being who was born of a woman, he falls away from the truth.
Rather, it is fitting for godliness to understand what Christ said: “The Father judges no one,
but has given all judgment to the Son, so that everyone may honor the Son just as they honor the Father.”
For God the Word, who became human and was numbered among human beings,
and was given a name among us like us, is no less the judge as God and Lord.
For there is one Son, in whom is God the Father. For, as I said, the one who begot him is in him.
And he, in turn, is in him. For just as there is one God the Father, from whom are all things,
so there is also one Lord Jesus Christ, through whom are all things. But they twist into something improper
also the statement made by blessed Paul. For he rightly said that God was in Christ, reconciling the world to his majesty.
They, in turn, introduce a crude division into the one Christ and separate God the Word,
as though he were in another Christ, understood to exist separately, so that he would be thought to have dwelt in a human being,
and not to have become human. But the intention of divine Scripture does not permit it to be understood this way, you wise men.
For you confuse the reading by directing the force of its meaning toward something improper.
For you ought to have taken every thought captive to obedience to Christ, as it is written.
For it was God who was reconciling the world to his majesty in Christ.
For when we were being reconciled in Christ, our reconciliation was with God the Father.
For God the Word, who is from him, was not another, apart from him in nature.
For the Son’s nature suffered no harm, even though he became human. For he remained one and the same, together with his body.
But that reconciliation came to us in Christ, and that he is our peace—
who dares deny it? For he is the way and the door, and in him all the fullness of the Godhead dwelt bodily.
But again this bitter, oppressive, crafty man pricks up his ear toward me on hearing this and says:
“If, for us, the one who dwelt is one, and the one in whom he dwelt is another,
how is it not necessary for the persons to be distinguished and recognized separately? Tell me.”
Where, then, does that claim of one person stand? For they say that Christ has one person.
But if there are two hypostases separate from one another, there will also be two persons.
Instead, they introduce a rule to suit themselves and say, “We distinguish
the hypostases, but unite the person.” How is this not foolishness,
something unheard of, and one of those things that cannot be? For in Christ, as I said,
it must be recognized that the nature of the flesh is different from that of the Word, with whom it became one.
But because the Scriptures speak of one Son and Lord, and the tradition of the faith also contains this,
we, for our part, have introduced an inseparable union, which took place between the Word from the Father and the body
that has a rational soul. We confess that there is one Son and one Christ.
And because there is one Son, we speak of one person, following in every respect the divine proclamation
and those who from the beginning were eyewitnesses and servants of the Word.
But those who understand something else beyond this, and through foolish questions of their own invention attach themselves to what is improper,
we exclude from our fellowship, saying to them, “Go into the brightness of your fire and into the flame of your burning.”
But because I have learned that some foolish people are going around saying
that the wicked thinking of Nestorius has taken hold of all the bishops of the East,
and that they say it is sound and ought to be followed, I wished to make this known as well.
All these bishops of the East, together with the honored lord John, bishop of Antioch, openly, in writing,
made known to everyone that the teaching of Nestorius is [?].
They condemned and anathematized him along with us, and they agree with the teaching of the holy apostles and of our fathers.
They too said with us that the holy Virgin is the Mother of God,
without adding that the mother of Christ is the mother of a man, as those wretched followers of Nestorius say.
Instead, they said openly that there is one Christ, Son, and Lord,
who was begotten of God the Father before all ages, who is God the Word.
But in the last times, this very same one was born in the flesh from a woman.
And they say that this very same one is perfect in his divinity and perfect in his humanity.
They confess that he is one person, without dividing him in any way into two sons or two Christs.
Therefore, if anyone falsely accuses them of believing anything beyond these things, let us not allow him [?].
Instead, let him be cast out as a deceiver and a son of the devil, so that they may not drive away those who wish to walk uprightly.
And if they produce writings purportedly coming from persons who are [?], these are not to be accepted.
For they have already professed their faith in writing, and they cannot write anything contrary to it afterward.
Here ends the letter that Cyril sent to the blessed Valerian.
A statement presented to Archbishop Cyril by Paul, bishop of Emesa, who was sent by John.
To my lord Cyril, the bishop who is holy and reverend in every respect, from Paul. Greetings in our Lord.
Our God-fearing and victorious emperors, showing the care and concern
that they have long had for those under their rule, and especially for the holy churches of God
and for the orthodox, true, and pure faith that they received from their fathers,
sent letters through the illustrious tribune and notary Aristolaus to Your Reverence,
to the reverend and holy Bishop John, and to our reverend and holy father Acacius, bishop of Aleppo,
commanding that, by coming together either face to face or in peaceful agreement, you should resolve the disputes that have arisen
between the God-loving bishops who assembled at Ephesus and ourselves,
and establish in the holy churches of God the peace that is pleasing to God,
and put an end to the disturbances that continually occur in the holy churches of God.
You should also agree to the deposition of Nestorius and anathematize his evil teaching.
When they received these letters expressing fear of God and love for Christ—
the holy Bishop John mentioned above and the holy Bishop Acacius—
and considered that there were many matters requiring a face-to-face meeting with you,
so that much time would not pass in delay, they sent me to Your Reverence to discuss with Your Holiness
how the matters concerning peace should be carefully managed, and how this excellent undertaking
might be brought to a fitting and beneficial conclusion. So, when I came, met with you, and spoke,
I found Your Reverence ready to manage this matter calmly and peacefully, as befits priests.
I also gave your holiness a document proclaiming the faith that we received from the fathers:
the orthodox and undefiled faith. This was the principal matter, deserving effort and care.
But since the matters concerning Nestorius also needed to receive a decision—the decision that had already seemed good to us—
I am writing this letter as I approach your reverence, who is nearby.
In it I declare that we accept the ordination of the reverent and holy Maximian,
and agree to the deposition of Nestorius, who was formerly in Constantinople.
We also anathematize the things he has impiously said in matters of doctrine.
And we gladly accept pure and genuine communion with you, in accordance with the statement we gave your God-fearing self
concerning the incarnation of God the Word. You also praised this statement and accepted it as your own faith;
a copy of it is also included in this letter. And in this pure communion,
we grant pardon for everything that happened in the meantime on both sides during the turmoil.
And by the grace of God we return to the churches’ former peace.
Letter of Mar John of Antioch to Mar Cyril of Alexandria.
To the reverent and God-loving Bishop Cyril: John sends greetings in our Lord.
Some time ago, by the command of our God-fearing emperors, it was ordered
that a council of God-loving bishops should assemble in the metropolis of Ephesus concerning church affairs and the orthodox faith.
We too assembled in the city just mentioned, but returned without meeting one another.
But it is unseemly to speak of the causes of divisions in a time of peace.
The churches were thereby driven into divisions, whereas everyone should have been especially concerned about this:
how they might come into harmony, with every division removed from their midst.
The God-fearing and Christ-loving emperors also commanded that this very thing should happen: that we should bring Christ’s churches into unity.
For this very purpose they sent my lord, the admirable and distinguished tribune Aristolaus,
to bring their authoritative letters, commanding that from now on we should be of one mind,
remove the stumbling blocks from our midst, and put an end to all disturbances and every distress.
In response to these authoritative letters, we immediately, at that very hour, sent:
To my lord Paul, holy in every way, the God-loving bishop, since this was pleasing
also to our holy and reverend father Acacius and to the God-loving bishops with us.
We did this out of great caution, since we could not meet with one another
and carry out face to face what our God-fearing emperors had commanded.
We instructed him to manage the matters concerning peace in our place, on our behalf, and as our representative,
since peace comes before everything else, and to deliver to your piety
the statement jointly drawn up by us concerning the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ.
This statement, which we sent to your piety through the God-loving man mentioned above, is as follows.
Concerning the Virgin, the Mother of God, and what we think
and say about her, and concerning the manner of the incarnation of the only-begotten Son of God,
we must speak, not by way of addition, but to provide confirmation, in accordance with what, from the beginning, from the Holy Scriptures
and from the tradition of the holy fathers, we have received and held fast. We state this briefly,
adding absolutely nothing to the faith established by the holy fathers at Nicaea.
For, as we have already said, it is sufficient for the whole knowledge of godliness and refutes all the wicked teaching of the heretics.
We speak while passing over matters beyond comprehension; rather, by acknowledging our weakness,
we bar the way to those who wish to attack us over matters that we consider beyond human understanding.
We therefore confess our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God,
to be perfect God and a perfect human being, consisting of a rational soul and a body.
He was begotten of the Father before the ages in his divinity, and in the last days,
the very same was born of the Virgin Mary in his humanity, for us and for our salvation.
He is of the same nature as the Father in his divinity and of the same nature as we are in his humanity.
For a union of two natures took place, and therefore we confess one Christ, one Son, one Lord.
According to this understanding of the union without confusion,
we confess the holy Virgin to be the Mother of God, because God the Word became flesh and became human, and from the very
conception he united to himself the temple taken from her. As for the statements about our Lord made by the apostles and evangelists:
We know that those who speak of divine matters [?] treated some of these sayings in common, as referring to one person.
Others, however, they distinguished as referring to two natures, assigning those that befit God to Christ’s divinity.
But the lowly sayings they assigned to his humanity. Once this was accepted, agreement was reached.
For the sake of removing every controversy and allowing worldwide peace to dwell in the holy churches,
and of removing from our midst the stumbling blocks that have arisen, we accept the deposition of Nestorius,
who formerly was bishop in Constantinople, and we anathematize his wicked and impure statements,
since the holy churches among us possess the right and sound faith.
They preserve this and hand it down to the peoples, just as Your Holiness also does [?]. We also agree
to the ordination of the holy and God-fearing bishop Maximian, of the holy church of God in Constantinople.
And we are in communion with all those throughout the whole world,
the God-fearing bishops who hold fast to and preserve the right and unblemished faith.
May you remain in good health and pray for us, my God-fearing and holy lord, our true brother.
Letter of the blessed Cyril to John of Antioch.
To my lord John, our beloved brother and fellow minister: Cyril sends greetings in our Lord.
Let the heavens rejoice and the earth be glad! For the dividing barrier has been broken down, and what caused distress has been abolished.
Every form of division has been removed, for Christ, the Savior of all, has given peace to his churches.
The faithful and God-loving emperors also urged us toward this,
for they are zealous and devoted champions of the faith of their fathers.
And indeed, with care and without wavering, the right faith
they preserve in their souls, so that they may gain a name of praise forever, while making their reign illustrious.
To them the Lord of hosts also distributes good things with a generous hand.
He grants them the power to overcome those who stand against them, and bestows victory upon them.
For he does not speak falsely when he says, “As I live, says the Lord, I will glorify those who glorify me.”
So when our God-loving brother and fellow minister, my lord Bishop Paul, came to Alexandria, we were filled with joy, and very
rightly so, since such a man had become a mediator and had undertaken to engage in labors beyond his strength.
So that he might overcome the [?] of the devil and bring together those who had become divided from one another,
removing the obstacles that lay between them, he might crown the churches among you and among us with harmony and peace.
For it is unnecessary to speak of the circumstances that caused the division.
But I think it is right to consider and say what is fitting for a time of peace.
We therefore rejoiced at meeting the God-loving man whom we mentioned above.
He perhaps thought that he would face a great struggle to persuade us
that we ought to bring the churches of God to peace and put an end to the ridicule of outsiders.
Along with this, we should also blunt the sting of the devil’s wickedness.
But he found us so ready for this that he had no trouble whatsoever.
For we remember our Savior, who said, “My peace I give you; my peace I leave with you.”
We have also learned to say in our prayers, “Lord our God, give us peace, for everything
you have given us.” Thus, if someone shares in the peace given by God,
he lacks none of the good things. And that it was entirely unnecessary
and without any worthy cause that the churches were divided, we are now all the more firmly convinced, because
the God-loving bishop, Mar Paul, gave us a document containing a blameless confession of faith.
In conclusion, he said that it had been drawn up by Your Holiness and by the God-loving bishops there.
The text of that document is as follows, and it has been included word for word in this letter.
Concerning the Virgin, the Mother of God—how we think and speak of her—
and concerning the manner in which the only-begotten Son [?] of God became human, we speak out of necessity, not by way of an addition,
but by way of confirmation, in accordance with what, from the beginning, from the holy Scriptures
and from the tradition of the holy fathers, we have received and held fast. We state this briefly,
adding nothing whatsoever to the faith set forth by the holy fathers at Nicaea.
For, as we have already said, it is sufficient for the whole knowledge of godliness and refutes all the evil teaching of the heretics.
We speak, however, not by venturing into things beyond comprehension, but by acknowledging our weakness,
we bar the way to those who wish to attack us over matters that we consider beyond human understanding.
We therefore confess our Lord Jesus Christ, the only Son of God,
perfect God and perfect man, consisting of a rational soul and a body.
He was begotten from the Father before the ages in his divinity, and at the end of days, the very same one, for our sake
and for our salvation, was born of the Virgin Mary in his humanity. He is of the same nature as the Father in his divinity and of the same nature as we are in his humanity.
For a union of two natures took place. Therefore we confess one Christ, one Son, one Lord.
In accordance with the meaning of this union without confusion, we confess the holy Virgin to be the Mother of God,
because God the Word became flesh and became man, and from the very moment of conception united to himself the temple that he took from her.
As for the statements about our Lord made by the apostles and evangelists, we know that those who speak of divine things
treated some of them as shared, referring to one person, but distinguished others as referring to two natures.
They assigned those befitting God to Christ’s divinity, and the lowly ones to his humanity.
When we encountered these divine words of yours and found that we ourselves also believe this way—
for there is one Lord, one faith, one baptism—
we praised God, the Savior of all, rejoicing with one another that the faith which agrees with the divine Scriptures
and the tradition of the holy fathers is held by the churches among us and among you.
But because I learned that some people, who habitually make themselves blameworthy and buzz like wild wasps,
are spewing evil words against me, as though I say that Christ’s holy body came from heaven
and not from the Virgin, I thought it necessary to address a few words to them about this: O fools, who know only
how to slander, how did you embrace this opinion
and devise all this foolishness? You ought to have considered carefully that, for the most part,
our entire struggle for the faith has been over our assertion that the Virgin is the Mother of God.
But if we say that the holy body of Christ, the Savior of us all, came from heaven and not from her,
how is she recognized as the Mother of God? For whom did she bear,
if it is not true that she bore Emmanuel in the flesh? Let those who invented these things about me, then, be put to shame.
For the blessed prophet Isaiah does not lie when he says, “Look, the virgin will conceive and bear a son,
and they will call his name Emmanuel,” which means, “Our God is with us.”
And blessed Gabriel, who spoke to the blessed Virgin, is certainly truthful in every respect:
“Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God.
For look, you will conceive and give birth to a son, and you will name him Jesus, for he will save his people from their sins.”
But whenever we speak of our Lord Jesus Christ as being from heaven and from above, we do not mean that his holy body descended from above and from heaven
when we say such things. Rather, we are following blessed Paul, who declares plainly:
“The first man was of dust, from the earth; the second man is the Lord from heaven.” We also remember
our Savior himself, who said, “No one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven, the Son of Man,”
although in the flesh he was from the holy Virgin, as I have just said.
But because God the Word, who came from above and from heaven, emptied himself and took the form of a servant,
he was called the Son of Man, while remaining what he was, namely, God.
For in his nature he is unchanging and unalterable. Since he is recognized as one with his body, he is said to have descended from heaven.
He was also called the man from heaven, being perfect in his divinity and himself also perfect in his humanity.
And he is recognized as being in one person. For there is one Lord Christ, even though the distinction between the natures is recognized,
from which we say an inexpressible union has come about. But as for those who say,
“There was a mixture or confusion or intermingling of God the Word with the flesh,” may Your Holiness be persuaded to silence them.
For how often people spread these things about me too, as though I had thought or said such things!
But I utterly reject entertaining any such thought,
for I consider those people mad who have even supposed that a shadow of change could touch the nature of God.
For he remains forever what he is, and he has not changed. Nor does he change
in any respect or undergo alteration. Along with this, we also confess that the Word of God is not subject to suffering,
although, in his exalted wisdom, in his ordering of the mystery, we see that the sufferings that befell his flesh, to himself [?]
in his ordering of the mystery, we see that he claims as his own the sufferings that befell his flesh.
Thus Peter, too, who was wise in all things, said, “Christ suffered for us in the flesh,”
and not in the nature of his inexpressible divinity. For, so that he may be believed to be the Savior of all,
he makes the sufferings of the flesh his own in his saving plan and, as I said, refers them to himself.
As was said long ago through the voice of the prophet, as though spoken by him:
“I gave my back to blows and my cheeks to slapping, and I did not turn my face away from the shame of spitting.”
We agree in every respect with the teaching of the fathers, and especially with that of our blessed and illustrious father Athanasius.
Let Your Holiness be assured that we take care not to depart from him in anything whatsoever; nor does any of the others doubt this.
I would also have presented many proofs from their writings, confirming my words by them,
if I had not feared that the length of the letter might make someone weary of reading it.
But we do not accept, in any way whatsoever, that anyone should unsettle the faith that has been defined. This is the statement of faith
established by our holy fathers who assembled at Nicaea at that time.
Nor do we permit ourselves or others either to change a word in what was established there or to omit even a single letter.
For we remember the one who said, “Do not change the ancient boundaries that your fathers established.”
For it was not they themselves who spoke, but the Spirit of God the Father, who proceeds from him.
Nor is he foreign to the Son with respect to being.
And on this very point, the words of the saints, my fellow initiates in the mysteries, confirm us.
For in the Acts of the Apostles it is written, “When they came to Mysia,
they sought to go to Bithynia, but the Spirit of Jesus did not allow them.”
The blessed Paul also writes, “Those who are in the flesh cannot please God.
But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you.
But if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, that person does not belong to him.”
But when certain people, who are accustomed to twisting what is right,
alter my words to suit themselves, let Your Holiness not be surprised at this,
knowing that all heretics gather material for their error from the divine Scriptures,
while, through their wicked thoughts, they distort what was rightly spoken through the Holy Spirit,
and heap upon their own heads a flame that cannot be extinguished.
But since we have learned that even the letter of our illustrious father Athanasius to the blessed Epictetus,
which contains the true faith, has been altered and circulated by certain people, so that many might suffer harm from it,
For this reason, when we find something useful and necessary for the brothers in the original copy in our possession,
the one in which there is no error, we have sent a copy to Your Holiness.
Copy of the letter written to the blessed Epictetus, bishop of Corinth,
by Saint Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria,
who endured persecution from the Arians for the true faith and distinguished himself by confessing it.
1. I had thought that by now all the empty talk of the heretics everywhere had fallen silent,
after the holy council held at Nicaea. For the faith confessed there was in accordance with the divine Scriptures,
and it is sufficient to uproot all impiety and establish the true faith in Christ.
For this very reason, even recently, separate councils were held in Gaul, Spain, and Rome.
And all those who assembled, with regard to those
who were still concealing their allegiance to the thinking of Arius—I mean Auxentius of Milan,
and Ursacius, Valens, and Gaius from Pannonia—pronounced anathema with one mind, as though moved by one Spirit.
And they wrote everywhere, because these men were devising and adopting names of councils for themselves,
that no council should be recognized by name in the catholic Church except the one at Nicaea,
which is the defeat and uprooting of every heresy, especially Arianism, on account of which they were compelled to assemble at that time.
How, then, after all this, do some people again dare to dispute or distort these things,
unless they are Arians? For they are doing nothing surprising
if they revile what has been written against them, just as the pagans, when they hear
that the idols of the nations are silver and gold, consider the teaching of the divine cross foolishness.
But if it is people who are thought to believe rightly
and to love what has been handed down from the fathers who want to cause confusion through investigations,
they are doing nothing other than, as it is written, giving their neighbors the muddy drink of wrath.
They engage in useless disputes, to the ruin of the simple.
2. I write these things in this way because I came across the matters that took place before Your Fatherhood and were put down in a memorandum.
But I wish they had not been written down, so that we might not even leave a record of these things.
that afterward. For who has ever heard, or who has learned or taught? For the law went out from Zion,
and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem. From where did these things spring up? Or what Sheol spewed them out,
that it should be said that the body from Mary is of the same nature as the divinity of the Word? Or that the Word himself was changed into flesh and bones and hair
and the entire body, and was transformed from his own nature? Who has heard in the church, or indeed from Christians at all,
that our Lord put on a body in appearance and not in reality? Or who has been so ungodly as to think and say
that the divinity itself, which is of the same nature as the Father, was divided and became imperfect instead of perfect,
and that what was fastened with nails to the [?] was not that body,
but, they say, that nature which gives Wisdom its being? And who has heard that it was not from Mary,
but from his own nature that the Word himself fashioned for himself a body capable of suffering? And would anyone call those who say these things Christians?
And who devised this lawless ungodliness, even to entertain the thought and say
that whoever says that our Lord’s body is from Mary thinks of the Godhead not as a Trinity,
but as a group of four? And for this reason those who speak this way
declare that the body which our Savior put on is from the nature of the Godhead.
And from where, again, did some people invent an ungodliness comparable to what has been mentioned,
so as to say that the body did not come later than the divinity of the Word, but exists eternally with him, because from the nature
of Wisdom it came into being? And how did these people who are called Christians dare to speak so recklessly,
saying that our Lord, who appeared from Mary, is the Son of God by nature, but only in appearance is he from the offspring of the house of David,
from the body of the pure Mary? And were these people so bold as to say that Christ, who suffered in the flesh and was crucified,
is not, they say, the Lord and Savior and God and the Son of the Father? Or how do they wish to be called Christians,
those who say that the Word came upon a righteous man as upon one of the prophets,
and that he himself did not become the Son of Man by taking a body from Mary?
Rather, they say, Christ is one, and the Word who existed before Mary is another,
and before the ages he is the Son of the Father. And they regard [?] the Son of Man as one,
and speak of God the Word as another? 3. These things mentioned in the memorandum had been set out so explicitly,
sharing one intention, directed toward a single goal of utter ungodliness.
And over these matters they were arguing and quarreling with one another—these people who boast of the confession of the fathers made at Nicaea.
But I was astonished at your fear of God, because you endured this and did not rebuke those who say such things.
Instead, you set before them the faith that accords with the fear of God,
so that, upon hearing it, they might either keep silent or, if they persist in arguing, be counted with the rest of the heretics.
For these things that have been said should neither be spoken nor heard among Christians; rather, they are foreign in every [?] to the teaching
of the apostles. For this reason I too have had the things they said set down plainly in a letter,
so that merely by hearing them, everyone may clearly see the shame and wickedness in them.
Although it would have been proper to accuse and rebuke at length the ignorance of those who devised these things,
it is enough for our letter to go this far, so that we do not go on writing down their blasphemy.
For things whose ugliness is so obvious should not be turned over and examined at greater length,
lest those who argue in their favor suppose that there is some doubt about them.
Rather, it is enough simply to reply and say against these things:
These are not the teachings of the holy Church throughout the world, nor did our blessed fathers hold these views.
But so that these inventors of evil may not take this brief statement as an excuse,
it is good to recall a little from the divine Scriptures, so that perhaps even in this way they may be put to shame and turn away from their filthy thoughts.
4. Where do you get the claim, you wrongdoers, that the body is of the same nature as the divinity of the Word? For it is good to begin with this,
so that, when this claim is shown to be weak, the others too may be recognized as being like it.
These things cannot be found in the Scriptures. For they say that God came to be in a human body.
And again, our fathers who contended at Nicaea did not say of the body,
but of the Son himself, that he is of the same nature as the Father. But they confessed that the body was from Mary,
according to the divine Scriptures. Either, then, reject the Council of Nicaea,
and it is clear that you are introducing these things as heretics do,
or, if you wish to be children of the fathers, do not hold views beyond what [?] wrote.
For from this too you can understand the ugliness of your words.
For if the Word is of the same nature as the body, whose nature is from the earth, and the Word is of the same nature as the Father,
According to the confession of our fathers, the Father himself is also found to have the nature of the body, which is from the earth.
Why, then, do you blame the Arians for calling the Son a created being, when you yourselves make even the Father
of the same nature as creation? And you slip again into another form of impiety,
by saying that the Word was transformed into flesh, bones, hair, sinews, and the whole body, and was changed from his own nature.
Why, then, do you not say openly that he came from the earth? For the nature of the body is from the earth.
Where does all this foolishness come from, that you contradict yourselves? For even when you say that the Word is of the same nature as the body,
you acknowledge one alongside the other. But through the transformation into flesh,
you see a change in the Word himself, as though in mirages.
Who, then, will tolerate you when you say these things? For you have inclined toward impiety more than any heresy.
For if the Word is of the same nature as the body, mentioning Mary's service is unnecessary.
For it is possible for the body to exist eternally, just as the Word himself exists.
If, as you think, he is of the same nature as the body, why was the coming of the Word necessary,
either to put on something of his own nature, or to change from his own nature and become a body? For the Godhead did not take on itself
or put on something of its own nature. For the Word, who saves others from sins, did not sin,
so that he should change into a body, offer himself as a sacrifice on his own behalf, and redeem himself.
5. But it is not so—far from it! For he took on the offspring of Abraham, as the apostle said,
and therefore he had to become like his brothers and take on a body like ours.
For this reason Mary was indeed necessary, so that he might take it from her and offer it as his own on our behalf.
Isaiah indicated this in his prophecy when he said, “Look, the virgin will conceive and bear a son, and his name will be called Emmanuel.”
And Gabriel, who was sent to her, was not sent simply to a virgin,
but to a virgin who was betrothed to a man, so that through her betrothed he might show that Mary was truly a woman.
Scripture recounts his birth and says that she wrapped him in swaddling clothes and laid him in a manger.
And again there are other passages, calling blessed the breasts that nursed him,
and that he presented an offering because the one who was born opened the womb. All these things, then, were indications
of the virgin's giving birth. Gabriel, too, carefully announced the good news to her and said:
Not simply, “the one who is born in you,” so that it would not be supposed that a body entered him from outside,
but “from you,” he says, so that it might be believed that the one who is born is from her by nature.
For nature itself also clearly shows this: a virgin cannot produce milk
unless she has first given birth, nor can a body be nourished with milk and wrapped in swaddling clothes
unless it has first truly been born by nature. This is the one who was circumcised when he was eight days old.
Simeon received him in his arms. He was a child and grew, and reached twelve years of age,
and reached his thirtieth year. It was not as some people supposed:
that the very nature of the Word was changed and circumcised, although he is unchangeable and unalterable.
As our Savior himself said, “Look at me, look at me: I am he, and I have not changed.”
And Paul the apostle writes, “Jesus Christ is the same yesterday and today and forever and ever.”
Rather, in that body which was born, was circumcised, was carried, ate, and grew weary [?]—
and was fastened to the wood with nails and suffered—in it was the Word, God, who cannot suffer and has no body.
This was what was laid in the tomb, while he went in his soul to preach to the spirits in prison, as Peter said.
6. What further reveals the ignorance of those who say that God the Word was changed into bones and flesh.
For if this had been so, no tomb would have been needed;
instead, the body itself would have gone to preach to the souls in Sheol.
But as it was, he went in his soul, while Joseph wrapped the body in a shroud and laid it at Golgotha.
It is clear to everyone that the body itself was not the Word, but was the Word’s body.
And after he rose from the dead, Thomas touched this body and saw the marks of the nails,
which the Word himself endured as they were driven into his body. Although he could have stopped it [?], he did not.
Instead, he took upon himself as his own the things that belonged to the body.
Thus, when the body was struck, he said [?], as though he himself were suffering,
“Why do you strike me?” And although by nature he has no body, he had said beforehand,
“I gave my body to blows and my cheeks to slaps, and I did not turn my face away from spitting.”
For the things that the Word’s body suffered, the Word himself bore along with it, so that we might be saved through the suffering of God’s only Son.
And it was wonderful and extraordinary that he was one and the same, the one who suffered and did not suffer.
For he suffered because his own body was suffering, and he was present in that which suffered.
Yet he did not suffer, because he, the Word, is by nature incapable of suffering.
And he who is incorporeal was present in that body capable of suffering, while the body
belonged to God the Word, who is incapable of suffering. For he did this because of our debt, which he paid in his own person,
so that, when he had taken upon himself what was ours and offered us in himself as a sacrifice to his Father, [?] our wrongdoing might be forgiven through his atonement,
and he might renew us again through his gift, according to the apostle’s statement that everything should be renewed afresh in Christ.
7. These things did not happen merely in appearance, as some have supposed,
but truly and in reality, in that our Savior became a human being, so that he might be the Savior of the whole human being.
For if God the Word was in a body merely in appearance, as these people think,
he would have been a phantom, and it follows that our salvation is spoken of falsely,
as is the resurrection from the dead, according to the destructive wickedness of Mani. But look: our salvation is not imaginary,
nor is it the salvation of the body alone, but of the whole human being, both soul and body. For our salvation truly took place.
Therefore, what came from Mary is human by nature, according to the meaning of the divine Scriptures.
And our Savior’s body was truly a body, because it was the very same as this body of ours.
For Mary is our sister, because we are all descended from the one Adam.
And no one can doubt this if he remembers what Luke wrote.
For after our Lord rose from the dead, when the disciples supposed
that they were not seeing him in the body that came from Mary, but were looking instead at a spirit, he said to them,
reassuring them in their alarm, “Look at my hands and my feet, and the marks of the nails: it is I.
Touch me and see: a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see that I have.”
And when he had said these things, he showed them his hands and his feet.
These words can also refute those who have dared to say that our Lord was transformed into flesh and bones.
For he did not say, “As you see that I am flesh and bones,” but, “that I have them,”
so that it should not be supposed that God the Word himself was changed into these things, but rather that he came to be in them.
And let it be believed that he exists both before death and after the resurrection.
8. If, then, the demonstration of these things is thus established, it is unnecessary to approach these other matters
and to discuss anything about them, since that body in which the Word was
was not of the same nature as the Godhead, but was truly born of Mary.
And the Word himself was not changed into flesh and bones, but dwelt in the flesh and made it his own, and is one with it forever.
This is the meaning of what the blessed John said: “The Word became flesh.”
We can understand this from a similar statement, as Paul said: “Christ became a curse for us.”
He did not himself become a curse in his own person. Rather, because he took upon himself the curse that clung to us, he is said to have become a curse.
Likewise, the statement that he became flesh does not mean that he was changed into flesh, but that he took a body
for us, and we say that he became human. For to say that the Word became flesh is the same as saying that he became human.
It is like what is written in Joel: “I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh.”
Now the promise did not extend even to animals,
but only to human beings, for whose sake our Lord also became human.
When, therefore, someone understands the meaning of this statement, it rightly refutes
those who supposed that what was taken from Mary existed before her,
and that the Word had a human soul before her, and had always existed in it before his coming.
Let those also be silenced who said that our Lord’s body was not subject to death, but was, they claim, of that immortal nature.
For if he did not die, how could Paul hand on to the Corinthians what he himself had received from the apostles before him, saying:
“Christ died for our sins, as it is written, and was received [?] and rose on the third day,
as it is written”? Or how did he rise unless he first died? ... Let those also be restrained [?] who thought
that there could be a group of four instead of the Trinity if the body is said to be from Mary.
“But if,” they say, “the body is of the same nature as the Word, the Trinity remains intact [?],
because the Word introduces nothing new into it. But if someone calls the body from Mary human,
then, because the body is foreign to him in its nature and the Word is in it, it necessarily follows
that there will be a group of four and not the Trinity, because of the addition of the body.”
9. While saying these things, they do not realize how they themselves fall into precisely the same error.
For even if they say that the body is not from Mary, but is of the same nature as the Word,
they are no less exposed to what they feared: that they might be thought to introduce a group of four.
For, according to their own reasoning, they are found to be saying precisely the same thing.
For just as the Son is from the Father and, although he is of the same nature as the Father, is not himself the Father,
but is called Son in relation to the Father, so also, if the body is said to be of the same nature as the Word,
it is not itself the Word, but is something other than the Word.
But if it is something other, then even on this reasoning of theirs the Trinity turns out to be a group of four.
Yet it is not the true Trinity, truly perfect and indivisible, that receives an addition,
but the one invented by these people. Again, it is easy to discern their ignorance from their own empty wisdom.
For if, because our Savior’s body is from Mary and is human, as the Scriptures say,
they think that there turns out to be a group of four instead of a Trinity,
as though an addition had been made to the Godhead because of the body, they are greatly mistaken in placing what was made on an equal footing
with its Maker, and in thinking that the Godhead can receive an addition.
They have not understood that the Word came to be in a body not to add to the Godhead, but so that the body itself might rise.
Nor did the Word come forth from Mary to gain greater glory himself, but so that the human race might be saved.
How, then, can that body, which was saved and raised to life through [?] the Word,
make an addition to the Godhead in the Word? Rather, the truth is this:
it was the human being himself who received an increase and a great advancement through the Word’s union and fellowship with him.
For from being mortal he became immortal; from being natural he became spiritual.
Although made from dust, he passed through the gates of heaven and sat down at the Father’s right hand on high.
But the Trinity, even after the Word took a body from Mary,
remains the Trinity as it is, receiving neither addition nor diminution.
Rather, it is always perfect, and in the Trinity the one Godhead is [?].
And so in the Church one God is proclaimed, the Father of the Word.
10. Let this, then, restrain those who once said that the one who appeared from Mary is not the Christ and Lord and Jesus.
For if he was not God in the body, how was he called Immanuel as soon as he appeared from Mary,
which means “Our God is with us”? And Paul—if God the Word was not born
in the body, how does he write to the Romans, “From them,” he says, meaning the Jews, “Christ appeared in the flesh,
who is God over all”? Therefore, let those too who previously denied this, saying, “The one who was crucified is not God,”
be persuaded by all the divine Scriptures. Let them acknowledge that they acted foolishly and went astray, and let them repent, and they will be accepted.
Above all, let them agree with the apostle Thomas, who, after seeing the marks of the nails on him, cried out in a loud voice and said, “My Lord and my God!”
For although the Son is God and the Lord of glory, he was nailed up and dishonored in a body without glory.
For although it was the body that actually suffered, and blood and water flowed from his side, nevertheless all the suffering was attributed to God.
For this reason, when the sun saw its Maker being dishonored in his body and allowing it, it withdrew its rays and darkened the earth.
But that body, whose nature was subject to decay, transcended its nature because of the power within it.
It was exalted and freed from the decay inherent in its nature,
because it had become the body of God the Word, who is above these things. 11. As for what some people suppose and say,
that just as the Word used to come to one of the prophets, so he also came upon a certain individual, the man from Mary,
it is unnecessary even to discuss it, for the shame of their ignorance rests upon their faces,
