so that everyone may recognize them by their error. For if he came as he did into one of
the prophets, why was this one alone born of a virgin,
and not also of a man and a woman? For that is how each one of the righteous was born.
Or why is the death of each one of them not said to have taken place for our sake,
but only this one's death? And why, although he used to come upon each one of them, is he not spoken of as the Son of God,
except in the case of the one from Mary, as one who came once at the end of the ages? Or if he came in this way,
as he came into the saints of old, why did all these die and still not rise,
while the one who appeared from Mary alone rose after three days? Or why, if the Word came in the same way as he did to those others,
is the one from Mary alone called Immanuel, as God who was born from her in the body? For Immanuel means “Our God is with us.”
And why, if he came in this way, while each of the saints ate and drank and toiled and died,
It is not said as though the Word himself ate, drank, toiled, and died,
but only in the one who was from Mary. For the things that the body suffered are spoken of as though he himself suffered them.
And although all are said to have come into being and been born, only concerning the one who was from Mary is it said that the Word became flesh.
12. This is well known: with all the others, the Word was present through his Spirit for the purpose of prophecy.
But from Mary the Word himself, in his own person, took flesh for himself and appeared as a human being,
while being in his nature and his essence God the Word.
But in the flesh he became a human being from the offspring of the house of David, from Mary's flesh, as Paul said.
The Father pointed him out at the Jordan and on the mountain, saying, “This is my Son and my beloved, in whom I am pleased.”
The Arians denied him, but we acknowledge and worship him, without separating the Son, the Word, from his body.
Rather, we worship him himself, knowing him to be the Son of God, through whom everything came into being, and we were [?].
For this reason we are also amazed. How, then, over things so clear,
did a dispute arise among you? But give thanks to our Lord that, just as we were distressed by reading the memorandum, so we rejoiced at the outcome of the matter.
For they departed from us in peace and harmony, with a confession of devotion to God and with an upright and true faith.
This, then, also persuaded me, after much thought, to write these few things that I had considered,
lest my silence bring sorrow instead of joy to those whose agreement had become a cause of joy for us.
I therefore ask first your Holiness, and secondly everyone who hears, to receive these things with a good conscience.
And if anything in them falls short of devotion to God, correct it and let me know.
But if I have written as someone unskilled in expression, or in a manner that was not fitting, and incompletely,
may you all forgive the weakness of our discourse. The letter of Athanasius to Epictetus is finished.
Copy of the petition submitted by the bishops and priests in Greater Armenia,
to Proclus, the faithful bishop of Constantinople, concerning the writings of Theodore of Mopsuestia.
To the holy and God-loving Proclus, bishop of the catholic church and of the needy,
from Leontius and Abel, priests of Greater Armenia, and from the brothers who are with us.
We, holy one, in accordance with the tradition of our fathers, the bishops who were in the city of Nicaea,
believe and profess the true and [?] confession.
Now, because some people from the East came to us and wanted to unsettle us, treating us as simple people,
bringing with them a book by Theodore, the one who was bishop of Mopsuestia,
and because this man, as we learned from the writings of the holy Mar Rabbula, bishop of Edessa,
and from Mar Acacius of Melitene—for they made it known with certainty—was a corruptor, this Theodore,
and a disturber of the faith that cannot be disturbed; and because some people from Cilicia came to us
and brought accusations against Saint Acacius, bishop of Melitene, and the God-loving Rabbula, bishop of Edessa, saying
that they had rejected Theodore’s writings out of hostility and hatred:
for this reason all the holy bishops, because of your love for God and with much thought and concern, judged it right
that we should be sent here to learn from you with certainty whether those books and the passages from the compositions are truly perverse.
We therefore ask you to grant us writings from which we and those who sent us may learn
whether we ought to agree with those who came from Cilicia and brought Theodore’s books,
or whether we ought to direct our minds to the writings of the holy bishops Rabbula and Acacius.
Furthermore, we also have in our possession books containing Theodore’s compositions.
As we ask this very thing of you, see whether anything in it is well written [?].
So that, through the examination of Your Holiness, the men, women, and children who are in Greater Armenia,
the entire people of the holy church, may be instructed in the faith that has been established fully and firmly among the Romans.
And further, along with these, by the grace of God, may those who came from Cilicia to lead us astray
be corrected through the writings of your faith and turn back from that perversion,
and may they too be joined to the faith of the apostles, which the three hundred and eighteen fathers established after examination,
which we too profess. Then, when this has come about for us, with one mind and in one accord,
like true brothers and like members of a body, we may be joined to one another at every joint. And we,
who were not thrown into confusion, and those who held opposing views may be in harmony, confessing one Lord
and one true faith firmly established in our souls. We have kept your reverence for God in mind.
Another letter by the same blessed Mar Proclus, the bishop, to the bishops of Armenia.
To the chaste and God-loving partners in my ministry, the bishops, priests, and monks who are in Armenia:
To the children of the holy church of true teaching: Proclus sends greetings in our Lord.
1. The news, my brothers, of the error of these new weeds has afflicted our soul beyond measure and struck our mind with severe distress:
those whom the enemy of the whole of our common nature cunningly sowed in your land some time ago.
For news of evil commonly causes severe pain to a soul that has not been trained by practice in hearing it.
And in this way it drives its arrows deeper still, since the report of destruction itself
does not concern only the body and its gross substance, stopping there,
but takes captive through such reports the soul, which is lofty in its subtlety, so that the perfect vessel of faith is forced either
to be emptied without mercy or to be completely stripped bare.
For every virtue is desirable to those in whom the beauty of both body and soul has not been corrupted by the passions.
And every evil is rightly considered repulsive by those who have understanding,
because it is contrary to nature and brings what is unnatural into conflict with what is natural.
For just as help is desirable to those who need it, so too, regarding harm,
one ought either to flee from it when it is near or, when it is far away, take care that it does not come.
The forms of virtue, then, are numerous. The pagans, choked by error, wrote about it in detail,
but were blinded to precise discernment because they did not know God.
Christians, however, through their faith, have had the eyes of their hearts enlightened.
And through their confession of faith they have been able to gaze clearly at the Sun of Righteousness.
2. For the pagans, like people deprived of a guiding mind and stumbling in darkness, proceed confusedly in their words.
They have merely groped at this visible natural world, which moves without rest, and written about it in their teachings.
But as for grasping the truth, they were either dazzled by the passage of time or blinded by error.
For they say that there are four forms of virtue:
namely, justice, wisdom, self-control, and courage. Although these seem beautiful,
they move downward, flutter along the earth, and remain on this side of the vault of heaven.
For they say that courage is combat with fierce creatures;
self-control is victory over the passions; and wisdom is successful government of cities.
And as for justice, they established fair divisions according to law and laid them down for the world; they set limits to oppression and restrained it on both sides.
But they did not understand anything more excellent and higher than this visible world, nor were they able to write about it.
Instead, in the blindness of their minds, they crippled virtue [?].
They confined it to visible things alone and did not allow it anything lofty and comparable to the beauty of heaven.
3. Christians, whose hearts’ eyes have been enlightened by their faith,
whose instructor and teacher is the blessed Paul, said that virtue is what raises people toward God
and governs earthly affairs in an orderly way. This Paul, then, outstanding in every respect, enumerated many forms of virtue.
But he proclaimed these three especially: faith, hope, and love.
For faith gives human beings something beyond nature.
It brings into fellowship with spiritual beings the person who is still clothed in the garment of a body subject to many passions.
For what the angels and the nature of the spiritual powers did not know because of its greatness,
faith in him has given knowledge of it to human beings who walk on the earth and roll about on the ground in the dust.
It brings them near the throne of the true kingdom, and through the sure radiance that comes from it,
it makes known the nature that is without beginning and uncreated. With the ray that comes from it, it drives away the fog of the passions.
And once it has cleansed the heart of all darkness and dullness,
it enables that which is seen without being comprehended, and comprehended without being seen, to be seen clearly.
Hope, however, reveals what is to come here and now—not as in a dream, as one might say, but with certainty.
Without doubt, it establishes what is to come in the mind as firmly as something visible.
And, one might say, it depicts what a person awaits before that person’s eyes. For hope rises above every delay.
It brings what is awaited to the one awaiting it, without disturbance.
It overcomes the passage of time through the nearness [?] of what is to come. Love, however, is the head of our entire mystery.
For it persuaded God the Word, who exists eternally, to come to earth through clay.
These two, then, fit together.
For faith is the mirror of love, and love is the perfection of faith.
We believe, then, that God the Word became embodied without suffering, and we are right to believe this.
For this is the foundation of our salvation. But we also love him who took the form of a servant for our sake.
His nature underwent no change, and he made no addition to the Trinity.
Therefore, any Christian who is not rich in faith, hope, and love is not what he claims to be. But even if
he seems to have subjected his body and freed himself from the passions of the soul, he is not worthy of the crown of victory.
For he has observed the outward forms of virtue but has not drawn near to the one who awards the crown of victory
to those who have struggled earnestly for virtue.
4. Faith, then, as we have said, is the chief of all good things.
Let us therefore preserve it without deceit. Let us not stain it with the falseness of human thoughts or disturb it with troubling expressions.
Rather, let it remain within the boundaries [?] of the Gospel and the apostles, with no one daring to fight against the faith
through which he was saved and which he confessed at baptism, by means of the writings of his tongue.
For the height of faith checks every assault of insolence and audacity,
not only one that comes from human beings, but even one strengthened by a spiritual nature.
Paul bears witness, crying out, “If we or an angel from heaven should preach to you anything beyond what you have received, let him be accursed.”
For an angel is appointed to serve, not to proclaim teaching.
And he brings punishment upon [?] anyone who does not remain within what he has been commanded, but occupies himself with what is above his nature.
But even if he displays the excellence of his [?], let the novelty of his proclamation not be accepted.
5. Let us therefore guard what we have received without falling asleep. And may the sweetness of our faith open the eyes [?] of our soul at every moment.
What have we received from the Scriptures, except this: that God created the world by his Word,
and brought creation, which had not existed, into being; and honored humanity with the [?] of nature.
He gave salvation to free will and showed it its means of help: that by choosing good it should flee from evil.
And humanity’s folly, in voluntarily turning toward evil, drove the disobedient man out of Paradise.
And again, through the fathers and patriarchs, and through the law, judges, and prophets,
the Creator instructed our nature to keep away from sin and take care to do good.
But finally, when it ruled over us by our own choice, and the evil one was exacting vengeance through the destruction of our entire nature—
for even the law of nature had been corrupted, and the written law had been despised.
And the prophets, as human beings, recounted what had happened, but they did not lift humanity out of the depths of evil.
He himself, God the Word, who is without beginning, incomprehensible, and invisible,
and almighty—God the Word—came and became incarnate.
For he could become whatever he wished. Yet he took the form of a servant, became flesh, and was born of a virgin.
And in every respect he wished to show that he had truly become human.
For a beginning, forms, and experiences of suffering necessarily accompany nature.
For the evangelist did not say that he entered a fully formed human being, but that he became flesh.
For he spoke of the beginning of the nature and went back to the very beginning of conception. For [?] a human
being who is born naturally does not emerge immediately with a fully developed capacity for action.
Rather, the natural seed first becomes flesh, and afterward, little by little,
over time it acquires the capacity for sensations and every kind of activity.
In this way God the Word went back to the beginning and origin of human conception,
and first became flesh, without being changed into flesh—far from it!
For if divinity is above change, because change is something undergone by a transitory nature,
unchangeability alone belongs to his person, to him who is as he is.
6. We therefore use both expressions of Scripture [?], and we say that he became flesh,
and that he took the form of a servant. Both, if we understand them correctly, are the cause of our life.
For by saying that he became flesh, the evangelist showed us the inseparability of the perfect union.
For just as a union is not divided into two—and if it is separated, it is no longer a union but a duality—
so that one who is in perfect union is not divided into two.
But the statement that he took proclaims the absence of change in his [?].
For everything that came to be came into existence when it did not exist, like the heavens, which did not previously exist,
or like something that already existed and underwent a change, like the waters of the Gihon, which were changed into blood.
But neither applies to the divine nature. For it was not when he did not exist
that the unchangeable God the Word [?] underwent change. For this reason, through both expressions, the unchangeability of the divinity:
and not a division of the mystery, as Holy Scripture makes clear: it stated what he became and proclaimed what he assumed.
By the first expression, “he became,” we establish unity in person.
And by the second, we proclaim the unchangeableness of his nature. 7. God the Word, then, became a complete human being,
without diminishing that unchangeable nature through the wonder he performed, which had never entered anyone’s mind.
But we learned these things through faith; we did not grasp them through investigation.
And when he became a human being, he gave life to the whole human race through the body he assumed.
And he paid the debt of sin by dying for everyone as a human being.
But as God, who hates evil, he rendered powerless the one who holds the power of death, namely Satan.
He showed that the law could be fulfilled by fulfilling all righteousness, and he restored our nature’s original beauty.
And by becoming a human being, he honored the nature formed from earth, whose maker he himself is. The Son, then, is one.
For we worship the Trinity in one being, and we do not introduce a fourth in addition to this.
Rather, there is one Son, begotten of his Father without beginning, through whom we believe the worlds came into being.
He is the branch from that root, the one who shone forth from his Father without any outflow,
that Word who remains in the Father without departing. For although he appeared on earth,
he did not depart from the one who begot him. He therefore wished to give life to the one he had formed,
and he dwelt in the womb, which is the gateway for the whole of our common nature, and gave it life. By dwelling there, he blessed the womb.
And when he came out, he sealed it. Through his birth beyond the order of nature, he showed that he himself had become embodied in a way beyond words.
8. Christ, then, is not one and God the Word another. Far from it!
For that divine nature knows no two sons. The Only-begotten, then, was begotten of one.
For where there is no union of parents, there is no duality of offspring.
“At the name of Jesus Christ,” it says, “every knee shall bow, in heaven, on earth, and beneath the earth.”
But if Christ is someone else, and is not himself God the Word, it necessarily follows
that Christ is a mere human being, even if he is a temple of God, as those madmen say.
But if Christ is a mere human being, how can the exalted nature of the heavenly beings
bend the knee and worship the name of one who is lesser? Or how shall we accept the utterances of the prophets, which cry out:
That our God appeared on earth and lived among human beings? For when he said, “He appeared,” he was speaking of his revelation in the flesh.
And by saying, “He lived among them,” he made known his life among human beings at the end of the ages.
For through this very thing, he who is exalted in his greatness displayed his power in everything.
As the Almighty, he remained what he is for his own sake; and because he willed it, he came into being for our sake.
9. If, then, the swaddling clothes and the feeding trough in the stable are a stumbling block to some people,
along with the hunger he experienced at times and everything that happened to him who truly became a human being,
let them know that, by questioning the sufferings, they deny the nature.
And when they deny the nature, they do not believe in the divine plan of salvation. And when they do not believe in the divine plan of salvation, they forfeit their lives.
For if, ever since the foundations of the world, a human being has been born who followed such a path of birth,
let those quarrelers show us, and then the falsehood of their obstinacy will be exposed.
But if this is the beginning of our common nature, and God the Word truly became a human being,
how can they acknowledge the nature along with us, yet deny the sufferings? Let them therefore choose one of two things:
either, being ashamed of the sufferings, let them deny the nature, so that they may be silenced along with Mani and counted among the wicked;
or, if they accept the benefit that comes from his taking a body, let them not be ashamed of the sufferings that befell that nature.
But I am astonished at the blindness of heart of those who have recently blazed a path of error.
For I know one Son, as I have rightly learned, and I confess one person [?]: God the Word, who put on a body.
Since the one who endured sufferings and performed miracles is one, why do they remain silent about the divine acts,
yet make an uproar about the weaknesses? For to show that he is God and that he is the Word, he remained what he is
and became flesh, a child, and a human being without change, without dishonoring our mystery in any of these things.
And he himself both performed miracles and suffered, so that through the signs he might show that he remained as he is,
as he demonstrated through the wonders; and through [?] sufferings, that it might be believed that he became what he had fashioned.
He is therefore one and the same, who is from our world; he himself became embodied at the end of the ages.
And we confess that he is the Son, and we introduce nothing counterfeit into the divine nature.
For there is nothing additional in that throne of being.
10. But perhaps, in their confusion, they contend with us about this, merely fabricating feeble arguments from [?].
For if, they say, the Trinity is one essence, then the Trinity is not subject to suffering.
And God the Word is counted as one of the Trinity. Therefore the Word himself is also not subject to suffering.
But if God is not subject to suffering, it follows that the one who was crucified is someone else.
And he is not God the Word, who is truly incapable of suffering.
Those who say such things are weaving a spider’s web.
And those who devise these new demonstrations are writing on water.
While claiming to be wise, they became foolish, and their uncomprehending hearts became darkened [?].
For an eye dazzled by the sun’s rays cannot see clearly.
And a feeble mind cannot grasp the heights of faith.
What, then, do we say in accordance with the theological teaching of the faith?
The Trinity is indeed one essence and is above suffering. And when we say
that the Son suffered, we do not say without qualification that God the Word suffered. For the divine nature is above all suffering.
Rather, when we confess that God the Word, one of the Trinity, became incarnate,
we provide a basis for understanding to those who ask in faith why he became incarnate.
For God the Word himself wished to abolish those sufferings whose end is death,
but that incorruptible nature could not undergo suffering.
For all sufferings are assaults [?] of all composite beings.
For there is no composition in him who alone is above everything.
Suffering, therefore, could not reach where [?] composition is found.
He therefore wished to abolish the sufferings that rule over the nature capable of suffering,
as we said before, those whose destination was death.
And he took a body from the Virgin Mary, in a manner known to God the Word himself, and became human.
For this was his will, and he emptied himself in the likeness of a servant, while his divinity was in no way confined.
And in this way he gives life to the human race. For in his body he abolished sufferings, but kept his divinity free from suffering.
11. For this reason Gabriel too, when announcing the power and authority of the one who was born:
He was crying out to the blessed Mary, saying, “He will save his people from their sins.” But the people were not
a man's people, but God's. Someone who entered the world through corruption cannot rescue the world from sins,
and whose birth is open to accusation from its very beginning. Rather, he himself must be both God and a human being,
not divided into two, but remaining one.
By being born of a woman, he shows that he is a human being.
But by preserving and demonstrating his mother's virginity without sexual union, he made it known that he is God.
Jesus Christ gave life to the world—he who came into the world and lived among human beings.
But if Christ is merely a human being, and is not God the Word,
how did he create everything in the beginning, when he did not exist? For if, as a human being, he is younger than the created things,
it is clear that Christ did not bring into existence those things that preceded him,
because he was created after them, like an ordinary human being. How, then, does Paul cry out,
“There is one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom everything came into being”? For if everything came into being through Christ, it is clear that Christ is God the Word.
The evangelist also bears witness when he cries out, “In the beginning was the Word,
and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
He was in the beginning with God, and everything came into being through him.” If, then, the evangelist cries out that through the Word
everything came into being, and Paul explains this and says, “There is one Lord, Jesus Christ,
through whom everything came into being,” it is clear that Christ is God the Word.
12. But if they cite to us expressions from the Scriptures in which he was called a human being—what Peter said,
“Jesus of Nazareth, a man,” and what Paul proclaimed, “Through a man whom God appointed to give assurance,”
and what our Lord himself said about himself, “Why do you seek to kill me, a man?”—
let them know that either through their dullness they have failed to grasp the meaning of Scripture,
or through their wickedness they twist what was rightly written to suit their own perversity.
For Christ truly became a human being as well. But he became one, whereas previously he had been nothing but God.
Therefore, just as he is God, not a creature, so the very same one is truly a human being.
And just as he shares his Father's nature in his divinity, so he shares the Virgin's nature in his bodily existence.
For the truth of our mystery shines everywhere, far removed from all my error.
But if the Virgin did not give birth to God, then her remaining uncorrupted is not even worthy of wonder.
For many other women have also given birth and given righteous people to the world.
But if the tongues of the prophets, foretelling the incomprehensibility of our mystery, cried out, “Look, the virgin will conceive
and give birth to a son, and they will call his name Emmanuel”—which Gabriel explains by saying, “Our God is with us”—
why do they deny the mother her [?] because of the condescension of the one who was born? But perhaps they say this against us:
“Everyone who is born,” they say, “shares the nature of the woman who gave birth to him.
Therefore, if the woman who gave birth is human, the one who was born must necessarily also be human.”
You speak well, you who are mistaken! But the child shares her nature only then:
the nature of the woman struck by labor pains, when the one being born comes forth according to nature.
Natural childbirth involves labor pains from its beginning, since sexual union also comes before labor pains.
But here this shame does not even enter the mind; rather, a wonder beyond words has occurred.
Where the birth is beyond nature, there the one who was born is God.
We therefore confess that he is the one who created the worlds, gave the Law, and also gave the Spirit to the prophets [?],
and in the last times became embodied and sent apostles, apostles to the peoples and nations.
13. Let us therefore flee from the muddy pools and the [?] of error. I mean the teachings that contend with God:
from the madness of Arius, which divides the indivisible Trinity;
and from the audacity of Eunomius, who confined within his knowledge that nature which cannot be comprehended; and from the recklessness of Macedonius,
who excludes the Spirit from divinity—excluding him although he does not depart—and from this new teaching and contrived blasphemy,
which far surpasses Judaism in blasphemy. For those people deny the Son who exists,
and deprive the root of its fruit. But these people introduce weeds among what is wheat,
so that they may establish many sons for that incorruptible nature.
Let us therefore say with Paul that Christ is our peace, the one who made both one.
For through baptism he created Jews and Gentiles into one new human being.
And through his [?] he made one what had been divided through its freedom.
Let those troublemakers of wickedness therefore fear the sentence of judgment. For if what was divided became one through unity,
yet the one who made them one has, at their hands, been divided into two.
14. But now let us leave lengthy discussion behind and turn to concise statements of the true teaching.
Whoever wishes to know that truly he himself alone is the Son—
the one who existed before Abraham came into being, and who in later times grew bodily in stature and wisdom,
for his divinity possesses perfection at all times—let him ask Paul, and let Paul thunder forth, rightly declaring:
The one who was born bodily from the Jews is himself God from eternity. For when he speaks and sets forth
the wrongdoing of the Hebrews and the people's contention with God, and the root, which is Abraham,
and the offspring, which is Christ our Lord, he says this: “Theirs was the adoption as children.”
For God cried out through the prophet: “Israel is my son, my firstborn, and my glory.”
For they reaped glory beyond measure from abundant wonders,
and from the covenants with Abraham, which spoke of the people's great numbers and of blessings.
And the giving of the law, the law on Mount Sinai, which was written by the finger of God.
And the promises: the land of Palestine, and that the nations would be blessed through Abraham's offspring. From them came the fathers,
who shone through faith like stars in the night of error; and from them Christ appeared in the flesh.
Paul did not say only this and leave it at that. For it was not when he was born of Mary
that God the Word, who is without beginning, had his beginning.
Rather, he immediately said, “in the body,” so that, along with his bodily manifestation, he might also make known his divine birth.
Who, then, is this Christ? He is the one who was born of the Virgin, who was confined within the womb in a way that he himself knows.
He is the one who lay in a manger, the one who grew bodily, the one who descended to the lowest parts of the earth.
He is the one who endured all these bodily experiences so that he might be believed to be truly human.
He is not someone else apart from the one who descended, but he is
the very same one who descended and who ascended. For he did not first ascend, but descended. He did not become God through something added to him—far from it!
Rather, in his mercy he became human. For this was what we needed.
Do not learn this from me or from someone else, but from Paul, who learned about the Son from the Father through revelation and said:
“But when God, who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me by his grace, was pleased to reveal his Son through me.”
For this man truly teaches you who Jesus Christ is when he cries out:
“From them Christ appeared in the flesh, he who is God over all, blessed forever.”
What height of insolence do Paul’s words not bring down in those who love insolence? For he called him Christ:
To show that he truly became a human being, he said that he came from the Jews in the body.
To show that he did not begin to exist only from the time when he took bodily form,
he called him “he who is,” to proclaim thunderously through his words that he exists without a beginning.
He called him “he who is over all,” to proclaim him Lord of creation.
He said that he is God, so that his appearance and sufferings might not shake us into denying his incorruptible nature.
He called him “blessed,” so that everyone might worship him as sovereign over all, rather than dishonor him as a fellow servant.
He said “forever,” to show that he alone has surpassed the ages by his word, and that his divinity is glorified in them.
15. We therefore have Christ, he who is, who is God and is blessed. Let us worship him.
And let us say to the heretics, “Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him. For we have the mind of Christ.”
For this reason we await the revelation of the glory of the great God, our Savior Jesus Christ,
who will himself reward those who do good with a crown of glory, but will repay the unjust for their insolence.
We have written these things to you, beloved, having first been prompted by your letters,
in which you informed us about certain contentious men who speak novelties and have entered your country,
and who wish, through impious speech and futile knowledge, to overturn the simplicity and lack of adornment of the pure beauty of the faith.
But once again I repeat this word to you:
“See that no one takes you captive through philosophy and the empty deception of the tradition of people who devise evil, and not according to Christ.”
For no one can lay another foundation of the true faith besides the one already laid, which is Jesus Christ.
Stand firm, therefore, in one spirit and with one soul, and contend for the faith of the gospel.
Do not be shaken in anything by those who oppose you.
Instead, preserve the tradition that you received from our holy and blessed fathers,
who proclaimed the truth in the city of Nicaea. And from that among the blessed
And the saints Basil and Gregory and the rest of the others who shared their views, whose names are written in the book of life.
End. Felix, bishop of Rome. On the incarnation of God the Word and his faith.
We believe that our Lord Jesus Christ, who was born of the Virgin Mary, is himself the Son of God from before the ages.
He is not a man assumed by God, so as to be someone else apart from him.
For neither did the Son of God assume a man who would be someone else apart from him.
Rather, while being perfect God, he became a perfect human being and took flesh from the Virgin.
[?]. II. Canons established at the Second Council of Byzantium concerning the Three Chapters.
That is, concerning the writings of Theodore, Theodoret, and Ibas, in the year of our Lord 553. First canon.
If anyone does not confess that in the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit we must worship one nature or being,
one power and authority, the Trinity in one substance,
one Godhead in three hypostases or persons, let him be accursed.
For there is one God, the Father, from whom all things are; and one Lord Jesus, through whom all things are; and one Holy Spirit, in whom all things are.
Second canon. If anyone does not confess two births of God the Word:
one from the Father, spiritually, before the ages and outside time;
and the other in the last days, when he came down from heaven, took flesh from my Lady Mary, the glorious ever-virgin Mother of God, and was born of her,
let him be accursed. Third canon.
If anyone says that the Word of God who performed miracles is one, and the Christ who endured sufferings is another;
or says that God the Word was with Christ when he was born of a woman, or was in him as one in another;
and that the Word of God who took flesh is not himself the one and same Lord Jesus Christ, and that the wonders he performed and the sufferings
he willingly endured in his body do not belong to the one and same hypostasis, let him be accursed.
Fourth canon. If anyone says that God the Word was united to a man by grace, or by activity,
or by rank, or by equality of honor, or by authority, or by association, or by action, or by power,
or by favor, as though God the Word favored the man because he was pleasing in his eyes, as Theodore foolishly said;
or merely by sharing a name, by which the Nestorians call God the Word Jesus and Christ,
and name the man separately Christ and Son, while explicitly asserting two hypostases;
And they suppose that they confess one person and one Christ only in honor, rank, and worship.
But he does not confess, as the holy fathers taught,
the union of God the Word with a body animated by a rational and intelligent soul—a union that took place by composition, that is, hypostatically.
And for this reason there is one hypostasis, who is our Lord Jesus Christ, one of the Holy Trinity.
Let him be anathema. Now, because unity is understood in many senses,
there are some who follow the impiety of Apollinaris and Eutyches, teaching the abolition of the natures that became one and proclaiming their union through mixture.
But those who share the views of Theodore and Nestorius accept their separation and introduce a union of affection.
But the holy church of God anathematizes the impiety of both these heresies,
and confesses the union of God the Word with the body by composition, that is, by a hypostatic union.
For union by composition in the mystery of Christ’s incarnation not only preserves without mixture the natures [?] that were united,
but also does not admit their separation into two hypostases. Canon Five.
If anyone understands the one hypostasis of our Lord Jesus Christ as embracing the meaning of many hypostases,
and therefore strives to introduce two hypostases or persons into the mystery of Christ’s incarnation,
and, after introducing them, calls them one person in rank, honor, and worship,
as Theodore and Nestorius mistakenly wrote, and they misrepresent the holy Council of Chalcedon, saying
that it used this expression, “one hypostasis,” in this impious sense,
but he does not confess that the Word of God was united substantially with the body and therefore became one hypostasis and one person,
and that this is how the holy Council of Chalcedon confesses one hypostasis in our Lord Jesus Christ, let him be anathema.
For the Holy Trinity did not receive an additional person or hypostasis,
even after one of that same Holy Trinity, God the Word, became human. Canon Six.
If anyone says that the glorious Lady Mary, ever virgin, is falsely and not truly called the Mother of God,
or only figuratively, as though the one born from her were a mere human being and not God the Word who became incarnate from her,
and that the birth of that human being, as they say,
is figuratively attributed to God the Word, who was attached to the human being who was born,
and falsely accuses the holy Council of Chalcedon of teaching this:
that the Virgin is the Mother of God in this impious sense explained by Theodore.
Or if anyone calls her the mother of a man, or the Mother of Christ as though Christ were not God,
and does not acknowledge, in the proper sense, that she is truly the Mother of God,
because God the Word, who was begotten of the Father before [?], became incarnate from her and was born in the last days,
and the holy Council of Chalcedon thus rightly acknowledges her to be the Mother of God,
let him be condemned. Canon Seven. If anyone says “in two natures,”
and does not acknowledge that the one Lord Jesus Christ is recognized [?] in divinity and humanity,
so as to indicate by this the distinction between the natures from which the union was accomplished without confusion and beyond expression,
without the Word being changed into the nature of the flesh or the flesh being transformed into the nature of the Word,
because both remain what they are in their nature even after their hypostatic union,
but takes this expression in the mystery of Christ’s becoming human as indicating a division into parts;
or acknowledges a number of natures in the one Lord Jesus Christ himself, God the Word made flesh,
without understanding the distinction between those things of which he is composed as a distinction in thought alone, while their distinctive character is not abolished by the union,
because he is one from both, and in one are
both; but instead uses the number as though Christ had natures that are divided
and each subsists in its own hypostasis, let him be condemned. Canon Eight.
If anyone acknowledges that the union came about from two natures, from divinity and humanity,
or says that there is one incarnate nature of God the Word, and does not understand these expressions as the holy fathers taught:
that from the divine nature and the human nature, after they were united hypostatically, there came to be one Christ;
but strives through such expressions to introduce one nature or one substance of Christ’s divinity and humanity,
let him be condemned. For when we say that the only-begotten Word was united hypostatically to a body,
we do not say that there was some blending of the natures into one another; rather, we understand [?]
that the Word was united to a body while each remained what it was.
For this reason Christ is one, the same being both God and man, of the same nature as his Father in his divinity and of the same nature as us in his humanity.
For in the same way the catholic Church of God also rejects and anathematizes those who divide and cut into parts the mystery of Christ’s saving dispensation.
and also with those who blend him. Canon Nine. If anyone says that Christ is worshiped in two natures,
and thereby introduces two acts of worship, one separately for God the Word and another separately for the man;
or if anyone, to abolish the body or to mingle the divinity and humanity,
blasphemes and says that those things that were united have one nature and one essence, and worships Christ in this way,
but does not worship God the Word made flesh together with his body in a single act of worship,
as has been handed down from the beginning to God's holy church, let him be accursed.
Canon Ten. If anyone does not confess that our Lord Jesus, who was crucified in the flesh, is true God,
and the Lord of glory, and one of the Holy Trinity, let him be accursed.
Canon Eleven. If anyone does not anathematize Arius, Eunomius, Macedonius,
Apollinaris, Nestorius, Eutyches, and Origen—them and their wicked writings—
and all the other heretics who have been condemned and anathematized by God's holy, apostolic, and catholic church,
or by the four holy councils mentioned above,
and also those who have held, or are known to hold, the same views as the heretics listed above,
and persisted in their unbelief to the end, let him be accursed. Canon Twelve.
If anyone takes the side of the impious Theodore of Mopsuestia, who said
that God is one and Christ is another, who was troubled by the passions of the soul and the desires of the body;
and that little by little he freed himself from evils, and thus improved himself by advancing in his deeds;
and through his way of life became blameless;
that he was baptized as an ordinary man in the name of the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, and in baptism received the grace
of the Holy Spirit and was deemed worthy of adoption as a son; and that, like the image of a king, he is worshiped in the person of God the Word;
that after his resurrection he became unchangeable in his understanding and became wholly and completely without sin.
And again, this same wicked Theodore said that the union of God the Word with Christ took place in this way:
as the apostle said about a man and a woman, “The two shall become one flesh.”
And in addition to his countless other blasphemies, he went further and shamelessly said that when our Lord, after his resurrection, breathed on his disciples and said,
“Receive the Holy Spirit,” he did not give them the Holy Spirit, but only breathed on them symbolically.
This Theodore, however, dared to say that even when Thomas touched our Lord’s hands and side after his resurrection and confessed, saying,
“My Lord and my God,” Thomas did not say this about Christ, because he did not say that he was God.
Rather, Thomas marveled at the wonder of the resurrection and gave glory to God, who had raised Christ.
Worse than all these things is this: this same Theodore,
also in the commentary he wrote on the Acts of the Apostles, actually compares Christ to Plato,
or to Mani, Epicurus, and Marcion, and says that just as each of these devised a particular doctrine
and caused his disciples to be called Platonists, Manichaeans, Epicureans, and Marcionites,
in the same way Christ too, when he devised his teaching, had people named after him
Christians. Therefore, if anyone takes the side of the aforementioned impious Theodore,
or of his impious books, in which he spewed out the blasphemies described above and countless others against our great God and Savior Jesus Christ,
and does not anathematize him and his impious writings, and all those who accept him and take his side or say that he interprets correctly,
and those who wrote on his behalf and thought as he did, or who write in defense of him or his impious books,
and those who think or have thought as he did,
and have persisted or persist to the end in such unbelief, let him be accursed. Canon Thirteen.
If anyone takes the side of the impious books of Theodoret that were written against the orthodox faith,
and against the first holy Council of Ephesus, and against the twelve chapters of Saint Cyril,
and of the things he wrote on behalf of the impious Theodore and Nestorius and on behalf of others
who wickedly thought like the aforementioned Theodore and Nestorius, and accepts them or their unbelief,
and for this reason calls the teachers of the Church unbelievers, although they confess the hypostatic union of God the Word with the flesh,
and does not anathematize the aforementioned impious writings and those who have thought or think as they do,
but also all those who wrote against the orthodox faith or against Saint Cyril, whose memory is blessed, or against his twelve chapters,
and died in this unbelief, let him be accursed. Canon Fourteen.
If anyone takes the side of that letter which they say Ibas wrote to Mari the Persian,
in which he denies and refuses to accept that the Word of God became flesh and became a human being from our Lady Mary, the ever-virgin Mother of God,
but says that a mere man was born from her and calls him a temple,
As in the claim that God the Word is one and the man is another.
But he also condemns as a heretic Saint Cyril, who proclaimed the true faith of Christians,
and writes teachings resembling those of the wicked Apollinaris,
and accuses the holy council of Ephesus of sacrilege, alleging that it deposed Nestorius from his rank without a trial or an investigation.
And in the wicked letter mentioned above, he calls the Twelve Chapters of Saint Cyril, whose memory is blessed, wicked and opposed to the true faith,
and supports Theodore and Nestorius and their doctrines and wicked writings.
If, therefore, anyone supports that letter,
and does not anathematize it together with those who support it and say that all or part of it is correct,
and those who have written or write in its defense, or in defense of the blasphemies it contains, daring to support it,
or to support the wicked statements contained in it in the name of the holy fathers or of the holy council
of Chalcedon, and have persisted in them to the end, let him be accursed.
Therefore, after we have thus confessed these things that we have received from divine Scripture and from the teaching of the holy fathers,
and that were defined by the four holy councils mentioned above concerning that same one faith,
and after we too have pronounced anathema against the heretics or against their wickedness,
and also against those who have dared to support, or who support, the Three Chapters mentioned above,
or who have persisted, or persist, in their error and their condemnation,
if anyone strives to transmit, teach, or write anything contrary to these things rightly defined by us,
whether he is a bishop or is numbered among the clergy,
the person who has done such things, which are contrary to the canons of the church and the priesthood,
shall be stripped of his episcopal office or his clerical office. And if he is a monk or a layperson, let him be anathematized. The end.
